title: 5.43.12 The curve of fiber components
text: Dropping the connected-fiber hypothesis requires replacing the base by the curve of fiber components. The following construction is the curve case of Stein factorization. It also identifies the multiplicities needed when pulling back curvature measures. Proposition 5.43.13 . F2BB0D2DE2F4 Let $p:X\to C$ be a surjective holomorphic map, where $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ and $C$ is a connected compact Riemann surface. There is a factorization \[  X\xrightarrow {q}C'\xrightarrow {r}C,\qquad p=r\circ q,  \] where $C'$ is a connected compact Riemann surface, $q$ is surjective and holomorphic with connected fibers, and $r$ is a finite holomorphic map. The points of $r^{-1}(s)$ correspond to the connected components of $p^{-1}(s)$, which are the fibers of $q$ over those points. The factorization is unique up to a unique isomorphism commuting with $q$ and $r$. If $t\in r^{-1}(s)$ has ramification index $e_ t$, then, as effective divisors with multiplicities, \[  [p^{-1}(s)]=\sum _{t\in r^{-1}(s)}e_ t[q^{-1}(t)].  \] The degree of $r$ is the number of components of a regular fiber of $p$. Proof. We first construct the covering over the regular values, complete it across the critical values, and then extend its component quotient to $X$. The critical values form a finite set $D\subset C$, by the critical-set argument in the proof of 5.43.7 ; that argument does not use connectedness of the fibers. Over $C^\circ =C\setminus D$, the map $p$ is a proper submersion. The local construction in lemma 5.43.4 applies there: horizontal transport over a disk has compact inverse image over its closure. Compact fibers have finitely many components, and the resulting local labels are glued by locally constant permutations. We obtain \[  X^\circ \xrightarrow {q^\circ }C'^\circ \xrightarrow {r^\circ }C^\circ , \qquad X^\circ =p^{-1}(C^\circ ),  \] with $q^\circ $ a holomorphic submersion with connected fibers and $r^\circ $ a finite unramified covering of degree $d$. The complement of a proper analytic subset in a connected complex manifold is connected, so $X^\circ $ and its image $C'^\circ $ are connected. Here only the fiber divisor is removed. Locally, the complement of the zero set of a nonzero holomorphic function in a ball is path connected: join two outside points through an outside intermediate point by two complex-line disks. Each restriction is nonzero because it contains an outside endpoint, and its isolated zeros can be avoided. Applying this local argument along a chain of balls proves the required global connectedness. For each $s\in D$, take a small coordinate disk centered at $s$ and disjoint from the other critical values. A connected component of the covering over its puncture is a finite connected covering of a punctured disk, of some degree $e$. It has a coordinate $w$ in which $r^\circ (w)=w^ e$: the universal cover of the punctured disk is a half-plane with projection $z=\exp \zeta $, and the index-$e$ subgroup of its deck group is generated by $\zeta \mapsto \zeta +2\pi \mathrm i e$. The coordinate $w=\exp (\zeta /e)$ gives the asserted form. Attach one point $w=0$ to each such component. There are finitely many, with their degrees summing to $d$. Gluing these disks to $C'^\circ $ gives a connected Riemann surface $C'$ and a finite holomorphic map $r:C'\to C$. The new points have disjoint disk neighborhoods, so this gluing is Hausdorff. The inverse image of a small closed base disk is a finite union of closed disks; over the complement of their interiors, the original finite covering is proper. Thus $C'$ is compact. We extend $q^\circ $. Fix $x\in p^{-1}(s)$, $s\in D$. On a small coordinate ball $B$ about $x$, the image of $p$ lies in the chosen disk. The complement $B\setminus p^{-1}(s)$ is connected. Its image under $q^\circ $ therefore lies in a single punctured disk just attached to $C'$, since those disks are the connected components of $r^{-1}$ of the punctured base disk. In its coordinate $w$, the function $w\circ q^\circ $ is holomorphic and bounded, and \[  (w\circ q^\circ )^ e=p-s.  \] The bounded holomorphic removable-singularity theorem extends it across $p^{-1}(s)\cap B$. To see this without assuming that the divisor is smooth, first extend at its smooth points by the one-variable theorem in transverse coordinates. The singular locus of the reduced divisor has complex codimension at least two in the ambient manifold, so Hartogs extension across that locus completes the extension. In dimension one there are only isolated points. Its $e$th power remains $p-s$ by the identity theorem, and hence its value is zero on that fiber. This defines a holomorphic map from $B$ to the attached disk. The local extensions agree on their dense common regular locus and therefore glue to $q:X\to C'$ with $p=r\circ q$. Its image is closed, by compactness, and contains the dense set $C'^\circ $, so $q$ is surjective. Every fiber of $q$ is connected. Otherwise write one fiber as a union of two disjoint nonempty compact subsets and put them in disjoint open neighborhoods $U_1,U_2$. Properness gives a disk $V$ about their base point $t$ such that \[  q^{-1}(V)\subset U_1\cup U_2.  \] The map $q$ is open: at any point, a complex line on which the nonconstant germ $q-t$ has its first nonzero term gives an open one-variable restriction. Consequently both $q(U_ i)$ contain a neighborhood of $t$. A nearby point of $C'^\circ $ then has a fiber meeting both neighborhoods, contradicting connectedness of the regular fibers. The fibers of $p$ are the disjoint union of these connected $q$-fibers over the finitely many points of $r^{-1}(s)$. They are its components. Locally at $t$, the formula for a finite map is $r(w)-s=w^{e_ t}$ after changing the coordinate by a holomorphic root of a nonvanishing factor. Pulling back this equality by $q$ gives the divisor multiplicities stated above. Over $C^\circ $, $r$ is unramified and each sheet is one component, proving the degree assertion. Finally, any factorization with the stated properties has over $C^\circ $ precisely this covering of fiber components. It is unramified there: a critical point of its finite map, together with surjectivity of its first factor, would make $p$ critical over that base point. Thus the component identification is holomorphic on $C'^\circ $. On every punctured disk it identifies two completions of the same finite covering, and the coordinates $w^ e$ above extend it biholomorphically across the added point. It gives a global isomorphism; density and surjectivity make it unique and give commutation with both maps. $\square$

title: 5.43.14 Finite maps between curves
text:
Let $r:C'	o C$ be a finite surjective holomorphic map of degree $d$ between connected compact Riemann surfaces. Write $e_ x$ for its local degree at $x\in C'$, so that $\sum _{r(x)=s}e_ x=d$ for every $s\in C$. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $ eta $ on $C$ and put $\sigma =r^* eta $. Potentials in background $\sigma $ need not descend to $C$. Taking the maximum on each fiber nevertheless gives a base potential that dominates the original potential after pullback. Its Lelong numbers are the smallest ramification-adjusted Lelong numbers on the fiber. Lemma 5.43.15 . 0018DC5A7DD0 For $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(C',\sigma )$, the function \[  m_ h(s)=\max _{r(x)=s}h(x)  \] belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$ and satisfies $h\leq m_ h\circ r$. For every $s\in C$, \[  
u (m_ h,s)=\min _{r(x)=s} rac{
u (h,x)}{e_ x}.  \] If $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$, then $h\preceq v\circ r$ implies $m_ h\preceq v$. The analogous implication holds for the all-weight ideal order. Proof. On a base disk choose a smooth function $a$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a= eta $. Off the branch values, $m_ h+a$ is the maximum of finitely many subharmonic functions obtained from $h+a\circ r$ by inverse branches. It is subharmonic there and locally bounded above. The removable-singularity theorem extends it across the branch values. This extension has the stated value: upper semicontinuity and properness give the upper bound at the fiber, while the genuine upper limits of $h+a\circ r$ at its points give the reverse bound. Thus the extensions glue. The function is not identically $-\infty $, since $h$ is finite at some point. This proves the curvature inequality and $h\leq m_ h\circ r$. Choose coordinates in the disjoint disks over $s$ so that the map on the disk centered at $x$ is $t=z^{e_ x}$. Then \[  \sup _{|t|<\delta }m_ h(t) =\max _{r(x)=s}\sup _{|z|<\delta ^{1/e_ x}}h(z).  \] Divide by $\log \delta ^2<0$ and use the supremum definition of Lelong number. Each quotient on the right tends to $
u (h,x)/e_ x$, and the maximum becomes the minimum after division. Smooth local corrections do not affect these limits. An ordinary bound $h\leq v\circ r+c$ gives $m_ h\leq v+c$ on every fiber. On a curve, the all-weight ideal order is equivalent to the pointwise Lelong inequalities, by theorem 5.37.3 . The pullback formula 5.43.8 makes $h\preceq _{\mathcal I}v\circ r$ equivalent to $
u (h,x)\geq e_ x
u (v,r(x))$ at every $x$. The minimum formula gives the required base inequalities. $\square$ Finite pullback of measures includes ramification at atoms. For a continuous real function $f$ on $C'$, put \[  (\operatorname {Tr}_ r f)(s) =\sum _{r(x)=s}e_ xf(x).  \] This function is continuous: in the local description $t=z^ e$, the $e$ values tend to the same value at the branch point. For a finite positive measure $\mu $ on $C$, define $r^*\mu $ by \[  \int _{C'}f\, \mathrm d(r^*\mu ) =\int _ C\operatorname {Tr}_ r f\, \mathrm d\mu ,  \] and extend the definition to signed measures by linearity. Positivity and the bound $|\operatorname {Tr}_ r f|\leq d\| f\| _\infty $ give a finite measure by the Riesz representation theorem. Lemma 5.43.16 . 151A1D744DE7 For every finite signed measure $\mu $ and Borel set $B\subset C$, \[   egin{gathered} r_*r^*\mu =d\mu ,\qquad \| r^*\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}=d\| \mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}},\ r^*(\mathbf1_ B\mu )=\mathbf1_{r^{-1}(B)}r^*\mu , \qquad r^*\delta _ s=\sum _{r(x)=s}e_ x\delta _ x. \end{gathered}  \] For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(C, eta )$, writing $T_ v= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $\mu _ v=\mathbf1_{\{ v=-\infty \} }T_ v$, one has \[  T_{v\circ r}=r^*T_ v,\qquad \mu _{v\circ r}=r^*\mu _ v.  \] Images and inverse images of polar sets under $r$ are polar. Pullback and pushforward of positive measures commute with taking the atomic part. Proof. The trace of $g\circ r$ is $dg$, giving the pushforward identity. The same weighted fiber formula for Borel test functions follows from the monotone-class theorem and gives the restriction and atom formulas. The positive and negative Jordan parts of a signed measure have disjoint Borel carriers; their pullbacks are positive with disjoint inverse-image carriers. Each has $d$ times its original mass, which proves the total-variation identity. Choose a local smooth $a$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a= eta $; then $v+a$ is a subharmonic potential of $T_ v$. Its Riesz representation is a logarithmic potential plus a harmonic function. In coordinates $t=z^ e$, the identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ z\log |z^ e-t|^2 =\sum _{z^ e=t}\operatorname {ord}_ z(z^ e-t)\delta _ z  \] shows that pulling back this potential gives the weighted measure above. Fubini's theorem applies locally: factorization of $z^ e-t$ into its $e$ linear factors gives a uniform local $L^1$ bound for these logarithmic kernels as $t$ varies on a smaller disk. The harmonic term has zero Hessian after pullback. This proves $T_{v\circ r}=r^*T_ v$. The pole set of $v\circ r$ is exactly $r^{-1}\{ v=-\infty \} $, so the restriction formula proves the polar identity. Inverse images of polar sets are polar by composition of local subharmonic witnesses. For images, take local witnesses on the finitely many inverse-image disks of a small base disk. Off the branch values, the sum of their values over the inverse branches is subharmonic and is $-\infty $ wherever any witness has a pole. It is locally bounded above and is not identically $-\infty $. Its extension across the branch values is subharmonic. Adding the finitely many branch values to the resulting polar set still gives a polar set. This proves the image assertion locally, hence globally. The pullback of a nonatomic measure has no atoms by the atom formula. The pushforward of a nonatomic measure has no atoms because every fiber is finite. Atomic measures pull back and push forward to atomic measures. Splitting a positive measure into these two parts proves the last assertion. $\square$

u (m_ h,s)=\min _{r(x)=s} rac{

u (h,x)\geq e_ x

title: 5.43.17 Modifications
text: Proposition 5.43.18 . A7090F92CA39 Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds, and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Pullback gives a bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] Proof. Let $S\subset X$ be a proper analytic subset over whose complement $\pi $ is an isomorphism, and put $D=\pi ^{-1}(S)$. By lemma 5.43.2 , pullback preserves the curvature inequality, and the pullback of a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function is not identically $-\infty $, since $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $D$. The pullback map is injective because $\pi $ is surjective. To prove surjectivity, let $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$, and define $u=b\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $S$. On a coordinate neighborhood in $X$, choose a smooth function $\rho $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \theta $. Then $b+\rho \circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic on the inverse image of this neighborhood. By properness, its local upper bounds give a local upper bound for $u+\rho $ near $S$, so the removable-singularity theorem extends $u+\rho $ plurisubharmonically across $S$. The resulting quasi-plurisubharmonic extensions of $u$ agree almost everywhere on overlaps, hence everywhere, and glue to a function on $X$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is positive off $S$. Locally it is the sum of the positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\rho )$ and the smooth form $\theta -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $. The smooth form gives $S$ zero mass, so the restriction of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to $S$ is positive as well. Thus $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The plurisubharmonic functions $b+\rho \circ \pi $ and $(u+\rho )\circ \pi $ agree off $D$, hence almost everywhere, hence everywhere. Therefore $b=u\circ \pi $. $\square$ Pullback by a modification preserves $L^1$ convergence within a family with a common lower curvature bound. Compactness controls the pullbacks near the exceptional locus, where a direct change of variables would involve a vanishing Jacobian. Lemma 5.43.19 . C07C7BB26EF8 Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification between connected complex manifolds, and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. If $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ and all $v_ j,v$ belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then \[  v_ j\circ \pi \longrightarrow v\circ \pi \quad \hbox{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Y).  \] In particular, on compact manifolds this is convergence in $L^1$. Proof. By lemma 5.25.1 , the functions $v_ j$ are uniformly bounded above on relatively compact subsets of $X$. The pullbacks are therefore locally uniformly bounded above and have the common smooth lower curvature bound $-\pi ^*\theta $. After a smooth local correction, the compactness theorem for plurisubharmonic functions shows that every subsequence has a further subsequence that either converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ or tends locally uniformly to $-\infty $ on each connected coordinate region in $Y$. Every such region meets the complement of the exceptional locus. There $\pi $ is a biholomorphism, and change of variables gives $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence to $v\circ \pi $, which excludes convergence to $-\infty $. Each subsequential limit agrees with $v\circ \pi $ off the exceptional locus, hence almost everywhere, since this analytic set has smooth volume zero. Thus the limit is unique, and applying this argument on a countable cover by coordinate regions proves convergence of the whole sequence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Y)$. $\square$ Convergence in capacity is also preserved by modifications. The comparison takes place away from small neighborhoods of the exceptional sets, so no uniform comparison of capacities on the whole manifolds is needed. Lemma 5.43.20 . D7CDD8CAD2AC Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification between connected compact complex manifolds, equipped with Hermitian forms $\omega _ Y,\omega _ X$. Write $\operatorname {Cap}_ Y=\operatorname {Cap}_{\omega _ Y}$ and $\operatorname {Cap}_ X=\operatorname {Cap}_{\omega _ X}$ for the Hermitian capacities of section 5.29 . For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j,v$ on $X$, \[  v_ j\longrightarrow v\text{ in capacity on }X \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v_ j\circ \pi \longrightarrow v\circ \pi \text{ in capacity on }Y.  \] Proof. Choose a proper analytic subset $S\subset X$ such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism outside $D=\pi ^{-1}(S)$. Both $S$ and $D$ have capacity zero. For $\epsilon >0$, choose an open neighborhood $V$ of $D$ of capacity less than $\epsilon $. By properness, there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $S$ with $\pi ^{-1}(U_0)\subset V$; shrink it to an open set $U$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ X(U)<\epsilon $. The inverse of $\pi $ is biholomorphic near the compact set $X\setminus U$. A finite cover by nested coordinate charts and the comparison of local and global capacities in section 5.29 give a constant $C_\epsilon $ such that, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \begin{split}  \operatorname {Cap}_ Y(\pi ^{-1}E)& \leq \epsilon +C_\epsilon \operatorname {Cap}_ X(E),\\  \operatorname {Cap}_ X(E)& \leq \epsilon +C_\epsilon \operatorname {Cap}_ Y(\pi ^{-1}E). \end{split}  \] Apply these inequalities to $E=\{ |v_ j-v|>\delta \} $ for each fixed $\delta >0$, omitting the pluripolar pole sets, and let first $j\to \infty $ and then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 5.43.21 Multiplier ideals under modifications
text:
Throughout this subsection, $\pi :Y	o X$ is a modification of connected compact complex manifolds of dimension $n$. There is an analytic subset $S\subset X$ of codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus S$. Let $K_ X$ and $K_ Y$ be the canonical line bundles. Set $D=\pi ^{-1}(S)$ and \[  R_\pi =K_ Y\otimes \pi ^*K_ X^{-1}.  \] The determinant of the differential of $\pi $ is a canonical holomorphic section $J_\pi $ of $R_\pi $; in local coordinates its coefficient is the holomorphic Jacobian determinant $\operatorname {Jac}\pi $, and its zeros are contained in $D$. These standard facts about modifications of complex manifolds include the case $n=1$, in which every modification is an isomorphism. Lemma 5.43.22 . 599D8A3D42BC Let $a$ be quasi-plurisubharmonic on $X$. Pullback followed by multiplication with $J_\pi $ induces an isomorphism \[  \pi _* igl (R_\pi \otimes \mathcal I(a\circ \pi ) igr ) =\mathcal I(a).  \] More precisely, for every holomorphic line bundle $M$ on $X$, the map \[  s\longmapsto J_\pi \, \pi ^*s  \] is an isomorphism \[  H^0 igl (X,M\otimes \mathcal I(a) igr ) \simeq H^0 igl (Y,\pi ^*M\otimes R_\pi \otimes \mathcal I(a\circ \pi ) igr ).  \] Proof. The assertion is local on $X$. In coordinates and local frames, the map sends a holomorphic coefficient $f$ to $(f\circ \pi )\operatorname {Jac}\pi $. By the change-of-variables formula, local integrability of \[  |f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-a} \quad \hbox{and}\quad |f\circ \pi |^2|\operatorname {Jac}\pi |^2\mathrm{e}^{-a\circ \pi }  \] are equivalent. For the implication from integrability on $Y$ to integrability near a point of $X$, take a smaller relatively compact neighborhood of the point; by properness, its inverse image has compact closure, so finitely many charts on which the integrability holds suffice. Smooth positive coordinate densities are comparable on these charts, and analytic exceptional sets have smooth volume zero, so they do not change the integrals. It remains to show that every section on $Y$ is of the form $J_\pi \pi ^*s$. Divide it by $J_\pi $ off $D$ and use the inverse of $\pi $ there; this gives a holomorphic section of $M$ off $S$. Since $S$ has codimension at least two, Hartogs' extension theorem gives a holomorphic section $s$ on $X$. Its image $J_\pi \pi ^*s$ agrees with the given section off $D$, hence everywhere by the identity theorem. The integrability equivalence then places $s$ in the required multiplier ideal. The same argument on each open set proves the sheaf identity as well as the global identification. $\square$ Note that the lemma does not identify $\pi ^*\mathcal I(a)$ with $\mathcal I(a\circ \pi )$: the Jacobian is part of the holomorphic coefficient on $Y$ and cannot be removed from the integrability test. We also need the invariance of the ideal order $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ of section 5.33 , which involves all positive weights. The proof is local, so that we never have to extend a modification of a small open subset of $Y$ to a global one. Lemma 5.43.23 . 6AA2493173A9 For quasi-plurisubharmonic $a,b$ on $X$, \[  a\preceq _{\mathcal I}b \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a\circ \pi \preceq _{\mathcal I}b\circ \pi .  \] The assertion is local on $X$ and also holds for a proper bimeromorphic map between noncompact smooth complex manifolds. Proof. The reverse implication follows at every positive weight from the sheaf identity in lemma 5.43.22 : tensor the inclusion of ideals on $Y$ with $R_\pi $ and apply the left-exact direct image functor. The proof of that sheaf identity is local on the target, since properness makes each fiber compact and gives the required finite cover by integrability charts; compactness of the manifolds themselves is not needed. For the forward implication, fix a coordinate neighborhood $W\subset Y$, a local modification $\sigma :Z	o W$ with smooth source, and a prime divisor $E$ on $Z$. After shrinking $W$ around the point under consideration, its image is contained in a coordinate neighborhood $U\subset X$. Put $F=\pi \circ \sigma $ and \[  A_ F(E)=1+\operatorname {ord}_ E\operatorname {Jac}F.  \] The map $F$ is holomorphic, and it is injective and biholomorphic off a proper analytic subset; it need not be a proper modification of $U$. Let $m$ be a positive integer, and let $
u _ E$ and $\operatorname {ord}_ E$ be the generic Lelong number and the generic vanishing order along $E$, as in section 5.38 . The proof of lemma 5.38.9 applies to the map $F$ on relatively compact coordinate patches and gives \[  \max \left\{ 
u _ E(a\circ F)- rac{A_ F(E)}m,0ight\}  \leq  rac1m\operatorname {ord}_ E igl (\mathcal I(ma)\mathcal O_ Z igr ) \leq 
u _ E(a\circ F).  \] In more detail, the upper inequality follows by pulling back the local Bergman lower bound on $U$. For the lower one, a germ $f\in \mathcal I(ma)$ pulls back to a coefficient $(f\circ F)\operatorname {Jac}F$ that is square integrable against $\mathrm e^{-ma\circ F}$, because on a relatively compact patch of $Z$ the change-of-variables integral is bounded by the integral over the image of the patch. Generic divisorial removal and the one-variable integral then give \[  \operatorname {ord}_ E(f\circ F)+A_ F(E)>m
u _ E(a\circ F).  \] This estimate only uses the injectivity of $F$ off the exceptional set and the compactness of the patch, not properness of $F$ over $U$. The same estimates hold for $b$. The hypothesis gives $\mathcal I(ma)\subseteq \mathcal I(mb)$ for every $m>0$, so the orders of the pulled-back ideals satisfy the reverse inequality. Letting $m	o \infty $ in the two estimates proves \[  
u _ E(a\circ F)\geq 
u _ E(b\circ F).  \] This holds for every local divisor over $Y$. Blowing up a point on the source of any local modification recovers the Lelong number at that point as a generic Lelong number along the exceptional divisor; in dimension one the point already is a divisor. The local criterion in theorem 5.37.3 now gives $a\circ \pi \preceq _{\mathcal I}b\circ \pi $. No extension of $\sigma $ beyond its local domain was used. $\square$ Lemma 5.43.24 . 83C3A394E5BB For a proper bimeromorphic map $ho :Z	o Y$ between complex manifolds and quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ on $Y$, \[  a\sim _{\mathcal I}b \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a\circ ho \sim _{\mathcal I}b\circ ho .  \] The statement is local on $Y$. Proof. Apply the local order equivalence of lemma 5.43.23 to both $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$. Together, the two order relations are equivalent to equality of the multiplier ideals at every positive weight. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.43.24
text: Lemma 5.43.24 . 83C3A394E5BB For a proper bimeromorphic map $\rho :Z\to Y$ between complex manifolds and quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ on $Y$, \[  a\sim _{\mathcal I}b \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a\circ \rho \sim _{\mathcal I}b\circ \rho .  \] The statement is local on $Y$. Proof. Apply the local order equivalence of lemma 5.43.23 to both $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$. Together, the two order relations are equivalent to equality of the multiplier ideals at every positive weight. $\square$

title: 5.43.25 Restriction of analytic approximants
text:
A quasi-plurisubharmonic function with zero generic Lelong number along a submanifold may still restrict to the function identically equal to $-\infty $ (section 5.34 ). Analytic regularization removes this obstruction: the restrictions of the analytic approximants are quasi-plurisubharmonic, and a fixed lower curvature bound controls their generic Lelong numbers along divisors on every fixed modification. Corollary 5.43.26 . 50D99B4B0660 Let $	heta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and let $u_ m$, with curvature errors $\epsilon _ m$, be the approximants of corollary 5.36.2 . Let $Y\subset X$ be a connected compact complex submanifold along which the generic Lelong number of $u$ vanishes: \[  
u (u,Y)=\inf _{y\in Y}
u (u,y)=0.  \] Then each restriction $u_ m|_ Y$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $Y$; in particular, it is not identically $-\infty $. If $\pi :Z	o Y$ is a modification with smooth compact source and $E\subset Z$ is a prime divisor, then \[  \sup _ m
u  igl ((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi ,E igr )<\infty .  \] Proof. For each $m$, choose $y\in Y$ with $
u (u,y)<1/m$. Skoda's local integrability criterion gives $\mathcal I(mu)_ y=\mathcal O_{X,y}$, so the image ideal $\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y$ does not vanish identically. Since $u_ m$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, proposition 5.34.1 shows that $u_ m|_ Y$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic on $Y$. Its pullback to $Z$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic as well, since $\pi $ is biholomorphic off a proper analytic subset. Restricting and pulling back the curvature inequality of corollary 5.36.2 , which is allowed by lemma 5.43.2 , gives \[  \pi ^*(	heta |_ Y)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl ((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi  igr ) \geq -\epsilon _ m\pi ^*(\omega |_ Y).  \] Since the errors $\epsilon _ m$ are bounded, a sufficiently large multiple of a single Hermitian form on $Z$ dominates $\pi ^*(	heta |_ Y)+\epsilon _ m\pi ^*(\omega |_ Y)$ for all $m$. Lemma 5.38.8 , applied on $Z$ in this fixed background, therefore bounds the generic Lelong numbers along $E$ uniformly in $m$. $\square$

title: 5.44 Integration against non-pluripolar measures
text: For uniformly bounded potentials, $L^1$ convergence with respect to a smooth volume form can be transferred to any fixed finite measure that does not charge pluripolar sets. Passing to bounded exponentials extends this to families that are only bounded above. The same mechanism applies to moving mixed Monge–Ampère measures of bounded potentials and to smoothings of a fixed measure.

title: 5.44.1 A fixed measure
Lemma 5.44.2
5.44.3 Vanishing exponents
text: Proposition 5.44.4 . A89FF7CB0129 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be unbounded below, and for each $\lambda >0$ let $u_\lambda $ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with $u_\lambda \sim \varphi $. Then, for each $\lambda >0$, the function $\lambda u_\lambda $ has infinite distance in $L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$ from every constant. In particular, $\lambda u_\lambda $ cannot converge uniformly on $X$ to a finite constant as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Proof. Since $u_\lambda \leq \varphi +C$ for a constant $C$, the function $u_\lambda $ is unbounded below. Every nonempty strict sublevel set $\{ u_\lambda <t\} $ of the upper semicontinuous function $u_\lambda $ is open, hence of positive smooth volume. Thus $u_\lambda $, and with it $\lambda u_\lambda $, is essentially unbounded below, and both conclusions follow. $\square$ A vanishing exponent gives convergence of the exponentials to one, even when the normalized potentials vary. Lemma 5.44.5 . D260E972F57C Let $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$, and let $\lambda _ j>0$ decrease to zero. For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $, \[  \int _ X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}-1\right|\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0.  \] If $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then more precisely \[  \int _ X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}-1\right|\, |f|\, \mathrm{d}V \leq C_ p\lambda _ j\| f\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] The constant depends on the fixed background, $p$ and $\mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $, so that $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega )$. By lemma 5.29.2 , for every $T>1$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (\{ v_ j<-T\} )\leq C/T  \] uniformly in $j$. Since $v_ j\leq 0$ and $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$, splitting the integral at this sublevel set gives \[  \int _ X(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j})\, \mathrm{d}\mu \leq \lambda _ jT\mu (X)+\mu (\{ v_ j<-T\} ).  \] By lemma 5.29.18 , the second term is uniformly small when $T$ is large, and for this fixed $T$ the first term tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. This proves the general assertion; here the exponential is given the value zero at a pole, and pole sets have zero $\mu $-measure. For the quantitative assertion, lemma 5.26.2 , applied in the background $\Omega $, gives a uniform $L^ q$ bound for $-v_ j$, where $q=p/(p-1)$. Hölder's inequality and the bound \[  0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_ j}\leq \lambda _ j|v_ j|  \] give the claimed estimate for every $j$. $\square$

title: 5.44.6 Measures with bounded potentials
text: The fixed measure can be replaced by moving mixed Monge–Ampère measures of uniformly bounded potentials, provided these potentials converge in capacity. Since $\omega $ need not be closed, the proof has to control the torsion terms that appear in integration by parts. Lemma 5.44.7 . 27CEBF2AA643 Let $a_ j,a,w_ j,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be uniformly bounded, and write $\omega _ v=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. If $a_ j\to a$ in $L^1(X)$ and $w_ j\to w$ in capacity, then, for $0\leq k\leq n$, \[  \int _ X|a_ j-a|\, \omega _{w_ j}^{k}\wedge \omega ^{n-k} \longrightarrow 0.  \] The same conclusion holds if, instead of $a_ j,a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j,a$ have any fixed smooth lower curvature bound. Proof. By lemma 5.25.1 , the tail envelopes $A_ j=(\sup _{\ell \geq j}a_\ell )^*$ decrease to $a$. Since $a\leq \max (a_ j,a)\leq A_ j$, monotone convergence in capacity of bounded potentials (lemma 5.29.19 ) implies \[  \alpha _ j:=\max (a_ j,a)\longrightarrow a\quad \text{in capacity}.  \] We split $|a_ j-a|=(\alpha _ j-a)+(\alpha _ j-a_ j)$. The integral of the first part against the moving products tends to zero by lemma 5.29.16 . For the second part, put $h_ j=\alpha _ j-a_ j\geq 0$. We compare its integrals against the measures with indices $j$ and $\ell $. The case $k=0$ follows from the assumed $L^1$ convergence. For $k\geq 1$, put $z=w_ j-w_\ell $ and \[  T=\sum _{s=0}^{k-1}\omega _{w_ j}^{s}\wedge \omega _{w_\ell }^{k-1-s}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}.  \] Factorization and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold $X$ give \begin{align*} & \int _ Xh_ j\bigl (\omega _{w_ j}^{k}-\omega _{w_\ell }^{k}\bigr ) \wedge \omega ^{n-k}\\ & \hspace{20mm}=\int _ Xh_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}z\wedge T =\int _ Xz\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jT). \end{align*} Since $\omega $ is not assumed to be closed, $T$ need not be closed, and the product rule reads CDF5AC2B6D12 5.44.8 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_ jT)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j\wedge T+\mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}T+h_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} None of the terms involving derivatives of $T$ need vanish. We estimate the four terms. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ j=\omega _{\alpha _ j}-\omega _{a_ j}$, the absolute contribution of the first is at most \[  \int _ X|z|(\omega _{\alpha _ j}+\omega _{a_ j})\wedge T.  \] It tends to zero as $j,\ell \to \infty $ by lemma 5.29.16 , since $w_ j-w_\ell \to 0$ in capacity. Differentiating each factor shows that $\mathrm{d}T=\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge R$, where $R$ is a positive linear combination of mixed products of bidegree $(n-2,n-2)$. Moreover, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a sum of terms consisting of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ times mixed products of degree $n-2$, or of $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ times mixed products of degree $n-3$; terms of negative degree are absent. These smooth torsion factors are bounded in absolute value by fixed multiples of $\omega ^2$ and $\omega ^3$, respectively. As $h_ j$ is uniformly bounded, the contribution of $h_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ also tends to zero, by the same capacity estimate. For the two gradient terms, the pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for a positive mixed product gives, for example, \[  \left|\int _ Xz\, \mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge R\right|^2 \leq C\left(\int _ X|z|\, \mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\wedge \omega \wedge R\right) \left(\int _ X|z|\, \omega ^2\wedge R\right).  \] The second factor tends to zero, and the first is uniformly bounded. Indeed, if $p$ is any of the uniformly bounded potentials and $S$ any positive mixed product of degree $n-1$ occurring here, then \[  \int _ X\mathrm{d}p\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}p\wedge S =\frac12\int _ Xp^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S-\int _ Xp\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge S.  \] Expand $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S$ with all its torsion terms as above, and write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=\omega _ p-\omega $. Boundedness of $p$ and lemma 5.29.16 bound both integrals uniformly. Finally, $\mathrm{d}h_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j\leq 2\mathrm{d}\alpha _ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\alpha _ j+2\mathrm{d}a_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}a_ j$ as positive quadratic forms, which proves the asserted bound. The other gradient term is estimated in the same way. In dimension one, $T=1$ and all torsion terms in ( 5.44.8 ) vanish. These integration-by-parts and energy identities hold for smooth potentials. They extend to bounded potentials through smooth decreasing approximations in the Hermitian background, using the local Bedford–Taylor chain rule, its gradient products and quasi-continuity; equivalently, they follow from the bounded current calculus of section 5.28 . Only the common bound on the potentials enters the estimates. We have shown that the difference between the integrals of $h_ j$ against the measures with indices $j$ and $\ell $ tends to zero as $j,\ell \to \infty $. For a fixed index $\ell $, the measure $\omega _{w_\ell }^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ is a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure, and lemma 5.44.2 , applied separately to $\alpha _ j\to a$ and $a_ j\to a$ in $L^1(X)$, gives \[  \int _ Xh_ j\, \omega _{w_\ell }^{k}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}\longrightarrow 0 \qquad \text{as }j\to \infty .  \] Choosing first $\ell $ large and then letting $j\to \infty $, we conclude that the integrals of $h_ j$ against $\omega _{w_ j}^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ tend to zero. Together with the estimate for $\alpha _ j-a$, this proves the result. If the $a_ j$ only have some other fixed lower curvature bound, choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \omega $ such that they are $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. By section 5.29 , convergence in capacity is unchanged by this replacement. Apply the result just proved with $\Omega $ in place of $\omega $; by positivity, the original mixed measures are bounded by their counterparts for $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 5.45 Curvature of line bundles
text: Let $M$ be a complex manifold and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $M$. To relate potentials to holomorphic sections, we ask when a current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, with $u$ locally integrable, can be the curvature current of a metric on a line bundle. The transition law for the local weights of such a metric forces a closedness condition on the background. Proposition 5.45.1 . 620B099907AB The curvature current of a singular Hermitian metric with locally integrable weights on a holomorphic line bundle is closed. In particular, a nonclosed form $\theta $ cannot itself be the curvature current of such a metric, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is not closed on any neighborhood of a point where $\mathrm{d}\theta \neq 0$. Proof. Let $h$ be a singular Hermitian metric on a holomorphic line bundle $L\to M$. Choose a local holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$ and write its squared norm as $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi }$; the curvature current is then locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. If $e'=ge$ is another frame, with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, the new weight is $\varphi -\log |g|^2$. Since $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic, these local currents agree on overlaps and glue to a global current, which is closed because $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$. The final assertion follows from the identity \[  \mathrm{d}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=\mathrm{d}\theta  \] of currents. $\square$ Accordingly, when we study sections subject to multiplier-ideal conditions, we specify both the line bundle, whose curvature is closed, and any auxiliary Hermitian form on $M$. An algebraic interpretation then requires relating the invariants of the line bundle to this analytic background.

title: 5.46 Polar curvature
text:
For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, the restriction of the current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to the pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} $ is called the polar curvature of $u$. A bounded change of the potential preserves more than its Lelong numbers: it preserves the whole polar curvature. Indeed, a local energy estimate puts the bounded difference of two potentials in a Sobolev space, while pole sets admit smooth test functions of arbitrarily small energy, and these test functions show that no coefficient measure of the Hessian of the difference charges the pole set. Polar curvature is closed even when the pole set is not closed, so a local elliptic equation recovers it from its scalar Hermitian trace. section: 11.1 Torsion and the variation of mass
text: Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$. If $\omega $ were closed, Stokes' theorem would make the total Monge–Ampère mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ independent of the potential $u$. For a nonclosed Hermitian form this invariance can fail. Integration by parts expresses the mass of a smooth potential as a polynomial whose coefficients pair the potential with the complex Hessians of the powers of $\omega $, and polarization shows that the vanishing of these Hessians is also necessary for invariance. When they do not vanish, even smooth potentials of the same singularity type can have different masses, and the usual global comparison principle fails. The masses may nevertheless remain bounded, and whether they do depends only on the manifold, not on the chosen Hermitian form.

text: Integration by parts moves the complex Hessian of a function onto the form against which it is integrated. When that form is a power of a nonclosed $(1,1)$-form, its complex Hessian contains, besides the complex Hessian of the form itself, a quadratic term in its exterior derivative. Lemma 11.1.2 . 3B0A8DD950AD For a smooth real function $f$ and a smooth form $T$ of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T=\int _ X f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] Proof. Since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ is a one-form, $\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T-\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}T$, and Stokes' theorem gives the first equality in \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T =\int _ X\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}T =\int _ X f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] For the second, recall that the integral of $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma $ vanishes for every form $\sigma $ of total degree $2n-1$, by Stokes' theorem for $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. We apply this to $\sigma =f\, \mathrm{d}T$ and use $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$. $\square$ Lemma 11.1.3 . BF56C7366FC6 For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and an integer $q\geq 1$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\theta ^ q) =q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\theta +q(q-1)\, \theta ^{q-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta ,  \] where the second term is omitted when $q=1$. Proof. For $q=1$ there is nothing to prove. For $q\geq 2$, since $\theta $ has even degree, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\theta ^ q)=q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta $. Applying $\mathrm{d}$ and using again that $\theta ^{q-1}$ has even degree, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\theta ^ q) =q(q-1)\, \theta ^{q-2}\wedge \mathrm{d}\theta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta +q\, \theta ^{q-1}\wedge \mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\theta .  \] $\square$ Thus the quadratic torsion term $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ can make the higher powers of $\omega $ fail to be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed even when $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. title: 11.1.4 The mass polynomial
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.1 Torsion and the variation of mass
text: For a smooth real function $u$ on $X$, write $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and set \[  \mathcal H_\omega =\{ u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R):\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0\} , \qquad \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] The set $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions is convex and open in the $C^2$ topology, while the mass $\mathrm M_\omega (u)$ is defined for every smooth real $u$. Expanding it along a smooth direction gives a polynomial whose nonconstant coefficients detect the complex Hessians of the powers of the background. Theorem 11.1.5 . 2B3316345A4A For every smooth real function $u$, EB2FF7F930E4 11.1.6 \begin{equation}  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^ n+ \sum _{k=1}^{n-1}\binom nk \int _ X u(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-k}). \end{equation} Proof. Expand $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ by the binomial theorem. The term with $k=n$ integrates to zero, since it is exact: \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{d}\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}\bigr ).  \] For $1\leq k\leq n-1$, apply lemma 11.1.2 with $f=u$ and $T=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-k}$. Since both $\mathrm{d}$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ annihilate $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-k}),  \] which gives the $k$th term of ( 11.1.6 ). When $n=1$, the sum is empty and the mass is constant. $\square$ If every $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)$ with $1\leq j\leq n-1$ vanishes, ( 11.1.6 ) shows that the mass is constant. Conversely, varying the potential in several independent directions recovers each of these forms by polarization. Theorem 11.1.7 (Chiose) . FB90FC741F25 Assume $n\geq 2$. The following conditions are equivalent: $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is independent of $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n-1$; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega =0$. They are also equivalent to the condition that $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ be the same for all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u$, where $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of section 5.28 . Under these conditions the common mass is $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Proof. Step 1: the first condition implies the second. Let $u$ be a smooth real function. For $|t|$ small, $tu$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\omega $ for both signs of $t$, so the polynomial $t\mapsto \int _ X(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is constant on an interval and its nonconstant coefficients vanish. For $1\leq j\leq n-1$ this gives \[  \int _ X\omega ^ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-j}=0.  \] Replace $u$ by a linear combination of $n-j$ smooth real functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_{n-j}$ and compare the coefficients of the monomial in which every parameter appears once. We obtain \[  \int _ X\omega ^ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n-j}=0.  \] Integrating by parts in the first factor and using that $u_1$ is arbitrary, we obtain the pointwise identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n-j}=0  \] for every choice of the remaining functions. At a given point, the complex Hessians of these functions can be prescribed arbitrarily: multiply a quadratic polynomial in a coordinate chart by a cutoff function equal to one near that point. Since the identity is multilinear, we may complexify it and use the quadratic monomials $z_ a\bar z_ b$. Wedge products of their complex Hessians give all coordinate forms of the complementary bidegree, and pairing with these forms shows that every coefficient of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ j)$ vanishes. When $j=n-1$ there are no remaining factors, and the same conclusion follows directly from the arbitrariness of $u_1$. This proves the second condition. Step 2: the remaining equivalences for smooth potentials. The second condition implies the first by theorem 11.1.5 . For $n\geq 3$, the identities for $j=1,2$ and lemma 11.1.3 give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ and \[  0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=2\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +2\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega ,  \] so the second condition implies the third. For $n=2$, the second condition is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, while $\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ vanishes for degree reasons; the implication is again immediate. Conversely, lemma 11.1.3 derives all the identities of the second condition from the third. Step 3: bounded potentials. Assume the first condition and let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. By theorem 5.32.1 , there are uniformly bounded functions $u_ j\in \mathcal H_\omega $ decreasing to $u$. Their masses all equal $\int _ X\omega ^ n$, and the continuity of the bounded products of section 5.28 along such sequences passes this common value to the limit. Conversely, every element of $\mathcal H_\omega $ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, so constancy for bounded potentials implies the first condition. The zero potential shows that the common mass is $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. $\square$ In particular, a closed background has invariant mass. Under the equivalent conditions above, ( 11.1.6 ) even gives $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^ n$ for every smooth real $u$, not only for $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. In dimension one the mass is always $\int _ X\omega $. Mass invariance can also hold in a nonclosed background. In theorem 12.18.15 , a pluriclosed metric with nonzero exterior derivative satisfies all the lower-power identities above. Those identities fix its bounded-potential mass, even though a family of scalar perturbations can have its least relative eigenvalue tend to zero. The first variation of the mass involves only the complex Hessian of the power $\omega _ u^{n-1}$ of the perturbed form. Proposition 11.1.8 . 5C29873687ED For smooth real functions $u,v$ on $X$, 0B024E0A2A47 11.1.9 \begin{equation}  \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm M_\omega (u+tv) =n\int _ X v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1}). \end{equation} If $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$ for every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Proof. Since $\mathrm M_\omega (u+tv)$ is a polynomial in $t$, its derivative at $t=0$ is \[  n\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1},  \] and lemma 11.1.2 turns this into the right-hand side of ( 11.1.9 ). For the second assertion, fix $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. For every smooth real direction $v$, the segment $u+tv$ lies in $\mathcal H_\omega $ when $|t|$ is sufficiently small, so the right-hand side of ( 11.1.9 ) vanishes for all smooth real $v$. Hence the smooth top-degree form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})$ vanishes. $\square$ Corollary 11.1.10 . 2C05FFD39C6D If $n=2$, then for every smooth real function $u$ on $X$, \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^2+2\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega .  \] Consequently, $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $ if and only if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Proof. The formula is the case $n=2$ of ( 11.1.6 ), and it shows that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ implies constancy. Conversely, if the mass is constant, proposition 11.1.8 at $u=0$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. $\square$ The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$ makes the first variation vanish at $u=0$; Hermitian forms satisfying it are the Gauduchon metrics of section 11.3 . On a surface this identity already gives mass invariance. In dimension three, however, ( 11.1.6 ) reads \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^3 +3\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2) +3\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega .  \] Vanishing of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$ removes the linear term, while $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ still governs the quadratic term. Thus stationarity of the mass at one potential must be distinguished from its invariance on $\mathcal H_\omega $; an explicit example is given in example 11.23.5 .

title: 11.1.11 Mass variation on a complex torus
search_title: Mass variation on a complex torus
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.1 Torsion and the variation of mass
text: By corollary 11.1.10 , the mass on a surface varies precisely through the pairing $2\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ of the potential with the complex Hessian of the background. A product of elliptic curves gives an explicit background and a family of smooth potentials for which this pairing is nonzero. Example 11.1.12 . F336FEED9D87 Let $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^2$. For $j=1,2$, let $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$ be the standard coordinates on the universal cover $\mathbb C^2$, with $x_ j,y_ j$ real, and put \[  \beta _ j=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j.  \] The forms $\beta _ j$ descend to $X$. For a real parameter $t$, define \[  b(x_1)=2+\cos (2\pi x_1),\qquad \omega =\beta _1+b(x_1)\beta _2,\qquad u_ t=t\cos (2\pi x_1).  \] Since $1\leq b\leq 3$, the form $\omega $ is Hermitian. It is not closed, because $\mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}b\wedge \beta _2$ is not identically zero. For a function $f$ of $x_1$ alone, one has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=(f''/4)\beta _1$, where the prime denotes differentiation in $x_1$. Hence \[  \omega _{u_ t} =\bigl (1-\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr )\beta _1+b\beta _2>0 \quad \text{if}\quad |t|<\pi ^{-2}.  \] Writing $B=\int _ X\beta _1\wedge \beta _2>0$, we have 914CB776FFB8 11.1.13 \begin{equation}  \mathrm M_\omega (u_ t)=(4-\pi ^2t)B. \end{equation} Indeed, \[  \omega _{u_ t}^2 =2\bigl (1-\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr ) \bigl (2+\cos (2\pi x_1)\bigr )\beta _1\wedge \beta _2,  \] and over a period the average of $\cos (2\pi x_1)$ is zero while that of its square is $1/2$. Although the complex torus is Kähler, the background $\omega $ chosen above is not closed, and this already allows the mass to vary. On non-Kähler manifolds even an upper bound for the mass can fail; the Hopf manifolds of section 23.1 give examples. Corollary 11.1.14 . 0C9AAEBBC04C In general, the total Monge–Ampère mass is not determined by the ordinary singularity type or by the multiplier ideals, even among smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials. Proof. The potentials $u_ t$ of example 11.1.12 are smooth on the compact manifold $X$, so any two of them differ by a bounded function and have the same singularity type in the sense of section 5.33 . For the same reason, their multiplier ideals are the structure sheaf for every positive multiple of the weight. By ( 11.1.13 ), their masses differ. $\square$

title: 11.1.15 Comparison and mass invariance
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.1 Torsion and the variation of mass
text: The global comparison principle of Kähler geometry compares the Monge–Ampère measures of two potentials on the set where one lies below the other. Adding a constant to a potential leaves its Monge–Ampère measure unchanged, and after a large constant shift this set becomes the whole manifold. Such an inequality would therefore compare total masses, and the varying mass of example 11.1.12 rules it out. Proposition 11.1.16 . 2A8C104899E8 Suppose that every pair $u,v\in \mathcal H_\omega $ satisfies F5F2F7988675 11.1.17 \begin{equation}  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation} Then $\mathrm M_\omega $ is constant on $\mathcal H_\omega $. Proof. Fix $u,v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. By compactness there is a constant $C$ such that $u<v+C$ everywhere. Since $\omega _{v+C}=\omega _ v$, applying ( 11.1.17 ) to $u$ and $v+C$ gives $\mathrm M_\omega (v)\leq \mathrm M_\omega (u)$. Exchanging the roles of $u$ and $v$ gives the opposite inequality. $\square$ Corollary 11.1.18 . 9578EA44189A The inequality ( 11.1.17 ) does not hold for every Hermitian form on a compact complex manifold. Proof. Let $X$, $\omega $, $u_ t$ and $B=\int _ X\beta _1\wedge \beta _2$ be as in example 11.1.12 . For $-\pi ^{-2}<t<0$, set $u=0$ and $v=u_ t+C$ with $C>|t|$. Then $\{ u<v\} =X$, but \[  \int _ X\omega _ v^2=(4-\pi ^2t)B>4B=\int _ X\omega _ u^2.  \] Thus this pair violates ( 11.1.17 ). $\square$ The modified comparison principle of theorem 14.19.6 compensates for the derivatives of the background. Conversely, under the equivalent conditions of theorem 11.1.7 , the ordinary comparison principle holds for bounded potentials, by 14.25.3 .

title: 11.1.19 Uniform mass bounds
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.1 Torsion and the variation of mass
text: Although the mass varies, it may remain bounded. Set \[  \overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\omega )=\sup _{u\in \mathcal H_\omega }\mathrm M_\omega (u)\in (0,+\infty ],  \] the supremum of the masses of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials. Comparing two Hermitian forms and rescaling the potentials shows that the finiteness of this supremum depends only on $X$. Proposition 11.1.20 . 682711871907 If $\eta $ is another Hermitian form and $\omega \leq C\eta $ for a constant $C>0$, then \[  \overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\omega )\leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] In particular, finiteness of $\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}$ is independent of the Hermitian form. Proof. Let $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. Since $C\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, the function $u/C$ belongs to $\mathcal H_\eta $. The top exterior power is monotone on positive $(1,1)$-forms: for positive Hermitian matrices $A\leq B$, all eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}$ are at least one, so $\det A\leq \det B$. Applying this pointwise gives \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n \leq C^ n\int _ X\bigl (\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u/C)\bigr )^ n \leq C^ n\overline{\mathrm v}_{\mathrm{sm}}(\eta ).  \] Taking the supremum over $u$ proves the inequality. Since any two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $X$ are comparable in both directions, the last assertion follows. $\square$ The smooth supremum considered here is also the upper mass over all bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials: proposition 13.14.15 proves this using approximation by smooth strict potentials and continuity of bounded products. In section 13.14 , we then pass to unbounded truncations. By corollary 13.14.19 , finiteness of this common supremum is equivalent to finiteness of the extended non-pluripolar mass of every $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential.

title: 11.2 Monge–Ampère energy and torsion
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, and $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and the space $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions are as in section 11.1 . For a Kähler form, the Monge–Ampère operator is the gradient of an energy: there is a functional on $\mathcal H_\omega $ whose derivative at $u$ in every smooth real direction $v$ is $\int _ Xv\, \omega _ u^ n$. For a Hermitian form, such a primitive exists exactly when $\omega $ is closed. Symmetry of its mixed second derivatives first forces $\mathrm d(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$, and varying the potential then forces $\mathrm d\omega =0$; this is stronger than the mass invariance of section 11.1 . For a nonclosed background, integrating the Monge–Ampère one-form along radial segments still defines a functional, and its first variation shows which torsion terms enter the corresponding Euler equation. A different energy is available for Hermitian symplectic forms on fourfolds: along potential variations, this completion energy changes by minus the change of the volume. It is therefore constant along potential variations exactly when the mass is invariant, although even then the Monge–Ampère one-form has no primitive unless $\omega $ is closed.

title: 11.2.1 Primitives of the Monge–Ampère one-form
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: On $\mathcal H_\omega $ consider the Monge–Ampère one-form \[  \alpha _ u(v)=\int _ Xv\, \omega _ u^ n,\qquad v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R).  \] Let $U\subseteq \mathcal H_\omega $ be open in the $C^2$ topology on smooth functions. A primitive of $\alpha $ on $U$ is a functional $E$ on $U$ such that, for every $u\in U$ and every smooth real direction $v$, the directional derivative \[  DE_ u(v)=\left.\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\right|_{t=0}E(u+tv)  \] exists and equals $\alpha _ u(v)$. Restrict $E$ to the intersection of $U$ with a finite-dimensional affine plane. Its first derivatives are values of $\alpha $, which depend smoothly on the parameters, so its mixed second derivatives agree. The following integration-by-parts criterion identifies the differential condition imposed by this symmetry. Lemma 11.2.2 . 8A9C3139B5B5 For a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Omega $, the pairing $B(v,w)=\int _ Xw\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega $ is symmetric on smooth real functions if and only if $\mathrm{d}\Omega =0$. Proof. By lemma 11.1.2 , $B(v,w)=\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\Omega )$. Since $v$ is arbitrary, symmetry is therefore equivalent to the pointwise identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w\Omega )-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \Omega =w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega +\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\Omega =0  \] for every smooth real $w$. Taking $w=1$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega =0$. The remaining expression is linear in the first jet of $w$, so we may complexify the test functions. At a chosen point, take a holomorphic linear function multiplied by a cutoff function, so that $\partial w=\lambda $ is an arbitrary $(1,0)$-covector and $\bar\partial w=0$ at that point. There the first-order expression equals \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\bigl (\partial w\wedge \bar\partial \Omega -\bar\partial w\wedge \partial \Omega \bigr ).  \] It follows that $\lambda \wedge \bar\partial \Omega =0$ for every $(1,0)$-covector $\lambda $. Since the wedge pairing between $(1,0)$-covectors and forms of bidegree $(n-1,n)$ is nondegenerate, $\bar\partial \Omega =0$, and $\partial \Omega =0$ because $\Omega $ is real. Conversely, if $\mathrm{d}\Omega =0$, then $\partial \Omega =\bar\partial \Omega =0$ by type, so $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega =0$, and the same product formula proves symmetry. $\square$ Lemma 11.2.3 . 8535B6F80ED4 Let $T$ be a form of type $(2,1)+(1,2)$ on a complex vector space of dimension $n\geq 2$. If $T\wedge A^{n-2}=0$ for every real $(1,1)$-form $A$ in an open neighborhood of a positive form, then $T=0$. Proof. For $n=2$ the assertion is immediate. Otherwise the expression $T\wedge A^{n-2}$ is polynomial in the real coefficients of $A$, so it vanishes for every real $(1,1)$-form $A$. Polarization and then complexification give $T\wedge A_1\wedge \cdots \wedge A_{n-2}=0$ for arbitrary complex $(1,1)$-forms $A_ j$, and such products span all forms of bidegree $(n-2,n-2)$. Since these wedges preserve type, the identity holds separately for the two type components of $T$. Wedging the identity for $T^{2,1}$ with arbitrary $(0,1)$-covectors, we obtain test forms spanning bidegree $(n-2,n-1)$, which pairs perfectly with bidegree $(2,1)$ into top degree. Thus $T^{2,1}=0$. The component $T^{1,2}$ is treated in the same way with $(1,0)$-covectors. $\square$ Theorem 11.2.4 . 7D069B347672 For $n\geq 2$, the one-form $\alpha $ has a primitive on $\mathcal H_\omega $ if and only if $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. In fact, a primitive on a $C^2$-open neighborhood of $0$ already forces $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. Proof. Suppose that a primitive $E$ exists on such a neighborhood $U$. For $u\in U$ and smooth real directions $v,w$, the mixed second derivatives of $(s,t)\mapsto E(u+sv+tw)$ at the origin agree. After division by $n$, this equality reads B4B9D0AD937E 11.2.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ Xw\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1} =\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge \omega _ u^{n-1}. \end{equation} By lemma 11.2.2 , \[  0=\mathrm{d}(\omega _ u^{n-1}) =(n-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-2}.  \] Fix a point $x$. A real quadratic polynomial in local coordinates, multiplied by a cutoff function equal to one near $x$, realizes any prescribed real $(1,1)$-form $H$ as $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u(x)$. These functions can be chosen to depend linearly on $H$, with global $C^2$ norms bounded by a fixed constant times the coefficient norm of $H$. Thus every sufficiently small $H$ is realized by a potential in $U$, and the preceding identity holds at $x$ with $\omega (x)+H$ ranging over an open neighborhood of the positive form $\omega (x)$. Applying lemma 11.2.3 with $T=\mathrm{d}\omega (x)$, we conclude that $\mathrm{d}\omega (x)=0$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$. Conversely, proposition 11.2.8 below constructs a primitive for a closed background. $\square$ In dimension one every real $(1,1)$-form is closed, and proposition 11.2.8 always gives a primitive. For $n\geq 2$, the symmetry condition at a single potential $u$ is $\mathrm d(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0$; the theorem uses it on an open set of potentials. Mass invariance alone does not suffice. Indeed, let $X$ be a compact complex surface admitting no Kähler metric, and let $\omega $ be a Gauduchon form on $X$, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ (definition 11.4.1 ); such forms exist by theorem 11.4.2 . The mass of $\omega $ is constant by corollary 11.1.10 , but $\omega $ is not closed, so its Monge–Ampère one-form has no primitive.

title: 11.2.6 Radial energy and closed backgrounds
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Integrating the Monge–Ampère one-form along the segment from $0$ to $u$ defines a functional for an arbitrary background. Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. For $u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, put $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and define the radial energy 1CE478F66A34 11.2.7 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  E_\theta (u) & =\int _0^1\int _ Xu(\theta +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\, \mathrm{d}t\\ & =\frac1{n+1}\sum _{j=0}^ n \int _ Xu\, \theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} To obtain the second expression, write $\theta +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(1-t)\theta +t\theta _ u$, expand, and use \[  \binom nj\int _0^1t^ j(1-t)^{n-j}\, \mathrm dt=\frac1{n+1}.  \] We write $DE_{\theta ,u}(v)$ for the derivative of $E_\theta $ at $u$ in the direction $v$. When $\theta $ is closed, integration by parts makes the derivatives of the mixed terms telescope. Proposition 11.2.8 . E345C8B2A48C If $\mathrm d\theta =0$, then $DE_{\theta ,u}(v)=\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ n$ for every pair of smooth real functions $u,v$. Proof. Differentiate the finite sum in ( 11.2.7 ). The term indexed by $j$ contributes \[  \int _ Xv\theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j} +j\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j},  \] the second summand being absent for $j=0$. For $j\geq 1$, the form $\theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j}$ is closed, so by lemma 11.2.2 we may interchange $u$ and $v$ in the second summand. Using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\theta _ u-\theta $, we can then write the contribution of the term with $j\geq 1$ as \[  (j+1)\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ j\wedge \theta ^{n-j} -j\int _ Xv\theta _ u^{j-1}\wedge \theta ^{n-j+1}.  \] Together with the contribution $\int _ Xv\theta ^ n$ of the term $j=0$, these expressions telescope to $(n+1)\int _ Xv\theta _ u^ n$. Dividing by $n+1$ completes the proof. $\square$ Thus, when $\mathrm d\omega =0$, the restriction of $E_\omega $ to $\mathcal H_\omega $ is the primitive required in theorem 11.2.4 .

title: 11.2.9 First variation in a nonclosed background
search_title: First variation in a nonclosed background
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: For the Hermitian background $\theta =\omega $, the functional ( 11.2.7 ) integrates $\alpha $ along the segment from $0$ to $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $. When $\omega $ is not closed, the derivative of $E_\omega $ differs from $\alpha $ by the terms produced when integration by parts differentiates the background powers. Computing this difference gives the Euler equation of $E_\omega $ even when no primitive exists. Proposition 11.2.10 . 4793125897B2 For $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ and $v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, put $\Omega _ t=(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Then 91AE93E20D38 11.2.11 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n =n\int _0^1t\int _ Xv\bigl (& u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega _ t +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega _ t\\ & -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\Omega _ t\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{split} \end{equation} Proof. Differentiating the radial integral in ( 11.2.7 ) in the direction $v$ gives \[  DE_{\omega ,u}(v) =\int _0^1\left(\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n +nt\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega _ t\right)\mathrm dt.  \] On the other hand, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n & =\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} \left(t\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\right)\mathrm dt\\ & =\int _0^1\left(\int _ Xv(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n +nt\int _ Xv\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Omega _ t\right)\mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] The terms without a factor $nt$ cancel in the difference, leaving \[  \begin{aligned}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n & =n\int _0^1t\int _ X (u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-v\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \Omega _ t\, \mathrm dt\\ & =n\int _0^1t\int _ Xv \bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\Omega _ t)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Omega _ t\bigr )\, \mathrm dt. \end{aligned}  \] The second equality is lemma 11.1.2 . Expanding the last parenthesis by the product rule in the proof of lemma 11.2.2 gives ( 11.2.11 ). When $n=1$, one has $\Omega _ t=1$ and the right-hand side vanishes. $\square$ Proposition 11.2.12 . 0009683E4137 If $n=2$, then every $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ satisfies \[  E_\omega (u)=\int _ Xu\omega ^2 +\int _ Xu\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u +\frac13\int _ Xu(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2.  \] For every smooth real direction $v$, its differential satisfies 173E9E78941E 11.2.13 \begin{equation}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^2 =\int _ Xv\bigl (u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega \bigr ). \end{equation} Proof. Expanding the radial integral gives the first identity. For $n=2$, one has $\Omega _ t=\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and since $\mathrm d$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ annihilate $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, the derivatives $\mathrm d\Omega _ t$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega _ t$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega _ t$ are those of $\omega $. Formula ( 11.2.11 ) and $2\int _0^1t\, \mathrm dt=1$ give the second identity. $\square$ Consequently, if $n=2$ and $\mu $ is a fixed smooth real $(2,2)$-form on $X$, a critical point $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ of the functional $E_\omega (u)-\int _ Xu\, \mu $ satisfies \[  \omega _ u^2+u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\omega =\mu  \] rather than the Monge–Ampère equation $\omega _ u^2=\mu $. The radial Euler equation can therefore differ from the Monge–Ampère equation even when the total mass is invariant.

Then 91AE93E20D38 11.2.11 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  DE_{\omega ,u}(v)-\int _ Xv\omega _ u^ n =n\int _0^1t\int _ Xv\bigl (& u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega _ t +\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Omega _ t\\ & -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{d}\Omega _ t\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{split} \end{equation} Proof.
