title: 11.2.14 Symplectic completions and potential variations
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
The radial energy is built from the Monge–Ampère one-form, and its first variation exhibits the torsion of the background. When a Hermitian form is the $(1,1)$-part of a closed real two-form, there is another natural energy: the squared $L^2$ norm of the smallest $(2,0)$-part needed to close it. In complex dimension four, adding a complex Hessian to the form changes this energy by minus the change of the volume. Its potential variations are therefore governed by the volume, and not by a primitive of the Monge–Ampère one-form. Throughout this section we assume $n=4$. A Hermitian form $\omega $ is Hermitian symplectic if there is a smooth $(2,0)$-form $ho $, called a completion of $\omega $, such that \[  \partial ho =0,\qquad  ar\partial ho =-\partial \omega .  \] Equivalently, the real two-form $\omega +ho + arho $ is closed. Applying $ ar\partial $ to the second equation shows that $\omega $ is pluriclosed, meaning $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Two completions differ by a closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form, so the completions of $\omega $ form an affine space over the finite-dimensional space of closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-forms. The quadratic norm \[  \| ho \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2 = rac12\int _ Xho \wedge  arho \wedge \omega ^2  \] is positive definite on $(2,0)$-forms, and minimizing it over this affine space gives a unique canonical completion $ho _\omega $. It is characterized by being orthogonal to every closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form. Define the completion energy and the volume of $\omega $ by \[  F(\omega )=\| ho _\omega \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2, \qquad V(\omega )= rac1{4!}\int _ X\omega ^4.  \] The completion energy is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when $\omega $ is Kähler: a zero canonical completion forces $\partial \omega =0$, while a closed $\omega $ has the zero completion. Since $\omega $ is pluriclosed, it defines an Aeppli cohomology class, whose real $(1,1)$-representatives are the forms $\omega +\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $, with $	au $ a smooth $(1,0)$-form. We call a real form $\psi =\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $ an Aeppli variation . If $ho $ completes $\omega $ and $\omega +t\psi $ is positive for a real $t$, then $\omega +t\psi $ has the completion $ho +t\partial 	au $. In particular, the positive representatives $\omega +\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au >0$ of the Aeppli class of $\omega $ are again Hermitian symplectic. Every positive potential variation $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ belongs to this class and has the same exterior derivative as $\omega $. We write $DF_\omega (\psi )$ for the derivative of $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\psi )$ at $t=0$. Lemma 11.2.15 . 19D4882CC9D5 Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic, with canonical completion $ho =ho _\omega $. Every Aeppli variation $\psi =\partial  ar	au + ar\partial 	au $ satisfies 7C73F0133C9D 11.2.16  egin{equation}  DF_\omega (\psi )=\int _ X\left( \operatorname {Re}(\partial 	au \wedge  arho \wedge \omega ^2) +ho \wedge  arho \wedge \psi \wedge \omega ight). \end{equation} Proof. The canonical completion of $\omega +t\psi $ is $ho +t\partial 	au -h(t)$, where $h(t)$ is a closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-form and $h(0)=0$. In a fixed basis of these holomorphic forms, the orthogonal projection defining $h(t)$ solves a positive definite Gram system whose coefficients are smooth in $t$. Since $ho $ is orthogonal to closed holomorphic $(2,0)$-forms, the contribution of $h'(0)$ to the first derivative of the squared norm vanishes. We may therefore differentiate using the completion $ho +t\partial 	au $. Differentiating its two factors and the factor $(\omega +t\psi )^2/2$ gives the formula. $\square$ Proposition 11.2.17 . AE6CE389C569 Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic. For every smooth real function $\varphi $ with $\omega _\varphi =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$, one has $ho _{\omega _\varphi }=ho _\omega $ and BAFFEA611460 11.2.18  egin{equation}  F(\omega _\varphi )+V(\omega _\varphi )=F(\omega )+V(\omega ). \end{equation} Moreover, $DF_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=0$ for every smooth real $\varphi $ if and only if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3)=0$. Thus a critical point of $F$ in its Aeppli class is Gauduchon. Proof. Fix any completion $\zeta $ of $\omega $ and put $\Theta _\zeta =\omega +\zeta + ar\zeta $. Expansion by type gives \[   rac1{4!}\int _ X\Theta _\zeta ^4 =V(\omega )+ rac12\int _ X\zeta \wedge  ar\zeta \wedge \omega ^2 + rac14\int _ X\zeta ^2\wedge  ar\zeta ^2.  \] Since $\partial \omega _\varphi =\partial \omega $, the forms $\omega _\varphi $ and $\omega $ have the same completions. With $\zeta $ fixed, replacing $\omega $ by $\omega _\varphi $ changes the closed form $\Theta _\zeta $ by an exact form, so the integral on the left is unchanged; so is the last integral on the right, which does not involve $\omega $. Hence \[  \| \zeta \| _{L^2(\omega _\varphi )}^2 -\| \zeta \| _{L^2(\omega )}^2=V(\omega )-V(\omega _\varphi ).  \] This difference is independent of $\zeta $, so the two norms have the same minimizer, which gives $ho _{\omega _\varphi }=ho _\omega $ and ( 11.2.18 ). Differentiating at $t=0$ along $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ and using lemma 11.1.2 , we obtain \[  DF_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=- rac16\int _ X\varphi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3).  \] Since $\varphi $ is arbitrary, this proves the remaining assertions. $\square$ The positive index of a real quadratic form on a real vector space is the supremum of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which it is positive definite; the negative index is defined in the same way. Thus the positive index is infinite when the form is positive definite on subspaces of arbitrarily large finite dimension. Theorem 11.2.19 . 04BD04D6C676 Let $\omega $ be Hermitian symplectic, and let $H_\omega $ be the Hessian of $F$ at $\omega $ along the affine space of real representatives of the Aeppli class of $\omega $, so that $H_\omega (\psi ,\psi )$ is the second derivative of $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\psi )$ at $t=0$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)
e 0$, the restriction of $H_\omega $ to potential directions $\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ has infinite positive and negative index. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$, then $F(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )=F(\omega )$ whenever $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. Consequently, every local minimum of $F$ in an Aeppli class satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$. Proof. Step 1: the Hessian formula. Pluriclosedness and Stokes' theorem give $\int _ X\omega \wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^3=\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^4=0$. Thus the volume and, by ( 11.2.18 ), the energy along a potential line $t\mapsto \omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ are polynomials of degree at most two in $t$. Differentiating twice and integrating by parts, we obtain 8B6CFC8EA37B 11.2.20  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}  H_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi ,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi ) & =- rac12\int _ X\omega ^2\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^2\ & = rac12\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)\wedge \mathrm d\varphi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\varphi . \end{aligned} \end{equation} For the second equality, apply lemma 11.1.2 once and then use the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi ^2/2)=\varphi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi +\mathrm d\varphi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\varphi $ against the closed form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$. Step 2: both indices are infinite if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)
e 0$. Put $\Psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)$. At each point, $\xi \mapsto \Psi \wedge \mathrm i\xi \wedge  ar\xi $, divided by a positive volume form, is a Hermitian quadratic form in the $(1,0)$-covector $\xi $, and these quadratic forms determine $\Psi $. Their traces with respect to $\omega $ are positive multiples of the density $\Psi \wedge \omega $, whose integral vanishes by Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. If the quadratic forms took no strictly positive value, they would be negative semidefinite everywhere, with nonpositive traces of integral zero; the traces, and hence $\Psi $, would vanish identically. The same argument applies with the signs reversed. Therefore, if $\Psi 
e 0$, the quadratic forms take a strictly positive value somewhere and a strictly negative value somewhere. Fix one of the two signs. Choose holomorphic coordinates on a ball such that, with $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, the density $\Psi \wedge \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x$ has that sign on the ball; this is possible because $\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x$ is a positive multiple of $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d ar z_1$. For a nonzero real cutoff function $a$ supported in the ball, set $\varphi _ N=a\cos (Nx)$. Formula ( 11.2.20 ) gives \[  H_\omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ N,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ N) = rac{N^2}{2}\int _ Xa^2\sin ^2(Nx)\Psi \wedge \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x+O(N),  \] where the constant in $O(N)$ depends on $\Psi $, the chart and the cutoff, but not on $N$. By integration by parts in $x$, the integral tends to half the same integral without the factor $\sin ^2(Nx)$. Hence the Hessian has the chosen sign for large $N$. For a positive integer $k$, apply this construction on $k$ disjoint smaller balls in that region. By the local integral formula, the resulting nonzero directions are linearly independent and pairwise orthogonal for the Hessian, so their span is a $k$-dimensional subspace on which $H_\omega $ is definite of the chosen sign. Repeating the argument with the opposite sign proves that both indices are infinite. Each finite-dimensional span admits sufficiently small variations preserving positivity. Step 3: flatness if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$. If $\Psi =0$, lemma 11.1.3 and pluriclosedness give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^3)=3\omega \wedge \Psi =0$. Both derivatives at $t=0$ of the quadratic polynomial $t\mapsto F(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ vanish, so it is constant on the interval of $t$ for which $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. This interval contains $0$ and $1$ whenever $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$. Finally, a local minimum cannot have a potential direction along which the Hessian is negative, so it satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$ by Step 2. $\square$ Corollary 11.2.21 . 67DF1C6C0509 For a Hermitian symplectic form $\omega $ on $X$, the following conditions are equivalent: $F(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ is independent of the smooth real function $\varphi $ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$; $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$; $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^4$ is independent of the bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u$. The common mass in the third condition is $24V(\omega )$. Every local minimum of $F$ in an Aeppli class has these properties. Proof. By ( 11.2.18 ), the energy is constant along smooth positive potential variations if and only if their volume is. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, lemma 11.1.3 , theorem 11.1.7 show that this smooth mass invariance is equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$ and to mass invariance for bounded potentials. The zero potential gives the common mass. The last assertion follows from theorem 11.2.19 . $\square$

title: 11.2.22 Completion energy on products of complex tori

title: 11.3 Gauduchon metrics and linear mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Throughout this chapter, $\omega $ is a fixed Hermitian form on $X$, and $n\geq 2$ unless a section specifies another setting. The mass variation in section 11.1 leaves a linear conservation law. If $\gamma $ is a Gauduchon metric, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, integration against $\gamma ^{n-1}$ annihilates every complex Hessian. Thus the trace mass $\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of a positive current depends only on its smooth background $\theta $, even when $u$ is unbounded. Gauduchon's theorem produces such a metric in every conformal class, providing conserved pairings when the background is not closed. These pairings determine positivity as well as mass. A smooth form $\theta $ admits a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ exactly when all its Gauduchon degrees are nonnegative. Normalizing the degrees gives the largest lower curvature bound obtainable by adding a complex Hessian. This bound is always attained by a potential; a minimizing test exists in the weak closure of the normalized smooth Gauduchon forms, although a smooth minimizing metric generally does not exist. Applied to $\omega _ u$, the conformal construction also gives the adjoint probability of the linearized Monge–Ampère operator. It identifies the compatibility condition for that operator and explains the extra term in entropy dissipation for a nonclosed background. For a holomorphic line bundle, the conserved pairing is the degree of its curvature, and a positive degree excludes a metric with nonpositive curvature. Fiber averaging extends this obstruction to plurisubharmonic norms near a direct sum of line bundles. Polar duality and homogeneous regularization then turn it into an obstruction to semipositive Finsler curvature. The stable ample bundles constructed on Hirzebruch surfaces show that ampleness alone does not remove the obstruction; their projective complements give a geometric way to measure it. The same scalar equation can improve curvature when the mean curvature is nonnegative: a conformal change spreads directional positivity from a nonempty open set to the whole manifold. Ricci-flat Kähler surfaces illustrate the distinction between this directional condition and positivity on every tangent and fiber pair. On a projective manifold, positivity on every such pair admits another duality criterion, expressed by positive measures over the dual bundle.

title: 11.4 Conformal Gauduchon metrics
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: By proposition 11.1.8 , the first variation of the mass at $u=0$ vanishes exactly when $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$. This condition can be achieved in every conformal class: finding a conformal factor amounts to finding a positive generator of the kernel of the adjoint of a scalar elliptic operator. Definition 11.4.1 . 70139B6ABDC2 A Hermitian form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon , or a Gauduchon metric , if \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0.  \] It is balanced if $\mathrm d(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, and pluriclosed if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma =0$. Theorem 11.4.2 (Gauduchon's theorem) . 3978AEB15BD7 Every Hermitian form $\eta $ has a conformal Gauduchon representative. More precisely, there is a smooth strictly positive function $\rho $, unique up to multiplication by a positive constant, such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1})=0.  \] The associated Gauduchon form is $\gamma =\rho ^{1/(n-1)}\eta $. Proof. For a smooth real function $v$ on $X$, define \[  Lv=n\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \eta ^{n-1}}{\eta ^ n}.  \] This real second-order operator has positive definite principal symbol and no zeroth-order term. By the maximum principle, its kernel consists of the constants. Its index is zero, since the linear path joining it to a Laplace operator consists of elliptic operators. Fredholm theory and elliptic regularity therefore show that the formal adjoint $L^*$ of $L$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$ has a one-dimensional kernel, generated by a nonzero smooth real function $\rho $. We first prove that $\int _ X\rho \eta ^ n\ne 0$. Otherwise the constant function $1$ would be orthogonal to the kernel of $L^*$, and the Fredholm alternative would solve $Lv=1$, which is impossible at a maximum point of $v$. We may therefore rescale so that $\int _ X\rho \eta ^ n=1$. Next we show that $\rho \geq 0$. Suppose instead that $\rho $ is negative somewhere. Choose a nonzero smooth function $h\geq 0$ supported where $\rho <0$, and put $c=\int _ Xh\rho \eta ^ n<0$. The function $h-c$ is strictly positive and orthogonal to the kernel of $L^*$, so the Fredholm alternative would solve $Lv=h-c>0$, which is again impossible at a maximum point of $v$. In real local coordinates $(x_1,\ldots ,x_{2n})$, write $L^*=A^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j+B^ i\partial _ i+C$, where $\partial _ i=\partial /\partial x_ i$, the coefficients are smooth, and repeated indices are summed from $1$ to $2n$. The leading symbol $(A^{ij})$ is positive definite. Since $\rho \geq 0$, \[  (L^*-\max (C,0))\rho =-\max (C,0)\rho \leq 0,  \] and the operator $L^*-\max (C,0)$ has nonpositive zeroth-order term. By the strong minimum principle, a zero of $\rho $ would force $\rho $ to vanish identically on the connected manifold $X$. Hence $\rho >0$. Finally, integration by parts gives \[  \int _ X\rho Lv\, \eta ^ n =n\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1}).  \] Thus the equation $L^*\rho =0$ is precisely $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \eta ^{n-1})=0$, and the one-dimensional adjoint kernel gives uniqueness up to positive scaling. Since $\gamma ^{n-1}=\rho \eta ^{n-1}$, the form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon. $\square$ A Kähler form, that is, a closed Hermitian form, is both balanced and pluriclosed, and every balanced form is Gauduchon. On surfaces, balanced forms are Kähler, and the Gauduchon and pluriclosed conditions coincide.

title: 11.5 Conservation of the trace mass
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: The power $\gamma ^{n-1}$ of a Gauduchon metric annihilates every complex Hessian under integration. It therefore assigns to a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ a mass depending only on its smooth background $\theta $, also when the potential $u$ is unbounded. Proposition 11.5.1 . 828FAD1A35BF Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, let $u$ be a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function, and let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric. Then 97DCB5703B01 11.5.2 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, distributional integration by parts gives \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\gamma ^{n-1}\rangle =\langle u,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})\rangle =0.  \] The product on the left of ( 11.5.2 ) is a positive measure, whose total mass is therefore the finite number on the right. $\square$ We call $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ the Gauduchon degree of $\theta $ with respect to $\gamma $. Here $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is the full distributional current, including any mass carried by the pole set of $u$. The non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of section 13.14 discards this mass; example 13.15.17 illustrates the difference on a curve. Corollary 11.5.3 . A9609E0AE7B9 There are constants $0<a\leq b<+\infty $, depending only on $\omega $ and a chosen Gauduchon metric, such that every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies \[  a\leq \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \omega ^{n-1}\leq b.  \] Proof. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$ and choose positive constants $c,C$ with $c\gamma ^{n-1}\leq \omega ^{n-1}\leq C\gamma ^{n-1}$. Wedging these inequalities with the positive current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and integrating, we obtain, by proposition 11.5.1 , the bounds $cA$ and $CA$, where $A=\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0$. $\square$ The trace bound controls the mass of positive currents and hence their weak compactness. By itself it gives no bound for the Monge–Ampère mass, since a bound on the integral of a trace does not bound the integral of its $n$th power. The pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality relates the conserved trace to the density in a smooth Monge–Ampère equation. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$. Proposition 11.5.4 . BFC1330527CA For any two Hermitian forms $\eta ,\gamma $, 1F99A7154650 11.5.5 \begin{equation}  \eta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{\eta ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \end{equation} pointwise. Consequently, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $f$ a smooth strictly positive function. If $u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $c>0$ satisfy $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, then B78F87EF7411 11.5.6 \begin{equation}  c^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{f\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \end{equation} for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. Proof. In a frame where $\gamma $ is the identity, let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $\eta $. The ratios of the two sides of ( 11.5.5 ) to $\gamma ^ n$ are $n^{-1}\sum _ j\lambda _ j$ and $(\prod _ j\lambda _ j)^{1/n}$, respectively, and their comparison is the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. For the second assertion, apply ( 11.5.5 ) with $\eta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, integrate, and use ( 11.5.2 ). $\square$ The corresponding density inequality for unbounded potentials in a Hermitian background is proved in lemma 13.14.12 .

If $u\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $c>0$ satisfy $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, then B78F87EF7411 11.5.6 \begin{equation}  c^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{f\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \end{equation} for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. Proof. In a frame where $\gamma $ is the identity, let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $\eta $. title: 11.6 The Gauduchon criterion for positivity
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: The trace identity gives a necessary condition for $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to be nonempty: every Gauduchon degree of $\theta $ must be nonnegative. The condition is also sufficient. A Hahn–Banach separation produces a positive current with the prescribed pairings, and a scalar elliptic equation shows that its difference from $\theta $ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Theorem 11.6.1 (The generalized Lamari criterion) . 88BE3B63D9E5 For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, the following conditions are equivalent: There exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0$ for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. To apply separation, we express the test in terms of smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $\Gamma $. Every strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $ has a unique strictly positive $(1,1)$-root $\gamma $, that is, $\Gamma =\gamma ^{n-1}$. Indeed, in a frame in which $\Gamma $ is diagonal, and with the same wedge normalization on both sides, the coefficients $g_ i$ of $\Gamma $ are the products $\prod _{j\neq i}\lambda _ j$ of the eigenvalues $\lambda _ j$ of $\gamma $. Hence \[  \lambda _ i=\frac{(\prod _ jg_ j)^{1/(n-1)}}{g_ i}.  \] This spectral formula uses only a positive determinant and a matrix inverse, so the root depends smoothly on the coefficients of $\Gamma $, also at repeated eigenvalues, and pointwise uniqueness makes the local roots agree on overlaps. Consequently, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$ says exactly that the root $\gamma $ is Gauduchon. of theorem 11.6.1 . Necessity is proposition 11.5.1 . For sufficiency, let $F$ be the real vector space of smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, and let \[  E=\{ \Gamma \in F:\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0\} ,\qquad \ell (\Gamma )=\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma \quad (\Gamma \in E).  \] Fix a strictly positive $\Gamma _0\in E$, which exists by theorem 11.4.2 . By the root calculation above, the hypothesis says that $\ell $ is nonnegative on the strictly positive elements of $E$. Adding $\epsilon \Gamma _0$ and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $\ell $ is also nonnegative on the semipositive elements of $E$. Step 1: a positive extension of $\ell $. For $\Phi \in F$ put \[  p(\Phi )=\inf \{ \ell (\Gamma ):\Gamma \in E,\  \Gamma \geq \Phi \} .  \] This is a finite sublinear function. To see finiteness, choose $C$ with $-C\Gamma _0\leq \Phi \leq C\Gamma _0$. The admissible element $C\Gamma _0$ gives an upper bound, while every admissible $\Gamma $ satisfies $\Gamma +C\Gamma _0\geq 0$ and hence $\ell (\Gamma )\geq -C\ell (\Gamma _0)$. Sublinearity follows by adding and rescaling competitors. For $\Phi \in E$, the nonnegativity of $\ell (\Gamma -\Phi )$ for admissible $\Gamma $ shows that $p(\Phi )=\ell (\Phi )$. The Hahn–Banach theorem gives a real linear extension $T$ of $\ell $ to $F$ with $T(\Phi )\leq p(\Phi )$ for all $\Phi \in F$. If $\Phi \geq 0$, the zero form is admissible for $p(-\Phi )$, so $T(-\Phi )\leq 0$, that is, $T(\Phi )\geq 0$. Moreover, the bounds by $C\Gamma _0$ show that $T$ is continuous for the uniform norm. It is therefore a positive $(1,1)$-current, and the current $S=T-\theta $ annihilates $E$. Step 2: $S$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. To recover a potential from $S$, consider the scalar operator \[  Dv=\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\Gamma _0)}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm dV$ is the smooth positive volume form fixed above. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _0=0$, this is an elliptic scalar operator with no zeroth-order term. Its kernel consists of the constants and its index is zero, while Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XDv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. Consequently its range is exactly the space of smooth functions of integral zero, and by elliptic estimates its inverse on functions normalized by $\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ is continuous in the smooth topology. For a smooth top-degree form $\zeta $ with $\int _ X\zeta =0$, solve $Dv=\zeta /\mathrm{d}V$ with this normalization and set $R\zeta =v\Gamma _0$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R\zeta =\zeta $, and $R$ is continuous. Define a distribution $u$ on such top-degree forms by \[  \langle u,\zeta \rangle =S(R\zeta ),  \] and extend it to all top-degree forms by assigning an arbitrary value on one fixed volume form of integral one. For every $\Phi \in F$, the form $\Phi -R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )$ belongs to $E$, and $S$ annihilates it. It follows that \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\Phi \rangle =S(R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi ))=S(\Phi ).  \] Thus $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=T\geq 0$, and proposition 5.22.2 gives a representative of $u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$ Applying the criterion to $\theta -a\omega $, for $a\in \mathbb R$, determines the largest lower curvature bound attainable in the background $\theta $. Corollary 11.6.2 . F83E15A1F529 For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, set \[  \kappa _\omega (\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \  \mathrm{Gauduchon}} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}.  \] This is a finite real number, and it is the largest real $a$ for which there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ satisfying \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq a\omega .  \] In particular, this largest value is attained, and $\theta $ is big, in the sense of section 5.40 , precisely when $\kappa _\omega (\theta )>0$. Proof. Since $\theta $ is smooth, $-C\omega \leq \theta \leq C\omega $ for some $C$, so the infimum lies in $[-C,C]$. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq a\omega $, the trace identity applied to the background $\theta -a\omega $ shows that $a$ is at most each of the ratios in the definition, hence $a\leq \kappa _\omega (\theta )$. Conversely, for $a=\kappa _\omega (\theta )$, all Gauduchon degrees of $\theta -a\omega $ are nonnegative, and theorem 11.6.1 applied to this smooth form gives the required $u$. The last assertion follows, since bigness means the existence of a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. $\square$ Whether the infimum defining $\kappa _\omega (\theta )$ is attained by a smooth Gauduchon metric is decided by a rigidity property of the trace: a positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with vanishing Gauduchon degree is zero. Lemma 11.6.3 . 91B8C8A3C10E Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $. If \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0  \] for one Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, then $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Conversely, a form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth has zero degree with respect to every Gauduchon metric. The same conclusions hold for $n=1$, with $\gamma ^{n-1}=1$. Proof. Choose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and put $S=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 11.5.1 , $\int _ XS\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0$. Since the trace measure $S\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of the positive current $S$ controls all its coefficient measures, $S=0$. Taking the trace of the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\theta $ with respect to $\omega $ gives an elliptic equation with smooth right-hand side, so $u$ is smooth by elliptic regularity, and $f=-u$ has the required property. The converse is Stokes' theorem. For $n=1$, the trace measure is $S$ itself and the same argument applies. $\square$ For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, put $a=\kappa _\omega (\theta )$. By corollary 11.6.2 , the form $\theta -a\omega $ admits a positive current $\theta -a\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. A Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum defining $\kappa _\omega (\theta )$ precisely when the Gauduchon degree of $\theta -a\omega $ with respect to $\gamma $ vanishes. Hence lemma 11.6.3 shows that the infimum is attained by a smooth Gauduchon metric if and only if \[  \theta -a\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\quad \text{for some }f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R),  \] and in that case every Gauduchon metric attains it. Thus a positive current at the threshold always exists, whereas a smooth minimizing Gauduchon metric exists only in this exceptional situation.

section: 11.7 Compactness and duality of Gauduchon currents
text: When no smooth Gauduchon metric attains the threshold, a minimizer can still be found among weak limits of normalized Gauduchon forms. The normalization bounds the coefficient measures and hence gives compactness. Let $\mathscr G_\omega $ be the set of positive $(n-1,n-1)$-currents $T$ on $X$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0,\qquad \int _ X\omega \wedge T=1.  \] We call them normalized Gauduchon currents . Let $\mathscr C_\omega $ be the weak closure of the set of smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. By the root calculation preceding the proof of theorem 11.6.1 , these smooth members are exactly the normalized powers $\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ of Gauduchon metrics $\gamma $. Proposition 11.7.1 . 155386134D9E The sets $\mathscr G_\omega $ and $\mathscr C_\omega $ are nonempty, compact and convex. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, 7F6E8313B3F8 11.7.2 \begin{equation}  \kappa _\omega (\theta ) =\min _{T\in \mathscr C_\omega }\int _ X\theta \wedge T. \end{equation} Moreover, a current $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ belongs to $\mathscr C_\omega $ if and only if EDF0C9D4A983 11.7.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\theta \wedge T\geq 0 \quad \text{for every smooth real }\theta \text{ with }\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing . \end{equation} Proof. Gauduchon's theorem gives a smooth strictly positive member of $\mathscr G_\omega $ after normalization. The fixed trace mass bounds the total variation of all coefficient measures in finitely many local frames, so weak compactness of finite measures gives compactness of the family of positive currents with this trace. Positivity, the trace normalization and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ pass to weak limits. On this bounded set, testing against smooth forms or against forms with continuous coefficients gives the same topology, by uniform approximation, and this topology is metrizable since the space of continuous test forms is separable. Thus the compactness can also be used sequentially. The defining conditions of $\mathscr G_\omega $ are convex. Its smooth strictly positive members form a convex set, so their closure $\mathscr C_\omega $ is compact and convex as well. Pairing with a fixed smooth $\theta $ is weakly continuous. Its minimum on the closure of the smooth members is therefore their infimum, which proves ( 11.7.2 ). The Lamari criterion shows that ( 11.7.3 ) holds for every smooth strictly positive member, and hence for every member of their weak closure. Conversely, suppose that $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ does not belong to $\mathscr C_\omega $, and separate this point from the compact convex set $\mathscr C_\omega $ in the space of currents with the weak topology. A continuous linear functional for that topology is evaluation against a smooth form. After changing its sign if necessary, we obtain a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ such that \[  \int _ X\beta \wedge T <\min _{R\in \mathscr C_\omega }\int _ X\beta \wedge R =\kappa _\omega (\beta ).  \] By corollary 11.6.2 , the smooth form $\beta -\kappa _\omega (\beta )\omega $ admits a positive current. Its pairing with $T$ is negative, because $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. This contradicts ( 11.7.3 ) and proves the converse. $\square$ Corollary 11.7.4 . A97DA8CE2358 The function $\kappa _\omega $ is concave, positively homogeneous and invariant under the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Let $\theta $ and $\eta $ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms and let $\varepsilon \geq 0$. If $-\varepsilon \omega \leq \theta -\eta \leq \varepsilon \omega $, then \[  |\kappa _\omega (\theta )-\kappa _\omega (\eta )|\leq \varepsilon .  \] If smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$ converge uniformly to a smooth form $\theta $ and $T_ j\in \mathscr C_\omega $ minimize their pairings, every weak cluster point of $(T_ j)$ minimizes the pairing with $\theta $. Proof. By ( 11.7.2 ), $\kappa _\omega $ is an infimum of linear functionals, which proves concavity and positive homogeneity. Invariance under the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ follows from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$. The normalization of the trace gives \[  \left|\int _ X(\theta -\eta )\wedge T\right|\leq \varepsilon \quad (T\in \mathscr C_\omega ),  \] and taking infima proves the estimate. For the last assertion, pass to a subsequence $T_ j\rightharpoonup T\in \mathscr C_\omega $. The estimate and the uniform convergence of the backgrounds give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge T =\lim _ j\int _ X\theta _ j\wedge T_ j =\lim _ j\kappa _\omega (\theta _ j)=\kappa _\omega (\theta ).  \] Thus $T$ is a minimizer. $\square$ In general, the closure $\mathscr C_\omega $ cannot be replaced by all of $\mathscr G_\omega $: the exceptional-curve example in example 10.18.3 separates the two sets by a smooth closed form. Testing against all of $\mathscr G_\omega $ instead detects smooth positivity and nefness, as shown in theorem 12.34.1 .

text: Let $\mathcal T_\omega $ be the smooth strictly positive members of the normalized current cone $\mathscr G_\omega $ of section 11.7 . Thus every $\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge \Theta =1$. These tests form a weakly relatively compact family, but their pairings with a form concentrating transversely to a hypersurface need not stay bounded. A uniform bound would, by duality, produce a potential whose curvature charges the local hypersurface. Analyticity of Lelong level sets then forces a global hypersurface. Choose a product coordinate chart $(z,\zeta )\in U\times \Delta _ r$, with $z\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and a smooth compactly supported $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ on $U$, equal to one on a nonempty connected smaller polydisk $U'$. Put $\sigma _\zeta =(\mathrm i/(2\pi ))\, \mathrm d\zeta \wedge \mathrm d\bar\zeta $. Fix $p\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb C)$, nonnegative and supported in the closed unit disk, with $\int p\, \sigma _\zeta =1$. For small $\delta >0$ extend \[  B_\delta =\chi (z)\delta ^{-2}p(\zeta /\delta )\sigma _\zeta  \] by zero to $X$, and set \[  C_\delta =\sup _{\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega } \int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta .  \] The form $B_\delta $ is smooth and semipositive. For fixed $\delta $ it is bounded above by a finite multiple of $\omega $, so $C_\delta <\infty $. Theorem 11.8.1 . B0762464DCDC If $C_{\delta _ j}$ stays bounded along a sequence $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$, then some global analytic hypersurface contains $U'\times \{ 0\} $. In particular, on a manifold without analytic hypersurfaces, $C_\delta \to \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Proof. Suppose $C_{\delta _ j}\leq M$ and put $\kappa =(M+1)^{-1}$. Normalizing any smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed complementary form gives \[  \int _ X(\omega -\kappa B_{\delta _ j})\wedge \Theta \geq 0.  \] The generalized Lamari criterion, theorem 11.6.1 , supplies $v_ j$ with \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq \kappa B_{\delta _ j},\qquad \sup _ Xv_ j=0.  \] Since $B_{\delta _ j}\geq 0$, the potentials belong to the fixed normalized $\omega $-plurisubharmonic family. By theorem 5.25.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$ to $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The transverse approximate identity converges to $\chi [\zeta =0]$, so passing in distributions gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \kappa \chi [\zeta =0].  \] On a smaller chart meeting the inner hypersurface, add a smooth $\rho $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $. The closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+\rho )$ dominates $\kappa [\zeta =0]$ where $\chi =1$. Hence the Lelong number of $v$ is at least $\kappa $ at every point of $U'\times \{ 0\} $. By Siu's theorem in 5.34.2 , the set $Z=\{ \nu (v,\cdot )\geq \kappa \} $ is analytic and has dimension at most $n-1$. Smooth local corrections do not change its definition. The compact analytic set $Z$ has finitely many global irreducible components. Their intersections with the connected inner hypersurface are analytic subsets covering it. At least one intersection is the whole hypersurface, since finitely many proper analytic subsets cannot cover an open polydisk. That component has dimension $n-1$ and is the required global hypersurface. If no such hypersurface exists, there is no bounded sequence $C_{\delta _ j}$ with $\delta _ j\downarrow 0$, which proves the asserted divergence. $\square$ Proposition 11.8.2 . 26C9605156BE Suppose an effective Cartier divisor agrees, with multiplicity one, with $\{ \zeta =0\} $ throughout the chosen coordinate chart. Then $C_\delta $ is uniformly bounded for all sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Let $s$ be the canonical section of its divisor line bundle. In the chart write $s=\zeta e$ with $e$ a nonvanishing holomorphic frame. Choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ with $|e|_ h=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname {supp}\chi \times \{ |\zeta |\leq \delta _0\} $ for a fixed small $\delta _0>0$. The smooth global functions $\psi _\delta =\log (|s|_ h^2+\delta ^2)$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq -C\omega $ with one $C\geq 1$. Off the divisor their Hessians are a bounded scalar multiple of the negative curvature of $h$, plus a semipositive gradient term; continuity gives the same lower bound at the divisor. Fix $0<\epsilon \leq (2C)^{-1}$, so $\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \omega /2$. On the flat-frame region, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta =\frac{\delta ^2}{(|\zeta |^2+\delta ^2)^2}\sigma _\zeta \geq \frac1{4\delta ^2}\sigma _\zeta \quad (|\zeta |\leq \delta ).  \] If $P=\| p\| _\infty $, then $B_\delta \leq P\delta ^{-2}\sigma _\zeta $ on its support. Therefore \[  \omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}B_\delta  \] globally for $\delta \leq \delta _0$. Every $\Theta \in \mathcal T_\omega $ gives, by smooth Stokes, \[  1=\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta )\wedge \Theta \geq \frac{\epsilon }{4P}\int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta .  \] Taking the supremum proves $C_\delta \leq 4P/\epsilon $. $\square$ The uniform bound requires the divisor to agree on the entire cutoff chart. A global hypersurface supplied by the preceding theorem can have further branches there, so the theorem does not provide this converse at arbitrary intersections. Divergence of the transverse pairing alone also gives no lower bound for the volume of the positive root of a test.

title: 11.9 Convex norms and Gauduchon degrees
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
For holomorphic line bundles, the trace identity of proposition 11.5.1 becomes a statement about curvature. Let $F$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ and $k$ a smooth Hermitian metric on $F$. In a local holomorphic frame $e$ of $F$ we identify $k$ with the positive function $|e|_ k^2$, and the curvature form of $k$ is $R_ k=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log k$. Let $\Theta $ be a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$; by the root calculation preceding the proof of theorem 11.6.1 , $\Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a unique Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. The degree of $F$ with respect to $\Theta $ is \[  \deg _\Theta F=\int _ XR_ k\wedge \Theta .  \] Two metrics on $F$ differ by a factor $\mathrm e^{-u}$ with $u$ smooth, which adds $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ to the curvature, so the degree is independent of $k$ by lemma 11.1.2 . It is the Gauduchon degree of the curvature form with respect to $\gamma $; the form $\Theta $ need not be $\mathrm d$-closed. The squared norm $v\mapsto |v|_ k^2$ is plurisubharmonic on the total space of $F$ off the zero section exactly when $\log k$ is plurisubharmonic, that is, when $R_ k\leq 0$; this follows from the Levi form computation in the proof of lemma 11.11.1 below. A line bundle of positive degree therefore admits no metric with plurisubharmonic squared norm. This section extends the obstruction to direct sums of line bundles of positive degree, to all holomorphic structures sufficiently close to such a direct sum, and to norms that need not be Hermitian. The mechanism is again integration against $\Theta $: averaging the horizontal complex Hessians of a norm near the line summands produces a negative multiple of the degrees, and this negativity is stable under small changes of the holomorphic structure. For a smooth complex vector bundle $F$, a smooth complex norm is a continuous function $p:F	o [0,+\infty )$, positive away from the zero section and smooth there, such that \[  p(\lambda v)=|\lambda |p(v),\qquad p(v+w)\leq p(v)+p(w)  \] for $\lambda \in \mathbb C$ and vectors $v,w$ in the same fiber. Its square $G=p^2$ satisfies $G(\lambda v)=|\lambda |^2G(v)$. Near each line summand of a direct sum, the triangle inequality controls the fiber derivatives of $G$, and these estimates control the averaged horizontal complex Hessians. Lemma 11.9.1 . A592FEE54E20 Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mu $ on $X$. Every holomorphic line bundle $F$ has a Hermitian metric $k$ satisfying \[  R_ k\wedge \Theta =\lambda \mu , \qquad \lambda = rac{\deg _\Theta F}{\int _ X\mu }.  \] Proof. Start with any metric $k^0$, and put $\mathcal Lu=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Theta )/\mu $. This scalar operator is uniformly elliptic, has no zeroth-order term, and its kernel consists of the constants by the maximum principle. On Hölder spaces, the homotopy to a Laplace operator used in the proof of theorem 11.4.2 shows that its index is zero, so its cokernel is one-dimensional. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0$, integration by parts gives $\int _ X\mathcal Lu\, \mu =0$, and therefore its image consists exactly of the smooth functions of zero $\mu $-mean. Hence we can solve \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \Theta =\lambda \mu -R_{k^0}\wedge \Theta ,  \] whose right-hand side has integral zero, and elliptic regularity makes $u$ smooth. Then $k=k^0\mathrm e^{-u}$ has the required curvature. $\square$ Let $F_0= igoplus _{s=1}^ rF_ s$ be a direct sum of holomorphic line bundles, with $r\geq 2$. Choose Hermitian metrics $k_ s$ on $F_ s$ and write $k= igoplus _ sk_ s$. Let $P_ s$ be the orthogonal projection onto $F_ s$, and let \[  \Sigma =\{ v\in F_0:|v|_ k=1\}   \] be the unit sphere bundle, with fibers $\Sigma _ x$. On each fiber sphere $\Sigma _ x$ we use the rotation-invariant probability measure $\mathrm d\sigma _ x$. Fix a nonnegative smooth function $\chi $ supported in $(-1,1)$ and positive near zero. For $0<\varepsilon <1/2$, define weights $ho _ s$ on $\Sigma $ by \[  ho _ s(v)=c_\varepsilon \chi \left( rac{|(I-P_ s)v|_ k^2}{\varepsilon ^2}ight), \qquad \int _{\Sigma _ x}ho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x=1.  \] In unitary frames respecting the splitting, these weights and the normalizing constant $c_\varepsilon $ are independent of the base point and of the index $s$. Independent phase rotations of the summands preserve them, so they are globally defined. The support of $ho _ s$ lies within distance $\varepsilon $ of the unit circle of $F_ s$. Lemma 11.9.2 . FD645EB1208B For a smooth complex norm on $F_0$ with square $G$, put \[  a_ s(x)=G(e_ s),\qquad N(x)=\sum _ sa_ s(x),\qquad D_ jG(v)=\mathrm d_ vG(P_ jv),  \] where $e_ s$ is any $k_ s$-unit vector in the fiber of $F_ s$ at $x$; complex homogeneity makes $a_ s$ well defined. Then \[  G(v)\leq N|v|_ k^2,\qquad |\mathrm d_ vG(w)|\leq 2N|v|_ k|w|_ k.  \] On the support of $ho _ s$, \[  |D_ jG|\leq 2\varepsilon N\quad (j
e s),\qquad |D_ sG-2a_ s|\leq 10\varepsilon N.  \] Proof. The triangle inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give $p(v)\leq \sum _ s|v_ s|_ k\sqrt{a_ s}\leq \sqrt N|v|_ k$. Differentiating $|p(v+tw)-p(v)|\leq |t|p(w)$ in the real variable $t$ gives $|\mathrm d_ vp(w)|\leq p(w)$, and both global bounds follow. For $v$ in the support of $ho _ s$, set $w=(I-P_ s)v$ and $e_ s=P_ sv/|P_ sv|_ k$. Then $|w|_ k<\varepsilon $ and $|v-e_ s|_ k\leq |w|_ k+1-|P_ sv|_ k<2\varepsilon $. The segment from $e_ s$ to $v$ stays in the unit ball and avoids zero, so integrating the derivative bound along it gives $|G(v)-a_ s|\leq 4\varepsilon N$. For $j
e s$, we have $|P_ jv|_ k<\varepsilon $, which gives the first axis bound. Euler's identity $\mathrm d_ vG(v)=2G(v)$ yields \[  D_ sG-2a_ s=2(G(v)-a_ s)-\sum _{j
e s}D_ jG.  \] The sum on the right is $\mathrm d_ vG(w)$, whose absolute value is at most $2\varepsilon N$. This proves the second axis bound. $\square$ Write $\pi :F_0	o X$ for the bundle projection. For $v\in F_0$ with $\pi (v)=x$, let $H_{0,v}:T_ xX	o T_ vF_0$ be the horizontal lift for the Chern connection of $k$. It is complex linear, and at unit vectors it is tangent to $\Sigma $, since the Chern connection preserves $k$. For a smooth real function $G$ on $F_0\setminus \{ 0\} $, define a $(1,1)$-form $ eta _ s(G)$ and functions $U_ s$, $V_{sj}$ on $X$ by \[   egin{aligned}   eta _ s(G)& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}ho _ s H_{0,v}^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G)\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x,\  U_ s& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}Gho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x,\  V_{sj}& =\int _{\Sigma _ x}D_ jGho _ s\, \mathrm d\sigma _ x. \end{aligned}  \] Lemma 11.9.3 . EE774D339C2C With $R_ j$ the curvature of $k_ j$, \[   eta _ s(G)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ s- rac12\sum _ jR_ jV_{sj}.  \] Proof. At a fixed base point, choose holomorphic frames of the line bundles with $k_ j=\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}$ and $\mathrm d\varphi _ j=0$ at that point. There the horizontal lift has zero vertical component. Write the smooth unitary fiber coordinates as $\zeta _ j=\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j/2}v_ j$ and $G(z,v)=g(z,\zeta )$. At the base point, the first base derivatives of $\zeta _ j$ vanish, and its mixed second base derivatives are $- rac12(\varphi _ j)_{\alpha  ar eta }\zeta _ j$ and their conjugates. The chain rule therefore gives \[  G_{\alpha  ar eta } =g_{\alpha  ar eta }- rac12\sum _ j(\varphi _ j)_{\alpha  ar eta } (\zeta _ jg_{\zeta _ j}+ ar\zeta _ jg_{ ar\zeta _ j}).  \] The expression in parentheses is $D_ jG$. Both the spherical measure and $ho _ s$ are independent of $z$ in unitary coordinates, so averaging the identity gives the result, since $R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$. $\square$ Theorem 11.9.4 . C222D1BB3C65 Suppose that for each $s$ there is a smooth strictly positive real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Theta _ s$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta _ s=0,\qquad \deg _{\Theta _ s}F_ s>0.  \] Then there is a $C^4$ neighborhood of the split Dolbeault operator on the underlying smooth bundle of $F_0$ such that no integrable Dolbeault operator in this neighborhood admits a smooth complex norm whose square is plurisubharmonic off the zero section. Proof. Step 1: the split structure. Fix $\mu $ and use lemma 11.9.1 to choose $k_ s$ with $R_ s\wedge \Theta _ s=\lambda _ s\mu $, where $\lambda _ s>0$. Put \[  \lambda _* =\min _ s\lambda _ s,\qquad C=5\sum _ s\lambda _ s+ \sum _ s\sum _{j
e s}\sup _ X\left| rac{R_ j\wedge \Theta _ s}{\mu }ight|.  \] For a squared norm $G$, define $I_0(G)=\sum _ s\int _ X eta _ s(G)\wedge \Theta _ s$. By lemma 11.9.3 , the term $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ s$ integrates to zero against $\Theta _ s$, and the axis estimates of lemma 11.9.2 then give \[  I_0(G)=- rac12\sum _{s,j}\int _ XV_{sj}R_ j\wedge \Theta _ s \leq -(\lambda _* -\varepsilon C)\int _ XN\mu .  \] Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $\varepsilon C<\lambda _*/2$, and keep all weights fixed. Step 2: nearby holomorphic structures. Write a nearby operator as $ ar\partial _ A= ar\partial _0+A$, with $ ar\partial _ A^2=0$. Its Chern connection for $k$ is $D_ A=D_0+A-A^{*k}$, where the adjoint changes the type from $(0,1)$ to $(1,0)$. Let $J_ A$ be the corresponding complex structure on the total space and $H_{A,v}$ the horizontal lift of $D_ A$. These depend smoothly on $A$, and $H_{A,v}$ is complex linear and tangent to the fixed sphere bundle $\Sigma $. For $g\in C^\infty (\Sigma ,\mathbb R)$, define its homogeneous extension by \[  (\mathcal Eg)(v)=|v|_ k^2g(v/|v|_ k),  \] and define a real differential operator on $\Sigma $ by \[  (\mathcal P_ Ag)(v)=\sum _ sho _ s(v)  rac{H_{A,v}^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_{J_ A}\mathcal Eg)_ v\wedge \Theta _ s(x)}{\mu (x)}, \qquad x=\pi (v).  \] It has order at most two. By the identity $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_ Jf=-(4\pi )^{-1}\mathrm df\circ J$, its coefficients depend on $A$ and its first derivatives, as well as on the fixed smooth data. Consequently they converge in $C^2$ as $A	o 0$ in $C^4$. Step 3: the adjoint operator. Take the formal adjoint $\mathcal P_ A^*$ for the fixed density $\mathrm d
u =\mathrm d\sigma _ x\, \mu (x)$ on the compact sphere bundle, and put $b_ A=\mathcal P_ A^*1$. Locally, if $\mathrm d
u =m(y)\, \mathrm dy$ and $\mathcal P_ A=\sum _{|\alpha |\leq 2}c_{\alpha ,A}\partial ^\alpha $, then \[  b_ A=m^{-1}\sum _{|\alpha |\leq 2}(-1)^{|\alpha |} \partial ^\alpha (mc_{\alpha ,A}).  \] Thus $\| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}	o 0$ as $A	o 0$ in $C^4$. For $g=G|_\Sigma $, homogeneity gives $\mathcal Eg=G$ and \[  I_ A(G):=\int _\Sigma \mathcal P_ Ag\, \mathrm d
u =\int _\Sigma gb_ A\, \mathrm d
u .  \] Since $0<g\leq N\circ \pi $ and the spherical measures have mass one, \[  |I_ A(G)-I_0(G)| \leq \| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}\int _ XN\mu .  \] Choose the neighborhood so that $\| b_ A-b_0\| _{C^0}<\lambda _*/4$ in it. Then $I_ A(G)\leq - rac14\lambda _*\int _ XN\mu <0$ for every smooth squared complex norm $G$. If $G$ were plurisubharmonic for $J_ A$, all horizontal pullbacks of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_{J_ A}G$ would be semipositive, and their pairings with $\Theta _ s$, weighted by $ho _ s\geq 0$, would give $I_ A(G)\geq 0$, a contradiction. $\square$ The neighborhood depends on the bundle and on the test forms $\Theta _ s$, and different line summands may require different tests. Its size is independent of all derivatives of the candidate norms: integration over the fixed sphere bundle transfers those derivatives to the coefficients of the adjoint operator. To apply theorem 11.9.4 to norms obtained by duality, we first need to regularize continuous norms while preserving a strict convexity margin. Polar duality then turns the obstruction into a failure of semipositive Kobayashi curvature on the dual bundle. Stable ample bundles on Hirzebruch surfaces provide concrete examples, and a fixed Stein hypersurface detects the failure for every Finsler metric on such a bundle. Dual support norms also connect this obstruction with the geometry of neighborhoods of the zero section. This leads to bounds for the convexity of a projective complement. Curvature supplies a second way to study these complements, through explicit exhaustions. A uniformly negative bundle over a Kähler base with a proper psh exhaustion instead gives logarithmic weights and a complete metric on its punctured total space ( 11.19 ). The distinction between these spaces matters: the final flat and Hopf examples use restrictions and topology to obtain further bounds for the projective complement.

title: 11.10 Homogeneous convex regularization
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 11.9.4 concerns smooth norms, whereas the norms produced by duality later in this section are in general only continuous. We show that a continuous homogeneous function with strict positivity margins can be approximated by smooth ones with the same margins, so the obstruction applies to it as well. The local step is Wu's convolution in projective coordinates, written as an average of holomorphic linear shears; the local approximations are glued by the argument of Greene and Wu. We give both steps in order to keep track of strict plurisubharmonicity and of strong convexity in the fibers; see section 25.5 for attribution. Let $\pi :F\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle, and write $F^\times $ for the complement of its zero section. A continuous real function $Q$ on $F$ is complex homogeneous of degree two if \[  Q(\lambda v)=|\lambda |^2Q(v)\qquad (\lambda \in \mathbb C).  \] We call $Q$ locally strongly convex in the fibers if, in a local bundle frame and near every point of $F^\times $, there is a constant $c>0$ such that $Q(z,v)-c|v|^2$ is convex on sufficiently small real fiber balls. For continuous functions, strict plurisubharmonicity means that subtracting a sufficiently small positive multiple of the Euclidean squared norm in local coordinates of the total space leaves a plurisubharmonic function. Both conditions are local, and on compact subsets of $F^\times $ they hold with uniform positive margins. The strong convexity required here holds with one constant on a neighborhood in the total space. Strong convexity of every fixed fiber is weaker, even for a plurisubharmonic squared complex norm. Example 11.10.1 . 196112D1B85A On the trivial bundle $D\times \mathbb C^2$, where $D=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z|<1/2\} $, put \[  Q(z,v)=\max \left\{  |v_1|^2+|v_2|^2, \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 \right\} .  \] This is a continuous plurisubharmonic function, positive off the zero section and complex homogeneous of degree two. Its square root is a complex norm on every fiber, and for each fixed $z$, the real function $Q(z,\cdot )$ is strongly convex. Nevertheless, $Q$ is not locally strongly convex in the fibers near $(z,v)=(0,(1,0))$ in the sense defined above. Proof. Write $t=|z|^2$. Both branches are continuous, positive semidefinite Hermitian quadratic forms in $v$, and the first is positive definite. Their square roots satisfy the triangle inequality and complex homogeneity; their maximum therefore is a complex norm. In particular $Q$ is positive off zero and continuous, also on the zero section. The first branch is plurisubharmonic on the total space. For the second, the locally uniformly convergent expansion \[  \frac{|v_1|^2}{1-|z|^2}+|z|^2|v_2|^2 =\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }|z^ kv_1|^2+|zv_2|^2  \] expresses it as a limit of sums of squared moduli of holomorphic functions. Thus it too is plurisubharmonic, and so is their maximum. For $0<t<1/4$, subtracting $t|v|^2$ gives \[  Q(z,v)-t|v|^2 =\max \left\{ (1-t)|v|^2, \left(\frac1{1-t}-t\right)|v_1|^2\right\} ,  \] which is convex. At $z=0$, one has $Q(0,v)=|v|^2$. Hence each fixed fiber has a positive strong convexity margin. To test a margin on a neighborhood of $(0,(1,0))$, fix any $c>0$ and choose a nonzero $z$ arbitrarily close to zero with $t<c$. At $v=(1,0)$ the second branch is strictly larger than the first, so it remains the maximum on a small fiber ball. Along the real line $v=(1,s)$ in this ball, \[  Q(z,(1,s))-c|(1,s)|^2 =\frac1{1-t}-c+(t-c)s^2.  \] Its second derivative is negative. Thus no positive $c$ makes $Q-c|v|^2$ convex on the fiber balls in any such total-space neighborhood. A fiber-linear change of smooth frame and its inverse are uniformly bounded on a smaller base neighborhood, so a positive quadratic margin in another frame would give one in this frame. This proves the failure of the local margin. $\square$ Lemma 11.10.2 . A2189A9C7D5A Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold and let $\mathcal S$ be a sheaf of germs of continuous real functions on $M$, whose elements we call sections. Suppose that $\mathcal S$ is closed under maxima and has the following two properties. Stability: if $f$ is a section near a compact set $K$, then $f+u$ is a section near $K$ whenever $u$ is smooth and sufficiently small in the $C^\infty $ topology on a neighborhood of $K$. Local approximation: every point has a neighborhood $U$ such that, for every compact $K\Subset U$, a section near $K$ can be approximated uniformly on $K$ by smooth sections near $K$, with arbitrarily small errors in any prescribed finite collection of derivative norms on compact subsets where the section is already smooth. Then every global section can be approximated uniformly on $M$ by smooth global sections. Proof. We first describe a gluing step. Let $f$ be a global section that is smooth near a compact set $L_1$, and let $L_2$ be a compact subset of one of the neighborhoods $U$ in the statement. Choose relatively compact open sets $W_3,W_4$ with $L_1\subset W_3$, $f$ smooth near $\overline W_3$, and $L_2\subset W_4\Subset U$. Choose a smooth function $0\leq \rho \leq 1$ equal to one near $\overline W_3$, with compact support in the region where $f$ is smooth. Put $V=W_3\cup W_4$, and choose a smooth function $-1\leq \psi \leq 1$ equal to one near $L_1\cup L_2$ and equal to minus one near $M\setminus V$. By stability, for sufficiently small $\xi >0$ the function $f_\xi =f+\xi \psi $ is still a global section. Approximate $f_\xi $ on $\overline W_4$ by a smooth section $g$, with uniform error less than $\delta <\xi /2$, and with arbitrarily small derivative errors near the compact set $\overline W_4\cap \operatorname {supp}\rho $, where $f_\xi $ is smooth. On $V$ define \[  h=f_\xi \quad \hbox{on }W_3,\qquad h=\rho f_\xi +(1-\rho )g\quad \hbox{on }W_4.  \] These definitions agree on the overlap, and $h$ is smooth. Where $\rho $ vanishes, $h$ is the section $g$. Where $\rho $ can be nonzero, $h-f_\xi =(1-\rho )(g-f_\xi )$, and stability applied to the smooth section $f_\xi $ makes $h$ a section if the derivative errors of $g-f_\xi $ are sufficiently small. Moreover, $|h-f_\xi |<\delta $. Define $f_1=\max \{ f,h\} $ on $V$ and $f_1=f$ outside $V$. Near $L_1\cup L_2$ we have $h>f$, and near the boundary of $V$ we have $h<f$. Thus $f_1$ is continuous, it is a section because $\mathcal S$ is closed under maxima, and it is smooth near $L_1\cup L_2$. Also $\| f_1-f\| _{C^0}<\xi +\delta $. Near $L_1$ it equals $f+\xi $, so the previous smoothness is preserved. Now cover $M$ by finitely many compact sets $L_2$ of this kind and repeat the step, starting with $L_1$ empty and then taking for $L_1$ the union of the previously treated compact sets. At every step choose $\xi $ and $\delta $ so small that the sum of the finitely many uniform errors is below the prescribed tolerance. The final section is smooth everywhere and has the required uniform error. $\square$ Lemma 11.10.3 . 047ADFD98AAF In a holomorphic bundle chart, write $v=(v',v_ r)$ and use the affine projective coordinate $w=v'/v_ r$ on the cone $v_ r\ne 0$. Suppose that a positive continuous complex homogeneous function $Q$ of degree two is strictly plurisubharmonic and locally strongly convex in the fibers on this cone, and put $q(z,w)=Q(z,(w,1))$. For a nonnegative smooth approximate identity $\eta _\delta (s,t)$ of integral one, define \[  q_\delta (z,w)=\int q(z-s,w-t)\eta _\delta (s,t)\, \mathrm ds\, \mathrm dt, \qquad Q_\delta (z,v)=|v_ r|^2q_\delta (z,v'/v_ r).  \] On every relatively compact projective subchart, for sufficiently small $\delta $, $Q_\delta $ is a smooth positive complex homogeneous function of degree two that is strictly plurisubharmonic and locally strongly convex in the fibers. As $\delta \to 0$, it converges to $Q$ uniformly on compact subsets of the cone consisting of vectors of norm one, and in every finite derivative norm wherever $Q$ is already smooth. Proof. Complex homogeneity gives the identity \[  Q_\delta (z,v) =\int Q(z-s,T_ tv)\eta _\delta (s,t)\, \mathrm ds\, \mathrm dt, \qquad T_ t(v',v_ r)=(v'-v_ rt,v_ r).  \] For fixed $(s,t)$, the map $(z,v)\mapsto (z-s,T_ tv)$ is holomorphic and invertible, and its restriction to each fiber is linear. On a compact subset of the cone consisting of vectors of norm one, all these maps with $(s,t)$ sufficiently small stay in a fixed compact subset of the original cone, and their differentials and inverses are uniformly bounded there. A positive local lower bound for the Levi form of $Q$, interpreted through quadratic barriers, therefore gives a positive lower bound for every pullback and for their average. The same argument with real quadratic barriers in the fibers preserves local strong convexity. Only fiber segments contained in the local cone neighborhood are used here. Ordinary convolution makes $q_\delta $ smooth, and the formula for $Q_\delta $ makes it smooth on the cone and complex homogeneous. Uniform convergence, derivative convergence on compact regions where $Q$ is smooth, and positivity for small $\delta $ follow from the corresponding properties of convolution and from the positive minimum of $Q$ on compact sets of vectors of norm one. $\square$ Theorem 11.10.4 . 3FA7CB52F1E5 Let $Q:F\to [0,+\infty )$ be continuous, positive on $F^\times $, complex homogeneous of degree two, strictly plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $, and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Then there are continuous complex homogeneous functions $Q_ j$ of degree two, smooth on $F^\times $, strictly plurisubharmonic there and locally strongly convex in the fibers, which converge to $Q$ uniformly on the unit sphere bundle of any fixed smooth Hermitian metric. Each $p_ j=\sqrt{Q_ j}$ is a smooth complex norm. Proof. Fix a smooth Hermitian squared norm $G$ on $F$, and let $M=\mathbb P(F)$ be the bundle of complex lines in $F$. The quotient $m=Q/G$ is a positive continuous function on the compact manifold $M$. Define a sheaf $\mathcal S$ on $M$ by requiring that the corresponding function $Gm$ on the cone be positive, strictly plurisubharmonic, and locally strongly convex in the fibers. This sheaf is closed under maxima. Indeed, multiplication by $G>0$ commutes with maxima. Near a point of the cone, subtract a common positive quadratic barrier from both functions; their maximum remains plurisubharmonic, and on sufficiently small fiber balls it remains convex. Positivity is also preserved. For stability on a compact subset $K$ of $M$, restrict to vectors of norm one lying over $K$, and to a fixed compact annulus around them. Finitely many bundle charts provide positive common lower bounds for both barriers. If $u$ is a smooth function on $M$ that is sufficiently small in $C^2$ near $K$, the Levi form and the real fiber Hessian of $Gu$ are smaller than half these bounds on that annulus. The perturbed function is therefore still positive and has both strict margins. Homogeneity transports the local conditions to the rest of the cone over $K$. This proves the stability required in lemma 11.10.2 . On a sufficiently small projective coordinate chart, lemma 11.10.3 gives local approximation, including derivative control on compact subsets where $m$ is smooth; dividing its regularizations by $G$ gives local smooth sections of $\mathcal S$. By lemma 11.10.2 , there are smooth positive global sections $m_ j\to m$ uniformly. Put $Q_ j=Gm_ j$ off the zero section and $Q_ j=0$ on the zero section. Homogeneity gives continuity at zero, uniformly over the compact base, as well as the asserted convergence on a fixed unit sphere bundle. It remains to see that $p_ j$ is a norm. Local convexity in the fibers away from zero implies convexity on the whole fiber. Indeed, the restriction of $Q_ j$ to a real line avoiding zero is locally convex and hence convex, while on a real line through zero, homogeneity gives $Q_ j(tv)=t^2Q_ j(v)$ for real $t$, which is convex including at zero. Thus the set $B_ x=\{ v:Q_ j(v)\leq 1\} $ is convex, balanced and absorbing, and its gauge is $\sqrt{Q_ j}$. If $v,w$ are nonzero, convexity applied to $v/p_ j(v)$ and $w/p_ j(w)$, with weights proportional to $p_ j(v)$ and $p_ j(w)$, gives the triangle inequality; the cases with a zero vector follow directly. Positivity, smoothness off zero and complex homogeneity give the remaining properties of a smooth complex norm. $\square$ Proposition 11.10.5 . 1263BBAE3998 Suppose that $F$ admits a smooth positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two that is strictly plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $. If a positive continuous complex homogeneous function $Q$ of degree two is plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $ and locally strongly convex in the fibers, then $F$ admits a smooth complex norm with strictly plurisubharmonic square on $F^\times $. Proof. For $\tau >0$, set $Q_\tau =Q+\tau H$; it is positive, complex homogeneous and strictly plurisubharmonic. On a compact annulus of vectors of norm close to one, local strong convexity of $Q$ in the fibers gives a positive uniform margin in finitely many frames, while the real fiber Hessian of $H$ is uniformly bounded there. Choose $\tau $ so small that the possible negative part of $\tau $ times this Hessian consumes less than half the margin. Homogeneity then gives local strong convexity of $Q_\tau $ in the fibers everywhere off zero. Apply theorem 11.10.4 to $Q_\tau $ and take one of its smooth regularizations; its square root is the required smooth complex norm. $\square$ Corollary 11.10.6 . F8EB48E98C63 For every holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 11.9.4 , there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is both strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. If that structure admits a function $H$ as in proposition 11.10.5 , there is also no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. For the first assertion, theorem 11.10.4 would produce a smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, contrary to theorem 11.9.4 . For the second, use proposition 11.10.5 and the same obstruction. $\square$ The second assertion requires the strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function $H$, which need not exist for an arbitrary holomorphic bundle; 11.11 shows that it exists when the dual bundle is ample. Without a strong convexity margin in the fibers, the regularization gives no obstruction for continuous fiber norms.

title: Proposition 11.10.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 11.10.5 . 1263BBAE3998 Suppose that $F$ admits a smooth positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two that is strictly plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $. If a positive continuous complex homogeneous function $Q$ of degree two is plurisubharmonic on $F^\times $ and locally strongly convex in the fibers, then $F$ admits a smooth complex norm with strictly plurisubharmonic square on $F^\times $. Proof. For $\tau >0$, set $Q_\tau =Q+\tau H$; it is positive, complex homogeneous and strictly plurisubharmonic. On a compact annulus of vectors of norm close to one, local strong convexity of $Q$ in the fibers gives a positive uniform margin in finitely many frames, while the real fiber Hessian of $H$ is uniformly bounded there. Choose $\tau $ so small that the possible negative part of $\tau $ times this Hessian consumes less than half the margin. Homogeneity then gives local strong convexity of $Q_\tau $ in the fibers everywhere off zero. Apply theorem 11.10.4 to $Q_\tau $ and take one of its smooth regularizations; its square root is the required smooth complex norm. $\square$

title: Corollary 11.10.6
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 11.10.6 . F8EB48E98C63 For every holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 11.9.4 , there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is both strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. If that structure admits a function $H$ as in proposition 11.10.5 , there is also no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. For the first assertion, theorem 11.10.4 would produce a smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, contrary to theorem 11.9.4 . For the second, use proposition 11.10.5 and the same obstruction. $\square$

The second part of corollary 11.10.6 requires a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function on $F^	imes $ that is complex homogeneous of degree two. Such a function is the squared norm of a vector, viewed as a point of the tautological line it spans, for a suitable metric on the tautological line bundle. Its Levi form is strictly positive exactly when the dual tautological metric is positively curved, so the function exists when $F^*$ is ample. Let $F	o X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank. In this subsection, $\mathbb P(F)$ parametrizes complex lines in $F$, $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)$ is the tautological line bundle whose fiber over a line is that line, and \[  L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(1) =\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)^*.  \] The map $v\mapsto ([v],v)$ identifies $F^	imes $ holomorphically with the complement of the zero section in $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)$. We use the curvature convention $R_ h=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h$ of section 11.9 . Lemma 11.11.1 . 40D29F4EF95B A smooth Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ determines a positive smooth complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two on $F^	imes $: the squared norm of $v$ in the dual metric on the tautological line $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P(F)}(-1)_{[v]}$. The function $H$ is strictly plurisubharmonic if and only if $R_ h$ is strictly positive on $\mathbb P(F)$. Proof. Take local holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $\mathbb P(F)$ and a holomorphic frame $e$ of the tautological line bundle, and write the metric of the dual frame as $h=\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$. The dual metric gives \[  H(y,\lambda e)=|\lambda |^2\mathrm e^{\varphi (y)},\qquad R_ h=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] Let $\mathcal L$ denote the complex Hessian, without the factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$ of the curvature normalization. Differentiating at a point with $\lambda 
e 0$ gives \[  \mathcal L H(u,t) =H\left(\mathcal L\varphi (u)+ \left| rac{t}{\lambda }+\partial \varphi (u)ight|^2ight), \qquad (u,t)\in T_ y^{1,0}\mathbb P(F)\oplus \mathbb C.  \] If $\mathcal L\varphi $ is positive definite, the right-hand side is positive for every nonzero $(u,t)$: the first term detects $u
e 0$, and the second detects $t
e 0$ when $u=0$. Conversely, for $u
e 0$, set $t=-\lambda \partial \varphi (u)$; strict positivity of $\mathcal L H$ then forces $\mathcal L\varphi (u)>0$. This is exactly positivity of $R_ h$. The squared tautological norm is independent of the chosen frame and is complex homogeneous, so the local functions define the asserted global function $H$. $\square$ A line bundle is very ample when its complete linear system defines a holomorphic embedding, and ample when some positive tensor power is very ample. With the convention above, a vector bundle $F^*$ is called ample when $L$ is ample. Proposition 11.11.2 . 68260DAF47D2 If $F^*$ is ample, there is a positive complex homogeneous function $H$ of degree two on $F^	imes $ that is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic there and, after extension by zero, continuous on $F$. Proof. Choose $m\geq 1$ such that $L^ m$ is very ample. Its complete linear system gives an embedding $\iota :\mathbb P(F)	o \mathbb P^ N$ with $L^ m=\iota ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$. Pull back the Fubini–Study metric to a metric $k$ on $L^ m$, and take its positive $m$th root $h$ on $L$: in a local frame $h=k^{1/m}$, and the transformation law for $L^ m$ makes these local roots a metric on $L$. Its curvature is \[  R_ h= rac1m\iota ^*\omega _{m FS}>0,  \] because the differential of the embedding is injective. Apply lemma 11.11.1 . Since the base is compact, the resulting $H$ is bounded on the unit sphere bundle of a fixed Hermitian metric. Homogeneity then gives $0<H(v)\leq C|v|^2$ off zero, which proves continuity of the extension by zero. $\square$ Corollary 11.11.3 . EB345AEE34BC Let $F$ carry a holomorphic structure in the neighborhood of theorem 11.9.4 . If $F^*$ is ample, there is no positive continuous complex homogeneous function of degree two on $F$ that is plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the fibers. Proof. By proposition 11.11.2 , ampleness of $F^*$ gives the function $H$ required in proposition 11.10.5 . title: 11.12 Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics
