section: 11.12 Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics
text: For a holomorphic vector bundle that is not assumed to carry a positively curved Hermitian metric, positivity can be measured by Finsler metrics and their Kobayashi curvature. Polar duality converts a Finsler metric on $E$ with semipositive Kobayashi curvature into a continuous norm on $E^*$ whose square is plurisubharmonic and uniformly convex in the fibers. With the regularization of 11.10 , theorem 11.9.4 therefore excludes such Finsler metrics on an ample bundle whose dual is close to a split bundle with positive Gauduchon degrees. Let $E\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank; in this subsection $n\geq 1$. Write $E^\times $ for the complement of its zero section. A squared Finsler metric on $E$ is a positive smooth function $G$ on $E^\times $ with \[  G(x,tv)=|t|^2G(x,v),\qquad t\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} ,  \] extended continuously by zero to the zero section. It is strongly pseudoconvex if its vertical complex Hessian $(G_{i\bar j})$ is positive definite; this does not require convexity in the real fiber variables. In local holomorphic base and fiber coordinates $(z,v)$, with Greek indices for base coordinates, Latin indices for fiber coordinates and summation over repeated indices, put \[  \begin{gathered} S_{\alpha \bar\beta } =G_{\alpha \bar\beta } -G_{\alpha \bar j}G^{\bar j i}G_{i\bar\beta },\\ \mathcal K_ G=-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi G} S_{\alpha \bar\beta }\, \mathrm dz^\alpha \wedge \mathrm d\bar z^\beta , \end{gathered}  \] where $(G^{\bar j i})$ is the inverse of the vertical Hessian. We use this convention for the Kobayashi curvature $\mathcal K_ G$, a horizontal $(1,1)$-form at each point of $E^\times $. Thus $\mathcal K_ G\geq 0$ means $S\leq 0$, and $\mathcal K_ G>0$ means that $S$ is negative definite. Lemma 11.12.1 . 82E28EBCB904 Let $G$ be a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric. If $\mathcal K_ G>0$, then for every $v_0\in E_{x_0}^\times $ there is a local holomorphic section $\sigma $ with $\sigma (x_0)=v_0$ and \[  G(z,\sigma (z))\leq G(x_0,v_0)  \] near $x_0$. Moreover, without any curvature assumption, on a coordinate ball, for $\varphi =|z|^2$ and $\varepsilon >0$, the metric $G_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }G$ is strongly pseudoconvex and satisfies \[  \mathcal K_{G_\varepsilon }=\mathcal K_ G+\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] Proof. Since the vertical Hessian is positive, the Levi-orthogonal complement $H_{G,v}$ of the vertical tangent space at $v$ projects isomorphically onto the base tangent space. The Levi form of $G$ on $H_{G,v}$ is the Schur complement $S$, which is negative definite when $\mathcal K_ G>0$. For the vertical radial vector $R=v_ i\partial _{v_ i}$, complex homogeneity gives \[  \partial G(R)=G,\qquad \mathcal L_ G(a,\bar R)=\partial G(a)  \] for every tangent vector $a$, where $\mathcal L_ G$ is the Levi form. Since $R$ is vertical, the second identity implies $\partial G|_{H_{G,v}}=0$. Choose a holomorphic section $\sigma _0$ through $v_0$ whose tangent space at $x_0$ is $H_{G,v_0}$. In coordinates centered at $x_0$, the function $G\circ \sigma _0$ has zero first derivative and Taylor expansion \[  G(x_0,v_0)+P(z)+\overline{P(z)} +S_{\alpha \bar\beta }z^\alpha \bar z^\beta +O(|z|^3),  \] where $P$ is a homogeneous holomorphic quadratic polynomial. The identity $\partial _ vG(v_0)(v_0)=G(v_0)>0$ gives a vertical vector $b$ with $\partial _ vG(v_0)(b)=1$. Set $\sigma =\sigma _0-bP$ in the local frame. This changes only the pure quadratic terms and cancels $P+\bar P$. The remaining quadratic form is negative definite, and therefore dominates the cubic remainder on a sufficiently small ball. The section stays nonzero there and satisfies the asserted inequality. For the last assertion, differentiate $\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }G$ in the Schur complement. Euler's identities give $G_{\bar j}=v_ iG_{i\bar j}$ and $G_\alpha =G_{\alpha \bar j}\bar v_ j$. Hence the terms containing $\partial \varphi $, including its square, cancel between the base Hessian and the mixed block product, leaving \[  S(G_\varepsilon )=\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi } \bigl (S(G)-\varepsilon G(\varphi _{\alpha \bar\beta })\bigr ).  \] Dividing by $G_\varepsilon $ gives the curvature formula. The vertical Hessian of $G_\varepsilon $ is the positive multiple $\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon \varphi }(G_{i\bar j})$, so $G_\varepsilon $ is again strongly pseudoconvex. $\square$ Proposition 11.12.2 . 672C05CD55F8 Let $G$ be a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with $\mathcal K_ G\geq 0$. Its polar square \[  Q(x,\xi )=\max _{[v]\in \mathbb P(E_ x)} \frac{|\xi (v)|^2}{G(x,v)},\qquad \xi \in E_ x^*,  \] is continuous and plurisubharmonic on the total space of $E^*$, positive off the zero section and complex homogeneous of degree two. The function $\log Q$ is plurisubharmonic off the zero section, and $\sqrt Q$ is a complex norm on each fiber. Proof. The ratio is invariant under complex rescaling of $v$, so the maximum can be taken over the compact unit sphere in a local frame, which proves continuity. Positive upper and lower bounds for $G$ on that sphere compare $Q$ with a Hermitian squared dual norm; this gives positivity off zero and continuity at zero, and complex homogeneity is clear. Moreover, \[  \sqrt{Q(x,\xi )}=\sup _{v\ne 0}\frac{|\xi (v)|}{\sqrt{G(x,v)}}.  \] Each term satisfies the triangle inequality in $\xi $, and so does their supremum. On a coordinate ball, set $G_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{-\varepsilon |z|^2}G$. By lemma 11.12.1 , its Kobayashi curvature is strictly positive, and its polar square is $Q_\varepsilon =\mathrm e^{\varepsilon |z|^2}Q$. At a point $(x_0,\xi _0)$ with $\xi _0\ne 0$, choose a maximizing line and a vector $v_0$ on it. The lemma, applied to $G_\varepsilon $, gives a holomorphic section $\sigma $ such that \[  \log Q_\varepsilon (z,\xi ) \geq \log |\xi (\sigma (z))|^2-\log G_\varepsilon (x_0,v_0),  \] with equality at $(x_0,\xi _0)$. The pairing $\xi (\sigma (z))$ is nonzero near that point, so the right-hand side is pluriharmonic there. Restriction to sufficiently small holomorphic disks centered at the point therefore gives the submean inequality for $\log Q_\varepsilon $. This argument applies at every point off the zero section, and together with continuity it shows that $\log Q_\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic there. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $\log Q_\varepsilon =\log Q+\varepsilon |z|^2$ converge locally uniformly off the zero section. Passing to the limit in the submean inequalities on disks proves that $\log Q$ is plurisubharmonic off the zero section. Since the exponential is increasing and convex, Jensen's inequality shows that $Q=\exp (\log Q)$ is plurisubharmonic there. At a point of the zero section, $Q=0$ and $Q\geq 0$, so every centered disk satisfies the submean inequality there. Together with continuity and the submean inequalities at nonzero points, this proves plurisubharmonicity on the whole total space of $E^*$. $\square$ Lemma 11.12.3 . BD7ECB0F942E Let $k$ be a smooth Hermitian metric on $E$, and let $G$ be a positive smooth complex homogeneous function of degree two on $E^\times $, extended by zero. Then its polar square $Q$, defined as in proposition 11.12.2 , has a constant $c>0$ such that \[  Q(x,\xi )-c|\xi |_{k^*}^2  \] is real convex on every dual fiber. Neither strong pseudoconvexity nor real convexity of $G$ is required here. Proof. The real fiber Hessian of $G$ is bounded above by $2L$ times $k$ on the compact unit sphere bundle of $k$, for some $L>0$, and homogeneity extends this bound to every nonzero vector. Also, $G$ is $C^1$ at zero with derivative zero, since its value is $O(|v|^2)$ and its first fiber derivative is $O(|v|)$, uniformly over the base. Integrating the Hessian estimate along a segment gives 7BB708C6E5FD 11.12.4 \begin{equation}  G(v+w)\leq G(v)+\mathrm d_ vG(w)+L|w|_ k^2; \end{equation} a segment passing through zero is handled by splitting it there and using the continuity of the first derivative. Complex homogeneity and completing the square on each complex line give the identity E21FC7F3990F 11.12.5 \begin{equation}  Q(x,\xi )=\max _{v\in E_ x} \{ 2\operatorname {Re}\xi (v)-G(x,v)\} . \end{equation} The maximum exists because $G(v)\geq a|v|_ k^2$ for a uniform constant $a>0$. Fix a maximizer $v_0$ for $\xi _0$. Differentiation, including the case $\xi _0=v_0=0$, gives $\mathrm dG(v_0)=2\operatorname {Re}\xi _0$. Evaluate the expression in ( 11.12.5 ) for $\xi _0+\zeta $ at $v_0+w$ and apply ( 11.12.4 ). The terms involving $\xi _0(w)$ cancel, and we obtain \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (w)-L|w|_ k^2.  \] Taking the supremum over $w$ yields \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +L^{-1}|\zeta |_{k^*}^2.  \] Set $c=L^{-1}$ and $\Phi =Q-c|\cdot |_{k^*}^2$. After subtracting the square, this inequality gives a real affine function on the whole dual fiber that lies below $\Phi $ and equals $\Phi $ at $\xi _0$. Hence $\Phi $ is the supremum of such affine functions, and therefore convex. Neither uniqueness of the maximizer nor real convexity of $G$ has been used. $\square$ Corollary 11.12.6 . 3DE300A9B2AD If $E$ is ample and has a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature, then $E^*$ admits a smooth complex norm whose square is strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the real fibers. Proof. By proposition 11.12.2 , the polar square is a positive continuous plurisubharmonic complex homogeneous function of degree two, and by lemma 11.12.3 it has the strong convexity in the fibers required in proposition 11.10.5 . Applying proposition 11.11.2 to $F=E^*$, whose dual $F^*=E$ is ample, gives the positive smooth strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function $H$ on $E^*$. Hence proposition 11.10.5 applies. Its proof uses theorem 11.10.4 , which preserves strong convexity in the fibers, and the square root of the resulting function is the asserted smooth norm. $\square$ Corollary 11.12.7 . 2984296C9B5A Let $F$ be the underlying smooth bundle of $F_0$ in theorem 11.9.4 , with a holomorphic structure in the neighborhood given there. If $F^*$ is ample, then $F^*$ admits no strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature. Proof. Apply corollary 11.12.6 to $E=F^*$. Such a metric would produce a smooth complex norm on $F$ with plurisubharmonic square, contrary to theorem 11.9.4 . $\square$ The corollary applies only near a split bundle whose line summands have positive Gauduchon degrees, and it is not vacuous only if such a neighborhood contains holomorphic structures with ample dual. On Hirzebruch surfaces, theorem 11.15.5 gives stable ample bundles whose duals lie in this neighborhood. Since the polar square need not be smooth, the regularization of 11.10 is an essential step of the argument.

Also, $G$ is $C^1$ at zero with derivative zero, since its value is $O(|v|^2)$ and its first fiber derivative is $O(|v|)$, uniformly over the base. Integrating the Hessian estimate along a segment gives 7BB708C6E5FD 11.12.4 \begin{equation}  G(v+w)\leq G(v)+\mathrm d_ vG(w)+L|w|_ k^2; \end{equation} a segment passing through zero is handled by splitting it there and using the continuity of the first derivative. Complex homogeneity and completing the square on each complex line give the identity E21FC7F3990F 11.12.5 \begin{equation}  Q(x,\xi )=\max _{v\in E_ x} \{ 2\operatorname {Re}\xi (v)-G(x,v)\} . \end{equation} The maximum exists because $G(v)\geq a|v|_ k^2$ for a uniform constant $a>0$. Fix a maximizer $v_0$ for $\xi _0$. Differentiation, including the case $\xi _0=v_0=0$, gives $\mathrm dG(v_0)=2\operatorname {Re}\xi _0$. Evaluate the expression in ( 11.12.5 ) for $\xi _0+\zeta $ at $v_0+w$ and apply ( 11.12.4 ). The terms involving $\xi _0(w)$ cancel, and we obtain \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (w)-L|w|_ k^2.  \] Taking the supremum over $w$ yields \[  Q(\xi _0+\zeta )\geq Q(\xi _0)+2\operatorname {Re}\zeta (v_0) +L^{-1}|\zeta |_{k^*}^2.  \] Set $c=L^{-1}$ and $\Phi =Q-c|\cdot |_{k^*}^2$. After subtracting the square, this inequality gives a real affine function on the whole dual fiber that lies below $\Phi $ and equals $\Phi $ at $\xi _0$. Hence $\Phi $ is the supremum of such affine functions, and therefore convex. Neither uniqueness of the maximizer nor real convexity of $G$ has been used. $\square$

title: Corollary 11.12.6

section: 11.12 Polar norms of semipositive Finsler metrics
text: Corollary 11.12.6 . 3DE300A9B2AD If $E$ is ample and has a strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature, then $E^*$ admits a smooth complex norm whose square is strictly plurisubharmonic off zero and locally strongly convex in the real fibers. Proof. By proposition 11.12.2 , the polar square is a positive continuous plurisubharmonic complex homogeneous function of degree two, and by lemma 11.12.3 it has the strong convexity in the fibers required in proposition 11.10.5 . Applying proposition 11.11.2 to $F=E^*$, whose dual $F^*=E$ is ample, gives the positive smooth strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function $H$ on $E^*$. Hence proposition 11.10.5 applies. Its proof uses theorem 11.10.4 , which preserves strong convexity in the fibers, and the square root of the resulting function is the asserted smooth norm. $\square$

title: 11.13 Ample comparison quotients on Hirzebruch surfaces
search_title: Ample comparison quotients on Hirzebruch surfaces

section: 11.13 Ample comparison quotients on Hirzebruch surfaces
text: To apply corollary 11.12.7 , we need ample vector bundles whose duals are close to a split bundle $F_1\oplus F_2$ with $\deg _{\Theta _ s}F_ s>0$ for suitable test forms $\Theta _ s$. The split bundle $F_1^*\oplus F_2^*$ is not ample itself: otherwise its quotient line bundles $F_ s^*$ would be ample, hence carry positively curved metrics, and each $F_ s$ would have negative degree for every test form. The ample bundles must therefore be obtained by deformation. On a Hirzebruch surface we choose a split bundle $E_0=L_1\oplus L_2$ whose dual summands have positive degree for suitable Kähler forms, and we construct an ample bundle $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ with the same Chern classes as a quotient of a trivial bundle. Both bundles belong to the family of bundles with these Chern classes that are prioritary for the ruling. This family is irreducible, which will allow us to find ample bundles in every neighborhood of $E_0$. Let $e\geq 0$ be an integer, and let \[  X=\mathbb F_ e=\mathbb P_{\mathbb P^1}(\mathcal O\oplus \mathcal O(e)), \qquad \pi :X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^1,  \] be the Hirzebruch surface, where the projective bundle parametrizes lines. Write $S$ for the section defined by the subbundle $\mathcal O(e)$ and $f$ for a fiber of $\pi $, called a ruling fiber; we identify line bundles with divisor classes and write $\mathcal O_ X(aS+bf)$. The normal bundle of $S$ is $\mathcal O(-e)$, so \[  S^2=-e,\qquad S\cdot f=1,\qquad f^2=0.  \] The dual of the tautological line bundle is $\mathcal O_ X(S)$. A line bundle of degree zero on the ruling fibers is pulled back from $\mathbb P^1$: its direct image has rank one, and the evaluation map from the pullback of the direct image is an isomorphism on each fiber. Consequently $\operatorname {Pic}(X)=\mathbb ZS\oplus \mathbb Zf$. Lemma 11.13.1 . 8FE2AABC7334 For integers $a\geq 0$ and $b$, \[  \pi _*\mathcal O_ X(aS+bf)= \bigoplus _{i=0}^ a\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(b-ie), \qquad R^1\pi _*\mathcal O_ X(aS+bf)=0.  \] A class $aS+bf$ is effective exactly when $a,b\geq 0$. If $a\geq 1$ and $b>ae$, its line bundle is very ample. In particular, \[  H=S+(3e+1)f, \qquad H^2=5e+2, \qquad h^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(H))=5e+4.  \] The canonical class is $K_ X=-2S-(e+2)f$. Proof. Over a trivializing chart of the base, sections of $\mathcal O_ X(aS)$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $a$ in the fiber coordinates. Their transition law gives \[  \pi _*\mathcal O_ X(aS)= \operatorname {Sym}^ a(\mathcal O\oplus \mathcal O(-e)),  \] and twisting by the base gives the formula. The first cohomology of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(a)$ on each fiber vanishes, which gives the assertion on the higher direct image. If $a<0$, restriction to a general ruling fiber excludes a nonzero section. For $a\geq 0$, the direct-image formula gives a nonzero section exactly when $b\geq 0$. Suppose that $a\geq 1$ and $b>ae$. All line bundles in the direct image then have degree at least one. Fiber polynomials of degree $a$ separate points and tangent directions within a fiber. To separate points over different base points, choose a fiber monomial that is nonzero at the first point and a coefficient section vanishing at the second base point but not at the first. At any point, choose such a nonzero monomial and a coefficient section with a simple zero at its base point; the resulting global section vanishes there, has nonzero derivative in a prescribed base direction and has zero vertical derivative. The complete linear system therefore separates points and first jets, so it defines an embedding. The formulas for $H^2$ and $h^0(H)$ follow from the intersection numbers and from the direct image $\mathcal O(3e+1)\oplus \mathcal O(2e+1)$. Finally, the relative Euler sequence gives $K_{X/\mathbb P^1}=-2S-ef$, and adding the pullback of the canonical class of $\mathbb P^1$ proves the last identity. $\square$ Put \[  L_1=\mathcal O_ X(5S-f),\qquad L_2=\mathcal O_ X(-S+(12e+5)f),\qquad E_0=L_1\oplus L_2.  \] Their Chern classes satisfy \[  c_1(E_0)=4H,\qquad c_2(E_0)=65e+26=13H^2.  \] An ample bundle with these Chern classes can be constructed as a quotient of a trivial bundle. The main point of the proof is to make the fibers of the associated map to projective space finite, which requires excluding common curves of the defining sections uniformly over the projective parameter. Proposition 11.13.2 . 6EA287558571 There exist linearly independent sections $a_0,\ldots ,a_3$ of $\mathcal O_ X(H)$ with no common zero. For any such quadruple and a general quadruple $b_0,\ldots ,b_3$ of sections of $\mathcal O_ X(3H)$, the sequence \[  0\longrightarrow \mathcal O_ X(-H)\oplus \mathcal O_ X(-3H) \xrightarrow {(a,b)}\mathcal O_ X^{\oplus 4} \longrightarrow E_{\mathrm{amp}}\longrightarrow 0  \] has a locally free ample cokernel $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ of rank two, with $c_1(E_{\mathrm{amp}})=4H$ and $c_2(E_{\mathrm{amp}})=13H^2$. Here general means outside a proper Zariski-closed subset of the space of quadruples. Proof. Step 1: the quadruple $a$. Since $\mathcal O_ X(H)$ is globally generated, a common zero at a fixed point imposes four independent linear conditions on a quadruple $a$. The incidence variety of quadruples with a common zero at some point of the surface therefore has codimension at least two in the space of quadruples, and its image there is closed by properness. Linear independence is also a nonempty open condition, because $h^0(H)\geq 4$, and the two open conditions intersect. Fix such an $a$ and write \[  V=H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H))^{\oplus 4},\qquad N=\dim V.  \] Step 2: local freeness. At a fixed point $x$, the map $(a,b)$ drops rank exactly when $b(x)$ is proportional to the nonzero vector $a(x)$. Since evaluation on $V$ is surjective, this is a condition of codimension three. Its incidence over $X$ has dimension at most $N-1$, and its image in $V$ is closed. Outside that image the cokernel is locally free of rank two. Step 3: the map to projective space. Dualizing the sequence identifies $E_{\mathrm{amp}}^*$ with a subbundle of $(\mathbb C^4)^*\otimes \mathcal O_ X$. This inclusion defines a proper morphism \[  q_ b:\mathbb P(E_{\mathrm{amp}}^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb P((\mathbb C^4)^*), \qquad \mathcal O_{\mathbb P(E_{\mathrm{amp}}^*)}(1) =q_ b^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1).  \] For $w=[w_0:\cdots :w_3]$, its fiber is the common zero scheme of \[  s_ w=\sum _ iw_ i a_ i\in H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(H)), \qquad t_ w=\sum _ iw_ i b_ i\in H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H)).  \] Linear independence of $a$ gives $s_ w\neq 0$ for every $w$. Step 4: no common curves. A nonzero effective subdivisor $D$ of $\operatorname {div}(s_ w)$ has class $uS+vf$, where \[  u\in \{ 0,1\} ,\qquad 0\leq v\leq 3e+1, \qquad (u,v)\neq (0,0).  \] Write $|D|=\mathbb P H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(D))$ for the complete linear system. For each of these finitely many classes $D_0$, let $T_{D_0}$ parametrize the triples $(w,[\sigma ],[\tau ])$ with \[  [\sigma ]\in |D_0|,\qquad [\tau ]\in |H-D_0|, \qquad [s_ w]=[\sigma \tau ].  \] Since products of nonzero sections are nonzero, this is a closed projective parameter scheme. Its fiber over $w$ consists of the finitely many effective subdivisors of the fixed divisor $\operatorname {div}(s_ w)$, counted with their possible multiplicities. Thus $\dim T_{D_0}\leq 3$. Vanishing on a nonzero effective divisor $D$ imposes at least four independent conditions on $H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H))$. Indeed, choose an integral curve $C$ in its support. Very ampleness gives sections $r_0,r_1$ of $\mathcal O_ X(H)$ with nonconstant ratio on $C$. The four cubic monomials in their restrictions are linearly independent, since a linear relation would make the nonconstant ratio algebraic over $\mathbb C$, hence constant. For fixed $(w,[\sigma ],[\tau ])$, the map $V\to H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H))$, $b\mapsto t_ w$, is surjective. The condition that $t_ w$ vanish on $D=\operatorname {div}(\sigma )$ therefore has codimension at least four in $V$. This condition is closed in families: the universal multiplication map \[  H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H-D_0))\otimes \mathcal O_{|D_0|}(-1) \longrightarrow H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(3H))\otimes \mathcal O_{|D_0|}  \] is injective on fibers, so its image is a subbundle, and the condition is the vanishing of the image of $t_ w$ in the quotient bundle. Its incidence over $T_{D_0}$ has dimension at most $N-1$, and its image in $V$ is closed. Step 5: conclusion. Choose $b$ outside these finitely many proper closed images and outside the image of Step 2. Then $s_ w$ and $t_ w$ have no common curve for any $w$, so every fiber of $q_ b$ is finite. A proper morphism with finite fibers is finite, and the pullback of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1)$ by a finite morphism is ample; hence $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is ample. Finally, the Whitney formula gives \[  c(E_{\mathrm{amp}})=\frac1{(1-H)(1-3H)}=1+4H+13H^2.  \] $\square$ A vector bundle $E$ on $X$ is called prioritary for the ruling if $\operatorname {Ext}^2_ X(E,E(-f))=0$. Since all ruling fibers are linearly equivalent, this condition does not depend on the chosen fiber, and by Serre duality it is equivalent to \[  \operatorname {Hom}_ X(E,E(K_ X+f))=0.  \] Prioritary bundles of fixed rank and Chern classes form an irreducible family, by the theorem of Walter recalled in 11.15 . Lemma 11.13.3 . 7055476D483C Both $E_0$ and $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ are prioritary for the ruling. Proof. Write $D=K_ X+f=-2S-(e+1)f$. The summands of $\operatorname {End}(E_0)(D)$ have classes \[  D,\quad D,\quad 4S-(13e+7)f,\quad -8S+(11e+5)f.  \] Each has a negative coefficient in the basis $S,f$, so by lemma 11.13.1 none of them has a nonzero section. This proves the required vanishing of $\operatorname {Hom}$ for $E_0$. Precomposition with the surjection $\mathcal O_ X^4\to E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ gives an injection \[  \operatorname {Hom}(E_{\mathrm{amp}},E_{\mathrm{amp}}(D)) \hookrightarrow H^0(X,E_{\mathrm{amp}}(D))^4.  \] Twist the defining sequence by $D$. Its middle term has no sections. For $j=1,3$, Serre duality and the formula of lemma 11.13.1 give \[  \begin{aligned}  H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X(D-jH))& =H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X(jH-f))^*,\\  \pi _*\mathcal O_ X(jH-f)& =\bigoplus _{i=0}^ j\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(j(3e+1)-1-ie). \end{aligned}  \] The higher direct image vanishes, and every degree in this sum is at least $j(2e+1)-1\geq 0$. Hence all these first cohomology groups vanish, and the long exact sequence of the twisted sequence gives $H^0(X,E_{\mathrm{amp}}(D))=0$. This proves the vanishing of $\operatorname {Hom}$ for $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$. $\square$ Proposition 11.13.4 . B6B9C2094631 For $F_ s=L_ s^*$, $s=1,2$, there are Kähler forms $\eta _ s$ with $\deg _{\eta _ s}F_ s=1$. Consequently, the split bundle $E_0^*=F_1\oplus F_2$ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 11.9.4 . Proof. The integral classes \[  A_1=6S+(6e+1)f,\qquad A_2=S+(13e+6)f  \] are very ample by lemma 11.13.1 . Pullbacks of normalized Fubini–Study forms under the corresponding embeddings give Kähler forms $\eta _ s$ representing $c_1(\mathcal O_ X(A_ s))$. A direct computation of intersection numbers gives \[  c_1(L_1)\cdot A_1=-1,\qquad c_1(L_2)\cdot A_2=-1,  \] so the degrees of the duals are equal to one. Since $n=2$, the closed positive $(1,1)$-forms $\eta _ s$ are admissible test forms $\Theta _ s$ in theorem 11.9.4 . $\square$

title: 11.14 Stable extensions approaching the split comparison bundle

section: 11.14 Stable extensions approaching the split comparison bundle
text:
The bundles near $E_0$ that we construct will also be slope-stable for a fixed polarization. The split bundle $E_0$ is unstable, and the ample bundle $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ need not be stable. Nonsplit extensions of $L_2$ by $L_1$ have the same Chern classes as $E_0$, are stable, and converge to $E_0$ as the extension class tends to zero; they are not ample, however. The next subsection combines them with $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$. Keep the Hirzebruch surface $X=\mathbb F_ e$, its ruling and the line bundles of 11.13 . Thus \[  L_1=\mathcal O_ X(5S-f),\qquad L_2=\mathcal O_ X(-S+(12e+5)f),\qquad E_0=L_1\oplus L_2.  \] We use the very ample polarization $P=4H-f=4S+(12e+3)f$. For a torsion-free coherent sheaf $E$ of positive rank on $X$, put \[  \deg _ PE=c_1(E)\cdot P, \qquad \mu _ P(E)=\frac{\deg _ PE}{\operatorname {rank}E}.  \] A vector bundle $V$ is $\mu _ P$-stable if $\mu _ P(M)<\mu _ P(V)$ for every coherent subsheaf $M\subset V$ with $0<\operatorname {rank}M<\operatorname {rank}V$. Since $\mu _ P(L_2)>\mu _ P(E_0)$ by the computation below, the split bundle $E_0$ is not $\mu _ P$-stable. Proposition 11.14.1 . A195B6162A49 The extension space has dimension \[  \dim \operatorname {Ext}^1_ X(L_2,L_1)=105e+35.  \] Every nonsplit extension \[  0\longrightarrow L_1\longrightarrow V\xrightarrow {q}L_2 \longrightarrow 0  \] is a locally free, $\mu _ P$-stable bundle with $c_1(V)=4H$ and $c_2(V)=13H^2$. Proof. Extensions of line bundles are locally free: the quotient is free on a small trivializing neighborhood, so the sequence splits there. Their classes form \[  \operatorname {Ext}^1_ X(L_2,L_1) =H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X(6S-(12e+6)f)).  \] By lemma 11.13.1 , the higher direct image of this line bundle vanishes and its direct image is the sum of the seven line bundles $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-12e-6-ie)$, $0\leq i\leq 6$. Their first cohomology groups have total dimension \[  \sum _{i=0}^6(12e+5+ie)=105e+35>0.  \] The Chern classes follow from the extension sequence. Direct computations of intersection numbers give \[  \mu _ P(L_1)=40e+11,\qquad \mu _ P(V)=40e+14, \qquad \mu _ P(L_2)=40e+17.  \] It suffices to test line-bundle subsheaves $M\hookrightarrow V$. Indeed, a rank-one torsion-free subsheaf on a smooth surface has a line bundle as its double dual, and its inclusion extends across the finitely many missing points by Hartogs extension in local bundle frames. The extended map remains injective and has the same first Chern class. This argument does not require the quotient to be locally free. If the composite $M\to L_2$ is zero, then $M$ maps nontrivially into $L_1$, so $\deg _ P M\leq \mu _ P(L_1)<\mu _ P(V)$. Otherwise its zero divisor $D$ is effective and $M=L_2(-D)$. If $D=0$, the composite is an isomorphism and its inverse splits $q$, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence $D\neq 0$, and \[  \deg _ P M=\mu _ P(V)+3-D\cdot P.  \] Every effective class is $aS+bf$ with $a,b\geq 0$, and \[  S\cdot P=8e+3,\qquad f\cdot P=4.  \] For $e\geq 1$, every nonzero effective divisor has $P$-degree at least four, which proves the strict slope inequality. For $e=0$, the only nonzero effective class of $P$-degree at most three is $S$. A lift of multiplication by a nonzero section $s\in H^0(X,\mathcal O_ X(S))$ from $L_2(-S)$ to $V$ would make the pullback of the nonzero extension class vanish. That pullback is the image of the class under the map \[  H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X(6S-6f)) \xrightarrow {\  \cdot s\  }H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X(7S-6f)).  \] On $X=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, order the factors so that $\mathcal O_ X(S)=\mathcal O(1,0)$ and $\mathcal O_ X(f)=\mathcal O(0,1)$. The Künneth formula identifies this map with \[  \bigl [H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(6)) \xrightarrow {\  \cdot s\  }H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(7))\bigr ] \otimes \operatorname {Id}_{H^1(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-6))}.  \] Multiplication by a nonzero section is injective on global sections, and tensoring with a vector space preserves injectivity. Thus the nonzero extension class cannot pull back to zero. This excludes the possible equality of slopes and proves stability also for $e=0$. $\square$ Proposition 11.14.2 . FD54983C4E79 Every extension of $L_2$ by $L_1$, including the split extension, is prioritary for the ruling and is not ample. Its restriction to every ruling fiber is $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(5)\oplus \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$. Proof. Put $D=K_ X+f=-2S-(e+1)f$. The four line bundles $L_ i^*\otimes L_ j(D)$ have classes \[  D,\quad D,\quad 4S-(13e+7)f,\quad -8S+(11e+5)f.  \] Each has a negative coefficient in the basis $S,f$, and hence no nonzero section. Applying $\operatorname {Hom}_ X(L_ i,\cdot )$ to the extension twisted by $D$ gives $\operatorname {Hom}_ X(L_ i,V(D))=0$ for $i=1,2$. Applying $\operatorname {Hom}_ X(\cdot ,V(D))$ to the original extension then gives $\operatorname {Hom}_ X(V,V(D))=0$. By Serre duality this is the prioritary condition $\operatorname {Ext}^2_ X(V,V(-f))=0$. Restriction to a ruling fiber is exact, because the quotient is locally free. The restricted line bundles have degrees five and minus one, and the restricted extension splits, since $\operatorname {Ext}^1_{\mathbb P^1}(\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O(5)) =H^1(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(6))=0$. The quotient of negative degree on this curve excludes ampleness. $\square$ Proposition 11.14.3 . 7215288BDF53 On the smooth bundle underlying $E_0$ there is a holomorphic one-parameter family of Dolbeault operators $\bar\partial _ t=\bar\partial _0+tA$, $t\in \mathbb C$, such that for $t\ne 0$ the holomorphic bundle defined by $\bar\partial _ t$ is $\mu _ P$-stable and prioritary, but not ample. As $t\to 0$, these operators converge to $\bar\partial _0$ in the $C^ m$ norm for every integer $m\geq 0$. Proof. Choose a nonzero extension class and a smooth Dolbeault representative $\eta \in \Omega ^{0,1}(X,L_2^*\otimes L_1)$ of it, so that $\bar\partial \eta =0$. On the smooth direct sum, set \[  A=\begin{pmatrix} 0

& \eta 

\\ 0

& 0

\end{pmatrix}.  \] The covariant Dolbeault derivative of $A$ is zero and $A\wedge A=0$, so $\bar\partial _ t^2=0$. Adding the Dolbeault operator of the base $\mathbb C$ of the parameter $t$ also gives an integrable operator on $X\times \mathbb C$, because the family depends holomorphically on $t$. This defines a holomorphic family of bundles whose extension class is $t[\eta ]$. It is nonsplit for $t\neq 0$, so the two preceding propositions apply. For a fixed smooth background connection and fixed metrics, \[  \| \bar\partial _ t-\bar\partial _0\| _{C^ m} =|t|\, \| A\| _{C^ m}\longrightarrow 0,  \] and the norm $\| A\| _{C^ m}$ is finite for every $m$ because $X$ is compact. $\square$ Thus stability and ampleness have been realized separately in the prioritary family of $E_0$: the nonsplit extensions are stable but not ample, while $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is ample. The deformation argument of theorem 11.15.5 joins the stable locus to the ample one and provides stable ample bundles arbitrarily close to $E_0$.

title: 11.15 Deforming to stable ample bundles
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
We keep the Hirzebruch surface $X=\mathbb F_ e$ and the data $H,P,L_1,L_2,E_0$ of 11.13 , 11.14 . The ample quotient $E_{\mathrm{amp}}$ and a nonsplit extension are two prioritary bundles with the same Chern classes as $E_0$; the former is ample and the latter is stable. Prioritary bundles with these invariants form an irreducible family in which ampleness and stability are open conditions, so bundles with both properties are dense in the family, and in particular they accumulate at $E_0$. We first prove the required openness assertions for algebraic families. Throughout this subsection, $T$ denotes a smooth complex algebraic variety. A flat family is a coherent sheaf $\mathcal E$ on $X	imes T$ that is flat over $T$, and its fiber $\mathcal E_ t$ at $t\in T$ is its restriction to $X	imes \{ t\} $. Lemma 11.15.1 . 0EEC7E1B2FB0 If a flat family $\mathcal E$ has a locally free fiber at $t_0\in T$, then $\mathcal E$ is a vector bundle on $X	imes T'$ for some Zariski-open neighborhood $T'$ of $t_0$. Proof. At a point of $X	imes \{ t_0\} $, lift a local basis of the fiber to $\mathcal E$. By Nakayama's lemma, the resulting map from a free module of finite rank is surjective near that point. Tensor its kernel sequence with the residue field of $t_0$. Flatness over $T$ makes the first Tor term zero, so the kernel restricts to the kernel of the chosen isomorphism on the fiber, namely zero, and Nakayama's lemma shows that the kernel vanishes near that point. Thus $\mathcal E$ is locally free near every point of the central fiber. The locus where $\mathcal E$ is not locally free is closed. Since the projection $X	imes T	o T$ is proper, the image of that locus is closed and misses $t_0$, and we remove this image. $\square$ Lemma 11.15.2 . 927EFEB9D586 For a vector bundle $\mathcal E$ on $X	imes T$, the parameters $t$ for which $\mathcal E_ t$ is ample form a Zariski-open subset of $T$. Proof. Put $Y=\mathbb P_{X	imes T}(\mathcal E^*)$, with the line convention, and let $p:Y	o T$ be the projection, a projective flat morphism. Write $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_ Y(1)$. If $\mathcal E_{t_0}$ is ample, then $\mathcal L_{t_0}$ is ample. Choose $k$ so that its $k$th power is very ample and has vanishing higher cohomology. By Serre vanishing, semicontinuity, and cohomology and base change, after shrinking $T$ around $t_0$ the sheaf $\mathcal V=p_*\mathcal L^ k$ is locally free and commutes with restriction to fibers. After a further shrinking, the evaluation map $p^*\mathcal V	o \mathcal L^ k$ is surjective: its cokernel vanishes on the central fiber, and the image of its support under the proper map $p$ is closed and misses $t_0$. Evaluation gives a proper morphism \[  g:Y\longrightarrow \mathbb P_ T(\mathcal V^*), \qquad g^*\mathcal O(1)=\mathcal L^ k,  \] whose restriction to the central fiber is a closed immersion. The locus where $g$ is quasi-finite is open; its complement has closed image in $T$ by properness and misses $t_0$, so after a further shrinking $g$ is proper and quasi-finite, hence finite. For a finite morphism, pushforward commutes with base change. The cokernel of \[  \mathcal O_{\mathbb P_ T(\mathcal V^*)}\longrightarrow g_*\mathcal O_ Y  \] therefore vanishes on the central fiber, and its support projects to a closed subset of $T$ missing $t_0$. After removing that subset, the map is surjective, so $g$ is a closed immersion. Consequently $\mathcal L^ k$ is very ample on every fiber, and $\mathcal E_ t$ is ample there. $\square$ Lemma 11.15.3 . EBF7EB73EABE For a family $\mathcal E$ of rank-two vector bundles on $X	imes T$ whose fibers have a fixed first Chern class, the parameters $t$ for which $\mathcal E_ t$ is $\mu _ P$-stable form a Zariski-open subset of $T$. Proof. Fix a stable fiber at $t_0$ and put $
u =c_1(\mathcal E_ t)\cdot P/2$, which is independent of $t$. Choose $k\geq 1$ such that $\mathcal E_{t_0}^*(kP)$ is globally generated and has vanishing higher cohomology. The argument with Serre vanishing, base change and evaluation used in the previous proof gives, over a neighborhood of $t_0$, maps \[  \mathcal E_ t\longrightarrow \mathcal O_ X(kP)^{\oplus N}  \] that are injective on every fiber. By the double-dual argument for rank-one subsheaves in the proof of proposition 11.14.1 , a destabilizing subsheaf of $\mathcal E_ t$ yields a nonzero map from a line bundle $M=\mathcal O_ X(aS+bf)$ with $\deg _ P M\geq 
u $. At least one component of its composite with the injection above is nonzero, and since effective classes have nonnegative coefficients, \[  a\leq 4k,\qquad b\leq (12e+3)k.  \] Since $\deg _ P M=(8e+3)a+4b$, the inequality $\deg _ PM\geq 
u $ also gives \[  a\geq  rac{
u -4(12e+3)k}{8e+3}, \qquad b\geq  rac{
u -4k(8e+3)}4.  \] Only finitely many integral pairs $(a,b)$ satisfy these four bounds. For each such pair with $\deg _ P M\geq 
u $, semicontinuity makes the set \[  \{ t:H^0(X,\mathcal E_ t\otimes M^*)
eq 0\}   \] closed, and it does not contain $t_0$. Conversely, a nonzero map from such an $M$ is injective as a map of sheaves and violates stability. Thus the set of parameters with unstable fibers is, on this neighborhood, exactly the finite union of these closed subsets, and removing the union proves the claim. $\square$ Lemma 11.15.4 . 319641577F72 Let $T$ be smooth and irreducible, let $U\subset T$ be a nonempty Zariski-open subset, and let $\mathcal E$ be a vector bundle on $X	imes T$. For every $t_0\in T$, there are points $t_ j\in U$ tending to $t_0$ in the analytic topology, together with smooth complex-linear identifications of the bundles underlying $\mathcal E_{t_ j}$ and $\mathcal E_{t_0}$, under which the Dolbeault operators of the fibers converge in the $C^ m$ norm for every integer $m\geq 0$. The dual operators converge in the same sense. Proof. The proper algebraic closed subset $T\setminus U$ has empty interior in the analytic topology. In an analytic coordinate ball $B$ around $t_0$, choose $t_ j\in U\cap B$ with $t_ j	o t_0$. Choose a smooth complex connection on $\mathcal E|_{X	imes B}$. Parallel transport along radial paths in $B$, keeping $x\in X$ fixed, gives identifications \[  \Phi _ t:\mathcal E_{t_0}^{\mathrm{sm}}\longrightarrow \mathcal E_ t^{\mathrm{sm}},\qquad \Phi _{t_0}=\operatorname {id},  \] depending smoothly on $(x,t)$, where the superscript $\mathrm{sm}$ denotes the underlying smooth complex bundle. These identifications need not be holomorphic. Transport the Dolbeault operators by these maps and write \[   ar\partial _ t=\Phi _ t^{-1} ar\partial _{\mathcal E_ t}\Phi _ t, \qquad A_ t= ar\partial _ t- ar\partial _{\mathcal E_{t_0}}.  \] Since both operators satisfy the same Leibniz rule, $A_ t$ is an endomorphism-valued $(0,1)$-form. Its coefficients are smooth in $(x,t)$, and $A_{t_0}=0$. Fix background metrics and a smooth connection on the central bundle. Compactness of $X$ and continuity of every finite collection of derivatives give \[  \| A_{t_ j}\| _{C^ m(X)}\longrightarrow 0 \qquad 	ext{for every integer }m\geq 0.  \] The dual identifications are $(\Phi _ t^{-1})^*$. In transported dual frames the perturbation is $-A_ t^{\mathsf T}$, so the same convergence holds for the dual Dolbeault operators. $\square$ We use Walter's theorem on prioritary stacks: on a birationally ruled surface, a nonempty stack of prioritary torsion-free sheaves with fixed rank $r\geq 2$ and fixed numerical Chern classes is smooth and irreducible. Here prioritary means that $\operatorname {Ext}^2(E,E(-f))=0$ for every ruling fiber $f$; on $X$ all ruling fibers are linearly equivalent. The theorem concerns the full prioritary stack and has no semistability hypothesis. Theorem 11.15.5 . E769519C862E For every $e\geq 0$, there are integrable Dolbeault operators on the smooth bundle underlying $E_0$ that converge to its split operator in every $C^ m$ norm, $m\geq 0$, and define ample $\mu _ P$-stable bundles of rank two with $c_1=4H$ and $c_2=13H^2$. The induced dual operators converge to the split dual operator in every $C^ m$ norm. Proof. Let $\mathcal P$ be the prioritary stack with invariants $(2,4H,13H^2)$. It contains $E_0$ by proposition 11.14.2 , and Walter's theorem makes it smooth and irreducible. Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal S$ be the loci of ample and of $\mu _ P$-stable vector bundles in $\mathcal P$. They are open by the three preceding family lemmas, which apply on smooth local charts of $\mathcal P$; the first lemma allows restriction to locally free families near a point given by a vector bundle. The ample bundle of proposition 11.13.2 is prioritary by lemma 11.13.3 , so $\mathcal A$ is nonempty. A nonsplit extension is stable and prioritary by proposition 11.14.1 , proposition 11.14.2 , so $\mathcal S$ is nonempty. By irreducibility, $\mathcal U=\mathcal A\cap \mathcal S$ is nonempty and dense. Choose a smooth local chart $q:T	o \mathcal P$ of finite type over $\mathbb C$, with a point $t_0$ representing $E_0$, and let $\mathcal E$ be the corresponding flat family on $X	imes T$. Fix an identification $\mathcal E_{t_0}\simeq E_0$. The variety $T$ is smooth because the stack and the chart are smooth. Shrink $T$ to an irreducible neighborhood of $t_0$ and use lemma 11.15.1 to make $\mathcal E$ a vector bundle on the whole product. The inverse image $q^{-1}(\mathcal U)$ is dense: every nonempty open $T'\subset T$ has nonempty open image $q(T')$ under the smooth map $q$, and this image meets $\mathcal U$. Apply lemma 11.15.4 to this dense open set. Each transported operator defines a bundle isomorphic to the corresponding ample stable fiber. The fixed invariants of the stack give its Chern classes, and the lemma also gives the convergence of the dual operators. $\square$ Corollary 11.15.6 . A2CE95B32341 For every $e\geq 0$, there is an ample $\mu _ P$-stable bundle $E$ of rank two on $X$ with $c_1(E)=4H$ and $c_2(E)=13H^2$ that admits no smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature. Proof. By proposition 11.13.4 , the two line summands of $E_0^*$ have positive degrees with respect to suitable test forms. The preceding theorem gives an ample stable bundle $E$ whose dual Dolbeault operator is as close to the split dual operator in $C^4$ as required. Apply corollary 11.12.7 to $F=E^*$. $\square$

title: Lemma 11.15.4
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 11.15.4 . 319641577F72 Let $T$ be smooth and irreducible, let $U\subset T$ be a nonempty Zariski-open subset, and let $\mathcal E$ be a vector bundle on $X\times T$. For every $t_0\in T$, there are points $t_ j\in U$ tending to $t_0$ in the analytic topology, together with smooth complex-linear identifications of the bundles underlying $\mathcal E_{t_ j}$ and $\mathcal E_{t_0}$, under which the Dolbeault operators of the fibers converge in the $C^ m$ norm for every integer $m\geq 0$. The dual operators converge in the same sense. Proof. The proper algebraic closed subset $T\setminus U$ has empty interior in the analytic topology. In an analytic coordinate ball $B$ around $t_0$, choose $t_ j\in U\cap B$ with $t_ j\to t_0$. Choose a smooth complex connection on $\mathcal E|_{X\times B}$. Parallel transport along radial paths in $B$, keeping $x\in X$ fixed, gives identifications \[  \Phi _ t:\mathcal E_{t_0}^{\mathrm{sm}}\longrightarrow \mathcal E_ t^{\mathrm{sm}},\qquad \Phi _{t_0}=\operatorname {id},  \] depending smoothly on $(x,t)$, where the superscript $\mathrm{sm}$ denotes the underlying smooth complex bundle. These identifications need not be holomorphic. Transport the Dolbeault operators by these maps and write \[  \bar\partial _ t=\Phi _ t^{-1}\bar\partial _{\mathcal E_ t}\Phi _ t, \qquad A_ t=\bar\partial _ t-\bar\partial _{\mathcal E_{t_0}}.  \] Since both operators satisfy the same Leibniz rule, $A_ t$ is an endomorphism-valued $(0,1)$-form. Its coefficients are smooth in $(x,t)$, and $A_{t_0}=0$. Fix background metrics and a smooth connection on the central bundle. Compactness of $X$ and continuity of every finite collection of derivatives give \[  \| A_{t_ j}\| _{C^ m(X)}\longrightarrow 0 \qquad \text{for every integer }m\geq 0.  \] The dual identifications are $(\Phi _ t^{-1})^*$. In transported dual frames the perturbation is $-A_ t^{\mathsf T}$, so the same convergence holds for the dual Dolbeault operators. $\square$

title: Theorem 11.15.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Theorem 11.15.5 . E769519C862E For every $e\geq 0$, there are integrable Dolbeault operators on the smooth bundle underlying $E_0$ that converge to its split operator in every $C^ m$ norm, $m\geq 0$, and define ample $\mu _ P$-stable bundles of rank two with $c_1=4H$ and $c_2=13H^2$. The induced dual operators converge to the split dual operator in every $C^ m$ norm. Proof. Let $\mathcal P$ be the prioritary stack with invariants $(2,4H,13H^2)$. It contains $E_0$ by proposition 11.14.2 , and Walter's theorem makes it smooth and irreducible. Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal S$ be the loci of ample and of $\mu _ P$-stable vector bundles in $\mathcal P$. They are open by the three preceding family lemmas, which apply on smooth local charts of $\mathcal P$; the first lemma allows restriction to locally free families near a point given by a vector bundle. The ample bundle of proposition 11.13.2 is prioritary by lemma 11.13.3 , so $\mathcal A$ is nonempty. A nonsplit extension is stable and prioritary by proposition 11.14.1 , proposition 11.14.2 , so $\mathcal S$ is nonempty. By irreducibility, $\mathcal U=\mathcal A\cap \mathcal S$ is nonempty and dense. Choose a smooth local chart $q:T\to \mathcal P$ of finite type over $\mathbb C$, with a point $t_0$ representing $E_0$, and let $\mathcal E$ be the corresponding flat family on $X\times T$. Fix an identification $\mathcal E_{t_0}\simeq E_0$. The variety $T$ is smooth because the stack and the chart are smooth. Shrink $T$ to an irreducible neighborhood of $t_0$ and use lemma 11.15.1 to make $\mathcal E$ a vector bundle on the whole product. The inverse image $q^{-1}(\mathcal U)$ is dense: every nonempty open $T'\subset T$ has nonempty open image $q(T')$ under the smooth map $q$, and this image meets $\mathcal U$. Apply lemma 11.15.4 to this dense open set. Each transported operator defines a bundle isomorphic to the corresponding ample stable fiber. The fixed invariants of the stack give its Chern classes, and the lemma also gives the convergence of the dual operators. $\square$

title: Corollary 11.15.6
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Corollary 11.15.6 . A2CE95B32341 For every $e\geq 0$, there is an ample $\mu _ P$-stable bundle $E$ of rank two on $X$ with $c_1(E)=4H$ and $c_2(E)=13H^2$ that admits no smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature. Proof. By proposition 11.13.4 , the two line summands of $E_0^*$ have positive degrees with respect to suitable test forms. The preceding theorem gives an ample stable bundle $E$ whose dual Dolbeault operator is as close to the split dual operator in $C^4$ as required. Apply corollary 11.12.7 to $F=E^*$. $\square$

Corollary 11.15.6 shows that no Finsler metric on $E$ has semipositive Kobayashi curvature, but it does not locate the failure. For a single metric, a point where the curvature is not semipositive gives a local hypersurface through that point on which the metric has a nondegenerate critical point with many positive Levi directions. Holomorphic approximation on a Stein manifold allows one hypersurface to serve for all metrics at once. In this subsection, $X$ is a connected smooth projective variety of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $E	o X$ is an algebraic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 2$, viewed as a holomorphic bundle. We use the squared Finsler metrics and the convention for Kobayashi curvature of 11.12 . A compact subset $K$ of a Stein manifold $Y$ is holomorphically convex if it coincides with its holomorphic hull $\{ y\in Y:|f(y)|\leq \sup _ K|f|	ext{ for all }f\in \mathcal O(Y)\} $. We use the classical Oka–Weil theorem in the following form: a function holomorphic near a holomorphically convex compact subset of a Stein manifold can be approximated uniformly there by global holomorphic functions. We also use polynomial Runge approximation in one variable on a union of two disjoint closed disks. Lemma 11.16.1 . 00BCE16BE996 Let $K,L$ be holomorphically convex compact subsets of a Stein manifold $Y$. If a global holomorphic function maps them into disjoint closed disks in $\mathbb C$, then $K\cup L$ is holomorphically convex. Proof. Write $h$ for the function and $\Delta _ K,\Delta _ L$ for the disks. Their union is polynomially convex, so testing with polynomials in $h$ shows that $h$ maps the holomorphic hull of $K\cup L$ into $\Delta _ K\cup \Delta _ L$. Suppose that $p
otin K\cup L$ and $h(p)\in \Delta _ K$. Holomorphic convexity of $K$ gives $a\in \mathcal O(Y)$ with $|a(p)|>\sup _ K|a|$. Choose polynomials tending uniformly to one on $\Delta _ K$ and to zero on $\Delta _ L$. Their compositions with $h$, multiplied by $a$, converge to $a$ at $p$ and on $K$, and to zero on $L$. A sufficiently good approximation therefore separates $p$ from $K\cup L$. The case $h(p)\in \Delta _ L$ is identical, with $K$ and $L$ interchanged. Thus no point outside $K\cup L$ belongs to its hull. $\square$ Lemma 11.16.2 . 8C1AF91F05D6 Let $U$ be a connected smooth affine variety and let $q\geq 0$ be an integer. Put $B=U	imes \mathbb C^*	imes \mathbb C^ q$, with coordinates $(x,t,s)$, and for $\lambda \in \mathbb C^*$ let $d_\lambda (x,t,s)=(x,\lambda t,\lambda s)$. For each $j\geq 1$, let $C_ j\subset B$ be a holomorphically convex compact set, let $g_ j$ be holomorphic near $C_ j$, and let $\delta _ j>0$. Suppose that $t(C_ j)$ lies in the disk $|t-t_ j|\leq |t_ j|/4$ for some $t_ j
eq 0$. Then there are $\lambda _ j\in \mathbb C^*$ and $f\in \mathcal O(B)$ such that \[  \sup _{d_{\lambda _ j}(C_ j)} |f-\lambda _ j g_ j\circ d_{\lambda _ j}^{-1}|<|\lambda _ j|\delta _ j \qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Proof. Choose an exhaustion $(L_ j)_{j\geq 0}$ of the affine, hence Stein, manifold $B$ by holomorphically convex compact sets with $L_ j\subset \operatorname {int}L_{j+1}$. We construct $f_ j\in \mathcal O(B)$ and compact sets $K_ j$ inductively, starting with $f_0=0$ and $K_0=L_0$. At stage $j\geq 1$, choose $M>0$ with $t(K_{j-1})\subset \{ |t|\leq M\} $, and choose $R>4M/3$. Dilation by $\lambda _ j=R/t_ j$ moves the $t$-projection of $C_ j$ into the disk $|t-R|\leq R/4$, which is disjoint from $|t|\leq M$. For the rest of the induction we replace $C_ j$, $g_ j$ and $\delta _ j$ by the dilated compact set $d_{\lambda _ j}(C_ j)$, the function $\lambda _ jg_ j\circ d_{\lambda _ j}^{-1}$ and the tolerance $|\lambda _ j|\delta _ j$, keeping the same notation. Lemma 11.16.1 , applied with the function $t$, makes $K_{j-1}\cup C_ j$ holomorphically convex. On disjoint neighborhoods of $K_{j-1}$ and $C_ j$, prescribe $f_{j-1}$ and $g_ j$, respectively. Oka–Weil approximation gives $f_ j\in \mathcal O(B)$ with \[  \sup _{K_{j-1}}|f_ j-f_{j-1}|<\epsilon _ j, \qquad \sup _{C_ j}|f_ j-g_ j|<\epsilon _ j, \qquad \epsilon _ j=2^{-j-2}\min (1,\delta _1,\ldots ,\delta _ j).  \] Let $K_ j$ be a member of the fixed exhaustion containing $K_{j-1}\cup C_ j\cup L_ j$ in its interior. The interiors of the sets $K_ j$ exhaust $B$, and the summable errors make $f_ j$ converge locally uniformly to some $f\in \mathcal O(B)$. For a fixed $j$, every later approximation controls its error on $C_ j$, since $C_ j\subset K_{m-1}$ for $m>j$. Consequently \[  \sup _{C_ j}|f-g_ j| \leq \sum _{m\geq j}\epsilon _ m \leq 2^{-j-1}\delta _ j<\delta _ j.  \] Returning to the original notation gives the stated tolerances. $\square$ Theorem 11.16.3 . 0A9CF0366804 Suppose that $E$ admits no smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric with semipositive Kobayashi curvature. Then there is a connected smooth Stein hypersurface $\mathcal S\subset E^	imes $, locally closed in the analytic topology, with the following property: for every smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric $G$ on $E$, the restriction $G|_{\mathcal S}$ has a nondegenerate critical point with at least $r$ positive Levi eigenvalues, and hence with at most $n-1$ negative ones. Proof. Step 1: coordinates. An algebraic frame trivializes $E$ over a nonempty affine open subset $U\subset X$. Since $X$ is smooth and connected, it is irreducible, so $U$ is dense and connected. Write the fiber coordinates as $(w,t,s)\in \mathbb C	imes \mathbb C	imes \mathbb C^{r-2}$, and put $B=U	imes \mathbb C^*	imes \mathbb C^{r-2}$. We seek $\mathcal S$ as a graph $w=f(x,t,s)$ over $B$; such a graph avoids the zero section because $t
e 0$. Step 2: a local test for one metric. Fix a candidate metric $G$. Since its Kobayashi curvature is not semipositive, its horizontal Schur complement has a positive direction somewhere. This condition is open, so it holds at a point $v_0=(x_0,w_0,t_0,s_0)$ with $x_0\in U$, $t_0
eq 0$ and $G_ w(v_0)
eq 0$. Indeed, the first two conditions define a dense open set, and the zero set of $G_ w$ has empty interior, since vanishing of $G_ w$ on an open set would give $G_{w ar w}=0$ there, contradicting the positivity of the vertical Hessian. Let $H$ be the Levi-orthogonal complement of the vertical tangent space $V$ at $v_0$. The Euler identities in the proof of lemma 11.12.1 give \[  K:=\ker \partial G(v_0)=H\oplus (V\cap K), \qquad \dim _{\mathbb C}(V\cap K)=r-1.  \] Indeed, $\partial G$ vanishes on $H$, and its value on the vertical radial vector is $G(v_0)>0$. The two summands are Levi orthogonal, the vertical summand is positive definite, and the horizontal summand has a positive direction. Thus the Levi form of $G$ restricted to $K$ has at least $r$ positive eigenvalues. Since $G_ w(v_0)
eq 0$, the space $K$ is the graph of a linear map defined on $T_{b_0}^{1,0}B$, where $b_0=(x_0,t_0,s_0)$. Choose a local holomorphic function $g$ near $b_0$ with $g(b_0)=w_0$ whose graph has tangent space $K$ at $v_0$. Then $F=G\circ \operatorname {Graph}(g)$ has a critical point at $b_0$, and its Levi form there is the restriction of the Levi form of $G$ to $K$. Keep this first jet of $g$ fixed and vary its quadratic jet. The mixed second derivatives of $F$ do not change, while in local coordinates $z$ on $B$ the pure second derivatives satisfy \[  F_{\alpha  eta }(b_0)=A_{\alpha  eta }+G_ w(v_0)g_{\alpha  eta }(b_0),  \] where $A$ is fixed. Since $G_ w(v_0)
e 0$, we can prescribe the pure quadratic part of $F$ to be $	au \operatorname {Re}\sum _\alpha z_\alpha ^2$, whose real Hessian has eigenvalues $\pm 2	au $. If $	au $ is larger than half the operator norm of the real Hessian of the fixed mixed part, the full real Hessian is invertible by the Neumann-series criterion. The critical point is then nondegenerate, with the same Levi form. Step 3: stability of the test. Choose compact neighborhoods $C'\subset \operatorname {int}C$ of $b_0$ on which $g$ is defined, with $C$ holomorphically convex and $t(C)\subset \{ |t-t_0|\leq |t_0|/4\} $. A small closed Euclidean ball in a closed affine embedding of $B$ is such a set $C$, since linear functions separate points outside the ball from the ball. Fix a smooth Hermitian background metric on $E$ and its compact unit sphere bundle $\Sigma $. By homogeneity, the $C^2$ distance between metrics on $\Sigma $ controls their $C^2$ distance on each fixed compact subset of $E^	imes $. Persistence of nondegenerate critical points and openness of the conditions on the Levi eigenvalues therefore give a neighborhood $\mathcal V_ G$ of $G|_\Sigma $ for the $C^2$ topology and a number $\delta _ G>0$ with the following property: for every metric whose restriction to $\Sigma $ lies in $\mathcal V_ G$ and every holomorphic function within $\delta _ G$ of $g$ uniformly on $C$, the restriction of the metric to the graph of the function still has a nondegenerate critical point over $C'$ with at least $r$ positive Levi eigenvalues. Here the Cauchy estimates on $C'$ turn uniform closeness on $C$ into $C^2$ closeness on $C'$. Step 4: one hypersurface for all metrics. The restrictions of the candidate metrics to $\Sigma $ form a subspace of the separable metrizable space $C^2(\Sigma )$. This subspace is second countable, hence Lindelöf, so the cover by the neighborhoods $\mathcal V_ G$ has a countable subcover $(\mathcal V_ j)_{j\geq 1}$, with associated data $C_ j,g_ j,\delta _ j$. For $D_\lambda (x,w,t,s)=(x,\lambda w,\lambda t,\lambda s)$, \[  G\circ D_\lambda =|\lambda |^2G.  \] Dilation therefore preserves critical points of restrictions to graphs, their real nondegeneracy and their Levi inertia, for every candidate metric. It maps the graph of a function $g$ over $C$ to the graph of $\lambda g\circ d_\lambda ^{-1}$ over $d_\lambda (C)$, with $d_\lambda $ as in lemma 11.16.2 . A function within $|\lambda |\delta _ j$ of $\lambda g_ j\circ d_\lambda ^{-1}$ on $d_\lambda (C_ j)$ pulls back under the dilation to a function within $\delta _ j$ of $g_ j$ on $C_ j$. In particular, the metric neighborhood $\mathcal V_ j$ needs no change. Applying lemma 11.16.2 , we obtain one function $f\in \mathcal O(B)$ that satisfies all the dilated tests. Its graph $\mathcal S$ is biholomorphic to the connected affine Stein manifold $B$, and it is smooth and closed in the open subset $\{ x\in U,\  t
eq 0\} $ of $E^	imes $. Every candidate metric belongs to some $\mathcal V_ j$, so its restriction to $\mathcal S$ has the required nondegenerate critical point. Since $\dim _{\mathbb C}\mathcal S=n+r-1$, at least $r$ positive Levi eigenvalues leave at most $n-1$ negative ones. $\square$ Corollary 11.16.4 . 40E5740882E3 For each $e\geq 0$, the bundle $E$ of corollary 11.15.6 can be chosen so that $E^	imes $ contains a connected smooth Stein hypersurface on which the restriction of every smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric on $E$ has a nondegenerate critical point with at least two positive Levi eigenvalues and at most one negative Levi eigenvalue. Proof. The bundle constructed in the proof of theorem 11.15.5 is a fiber of an algebraic family on a chart of the prioritary stack, so it is algebraic. Apply theorem 11.16.3 with $n=r=2$, using the curvature obstruction of corollary 11.15.6 . $\square$

text: Corollary 11.16.4 . 40E5740882E3 For each $e\geq 0$, the bundle $E$ of corollary 11.15.6 can be chosen so that $E^\times $ contains a connected smooth Stein hypersurface on which the restriction of every smooth strongly pseudoconvex squared Finsler metric on $E$ has a nondegenerate critical point with at least two positive Levi eigenvalues and at most one negative Levi eigenvalue. Proof. The bundle constructed in the proof of theorem 11.15.5 is a fiber of an algebraic family on a chart of the prioritary stack, so it is algebraic. Apply theorem 11.16.3 with $n=r=2$, using the curvature obstruction of corollary 11.15.6 . $\square$

title: 11.17 Concave neighborhoods and dual norms
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
A relatively compact neighborhood $\Omega $ of the zero section of a vector bundle $E$ determines a norm on $E^*$, the support function $\xi \mapsto \max _{v\in \overline\Omega \cap E_ x}|\xi (v)|$ of its fibers. If the boundary of $\Omega $ is sufficiently concave in the horizontal directions, holomorphic sections touching the boundary from inside show that this support norm has plurisubharmonic square, and supporting balls give it uniform convexity in the fibers. Consequently, when the dual norms are obstructed as in theorem 11.9.4 , such neighborhoods cannot exist. In terms of exhaustion functions, this bounds the convexity of the complement of the zero section in the projective completion of $E$. In this subsection, $E	o X$ is a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$, and $n\geq 1$. Fix a smooth Hermitian metric $k$ on $E$, with real inner product $k_{\mathbb R}=\operatorname {Re}k$ and dual norm $|\cdot |_{k^*}$. For a smooth real function $f$, write $\mathcal L_ f$ for its complex Hessian. Let $\Omega $ be an open set with smooth boundary, defined near $\partial \Omega $ by $f<0$ with $\mathrm df
e 0$ on $\partial \Omega $. We say that $\partial \Omega $ has at least $n$ negative Levi directions if, at every boundary point, $\mathcal L_ f$ has at least $n$ negative eigenvalues on $\ker \partial f$. Lemma 11.17.1 . 7A772B0D8822 Fix $\delta ,B>0$. On a finite-dimensional Hermitian vector space, put \[  s_ c(\xi )=|\xi (c)|+\delta |\xi |  \] for covectors $\xi $ and vectors $c$ with $|c|\leq B$. There is $\gamma >0$, depending only on $\delta $ and $B$, such that $s_ c^2-\gamma |\xi |^2$ is real convex for every such $c$. Proof. For $0<	au \leq 1$, replace $s_ c$ by the norm \[  s_{c,	au }(\xi )=\sqrt{|\xi (c)|^2+	au |\xi |^2}+\delta |\xi |,  \] which is smooth off zero. Its Lipschitz constant is at most $L=\sqrt{B^2+1}+\delta $, uniformly in $c$ and $	au $. All derivatives below are real derivatives on the dual space. At $\xi 
e 0$, set $u=\xi /|\xi |$ and decompose a vector as $w=\alpha u+b$ with $b$ orthogonal to $u$ for the real inner product. Write $s=s_{c,	au }$ and $A=\mathrm ds_\xi (w)$. Since the first summand of $s$ is convex and $s\geq \delta |\xi |$, \[  D^2s(w,w)\geq \delta  rac{|b|^2}{|\xi |},\qquad D^2(s^2)(w,w)\geq 2A^2+2\delta ^2|b|^2.  \] Homogeneity gives $\mathrm ds_\xi (u)=s(\xi )/|\xi |\geq \delta $. Since $|\mathrm ds_\xi (b)|\leq L|b|$, we have \[  |w|^2\leq  rac{2A^2}{\delta ^2} +\left(1+ rac{2L^2}{\delta ^2}ight)|b|^2.  \] Take $\gamma =\delta ^4/(\delta ^2+2L^2)$. Then $\gamma \leq \delta ^2/2$ and $\gamma (1+2L^2/\delta ^2)=\delta ^2$, so $D^2(s^2)(w,w)\geq 2\gamma |w|^2$. The homogeneous function $s^2-\gamma |\xi |^2$ of degree two extends as a $C^1$ function at zero with differential zero. Its restriction to every real line is convex, including at zero, because its second derivative is nonnegative away from zero and its first derivatives match there. Thus it is convex on the whole space. Finally, \[  0\leq s_{c,	au }(\xi )-s_ c(\xi )\leq \sqrt	au \, |\xi |,  \] and the locally uniform limit as $	au \downarrow 0$ proves the assertion with the same $\gamma $. $\square$ Theorem 11.17.2 . 854B49CB03B9 Suppose that a relatively compact neighborhood $\Omega \Subset E$ of the zero section has smooth boundary with at least $n$ negative Levi directions. Then \[  p(x,\xi )=\max _{v\in \overline\Omega \cap E_ x}|\xi (v)|  \] is a continuous complex norm on $E^*$ whose square $Q=p^2$ is plurisubharmonic on the total space of $E^*$. For some $\gamma >0$, each function $Q(x,\cdot )-\gamma |\cdot |_{k^*}^2$ is real convex. If $E$ is ample, $E^*$ also admits a smooth complex norm with strictly plurisubharmonic square off the zero section. Proof. Step 1: basic bounds. Put $A_ x=\overline\Omega \cap E_ x$. By compactness of $X$ there are $0<a_0<b_0$ such that, in every fiber, the closed $k$-ball of radius $a_0$ is contained in $\Omega $ and $\overline\Omega $ lies in the open ball of radius $b_0$. The maximum defining $p$ is attained, and \[  a_0|\xi |_{k^*}\leq p(x,\xi )\leq b_0|\xi |_{k^*}.  \] As a supremum of absolute values of linear functionals, $p$ is complex homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. Step 2: support points. Fix $\xi _0
e 0$ and a maximizing point $v_0\in A_{x_0}$. It lies on $\partial \Omega $, since at an interior point a small vertical displacement would increase $|\xi _0(v)|$. Multiply $\xi _0$ by a complex number of modulus one to obtain $\eta $ with $\eta (v_0)=p(x_0,\xi _0)=a>0$. Then $\ell =\operatorname {Re}\eta $ satisfies $\ell \leq a$ on $A_{x_0}$. Choose a smooth defining function $f$ near the boundary, with $\Omega =\{ f<0\} $ and $\mathrm df
e 0$ there. Let $V=T^{1,0}_{v_0}E_{x_0}$ be the vertical tangent space and $T=\ker \partial f(v_0)$. Choose an $n$-dimensional complex subspace $W\subset T$ on which $\mathcal L_ f$ is negative definite. We first show that the vertical differential $\mathrm d_ vf(v_0)$ is nonzero. Otherwise $V\subset T$, and counting dimensions gives $W\cap V
e \{ 0\} $. A vector in this intersection has negative vertical Levi form, and the two corresponding real directions show that the real vertical Hessian of $f$ has a negative direction. Its negative cone is open, hence contains a direction $w$ with $\ell (w)>0$. Since the vertical first derivative vanishes, Taylor expansion gives $f(v_0+tw)<0$ for small $t>0$, contradicting $\ell \leq a$ on $A_{x_0}$. The boundary of $A_{x_0}$ is therefore smooth at $v_0$. Since the supporting functional $\ell $ attains its maximum on $A_{x_0}$ there, \[  \mathrm d_ vf(v_0)=c\, \mathrm d\ell ,\qquad c>0;  \] the sign follows because an inward direction along which $\ell $ increases would contradict the maximality. On the affine hyperplane $\{ \ell =a\} $ of the fiber, the restriction of $f$ has a local minimum zero at $v_0$: a point there with $f<0$ would allow an additional displacement increasing $\ell $ within $\Omega $. The real vertical Hessian of $f$ is thus nonnegative on $\ker \mathrm d\ell $. Consequently $\mathcal L_ f$ is nonnegative on the complex space $V\cap T$, of dimension $r-1$. Hence $W\cap V=\{ 0\} $, and the projection $W	o T^{1,0}_{x_0}X$ is an isomorphism. Step 3: plurisubharmonicity. In local coordinates $z$ centered at $x_0$, choose a holomorphic section $\sigma _0$ through $v_0$ with tangent space $W$. The function $f\circ \sigma _0$ has zero first derivative and negative definite mixed Hessian. Its quadratic expansion is \[  f(\sigma _0(z))=\sum H_{\alpha  ar eta }z_\alpha  ar z_ eta +2\operatorname {Re}P(z)+O(|z|^3),  \] where $P$ is a holomorphic quadratic polynomial. Choose a vertical vector $b$ with $\partial _ vf(b)=1$, and replace $\sigma _0$ by $\sigma =\sigma _0-bP$. This preserves the first jet and cancels the pure quadratic part. Thus, after shrinking the chart, \[  f(\sigma (z))\leq -\epsilon |z|^2, \qquad \sigma (0)=v_0,  \] for some $\epsilon >0$. In particular $\sigma (z)\in A_ z$ throughout the chart. Compactness of $\overline\Omega $ makes $p$ upper semicontinuous: for convergent covectors, the corresponding maximizing vectors have a subsequence whose limit lies in the limiting fiber of $\overline\Omega $. The supporting section gives the opposite inequality $p(z,\xi )\geq |\xi (\sigma (z))|$, with equality at $(x_0,\xi _0)$. Therefore $p$ is continuous off the zero section, and its upper bound gives continuity at zero. The holomorphic pairing $\xi (\sigma (z))$ is nonzero near the contact point, and its logarithmic absolute value is a pluriharmonic function lying below $\log p$ and equal to it at $(x_0,\xi _0)$. The mean-value property on small holomorphic disks therefore gives the submean inequality for $\log p$ at every point off the zero section. Thus $\log p$, and then $Q=\exp (2\log p)$ by Jensen's inequality, are plurisubharmonic there. At the zero section the continuous nonnegative function $Q$ vanishes, so its submean inequality on disks also holds there. Step 4: uniform convexity in the fibers. Consider all maximizing triples $(x,\xi ,v)$ with $|\xi |_{k^*}=1$. They form a compact set, since $p$ is continuous, and by Step 2 the vertical differential $\mathrm d_ vf$ does not vanish at these support points. Thus there are uniform constants $m>0$, $ho >0$ and $C\geq 1$ such that, for vertical vectors $w$, \[  |\mathrm d_ vf|\geq m,\qquad f(v+w)\leq \mathrm d_ vf(w)+C|w|_ k^2\quad (|w|_ k\leq ho ).  \] Choose $0<\delta <\min \{ a_0/2,ho /2,m/(2C)\} $. At a support point, write $N$ for the outward real vertical unit normal and set $c=v-\delta N$. If $|w+\delta N|_ k\leq \delta $, then \[  k_{\mathbb R}(w,N)\leq - rac{|w|_ k^2}{2\delta },\qquad f(v+w)\leq -\left( rac{m}{2\delta }-Cight)|w|_ k^2\leq 0.  \] All these points lie in the neighborhood where $f$ is defined, so the closed ball $\overline B_ k(c,\delta )$ is contained in $A_ x$. The support function of this ball is $s_ c(\xi )=|\xi (c)|+\delta |\xi |_{k^*}\leq p(x,\xi )$. For a maximizing covector of unit norm, with its phase normalized as in Step 2, the real part $\operatorname {Re}\eta $ has real dual norm one and its metric dual vector is $N$. Hence $\operatorname {Re}\eta (N)=1$, and since $|\eta (N)|\leq 1$, also $\eta (N)=1$. We obtain $\eta (c)=a-\delta >0$, and therefore $s_ c(\xi )=a$. Homogeneity now gives \[  Q(x,\xi )=\sup _ c s_ c(\xi )^2,  \] where $c$ ranges over the centers of the supporting balls in the fiber. Every such center satisfies $|c|_ k\leq b_0+\delta $, so by lemma 11.17.1 all the functions $s_ c^2-\gamma |\xi |_{k^*}^2$ are convex for the same $\gamma >0$. Their supremum is finite, and it proves the asserted strong convexity of $Q$. Step 5: smoothing. Finally, if $E$ is ample, proposition 11.11.2 gives the smooth strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function on $E^*$ required in proposition 11.10.5 , and applying that proposition to $Q$ gives the smooth norm. $\square$ For a complex manifold of dimension $N$ and an integer $1\leq q\leq N$, we say that the manifold is $q$-convex if it has a smooth real exhaustion function with at least $N-q+1$ positive Levi eigenvalues outside a compact set; here an exhaustion function is one whose sublevel sets are compact. A $q$-convex manifold is also $q'$-convex for $q\leq q'\leq N$. We call such integers $q$ the smooth convexity indices of the manifold, and the smallest of them, when one exists, its least smooth convexity index . Lemma 11.17.3 . 9020E77B2318 Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$, and let $Z\subset Y$ be a closed complex submanifold of dimension $D\geq 1$. If the least smooth convexity index of $Z$ is $\kappa \leq D$, then every smooth convexity index of $Y$ is at least $\kappa $. Proof. Suppose that $Y$ is $p$-convex for an integer $1\leq p<\kappa $. Then a smooth exhaustion function $\psi $ has at least $N-p+1$ positive Levi eigenvalues outside a compact set $K\subset Y$. Its restriction to the closed submanifold $Z$ is an exhaustion function, since its sublevel sets are closed subsets of the compact sublevel sets of $\psi $, and $K\cap Z$ is compact. At a point of $Z\setminus K$, choose a complex subspace $P\subset T^{1,0}Y$ of dimension $N-p+1$ on which the Levi form of $\psi $ is positive definite. Then \[  \dim _{\mathbb C}(P\cap T^{1,0}Z)\geq (N-p+1)+D-N=D-p+1.  \] The Levi form of $\psi |_ Z$ is the restriction of the Levi form of $\psi $, since the inclusion is holomorphic, so it has at least $D-p+1$ positive eigenvalues. Since $p<\kappa \leq D$, this shows that $Z$ is $p$-convex, which contradicts the definition of $\kappa $. $\square$ In the following results, projectivizations parametrize complex lines. Corollary 11.17.4 . B53EB4EFC135 Suppose that $E$ is ample and that $E^*$ admits no smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square off the zero section. Then the complement \[  Z\setminus Y,\qquad Z=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E), \quad Y=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X),  \] is not $r$-convex. Proof. The chart of $Z$ where the $\mathcal O_ X$-coordinate is nonzero is identified with the total space of $E$, and $Y$ is its zero section. Suppose that $Z\setminus Y$ is $r$-convex. Since $\dim Z=n+r$, a smooth exhaustion function $\psi $ then has at least $n+1$ positive Levi eigenvalues outside a compact set $K$. Choose a relatively compact disk-bundle neighborhood $D\Subset E$ of $Y$. The set $Z\setminus D$ is compact and disjoint from $Y$. Choose a regular value $c$ of $\psi $ greater than its maximum on $Z\setminus D$ and on $K$. Since $\{ \psi \leq c\} $ is compact in $Z\setminus Y$, the set $\Omega =\{ \psi >c\} \cup Y$ is an open neighborhood of $Y$. Its closure is a compact subset of $D$, and its boundary is the regular level set $\{ \psi =c\} $. The defining function $f=c-\psi $ has at least $n+1$ negative Levi eigenvalues there. Restriction to the complex tangent hyperplane removes at most one negative direction, leaving at least $n$. Since $E$ is ample, theorem 11.17.2 produces a smooth complex norm on $E^*$ with plurisubharmonic square, a contradiction. $\square$ Corollary 11.17.5 . E29138267596 For every $e\geq 0$, there is an ample rank-two bundle $E$ on the Hirzebruch surface $X=\mathbb F_ e$ such that $\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)$ is not $2$-convex. The bundle may be chosen with the slope-stability and Chern classes of theorem 11.15.5 . Proof. Use theorem 11.15.5 to choose $E$ whose dual Dolbeault operator lies in the $C^4$ neighborhood of theorem 11.9.4 ; the split dual bundle satisfies the hypotheses of that theorem by proposition 11.13.4 . Thus $E^*$ admits no smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, and corollary 11.17.4 with $r=2$ gives the assertion. $\square$

text: Lemma 11.17.3 . 9020E77B2318 Let $Y$ be a complex manifold of dimension $N$, and let $Z\subset Y$ be a closed complex submanifold of dimension $D\geq 1$. Since $p<\kappa \leq D$, this shows that $Z$ is $p$-convex, which contradicts the definition of $\kappa $. $\square$

title: 11.18 Curvature and projective complement exhaustions
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
Corollary 11.17.4 excludes $r$-convexity of the complement of the zero section in the projective completion, but it does not decide which larger indices occur. Upper bounds come from curvature. The reciprocal of the squared norm of a Hermitian metric is an exhaustion near the removed zero section, and every positive direction of the curvature, evaluated at a fiber vector, contributes a positive Levi eigenvalue. For a stable bundle of positive Gauduchon degree, the Hermitian–Einstein metric provides such a direction at every fiber vector. In this subsection, $E	o X$ is a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$, $n\geq 1$, and $h$ is a smooth Hermitian metric on $E$. In a holomorphic frame, write the matrix of $h$ as $M$, using column vectors and an inner product linear in its first argument, so that $h(v,v)=v^*Mv$. Put \[  F_ h= ar\partial (M^{-1}\partial M) =\sum _{\alpha , eta }F_{\alpha  ar eta }\, \mathrm dz_\alpha \wedge \mathrm d ar z_ eta , \qquad R_ h(u, ar u)=\sum _{\alpha , eta }F_{\alpha  ar eta }u_\alpha  ar u_ eta .  \] For $v\in E_ x$, the real $(1,1)$-form $\alpha _{h,v}=\mathrm i\, h(F_ hv,v)$ has the Hermitian coefficient form $u\mapsto h(R_ h(u, ar u)v,v)$. For a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, the mean curvature of $h$ is the $h$-Hermitian endomorphism $K_{\omega ,h}=\Lambda _\omega (\mathrm iF_ h)$, where $\Lambda _\omega $ denotes contraction with $\omega $, so that $\Lambda _\omega ( eta )\, \omega ^ n=n eta \wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ for $(1,1)$-forms $ eta $. The curvature $F_ h$ is unscaled: for a line bundle, the curvature $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h$ of section 11.9 is $\mathrm iF_ h/(2\pi )$. Use the line convention for projectivization and put \[  U_ E=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X).  \] The chart $[1:v]$ identifies the total space of $E$ with an open subset of $\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)$, in which $\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)$ is the zero section; thus $U_ E$ contains $E^	imes $. Its complex dimension is $n+r$. Convexity is understood in the sense of the smooth exhaustions of 11.17 . Lemma 11.18.1 . 5022159B8350 Put $G(v)=h(v,v)$ and $ho =G^{-1}$ on $E^	imes $. In a holomorphic frame that is unitary and Chern-normal at $x$, meaning that $M(x)$ is the identity and the first derivatives of $M$ vanish at $x$, the complex Hessian of $ho $ at $(x,v)$ is \[  \mathcal L_ho (u,w) = rac{h(R_ h(u, ar u)v,v)}{G^2} - rac{|w|_ h^2}{G^2} + rac{2|h(w,v)|^2}{G^3}, \qquad u\in T_ x^{1,0}X,\quad w\in E_ x,  \] where $(u,w)$ are the horizontal and vertical components of a tangent vector. There are no mixed horizontal–vertical terms, and the vertical block has exactly one positive and $r-1$ negative eigenvalues. Proof. Such a frame is obtained by a constant change of frame making it unitary at $x$, followed by a holomorphic change of frame, linear in the coordinates, that cancels $\partial M$. Then $F_{\alpha  ar eta }=-\partial _\alpha \partial _{ ar eta }M$ at $x$. The horizontal first derivatives of $G$ and its mixed horizontal–vertical second derivatives vanish. The horizontal complex Hessian of $G$ is $-h(R_ h(u, ar u)v,v)$, its vertical complex Hessian is $|w|_ h^2$, and its vertical first derivative in the direction $w$ is $h(w,v)$. Apply \[  \partial  ar\partial (G^{-1}) =2G^{-3}\partial G\wedge  ar\partial G-G^{-2}\partial  ar\partial G.  \] The vertical block equals $G^{-1}>0$ at $w=v$ and equals $-|w|_ h^2/G^2$ when $w\perp _ h v$. These two subspaces are orthogonal for the vertical block, which proves the statement about its eigenvalues. $\square$ Theorem 11.18.2 . B93CB03C68B7 Let $s$ be an integer with $0\leq s\leq n$. Suppose that for every $x\in X$ and every $0
e v\in E_ x$, the coefficient form of $\alpha _{h,v}$ has at least $s$ positive eigenvalues. Then $U_ E$ is $(n+r-s)$-convex. Proof. By lemma 11.18.1 , the horizontal block of $\mathcal L_ho $ has at least $s$ positive eigenvalues and the vertical block has one. Their direct sum thus has at least $s+1$ positive eigenvalues at every point of $E^	imes $. Choose $\epsilon >0$ and a smooth function $\chi :[0,+\infty )	o [0,1]$ equal to one on $[0,\epsilon ]$ and to zero on $[2\epsilon ,+\infty )$. Define \[  \psi ([1:v])= rac{\chi (G(v))}{G(v)}\quad (v
e 0),  \] and extend $\psi $ by zero on the divisor at infinity $\mathbb P(E)$. This extension is smooth. Indeed, near a point $[0:v]$ with $v
e 0$, use a local representative $[u:v]$ in a projective chart. On its intersection with the affine chart, $G(v/u)=h(v,v)/|u|^2$ tends to infinity as $u	o 0$, so $\chi (G)$ vanishes in a neighborhood of the point. If $\det h'=\mathrm e^ f\det h$, the two curvature representatives differ by $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, whose integral against $\omega ^{n-1}$ vanishes by lemma 11.1.2 . Thus the degree depends only on the Bott–Chern class $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(E)$ of the closed form $\mathrm i\operatorname {tr}F_ h/(2\pi )$, and it is the pairing of this class with $\omega ^{n-1}$. This holds, in particular, when $\omega $ is Gauduchon, $E$ is $\omega $-slope-stable, and $\deg _\omega E>0$. Proof. For $v
e 0$, the trace of $\alpha _{h,v}$ with respect to $\omega $ is $h(K_{\omega ,h}v,v)>0$, and a Hermitian form with positive trace has a positive eigenvalue. Apply theorem 11.18.2 with $s=1$. Under the Gauduchon and stability hypotheses, the classical existence theorem for Hermitian–Einstein metrics on stable bundles gives a metric $h$ with $K_{\omega ,h}=\lambda \operatorname {Id}_ E$, where $\lambda $ is a constant. Taking the trace and integrating the contraction identity gives \[  r\lambda \int _ X\omega ^ n =n\int _ X\operatorname {tr}(\mathrm iF_ h)\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =2\pi n\deg _\omega E>0.  \] Here $\operatorname {tr}F_ h= ar\partial \partial \log \det M$, so $\mathrm i\operatorname {tr}F_ h/(2\pi )$ represents $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(E)$. Choose $E$ as in corollary 11.17.5 , $\mu _ P$-stable and with $c_1(E)=4H$. By the choice of $E$, the complement is not $2$-convex. Finally, $1$-convexity would imply $2$-convexity, so the least index is three. $\square$
