For the potential $U$ and its smooth decreasing approximants $U_ N$ constructed in the proof of theorem 13.14.18 , the current $T=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ has integrable coefficients and \[  \| \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N-T\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2^{1-N}M.  \] Its pointwise determinant satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U) \geq (\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n, \qquad \int _ X(\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n=+\infty .  \] Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N)^ n\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Proof. Write $T_ j=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ for the smooth positive forms in that construction, and put \[  S_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ jT_ j,\qquad \delta _ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j=2^{-N}.  \] The smooth positive forms $S_ N$ increase pointwise, and the Gauduchon identity gives \[  \int _ XS_ N\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=(1-\delta _ N)M.  \] By monotone convergence of their traces, the series of matrices has a finite positive limit $S$ almost everywhere. The coefficients of $S$ are integrable, because in a $\gamma $-unitary frame the absolute value of every coefficient of a positive matrix is bounded by its trace. Positivity and the same trace identity give \[  \| S-S_ N\| _{L^1(\gamma )}=\delta _ N M.  \] In particular, $S_ N\to S$ in the sense of distributions. Since \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N=S_ N+\delta _ N\omega \longrightarrow \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U  \] in the sense of distributions, by $L^1$ convergence of the potentials, we obtain $T=S$. The triangle inequality now gives \[  \| \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N-T\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq \| S_ N-S\| _{L^1(\gamma )} +\delta _ N\| \omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )} =2\delta _ N M.  \] To compare $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)$ with the determinant, fix $N$ and set $V_ N=U-U_ N$. The remaining partial sums give $\delta _ N\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ N\geq 0$ and $V_ N\leq 0$. For $t>0$, the function $W_{N,t}=U_ N+\max (V_ N,-t)$ is bounded, and its current is the sum of two positive terms: \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W_{N,t} =S_ N+\bigl (\delta _ N\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (V_ N,-t)\bigr ).  \] On $D_ t=\{ U>-t\} $, the inequality $U_ N\leq 0$ gives $V_ N\geq U>-t$, and consequently $W_{N,t}=U=\max (U,-t)$ there. Locality and positivity of bounded products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U) \geq \mathbf1_{D_ t}S_ N^ n.  \] The smooth measure $S_ N^ n$ gives no mass to the pluripolar pole set of $U$, so letting $t\to \infty $ proves $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)\geq S_ N^ n$. The positive matrices $S_ N$ increase to $T$ almost everywhere, so their determinants increase to $\det _\gamma T$. Monotone convergence on every Borel set gives the asserted inequality between $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)$ and the determinant measure. Finally, for every $N\geq j$, positivity gives $S_ N\geq a_ jT_ j$. Hence both the measurable limit and the smooth approximating forms satisfy \[  \int _ X(\det _\gamma T)\gamma ^ n \geq a_ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n\geq 2^ j, \qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ N)^ n \geq a_ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n\geq 2^ j.  \] The first bound holds for every $j$, and the second for every $N\geq j$; together they prove the two assertions about infinite mass. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.14.22
text: Corollary 13.14.22 . 1D7A78F6BD02 If the bounded mass property fails, there are nonpositive potentials $w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $0<\varepsilon <1$, such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon \geq (1-\varepsilon )\omega , \qquad \mathcal I(pw_\varepsilon )=\mathcal O_ X\quad (p>0),  \] and such that both the integral of the pointwise determinant $\det _\gamma (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )$ against $\gamma ^ n$ and the extended Monge–Ampère mass of $w_\varepsilon $ are infinite. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the potentials converge to zero in $L^1$, their currents converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, and their full trace measures $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ converge to $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation. Proof. Take $w_\varepsilon =\varepsilon U$, with $U$ and $T=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ as in proposition 13.14.21 . Its current is \[  T_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )\omega +\varepsilon T.  \] The lower bound and the two $L^1$ convergence assertions follow immediately. The full trace measures have integrable densities, and their distance from $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation is at most \[  \varepsilon \| T-\omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )}.  \] Every multiplier ideal is trivial by the exponential integrability of $U$ proved in theorem 13.14.18 . Since $T_\varepsilon \geq \varepsilon T$ almost everywhere, the determinant integral of $T_\varepsilon $ is at least $\varepsilon ^ n$ times that of $T$, hence infinite. The extended mass of $w_\varepsilon $ is infinite by the proof of corollary 13.14.19 . $\square$

title: Corollary 13.14.23
text: Corollary 13.14.23 . BED3510B9193 Suppose $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. Let $(\varepsilon _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ and $(b_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be real sequences with $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$, $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, and $b_ j>\int _ X\omega ^ n$. There are smooth potentials $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xw_ j=0$ such that \[  \begin{gathered} \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)\omega , \qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n=b_ j, \\ \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2M\varepsilon _ j. \end{gathered}  \] Moreover, $w_ j\to 0$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}\to 1$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every fixed $p>0$. The full Gauduchon trace measures converge to $\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ in total variation. Proof. By proposition 13.14.15 , we can choose a smooth $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n>\varepsilon _ j^{-n}b_ j.  \] Put $T_ j=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. The polynomial \[  F_ j(s)=\int _ X\bigl ((1-s)\omega +sT_ j\bigr )^ n, \qquad 0\leq s\leq \varepsilon _ j,  \] satisfies $F_ j(0)<b_ j$, and also $F_ j(\varepsilon _ j)\geq \varepsilon _ j^ n\int _ XT_ j^ n>b_ j$ by positivity of the mixed terms. The intermediate value theorem gives $s_ j\in (0,\varepsilon _ j)$ with $F_ j(s_ j)=b_ j$. Set $w_ j=s_ ju_ j$. Then $\sup _ Xw_ j=0$, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j=(1-s_ j)\omega +s_ jT_ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)\omega $, and $w_ j$ has the prescribed mass $b_ j$. The Gauduchon identity gives $\| T_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )}=\| \omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )}=M$. Hence \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\| _{L^1(\gamma )} =s_ j\| T_ j-\omega \| _{L^1(\gamma )} \leq 2M\varepsilon _ j.  \] Since the absolute value of the trace of a Hermitian matrix is bounded by the trace of its absolute value, the same bound holds for the total variation of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. With $K_\omega $ as in ( 5.26.1 ), we also have $\| w_ j\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq K_\omega \varepsilon _ j$. Finally, let $\alpha ,C$ be the constants of lemma 5.26.2 for $(X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V)$, and fix $p>0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, one has $ps_ j\leq \alpha $. Convexity of the exponential function, applied with weight $ps_ j/\alpha $, gives \[  0\leq \mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}-1 \leq \frac{ps_ j}{\alpha }\bigl (\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha u_ j}-1\bigr ).  \] Integrating, we bound the $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ norm of $\mathrm{e}^{-pw_ j}-1$ by $pC\varepsilon _ j/\alpha $, which proves the last convergence. $\square$

title: 13.15 Weighted Monge–Ampère measures
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, and let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form. Capacity refers to the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 5.29 . For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ we write \[  \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)  \] for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 , and we put \[  r_ n=\max (n-2,0).  \] By section 13.14 , the measure $\mu _ u$ can have infinite mass when the bounded mass property fails. Its mass above depth $t$, on the superlevel set $\{ u\geq -t\} $, is nevertheless bounded by a polynomial of degree $r_ n$ in $t$, because the masses of bounded potentials grow at most polynomially in their range. A weight that decreases sufficiently fast in the depth $-u$ compensates for this growth. If $w:[0,+\infty )\to [0,+\infty )$ is a nonincreasing function with $w(t)\to 0$ as $t\to +\infty $, we call \[  w(-u)\, \mu _ u  \] the damped Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ with weight $w$; the weight is set to zero on the pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which $\mu _ u$ does not charge. The main examples are the exponential weights $\mathrm{e}^{-pt}$ and the polynomial weights $(1+t)^{-q}$. For suitable weights the damped measures are finite, uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to capacity, and continuous under convergence in capacity, a property that the extended measures themselves lack. Removing the weight requires uniform control of the mass on deep sublevel sets; we characterize this control and show by examples that such mass can persist although the potentials converge in capacity.

title: 13.15.1 Range and restricted mass
text: We first bound the Monge–Ampère mass of a bounded potential polynomially in its range. The first mixed mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is bounded independently of $v$ by the Gauduchon trace. Local Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimates turn this into a bound of degree $j-1$ in the range for the $j$th mixed mass, and Stokes' theorem expresses the top mass in terms of the lower ones. Proposition 13.15.2 . 57A94BD59310 There is a constant $C_\omega $ such that, for every $A\geq 0$, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq C_\omega (1+A)^{r_ n} \quad \text{if }v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega ),\  0\leq v\leq A.  \] Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls whose concentric smaller balls, with compact closure in the larger ones, cover $X$. On each larger ball choose a fixed quadratic function $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \omega $, shifted so that $p=v+q$ is plurisubharmonic with $0\leq p\leq A+C$. Let $\kappa $ be the Euclidean form. In the identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-\omega ),  \] the integral of the first term against $\kappa ^{n-1}$ is bounded by a fixed multiple of the global trace mass, which is bounded by corollary 11.5.3 , and the second term is smooth and fixed. Thus $\int \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\wedge \kappa ^{n-1}$ is bounded uniformly in $v$ and $A$; in dimension one, Stokes' theorem replaces the trace bound. By ( 5.27.3 ), on each smaller ball, \[  \int (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)^ j\wedge \kappa ^{n-j}\leq C_ j(1+A)^{j-1} \quad (1\leq j\leq n).  \] Expand $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p+\omega -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ j$ and sum over the finite cover. Since the smooth factors have bounded coefficients, the positive mixed masses satisfy \[  0\leq M_ j(v):=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ j\wedge \omega ^{n-j} \leq C_ j(1+A)^{\max (j-1,0)} \quad (0\leq j\leq n).  \] For smooth $v$, the exact form $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ integrates to zero, as in the proof of theorem 11.1.5 ; the regularization of theorem 5.32.1 and the continuity of bounded products give the same identity for bounded $v$. Thus \[  0=\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n =\sum _{j=0}^ n(-1)^{n-j}\binom nj M_ j(v).  \] Since the mixed masses are nonnegative, it follows that \[  M_ n(v)\leq \sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\binom nj M_ j(v) \leq C_\omega (1+A)^{r_ n}.  \] The largest power is $n-2$ when $n\geq 2$; for $n=1$, only the constant term remains. $\square$ For $n\leq 2$ the bound is uniform, so every compact complex curve or surface has the bounded mass property. In higher dimensions the bound grows with the range, and truncation turns it into a bound for the mass of an unbounded potential above a finite depth. Lemma 13.15.3 . 357B2DE7779E Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. For $t\geq 0$ and every Borel set $E\subset X$, F3E7262939D2 13.15.4 \begin{equation}  \mu _ u(\{ u\geq -t\} )\leq C_\omega (1+t)^{r_ n}, \qquad \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} )\leq (1+t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E). \end{equation} Proof. Put $v_ t=\max (u,-t-1)+t+1$. It is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic and takes values in $[0,t+1]$, and by plurifine locality its Monge–Ampère measure equals $\mu _ u$ on $\{ u\geq -t\} \subset \{ u>-t-1\} $. The first estimate therefore follows from proposition 13.15.2 , after enlarging the constant. For the second, $v_ t/(1+t)$ is a test function for the capacity, and positivity gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t)^ n \leq (1+t)^ n\bigl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ t/(1+t))\bigr )^ n.  \] Restricting this inequality to $E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} $ proves the capacity bound. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.15.2
text: Proposition 13.15.2 . 57A94BD59310 There is a constant $C_\omega $ such that, for every $A\geq 0$, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq C_\omega (1+A)^{r_ n} \quad \text{if }v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega ),\  0\leq v\leq A.  \] Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls whose concentric smaller balls, with compact closure in the larger ones, cover $X$. Since the smooth factors have bounded coefficients, the positive mixed masses satisfy \[  0\leq M_ j(v):=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ j\wedge \omega ^{n-j} \leq C_ j(1+A)^{\max (j-1,0)} \quad (0\leq j\leq n).  \] For smooth $v$, the exact form $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ integrates to zero, as in the proof of theorem 11.1.5 ; the regularization of theorem 5.32.1 and the continuity of bounded products give the same identity for bounded $v$. title: Lemma 13.15.3
text: Lemma 13.15.3 . 357B2DE7779E Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. For $t\geq 0$ and every Borel set $E\subset X$, F3E7262939D2 13.15.4 \begin{equation}  \mu _ u(\{ u\geq -t\} )\leq C_\omega (1+t)^{r_ n}, \qquad \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} )\leq (1+t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E). \end{equation} Proof. For the second, $v_ t/(1+t)$ is a test function for the capacity, and positivity gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t)^ n \leq (1+t)^ n\bigl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ t/(1+t))\bigr )^ n.  \] Restricting this inequality to $E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} $ proves the capacity bound. $\square$

title: Equation 13.15.4
text: F3E7262939D2 13.15.4 \begin{equation}  \mu _ u(\{ u\geq -t\} )\leq C_\omega (1+t)^{r_ n}, \qquad \mu _ u(E\cap \{ u\geq -t\} )\leq (1+t)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E). \end{equation}

title: 13.15.5 Exponential damping
text:
The exponential weight can be handled directly. A convex increasing function with bounded range transforms $u$ into a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and the chain rule shows that the transformed current dominates an exponential multiple of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded transform therefore controls the damped measure. For $a>0$ put $F_ a(t)=a^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{at}$ for $t\leq 0$, with $F_ a(-\infty )=0$. Then $0\leq F_ a\leq a^{-1}$, while $0<F_ a'\leq 1$ and $F_ a''\geq 0$ at finite arguments. Proposition 13.15.6 . 8B51BF8706B7 If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $u\leq 0$, then $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is bounded. The chain rule ( 5.27.9 ) gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ a(u) =\mathrm{e}^{au}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(1-\mathrm{e}^{au})\omega +a\mathrm{e}^{au}\, \mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u.  \] All three summands are positive, and positivity of their bounded mixed products yields the claimed inequality. For general $u$, use the truncations $u_ t=\max (u,-t)$. The bounded functions $F_ a(u_ t)$ decrease and take values between zero and $a^{-1}$, so their limit $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. On the plurifinely open set $D_ t=\{ u>-t\} $, it agrees with $F_ a(u_ t)$. Locality and the bounded case therefore give \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mathbf1_{D_ t}\mu _ u \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Let $t	o +\infty $. The pole set is not charged by $\mu _ u$, and it has zero mass for the bounded product on the right. $\square$ Theorem 13.15.7 . 4394319FDE01 For $p>0$, the damped measures $
u _{p,u}=\mathrm{e}^{pu}\mu _ u$ satisfy \[  
u _{p,u}(X)\leq C_\omega (1+p^{-1})^{r_ n}, \qquad 
u _{p,u}(E)\leq \max (1,n/p)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)  \] for every Borel set $E\subset X$, uniformly over all nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Proof. Take $a=p/n$ in proposition 13.15.6 . Since $F_{p/n}(u)$ takes values in $[0,n/p]$, proposition 13.15.2 with $A=n/p$ gives the total mass bound, after enlarging $C_\omega $. For the capacity bound put $B=\max (1,n/p)$ and $v=F_{p/n}(u)$. Then $v/B$ is a test function for the capacity, and \[  B igl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v/B) igr ) =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(B-1)\omega \geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v.  \] Consequently $
u _{p,u}\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)\leq B^ n\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v/B)$, which gives the second bound. The measures $
u _{p,u}$ do not charge pluripolar sets, because $\mu _ u$ does not. $\square$ Since $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set, multiplication by $\mathrm{e}^{-pu}$ recovers $\mu _ u$ from $
u _{p,u}$, including when its mass is infinite. An additive shift $u\mapsto u+c$ multiplies the damped measure by $\mathrm{e}^{pc}$.

title: Proposition 13.15.6
text: Proposition 13.15.6 . 8B51BF8706B7 If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and $u\leq 0$, then $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is bounded. The chain rule ( 5.27.9 ) gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F_ a(u) =\mathrm{e}^{au}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+(1-\mathrm{e}^{au})\omega +a\mathrm{e}^{au}\, \mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u.  \] All three summands are positive, and positivity of their bounded mixed products yields the claimed inequality. For general $u$, use the truncations $u_ t=\max (u,-t)$. The bounded functions $F_ a(u_ t)$ decrease and take values between zero and $a^{-1}$, so their limit $F_ a(u)$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. On the plurifinely open set $D_ t=\{ u>-t\} $, it agrees with $F_ a(u_ t)$. Locality and the bounded case therefore give \[  \mathrm{e}^{na u}\mathbf1_{D_ t}\mu _ u \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_\omega (F_ a(u)).  \] Let $t\to +\infty $. The pole set is not charged by $\mu _ u$, and it has zero mass for the bounded product on the right. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.15.7
text:
Theorem 13.15.7 . 4394319FDE01 For $p>0$, the damped measures $
u _{p,u}=\mathrm{e}^{pu}\mu _ u$ satisfy \[  
u _{p,u}(X)\leq C_\omega (1+p^{-1})^{r_ n}, \qquad 
u _{p,u}(E)\leq \max (1,n/p)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)  \] for every Borel set $E\subset X$, uniformly over all nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Proof. Take $a=p/n$ in proposition 13.15.6 . Since $F_{p/n}(u)$ takes values in $[0,n/p]$, proposition 13.15.2 with $A=n/p$ gives the total mass bound, after enlarging $C_\omega $. For the capacity bound put $B=\max (1,n/p)$ and $v=F_{p/n}(u)$. Then $v/B$ is a test function for the capacity, and \[  B igl (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v/B) igr ) =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+(B-1)\omega \geq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v.  \] Consequently $
u _{p,u}\leq \mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)\leq B^ n\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v/B)$, which gives the second bound. The measures $

title: 13.15.8 Decreasing weights and capacity continuity
text:
For a general decreasing weight $w$, writing $w(s)=\int _ s^\infty (-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t$ and integrating the finite-depth estimate ( 13.15.4 ) in $t$ bounds both the total mass and the mass on deep sublevel sets. Above any fixed depth, the damped measure is a weighted product of bounded potentials, which is continuous under convergence in capacity; the tail bound then removes the restriction to a fixed depth. Theorem 13.15.9 . EE93EE2035F6 Let $w:[0,+\infty )	o (0,+\infty )$ be continuously differentiable and nonincreasing, with $w(t)	o 0$ as $t	o +\infty $. For $T\geq 0$ define \[  B_ w(T)=\int _ T^\infty (1+t)^{r_ n}(-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Assume $B_ w(0)<+\infty $. For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the damped measures $
u _{w,u}=w(-u)\mu _ u$ satisfy \[  
u _{w,u}(X)\leq C_\omega B_ w(0),\qquad 
u _{w,u}(\{ u<-T\} )\leq C_\omega B_ w(T).  \] For every Borel set $E$ and $T\geq 0$, \[  
u _{w,u}(E)\leq w(0)(1+T)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)+C_\omega B_ w(T).  \] In particular, these measures are uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to capacity. If nonpositive $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfy $u_ j	o u$ in capacity, then $
u _{w,u_ j}ightharpoonup 
u _{w,u}$. Proof. Write $s=-u$. Since $w(s)=\int _ s^\infty (-w'(t))\, \mathrm{d}t$ for finite $s$, and since $\mu _ u$ does not charge the pole set $\{ s=+\infty \} $, Tonelli's theorem and lemma 13.15.3 give \[  \int _ X w(s)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u =\int _0^\infty (-w'(t))\mu _ u(\{ s\leq t\} )\, \mathrm{d}t \leq C_\omega B_ w(0).  \] Restricting the integral to $\{ s>T\} $ gives the same bound with $B_ w(T)$ in place of $B_ w(0)$, since the inner set is then $\{ T<s\leq t\} $, which is empty unless $t>T$. For the capacity bound, the second estimate in ( 13.15.4 ) gives \[  \int _{E\cap \{ s\leq T\} }w(s)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u \leq w(0)(1+T)^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E).  \] Adding the tail estimate for $\{ s>T\} $ proves the asserted bound. Since $B_ w(T)	o 0$, choosing first $T$ large and then the capacity small gives uniform absolute continuity. To prove continuity, fix a continuous nonincreasing $\eta :[0,+\infty )	o [0,1]$, equal to one on $[0,1]$ and zero on $[2,+\infty )$, and put $\eta _ T(s)=\eta (s/T)$. u _{w,u_ j}$ is carried by $\{ u_ j<-T\} $, so by the tail bound its integral against a continuous test function $f$ is at most $C_\omega B_ w(T)\| f\| _\infty $, uniformly in $j$; the same holds for $u$. u _{p,u}(\{ u<-T\} ) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-pT/2}
u _{p/2,u}(X) \leq C_ p\mathrm{e}^{-pT/2}.  \] For polynomial weights, the general estimate takes the following explicit form. Theorem 13.15.11 . B72AF5B37CB7 For every $q>r_ n$, the damped measures \[  \sigma _{q,u}:=(1-u)^{-q}\mu _ u  \] have uniformly bounded mass for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $u\leq 0$. More precisely, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(\{ u<-T\} ) \leq C rac{q}{q-r_ n}(1+T)^{r_ n-q}\quad (T\geq 0),  \] where $C$ depends only on $\omega $. There is also a constant $C_ q$ such that, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(E)\leq C_ q\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{(q-r_ n)/(q+n-r_ n)}.  \] Proof. For $w(t)=(1+t)^{-q}$, direct integration gives \[  B_ w(T)=q\int _ T^\infty (1+t)^{r_ n-q-1}\, \mathrm{d}t = rac{q}{q-r_ n}(1+T)^{r_ n-q}.  \] Thus proposition 13.15.9 gives the mass and tail estimates. For the capacity bound put $\delta =\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)$. If $0<\delta \leq 1$, choose $T=\delta ^{-1/(q+n-r_ n)}\geq 1$ in that theorem. Both $T^ n\delta $ and $T^{r_ n-q}$ equal $\delta ^{(q-r_ n)/(q+n-r_ n)}$, so its two terms have the required bound. If $\delta =0$, let $T	o \infty $; if $\delta >1$, use the total mass bound. $\square$ For $n\geq 2$, the capacity exponent is $1-n/(q+2)$. The threshold $q>n-2$ comes from the mixed-mass estimate in proposition 13.15.2 . Logarithmic factors give weights at the threshold. For $n\geq 3$ and $a>1$, put $r=n-2>0$ and \[  w(t)=(1+t)^{-r}[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^{-a}.  \] Differentiation gives \[  (1+t)^ r(-w'(t)) = rac{r}{(1+t)[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^ a} + rac{a}{(\mathrm{e}+t)[\log (\mathrm{e}+t)]^{a+1}}.  \] The ratios $(\mathrm{e}+t)/(1+t)$ are bounded. The substitution $y=\log (\mathrm{e}+t)$ therefore bounds the integrals of the two terms over $[T,+\infty )$ by fixed multiples of $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$ and $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{-a}$, respectively. Since $a>1$ and $\log (\mathrm{e}+T)\geq 1$, we obtain $B_ w(T)\leq C_{n,a}[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$. Hence, by proposition 13.15.9 , the damped measures $(1-u)^{-(n-2)}[\log (\mathrm{e}-u)]^{-a}\mu _ u$ have uniformly bounded mass, their mass on $\{ u<-T\} $ is at most a constant times $[\log (\mathrm{e}+T)]^{1-a}$, and they are continuous under convergence in capacity. In dimensions one and two, $r_ n=0$ and $B_ w(T)=w(T)$, so every weight satisfying the monotonicity, differentiability and vanishing conditions of proposition 13.15.9 can be used. Damping can restore convergence when every undamped measure has infinite mass. When the bounded mass property fails, take the potential $U$ constructed in the proof of theorem 13.14.18 , whose current has integrable coefficients by proposition 13.14.21 , and normalize it by $\sup _ XU=0$. For $0<\varepsilon <1$, the potentials $\varepsilon U$ converge to zero in capacity as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$: by ( 5.29.4 ), the capacity of $\{ \varepsilon U<-\delta \} $ is at most $C\varepsilon /\delta $ for each fixed $\delta >0$ and small $\varepsilon $. Consequently, for $p>0$ and $q>r_ n$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{p\varepsilon U}\mu _{\varepsilon U}ightharpoonup \omega ^ n, \qquad (1-\varepsilon U)^{-q}\mu _{\varepsilon U}ightharpoonup \omega ^ n,  \] although $\mu _{\varepsilon U}(X)=+\infty $ for every $0<\varepsilon <1$. The full currents also converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm, and their Gauduchon traces converge in total variation.

title: Theorem 13.15.11
text: Theorem 13.15.11 . B72AF5B37CB7 For every $q>r_ n$, the damped measures \[  \sigma _{q,u}:=(1-u)^{-q}\mu _ u  \] have uniformly bounded mass for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $u\leq 0$. More precisely, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(\{ u<-T\} ) \leq C\frac{q}{q-r_ n}(1+T)^{r_ n-q}\quad (T\geq 0),  \] where $C$ depends only on $\omega $. There is also a constant $C_ q$ such that, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \sigma _{q,u}(E)\leq C_ q\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{(q-r_ n)/(q+n-r_ n)}.  \] Proof. title: 13.15.12 Uniform tails and undamped convergence
text: On deep sublevel sets the damping weight tends to zero, so convergence of the weighted measures can leave their undamped mass uncontrolled. Uniformly vanishing deep tails supply the additional control: the following condition gives a finite limit measure and weak convergence of the undamped measures $\mu _{u_ j}$. It can equivalently be expressed by an increasing integrability weight. Theorem 13.15.13 . 8B2A9680933C Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive and suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity. Assume \[  \lim _{T\to \infty }\sup _ j\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )=0.  \] Then $\mu _ u$ is finite and $\mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \mu _ u$. Proof. Choose $T_0$ such that every tail $\mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )$ with $T\geq T_0$ is at most one. By lemma 13.15.3 , $\mu _{u_ j}(X)\leq C(1+T_0)^{r_ n}+1$, so the tail condition already gives a uniform bound for the total masses. With the cutoffs $\eta _ T$ of ( 13.15.10 ), the fixed-level argument in the proof of theorem 13.15.9 , applied with $w\equiv 1$, gives \[  \eta _ T(-u_ j)\mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \eta _ T(-u)\mu _ u \quad \text{for every fixed }T>0.  \] The masses of the measures on the left are bounded by the uniform bound for the total masses. Since $\eta _ T(-u)$ increases to one off the pole set as $T\to \infty $, monotone convergence proves $\mu _ u(X)<+\infty $. For a continuous test function $f:X\to \mathbb R$, the error made by inserting $\eta _ T(-u_ j)$ is at most $\| f\| _\infty \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )$, which is small for large $T$, uniformly in $j$. For the limit potential, the corresponding error tends to zero because $\mu _ u$ is finite and does not charge the pole set. Let first $j\to \infty $ with $T$ fixed, and then $T\to \infty $. $\square$ Let $\chi :[0,+\infty )\to [1,+\infty )$ be continuous, nondecreasing and unbounded. For a nonpositive potential $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ define \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)=\int _ X\chi (-u)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u,  \] with the value $+\infty $ allowed. Since $\chi (T)\to +\infty $, a uniform bound for this functional forces the sublevel tails to vanish uniformly. Corollary 13.15.14 . 7312F05A4396 Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be nonpositive. If $u_ j\to u$ in capacity and $\sup _ jJ_{\chi ,\omega }(u_ j)\leq C$, then \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)\leq C,\qquad \mu _{u_ j}\rightharpoonup \mu _ u.  \] Proof. Since $\chi \geq 1$, the total masses are at most $C$, and \[  \mu _{u_ j}(\{ u_ j<-T\} )\leq C/\chi (T).  \] Thus theorem 13.15.13 applies. For the bound on $J_{\chi ,\omega }(u)$, use ( 13.15.10 ) with the compactly supported continuous function $s\mapsto \chi (s)\eta _ T(s)$ in place of $w\eta _ T$. The corresponding weighted integrals converge for each fixed $T$, and they are at most $C$. Let $T\to \infty $ and use monotone convergence. $\square$ Proposition 13.15.15 . ACA3FA133A3B For a family of nonpositive potentials in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the uniform tail condition of theorem 13.15.13 is equivalent to a uniform bound on $J_{\chi ,\omega }$ for some continuous nondecreasing unbounded function $\chi \geq 1$. Proof. One implication was proved in corollary 13.15.14 . Conversely, write the family as $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$. As in the proof of theorem 13.15.13 , the tail condition and lemma 13.15.3 give a uniform bound for the total masses. Choose numbers $T_ k\to +\infty $, with $T_{k+1}>T_ k+1$, such that $\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} )\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $i\in I$. Let $\rho _ k$ be a continuous nondecreasing function, equal to zero on $[0,T_ k]$ and to one on $[T_ k+1,+\infty )$, and define \[  \chi (s)=1+\sum _{k\geq 1}\rho _ k(s).  \] The sum is locally finite, so $\chi $ is continuous, nondecreasing and unbounded. Tonelli's theorem gives \[  J_{\chi ,\omega }(u_ i) \leq \mu _{u_ i}(X)+\sum _{k\geq 1}\mu _{u_ i}(\{ -u_ i>T_ k\} ) \leq \sup _{i\in I}\mu _{u_ i}(X)+1,  \] so this weight gives a uniform integrability bound for the whole family. $\square$

title: 13.15.16 Mass concentration
text:
The tail condition excludes mass carried by sublevel sets that disappear in the capacity limit. On a curve this mass can concentrate at a pole of the limit. When the bounded mass property fails, it can also persist along smooth potentials converging to zero. Example 13.15.17 . 446B53338035 On $X=\mathbb P^1$, let $z$ be the standard affine coordinate and let $\delta _0$ denote the unit Dirac measure at its origin. Take the Fubini–Study form \[  \omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad \int _ X\omega =1,  \] and the global nonpositive potential \[  u(z)=\log  rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad u_ j=\max (u,-j).  \] At infinity, in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, the function $u$ equals $-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, so it is smooth there. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\delta _0, \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=0.  \] The second identity holds because the extended measure discards the pole set and the current vanishes on its complement. Each $u_ j$ is bounded and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. Its measure $\mu _ j=\mu _{u_ j}=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ has mass one by Stokes' theorem, and $\mu _ j=0$ on the open set $\{ u>-j\} $ by locality. Hence \[  \operatorname {supp}\mu _ j\subset \{ u\leq -j\}  =\left\{ |z|^2\leq  rac{\mathrm{e}^{-j}}{1-\mathrm{e}^{-j}}ight\} .  \] These disks shrink to the origin, so $\mu _ jightharpoonup \delta _0$.  On their supports, $u_ j=-j$. Consequently, for $j>T$, \[  \mu _ j(\{ u_ j<-T\} )=1, \qquad \mathrm{e}^{pu_ j}\mu _ j=\mathrm{e}^{-pj}\mu _ jightharpoonup 0 \quad (p>0).  \] Nevertheless, $u_ j	o u$ in capacity. Indeed, outside any neighborhood of the origin the functions eventually agree with $u$, and the origin has arbitrarily small neighborhoods of arbitrarily small capacity. Thus bounded mass and capacity convergence do not prevent the undamped measures from acquiring mass at a pole of the limit. The damped limit is the extended measure of $u$, as predicted by theorem 13.15.9 . We return to a general compact Hermitian manifold $(X,\omega )$. Corollary 13.15.18 . 5804300415EA Assume $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $ and put $V_\omega =\int _ X\omega ^ n$. Fix a real number $b>V_\omega $ and a sequence $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$ tending to zero. The smooth potentials $w_ j$ of corollary 13.14.23 , chosen with mass $b$, converge to zero in capacity. For every $T>0$, \[  \left\| \mathbf1_{\{ w_ j\geq -T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n-\omega ^ n ight\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0, \qquad \int _{\{ w_ j<-T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n\longrightarrow b-V_\omega .  \] After passage to a subsequence, there is a positive measure $\sigma $ of mass $b-V_\omega $ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ nightharpoonup \omega ^ n+\sigma , \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ w_ j<-T\} }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ nightharpoonup \sigma \quad 	ext{for every }T>0.  \] Proof. The construction in corollary 13.14.23 gives $w_ j=s_ j u_ j$, where $u_ j$ is smooth and $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$ and $0<s_ j<\varepsilon _ j$. The sublevel estimate ( 5.29.4 ) gives, for every fixed $\delta >0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ |w_ j|>\delta \} ) =\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ u_ j<-\delta /s_ j\} ) \leq Cs_ j/\delta \longrightarrow 0.  \] Put $\mu _ j=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ n$. Fix $T>0$ and write $E_{j,T}=\{ w_ j\geq -T\} $. The lower bound in corollary 13.14.23 gives \[  \mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\mu _ j\geq \lambda _{j,T}:=(1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\omega ^ n.  \] Since $w_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$, the smooth volume of $X\setminus E_{j,T}$ tends to zero, and hence $\lambda _{j,T}	o \omega ^ n$ in total variation. For every $p>0$, theorem 13.15.9 gives $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pw_ j}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j	o V_\omega $, and therefore \[  \limsup _ j\mu _ j(E_{j,T}) \leq \mathrm{e}^{pT}\lim _ j\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pw_ j}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j =\mathrm{e}^{pT}V_\omega .  \] Letting $p\downarrow 0$ and combining with the lower bound, we obtain $\mu _ j(E_{j,T})	o V_\omega $. Positivity now yields \[   egin{split}  \| \mathbf1_{E_{j,T}}\mu _ j-\omega ^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} & \leq \mu _ j(E_{j,T})-\lambda _{j,T}(X) +\| \lambda _{j,T}-\omega ^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\ & \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] Subtracting this shallow mass from $\mu _ j(X)=b$ proves the assertion about the mass on $\{ w_ j<-T\} $. The positive measures $\mu _ j$ have fixed mass on the compact manifold $X$, so a subsequence converges weakly to a measure $
u $ of mass $b$. The inequality $\mu _ j\geq (1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\omega ^ n$ gives $
u \geq \omega ^ n$. Set $\sigma =
u -\omega ^ n$. For each $T>0$, subtracting the total-variation limit of the shallow restrictions from $\mu _ jightharpoonup 
u $ gives the last assertion along the same subsequence, for every $T$. $\square$ Thus the defect $\sigma $ in corollary 13.15.18 carries the whole excess mass $b-V_\omega $, although the currents $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ converge to $\omega $ in the coefficient $L^1$ norm and their Gauduchon traces converge in total variation. The location of $\sigma $ is constrained by the limits of the intermediate powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$, as we now show.

title: Example 13.15.17
text: Example 13.15.17 . 446B53338035 On $X=\mathbb P^1$, let $z$ be the standard affine coordinate and let $\delta _0$ denote the unit Dirac measure at its origin. Take the Fubini–Study form \[  \omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad \int _ X\omega =1,  \] and the global nonpositive potential \[  u(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad u_ j=\max (u,-j).  \] At infinity, in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, the function $u$ equals $-\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$, so it is smooth there. title: Corollary 13.15.18
text:

title: 13.15.19 Intermediate currents of a shrinking sequence
search_title: Intermediate currents of a shrinking sequence
text: We formulate the result for a connected compact complex manifold $Y$ of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $h$, since it will be applied with different metrics in section 23.1 . Consider smooth functions \[  v_ j=s_ ju_ j,\qquad u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,h),\qquad \sup _ Yu_ j=0,\qquad 0<s_ j\longrightarrow 0.  \] Suppose that their Monge–Ampère masses $\int _ Y(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n$ equal a fixed number $b$ and that \[  (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n\rightharpoonup h^ n+\sigma .  \] The lower bound $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq (1-s_ j)h$ shows that $\sigma $ is positive. Although $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\to 0$ in the trace norm, its intermediate powers can have nonzero limits, and these limits determine $\sigma $. Proposition 13.15.20 . 708664A6CF93 After passage to a common subsequence, the positive forms \[  H_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j+s_ jh=s_ j(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)  \] satisfy $H_ j^ k\rightharpoonup K_ k$ for $1\leq k\leq n$. The currents $K_ k$ are positive and closed, and $K_1=K_ n=0$. For every smooth real $(n-k,n-k)$-form $\eta $ with $\mathrm{d}\eta =0$ or $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, \[  \int _ Y K_ k\wedge \eta =0.  \] Moreover, 13C111AE3D65 13.15.21 \begin{equation}  \sigma =\sum _{k=2}^{n-1}\binom nk h^{n-k}\wedge K_ k. \end{equation} If $\vartheta $ is a smooth closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, then $\sigma $ is supported on $\{ \vartheta ^ n=0\} $. In dimension three the same conclusion holds for every smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form $\vartheta $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\vartheta =0$. Proof. For $s_ j<1/2$, positivity in the expansion \[  (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n =\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk(1-s_ j)^{n-k}h^{n-k}\wedge H_ j^ k  \] gives a uniform bound for each $\int _ Yh^{n-k}\wedge H_ j^ k$. In local unitary coordinates, the coefficient matrix of the smooth positive form $H_ j^ k$ on exterior powers is positive semidefinite, so its entries are bounded in absolute value by its trace, up to a dimensional constant. The trace bounds therefore bound every coefficient in total variation, and weak compactness of measures gives a common subsequence and positive limits $K_ k$. For $n\geq 2$, choose a Gauduchon form $\gamma $. By proposition 11.5.1 , \[  \int _ Y H_ j\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =s_ j\int _ Yh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $\gamma $ and $h$ are equivalent smooth metrics, it follows that $H_ j\to 0$ in coefficient total variation. For $n=1$ the same conclusion follows from $\int _ YH_ j=s_ j\int _ Yh$. Thus $K_1=0$ in all dimensions. Since $\mathrm{d}H_ j=s_ j\mathrm{d}h$, \[  \mathrm{d}(H_ j^ k)=ks_ j\mathrm{d}h\wedge H_ j^{k-1}\longrightarrow 0  \] as currents, because the preceding trace bounds control multiplication by the fixed smooth form $\mathrm{d}h$. Hence every $K_ k$ is closed. The smooth form $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ k$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-exact and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact: \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ k =\mathrm{d}\bigl (\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v_ j\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^{k-1}\bigr ) =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (v_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^{k-1}\bigr ).  \] Its integral against either kind of test form $\eta $ in the statement is therefore zero by Stokes' formula. Expanding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j=H_ j-s_ jh$ gives \[  \int _ Y\eta \wedge H_ j^ k =-\sum _{r=0}^{k-1}\binom kr(-s_ j)^{k-r} \int _ Y\eta \wedge h^{k-r}\wedge H_ j^ r =O(s_ j).  \] Each integral on the right is bounded by the trace bound for $H_ j^ r$. Taking $k=n$ and $\eta =1$ shows that the positive measures $H_ j^ n$ tend to zero in total variation, which proves $K_ n=0$; the other vanishing integrals follow by weak convergence. Finally, letting $j\to \infty $ in the positive expansion above, the terms with $k=0$ tend to $h^ n$ and those with $k=1$ and $k=n$ vanish in the limit, which proves ( 13.15.21 ). For closed semipositive $\vartheta $, apply the vanishing integrals to $\eta =\vartheta ^{n-k}$. The measure $K_ k\wedge \vartheta ^{n-k}$ is positive and has zero mass. On every relatively compact open set where $\vartheta >0$, it dominates a positive multiple of the trace measure of $K_ k$, so $K_ k$ vanishes there. The decomposition gives the asserted support. In dimension three only $K_2$ occurs, and the same argument applies to the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed test form $\vartheta $ itself. $\square$ In dimensions at most two the decomposition forces $\sigma =0$. A threefold carrying a pluriclosed Hermitian metric, that is, a Hermitian form $\vartheta $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\vartheta =0$, has no nonzero defect $\sigma $ of this form either. In higher dimensions, the vanishing integrals impose necessary conditions on each intermediate current; they do not by themselves produce a smooth sequence with prescribed intermediate limits.

title: 13.15.22 Damping for a smooth background
text: For a general smooth background $\theta $, truncation at a constant level may fail to preserve $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity. A larger Hermitian form makes the truncations plurisubharmonic and dominates the extended measure, and the local expansion of the $\theta $-product gives continuity at each fixed truncation level. Theorem 13.15.23 . 18CDC482A9DD Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and for nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ put $\mu _{\theta ,u}=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$. The mass bounds, capacity estimates and capacity-continuity statements for damped measures in this chapter, including proposition 13.15.9 , hold for the measures $\mu _{\theta ,u}$ in place of $\mu _ u$, with constants depending on $\theta $ and $\omega $. In particular, for $p>0$ and $q>r_ n$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pu}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{\theta ,u} \leq C(1+p^{-1})^{r_ n},\qquad \int _ X(1-u)^{-q}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{\theta ,u}\leq C_ q.  \] The undamped tail criterion of theorem 13.15.13 and the integrability criterion of corollary 13.15.14 also hold with $\mu _{\theta ,u}$ in place of $\mu _ u$. Proof. Choose $C_0\geq 1$ such that $\theta \leq \Omega :=C_0\omega $. Then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Omega )$, and theorem 13.14.3 gives \[  0\leq \mu _{\theta ,u}\leq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega (u).  \] All the mass, tail and capacity bounds therefore follow from the estimates already proved for $\Omega $. The metric comparison in section 5.29 gives, for every Borel set $E\subset X$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E) \leq \operatorname {Cap}_\Omega (E) \leq C_0^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E).  \] For continuity, let nonpositive $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ converge in capacity, and use ( 13.15.10 ) with the $\theta $-product. The truncations are bounded and $\Omega $-plurisubharmonic. The weighted capacity continuity of section 5.27 , section 5.29 applies term by term to the local expansion of their signed $\theta $-products, with the same bounded quasi-continuous coefficients. Since the cutoff vanishes at the truncation level, the result is exactly the restricted positive measure. The uniform tails obtained from the domination by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Omega $ remove the cutoff. Domination also gives the sublevel estimate, so the preceding proofs of the undamped tail and integrability criteria apply without change. $\square$

title: 23.1 Unbounded mass on Hopf manifolds
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: By proposition 13.15.2 , every compact complex curve or surface has the bounded mass property. The property can fail in dimension three even when the metric is Gauduchon. We prove this on a Hopf threefold, then extend the construction to every scalar Hopf manifold of dimension at least three. The threefold mass formula provides the starting point. Its linear term vanishes for a Gauduchon metric, and for the standard Hopf metric the quadratic term is a positive multiple of the Dirichlet energy along the elliptic fibers over $\mathbb P^2$. We therefore seek smooth potentials with large vertical energy whose perturbed forms stay positive. A fiber heat kernel supplies the concentration. Varying its time across the base controls the mixed derivatives; a function of the base then restores positivity without changing the vertical energy. The higher-dimensional extension follows by comparing the angular densities. We next use the fiber structure to study minimum mass, damping and weak limits. Fiber averaging identifies the bounded potentials of minimum mass. For normalized potentials invariant under unitary rotations of the last two coordinates, a positive fiber flux yields the sharp square-root damping threshold; concentration at the endpoint separates individual finiteness from uniform tails and capacity continuity. Finally, we classify the excess measures produced by shrinking smooth potentials. They are exactly the lifts of base measures by the normalized area measures on the elliptic fibers, for the standard metric and for every other Hermitian metric on this threefold. Theorem 23.1.1 (Xia–Zhang) . 92B2FB434C79 The compact threefold \[  X=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z\rangle  \] admits a Gauduchon form $\omega $ and smooth real functions $V_ j$ such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j>0,\qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] In particular, $X$ does not have the bounded mass property.

title: Theorem 23.1.1 (Xia–Zhang)
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 23.1.1 (Xia–Zhang) . 92B2FB434C79 The compact threefold \[  X=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z\rangle  \] admits a Gauduchon form $\omega $ and smooth real functions $V_ j$ such that \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j>0,\qquad \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] In particular, $X$ does not have the bounded mass property. of theorem 23.1.1 . Choose a smooth function $r_\eta \geq 0$ supported in $(-1/2,b+1/2)$ with \[  r_\eta >d_\eta \  \hbox{on }[0,b],\qquad m_\eta :=\int _\mathbb Rr_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x\leq \int _\mathbb Rd_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x+\eta =o(1).  \] Such a majorant exists by uniform approximation of the compactly supported continuous function $d_\eta $, followed by adding a positive bump on $[0,b]$; for each fixed $\eta $ the approximation error can be chosen small enough for the integral bound. Fix a smooth $\psi \geq 0$ supported in $(-2,-1)$ with integral one and set \[  g_\eta (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ x(x-s) (r_\eta (s)-m_\eta \psi (s))\, \mathrm{d}s, \qquad V_\eta =W+g_\eta .  \] The negative part of $g_\eta ''$ lies to the left of its positive part, and their integrals agree. Consequently, \[  -m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0, \qquad g_\eta '=0\  \hbox{for }x\leq -2 \  \hbox{and for }x\geq b+1/2.  \] Thus $g_\eta $ vanishes for $x\leq -2$ and is constant for $x\geq b+1/2$, and $V_\eta $ has the properties at the two ends required for smooth extension to $X$. Since $g_\eta $ is independent of $w$, the Schur complement changes by exactly its second derivative: \[  Q[V_\eta ]=Q[W]+r_\eta -m_\eta \psi .  \] This is positive on $[0,b]$ because $r_\eta >d_\eta $ there. On $(-2,-1)$ it is at least $2/27-m_\eta \| \psi \| _\infty >0$ for small $\eta $. Elsewhere $Q[W]>0$, $\psi =0$ and $r_\eta \geq 0$. The vertical coefficient remains above $1-\eta $ by ( 23.1.24 ). For the remaining coefficient, if $x\leq -2$, both $W_ x$ and $g_\eta '$ vanish; if $-2\leq x\leq 0$, then $W_ x=0$ and $\mu \geq \mu (-2)>0$, while $|g_\eta '|\leq m_\eta =o(1)$; and if $x\geq 0$, then $\mu \geq 1/2$ and $W_ x\geq -o(1)$. In all cases $\mu +(V_\eta )_ x>0$ for sufficiently small $\eta $. Therefore lemma 23.1.7 gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta >0$ on $X$. On the fixed ball $B=\{ |\xi |^2<\mathrm{e}^{-3}\} \Subset U_0$, one has $V_\eta =F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$, including at $\xi =0$. Thus \[  \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|(V_\eta )_ w|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E =2\eta ^2\log (1/\varepsilon )+O(\eta ^2) =2\log (1/\eta )+O(\eta ^2)\longrightarrow +\infty  \] uniformly for $y\in B$. Since $\int _ B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2>0$, the mass identity ( 23.1.5 ) shows that $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )^3\to +\infty $, and the theorem follows by taking $V_ j=V_{\eta _ j}$ along any sequence $\eta _ j\downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 23.1.2 The Hopf metric and its mass
search_title: The Hopf metric and its mass
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: The projection to $\mathbb P^2$ separates the horizontal and vertical parts of the metric. We normalize the fiber measure to have mass one; this fixes the constants in the mass formula. On the covering space $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $, with coordinates $z=(z_0,z_1,z_2)$, put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \beta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s, \qquad \omega =\alpha +\beta .  \] The contraction $z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z$ changes $s$ by the constant $-2$, so these forms descend to $X$. A closed spherical shell between two successive radii is a compact fundamental domain; this also proves that the quotient is compact. Let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$, given by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|\xi |^2)$ in affine coordinates $\xi =(\xi _1,\xi _2)$. Projectivization gives a holomorphic map \[  \pi :X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^2, \qquad \alpha =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},\qquad \int _{\mathbb P^2}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2=1.  \] The form $\alpha $ has rank two and is positive transversally to the fibers, while the rank-one form $\beta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their kernels intersect only in zero, and therefore $\omega >0$. We shall use the identities 25275E5CD565 23.1.3 \begin{equation}  \alpha ^3=0,\quad \beta ^2=0,\quad \mathrm{d}\alpha =0, \quad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =-\alpha ^2, \quad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0. \end{equation} The first three follow from the definitions and the dimension of the base. For the fourth, differentiating $\beta =\mathrm i\partial s\wedge \bar\partial s/(2\pi )$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =(\partial \bar\partial s)^2/(4\pi ^2)=-\alpha ^2$. Finally, $\omega ^2=\alpha ^2+2\alpha \wedge \beta $, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=-2\alpha ^3=0$. Thus $\omega $ is Gauduchon, although $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2\ne 0$. On the affine base chart $U_0=\{ [z_0:z_1:z_2]\in \mathbb P^2:z_0\ne 0\} \simeq \mathbb C^2$ write \[  \xi _ j=z_ j/z_0\quad (j=1,2),\qquad w=\log z_0.  \] The choice of logarithm and the contraction change $w$ by elements of $\Lambda =\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm i\mathbb Z$. Hence \[  \pi ^{-1}(U_0)\simeq U_0\times E,\qquad E=\mathbb C/\Lambda ,\qquad \mathrm{d}A_ E=\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w, \quad \int _ E\mathrm{d}A_ E=1.  \] On another base chart the fiber coordinate changes by a holomorphic function of the base. Consequently, the vertical derivative $\partial _ w$ and the fiber integral below are globally defined. For a smooth function $V$ on $X$, write $V_ w=\partial V/\partial w$. Proposition 23.1.4 . DDEBFFAFCD1F For every $V\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, C46F0B405DC2 23.1.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^3 =6+6\int _{\mathbb P^2} \left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|V_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E\right) \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2(y). \end{equation} In particular, positivity of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V$ is not required. Proof. Since $\beta $ restricts to $2\mathrm{d}A_ E$ on each fiber, \[  \int _ X\omega ^3=3\int _ X\alpha ^2\wedge \beta =6.  \] By ( 11.1.6 ) and ( 23.1.3 ), followed by an integration by parts against the closed form $\alpha ^2$, \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^3-\int _ X\omega ^3 & =3\int _ X V\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\\ & =-3\int _ X V\alpha ^2\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V =3\int _ X\mathrm{d}V\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}V\wedge \alpha ^2. \end{split}  \] Wedging with $\alpha ^2$ removes every component of $\mathrm{d}V\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}V$ except the vertical one, which is $\mathrm i|V_ w|^2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar w/(2\pi )=2|V_ w|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E$. Integration over the fibers proves the formula. $\square$

DDEBFFAFCD1F For every $V\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, C46F0B405DC2 23.1.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^3 =6+6\int _{\mathbb P^2} \left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|V_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E\right) \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2(y). \end{equation} In particular, positivity of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V$ is not required. The fiber potential will be built from the heat kernel of $E$. It has large vertical energy at small times and decays at large times, where it can be cut off, and a lower bound for its logarithmic Hessian controls vertical positivity. To control the radial–vertical block when the time varies, we also need an estimate relating the kernel to its logarithmic gradient. For $t>0$ define 097EB0CA92F4 23.1.10  egin{equation}  k_ t(w)= rac2t\sum _{\lambda \in \Lambda } \exp \left(- rac{|w-\lambda |^2}{t}ight). \end{equation} This is a smooth positive $\Lambda $-periodic function of integral one: unfolding the integral reduces it to the Gaussian integral on $\mathbb C$, since $\mathrm{d}A_ E=\mathrm{d}a\, \mathrm{d}b/(2\pi )$ for $w=a+\mathrm ib$. For $(p,q)\in \mathbb Z^2$ set \[  
u _{p,q}=p+ rac{\mathrm iq}{2\pi },\qquad \chi _{p,q}(w)=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm ip\operatorname {Re}w+ \mathrm iq\operatorname {Im}w}.  \] These characters form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(E,\mathrm{d}A_ E)$. Computing the Fourier coefficients by the same unfolding gives 27E901CC3829 23.1.11  egin{equation}  k_ t=\sum _{p,q}\mathrm{e}^{-\pi ^2|
u _{p,q}|^2t}\chi _{p,q}, \qquad \partial _ tk_ t=\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}k_ t. \end{equation} All differentiated series converge locally uniformly for $t>0$. Lemma 23.1.12 . 14E6CDA9AAC4 Let $0<\eta <1/10$ and define \[  F_\eta (t,w)=-\eta \int _ t^\infty (k_ r(w)-1)\, \mathrm{d}r.  \] Then $F_\eta $ is smooth and real, and 9CCEEAD6F62C 23.1.13  egin{align}  (F_\eta )_ t=(F_\eta )_{w ar w} & =\eta (k_ t-1),\  (\log k_ t)_{w ar w}& \geq -1/t,	ag{23.1.14}\  \int _ E|(F_\eta )_ w(t,w)|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E & =2\eta ^2\log (1/t)+O(\eta ^2)\quad (0<t\leq 1). 	ag{23.1.15} \end{align} The error term in ( 23.1.15 ) is uniform in $t$ and $\eta $. u _{p,q}|^2$ is $1/4$, and any fixed number of differentiations introduces coefficients of polynomial growth in $|
u _{p,q}|$. Factoring out $\mathrm{e}^{-t/4}$ for $t\geq 1$ therefore leaves a convergent Gaussian series, which proves ( 23.1.16 ). u _{p,q}|^2t}}{|
u _{p,q}|^2}, \qquad \mathcal E_\eta '(t)=-2\eta ^2(k_{2t}(0)-1).  \] The Gaussian formula at the origin implies \[  k_{2t}(0)= rac1t+ O\left(t^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-1/(4t)}ight)\quad (0<t\leq 1).  \] To see this, isolate the zero lattice vector and use $\mathrm{e}^{-|\lambda |^2/(2t)}\leq \mathrm{e}^{-1/(4t)}\mathrm{e}^{-|\lambda |^2/4}$ for $\lambda 
e 0$. The error term is integrable near $t=0$, and $\mathcal E_\eta (1)=O(\eta ^2)$. Choose a nearest lattice point $\lambda _0$, and put $d=|w-\lambda _0|$ and $s_\lambda =|w-\lambda |^2-d^2\geq 0$. The distance $d$ is bounded by the diameter of a fundamental rectangle. In the remaining case $G^2/t$ is bounded, and ( 23.1.18 ) follows from $tk_ t\leq C$ after increasing $C_0$. $\square$ Lemma 23.1.19 . For $0<\kappa <1/(200C_0)$, $0<\eta <1/10$, $0<t\leq 1$ and $1/2\leq \mu \leq 1$, define $\sigma >0$ and the functions $h,\zeta $ of $w\in E$ by \[  \sigma ^2= rac{2\kappa }{\eta }\log  rac1{\eta t},\qquad h=\eta k_ t,\qquad \zeta = rac{\sigma }{\mu }\, t\partial _{ ar w}\log k_ t.  \] Then ED58C2434E12 23.1.20  egin{equation}  \kappa tk_ t-  rac{\mu ^2(1-\eta )h}{1-\eta +h} \left|\zeta - rac1{1-\eta }ight|^2 \leq C\kappa \exp \left(- rac1{C\sigma ^2t}ight). \end{equation} Proof. If $\sigma ^2t\geq 1/100$, the bound $tk_ t\leq C_0$ gives ( 23.1.20 ) after enlarging $C$. Assume therefore that $\sigma ^2t<1/100$. If $|\zeta -(1-\eta )^{-1}|\geq 1/4$, the subtracted expression is at least $h/[100(1+h)]$. Since $\log (1/(\eta t))>2$, the definition of $\sigma $ gives \[  \kappa t(1+h)\leq  rac{\eta }{400}+C_0\kappa \eta < rac{\eta }{100}.  \] Multiplication by $k_ t/(1+h)$ shows that the left side of ( 23.1.20 ) is nonpositive. Otherwise $|\zeta |\geq 3/4$, so \[  |t\partial _{ ar w}\log k_ t|= rac{\mu |\zeta |}{\sigma } \geq  rac3{8\sigma }.  \] Discarding the nonnegative square and applying lemma 23.1.17 gives ( 23.1.20 ) in this case as well. $\square$

title: 23.1.21 Variation of the heat time
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: The heat time will remain small on a fixed base ball and then increase with the radial variable until the fiber potential can be cut off. We choose its rate of increase so that the negative part of the Schur complement has small integral in the radial variable. Fix $\kappa $ as in lemma 23.1.19 . All estimates below concern the limit $\eta \downarrow 0$, with $\kappa $ fixed. Write \[  L=\log (1/\eta ),\quad \varepsilon =\eta ^{1/\eta ^2},\quad q_0=\sqrt{\log \frac1{\eta \varepsilon }},\quad a=\sqrt{\frac\kappa {2\eta }}.  \] Fix a smooth nondecreasing $\chi :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, independent of $\eta $, equal to zero on $(-\infty ,0]$ and one on $[1,+\infty )$, with $\int _0^1\chi =1/2$. Define F445D65CCB92 23.1.22 \begin{equation}  q(x)=q_0-\int _0^{ax}\chi (s)\, \mathrm{d}s, \qquad t(x)=\eta ^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-q(x)^2}. \end{equation} Thus $t=\varepsilon $ on $x\leq 0$, and $q=q_0+1/2-ax$ on $x\geq a^{-1}$. Put \[  b=\frac{q_0-1/2}{a},\qquad x_* =\frac{q_0+1/2}{a}.  \] For small $\eta $, we have $0<a^{-1}<b<x_*$, with C76E171B8E17 23.1.23 \begin{equation}  q(b)=1,\quad q(x_*)=0,\quad b,x_*=O\bigl (\sqrt{L/\eta }\bigr ),\quad \eta b=o(1). \end{equation} Fix also a smooth cutoff $\vartheta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, independent of $\eta $, zero on $(-\infty ,0]$ and one on $[1,+\infty )$, and define \[  W(x,w)=\vartheta (q(x))F_\eta (t(x),w).  \] This function equals $F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$ for $x\leq 0$ and vanishes for $x\geq x_*$. Moreover, by ( 23.1.13 ), 03733983FD0F 23.1.24 \begin{equation}  1+W_{w\bar w}=1+\vartheta (q)\eta (k_ t-1)>1-\eta . \end{equation} Lemma 23.1.25 . 3F868B74CEBD For the functions just constructed, let \[  d_\eta (x)=\max _{w\in E}\max \{ -Q[W](x,w),0\} .  \] For all sufficiently small $\eta $, the function $d_\eta $ is continuous, supported in $[0,b]$, and 198FD1FE8553 23.1.26 \begin{equation}  \int _\mathbb Rd_\eta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x=o(1),\qquad \sup _{\mathbb R\times E}\max \{ -W_ x,0\} =o(1). \end{equation} On $[-2,-1]\times E$, one also has $Q[W]\geq 2/27$. Proof. We first derive an exact formula for $Q[W]$ on $[0,b]$, then bound its negative part separately on $[0,a^{-1}]$ and on $[a^{-1},b]$, integrate these bounds, and finally examine the ends of the radial line. Step 1: the Schur complement on $[0,b]$. Write $F=F_\eta $ for the heat potential. On $[0,b]$ we have $q\geq 1$, hence $\vartheta (q)=1$ and $W=F(t(x),w)$. Set \[  h=\eta k_ t,\qquad \sigma =(\log t)_ x,\qquad \zeta =\frac{\sigma t}{\mu }\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t.  \] The heat equation gives $F_ t=h-\eta $, and the chain rule gives \[  W_ x=\sigma tF_ t,\quad W_{xx}=(\sigma _ x+\sigma ^2)tF_ t+\sigma ^2t^2F_{tt}, \quad W_{x\bar w}=\sigma tF_{t\bar w}.  \] Substituting these in $Q[W]$, using $h_ t=h((\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}+|\partial _{\bar w}\log k_ t|^2)$, and completing the square, we obtain the exact identity 477FF03F5EC1 23.1.27 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  Q[W]={}& \sigma ^2t\{ h[1+t(\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}]-\eta \}  +\sigma _ xtF_ t+\mu (1-\mu )-\frac{\mu ^2\eta }{1-\eta }\\ & +\frac{\mu ^2(1-\eta )h}{1-\eta +h} \left|\zeta -\frac1{1-\eta }\right|^2. \end{split} \end{equation} By ( 23.1.14 ), the part $\sigma ^2th[1+t(\log k_ t)_{w\bar w}]$ is nonnegative. Step 2: the initial interval $[0,a^{-1}]$. Here \[  \sigma =2aq\chi (ax),\qquad \sigma _ x=-\frac\kappa \eta \chi (ax)^2 +\frac\kappa \eta q\chi '(ax).  \] Moreover $q_0-1/2\leq q\leq q_0$ and $t\leq \varepsilon \mathrm{e}^{q_0}$, and the latter tends to zero faster than any power of $\eta $. In particular, \[  \kappa q\chi '(ax)t\leq \eta ,\qquad \sigma ^2t\leq \eta ^2.  \] At each point where $\chi (ax)>0$, apply lemma 23.1.19 with $\kappa \chi (ax)^2$ in place of $\kappa $; its constant is uniform in $x$. The positive square in ( 23.1.27 ) then absorbs the negative term $-\kappa \chi ^2tk_ t$ coming from $\sigma _ xtF_ t$. The remaining part of $\sigma _ xtF_ t$, which involves $\chi '$, is at least $-\eta $, because $F_ t\geq -\eta $. The other negative terms in ( 23.1.27 ) are $O(\eta )$, and so is the exponential error of lemma 23.1.19 , since $\sigma ^2t\leq \eta ^2$. Thus $d_\eta \leq C\eta $ on this interval. At points where $\chi (ax)=0$, the smooth nonnegative function $\chi $ has a minimum, so $\chi '(ax)=0$ and directly \[  Q[W]=\mu -\frac{\mu ^2}{1-\eta +h}>0,  \] since $\mu \leq \mu (a^{-1})<1-\eta $ for small $\eta $. Step 3: the interval $[a^{-1},b]$. Finally, $Q[W]$ is continuous, with positive denominator, so the maximum of its negative part over the compact fiber $E$ is continuous in $x$. title: 23.1.31 A base correction and unbounded mass
search_title: A base correction and unbounded mass
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Adding a function of $x$ alone changes $Q[W]$ by its second derivative and leaves the vertical energy unchanged. The integral bound for $d_\eta $ lets us choose this second derivative larger than $d_\eta $ and compensate its integral on an interval where $Q[W]$ is uniformly positive. The correction has small first derivative, so the remaining horizontal coefficient stays positive as well. of theorem 23.1.1 . Choose a smooth function $r_\eta \geq 0$ supported in $(-1/2,b+1/2)$ with \[  r_\eta >d_\eta \  \hbox{on }[0,b],\qquad m_\eta :=\int _\mathbb Rr_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x\leq \int _\mathbb Rd_\eta \, \mathrm{d}x+\eta =o(1).  \] Such a majorant exists by uniform approximation of the compactly supported continuous function $d_\eta $, followed by adding a positive bump on $[0,b]$; for each fixed $\eta $ the approximation error can be chosen small enough for the integral bound. Fix a smooth $\psi \geq 0$ supported in $(-2,-1)$ with integral one and set \[  g_\eta (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ x(x-s) (r_\eta (s)-m_\eta \psi (s))\, \mathrm{d}s, \qquad V_\eta =W+g_\eta .  \] The negative part of $g_\eta ''$ lies to the left of its positive part, and their integrals agree. Consequently, \[  -m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0, \qquad g_\eta '=0\  \hbox{for }x\leq -2 \  \hbox{and for }x\geq b+1/2.  \] Thus $g_\eta $ vanishes for $x\leq -2$ and is constant for $x\geq b+1/2$, and $V_\eta $ has the properties at the two ends required for smooth extension to $X$. Since $g_\eta $ is independent of $w$, the Schur complement changes by exactly its second derivative: \[  Q[V_\eta ]=Q[W]+r_\eta -m_\eta \psi .  \] This is positive on $[0,b]$ because $r_\eta >d_\eta $ there. On $(-2,-1)$ it is at least $2/27-m_\eta \| \psi \| _\infty >0$ for small $\eta $. Elsewhere $Q[W]>0$, $\psi =0$ and $r_\eta \geq 0$. The vertical coefficient remains above $1-\eta $ by ( 23.1.24 ). For the remaining coefficient, if $x\leq -2$, both $W_ x$ and $g_\eta '$ vanish; if $-2\leq x\leq 0$, then $W_ x=0$ and $\mu \geq \mu (-2)>0$, while $|g_\eta '|\leq m_\eta =o(1)$; and if $x\geq 0$, then $\mu \geq 1/2$ and $W_ x\geq -o(1)$. In all cases $\mu +(V_\eta )_ x>0$ for sufficiently small $\eta $. Therefore lemma 23.1.7 gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta >0$ on $X$. On the fixed ball $B=\{ |\xi |^2<\mathrm{e}^{-3}\} \Subset U_0$, one has $V_\eta =F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$, including at $\xi =0$. Thus \[  \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}|(V_\eta )_ w|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E =2\eta ^2\log (1/\varepsilon )+O(\eta ^2) =2\log (1/\eta )+O(\eta ^2)\longrightarrow +\infty  \] uniformly for $y\in B$. Since $\int _ B\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2>0$, the mass identity ( 23.1.5 ) shows that $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )^3\to +\infty $, and the theorem follows by taking $V_ j=V_{\eta _ j}$ along any sequence $\eta _ j\downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 23.1.35
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 23.1.35 . D3E13E0C86B3 For every $n\geq 3$, the Gauduchon metric $\omega _ n$ admits smooth potentials $V_\eta $ with $\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta >0$ whose total Monge–Ampère masses tend to infinity as $\eta \downarrow 0$. Proof. Use exactly the functions $V_\eta =W+g_\eta $ constructed in the proof of theorem 23.1.1 , including the heat scale $\varepsilon =\eta ^{1/\eta ^2}$. Their endpoint properties give smooth potentials on every $H_ n$, and lemma 23.1.33 gives strict positivity. The slope bounds in lemma 23.1.25 and $-m_\eta \leq g_\eta '\leq 0$ imply \[  \mu +(V_\eta )_ x\geq \tfrac 14 \qquad (x\geq 0)  \] for all sufficiently small $\eta $. We must first localize the divergent threefold mass to this region. On $x<0$, the heat potential is $W=F_\eta (\varepsilon ,w)$ and has no $x$ derivatives. The determinant formula in the preceding proof and $\int _ E F_{w\bar w}\, \mathrm dA_ E=0$ give \[  \int _ E J_3(V_\eta ;x,w)\, \mathrm dA_ E =12(\mu +g_\eta ') \bigl (g_\eta ''+\mu (1-\mu )\bigr ).  \] Here $0<\mu +g_\eta '\leq \mu $, and $g_\eta ''=r_\eta -m_\eta \psi $ with $\int r_\eta =m_\eta $ and $\int \psi =1$. Hence \[  \int _{x<0}\! J_3(V_\eta )\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dA_ E \leq 12\int _{-\infty }^0\mu ^2(1-\mu )\, \mathrm dx +12\int _{\mathbb R}|g_\eta ''|\, \mathrm dx \leq \tfrac 32+24m_\eta .  \] No bound on the amplitude of the fiber Hessian is required; its mean has been integrated exactly. Since the total threefold mass tends to infinity, its mass on $x\geq 0$ tends to infinity. The dimensional comparison now gives \[  \int _{H_ n}(\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )^ n \geq \frac{n(n-1)}6\, 4^{-(n-3)} \int _{x\geq 0}J_3(V_\eta )\, \mathrm dx\, \mathrm dA_ E \longrightarrow +\infty .  \] $\square$

title: Corollary 23.1.36
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Corollary 23.1.36 . 77FC30E16968 Every Hermitian metric on $H_ n$, $n\geq 3$, fails the bounded mass property. Proof. For a Hermitian form $h$, compactness gives $h\geq c\omega _ n$ for some $c>0$. The potentials $cV_\eta $ satisfy $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(cV_\eta )\geq c(\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_\eta )>0$, and positivity of determinants bounds their masses below by $c^ n$ times the divergent masses in theorem 23.1.35 . $\square$

title: 23.1.37 Minimum mass and fiber averaging
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
We return to the threefold $X=H_3$ and its form $\omega $. Averaging along the elliptic fibers removes the variation measured by ( 23.1.5 ). The Poincaré inequality on the fibers bounds the distance from a potential to its average by the excess mass. Bounded regularization preserves this inequality, which therefore identifies all bounded potentials of minimal mass and shows that potentials of almost minimal mass are close to them. Let $E$ act on $X$ by scalar multiplication: $	au _ a[z]=[\mathrm{e}^ a z]$ for $a\in E$. The action preserves $\alpha $, $ eta $ and $\omega $, and $\mathrm{d}A_ E$ is the Haar probability measure of $E$. For a bounded Borel function $u:X	o \mathbb R$, set \[  \mathrm{d}
u = rac{\omega ^3}{6}= rac12\alpha ^2\wedge  eta , \qquad Au(p)=\int _ Eu(	au _ a(p))\, \mathrm{d}A_ E(a) \quad (p\in X).  \] Thus $Au$ is constant on each fiber, and $
u $ is the probability measure whose disintegration along $\pi $ has fiber measures $\mathrm{d}A_ E$ and base measure $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$. Proposition 23.1.38 . E42306969D71 For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, the average $Au$ is the pullback of a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2$, and 18B65325175F 23.1.39  egin{equation}  \| u-Au\| _{L^2(X,
u )}^2 \leq  rac23\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3-6ight). \end{equation} The coefficient $2/3$ is optimal, even for smooth $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=6 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\pi ^*v\quad 	ext{for some } v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})\cap L^\infty (\mathbb P^2).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is smooth and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Averaging the positive forms $	au _ a^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$ gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au>0$. Since $Au$ is smooth and constant on the fibers, $Au=\pi ^*v$ for a smooth function $v$ on $\mathbb P^2$. At each point, the kernel of $\partial s$ maps isomorphically onto the tangent space of the base, and $ eta $ vanishes on it. Restricting $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au=\pi ^*(\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+ eta $ to this kernel therefore shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. For a smooth function $f:E	o \mathbb R$, the nonconstant Fourier characters in ( 23.1.11 ), indexed by $(p,q)\in \mathbb Z^2\setminus \{ (0,0)\} $, have eigenvalues $\pi ^2p^2+q^2/4\geq 1/4$ for $-\partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}$. Parseval's identity therefore gives \[  \int _ E\left|f-\int _ Ef\, \mathrm{d}A_ Eight|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E \leq 4\int _ E|f_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E.  \] Applying this inequality on every fiber, integrating against $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$ and using the mass identity ( 23.1.5 ), we obtain ( 23.1.39 ). For bounded $u$, choose uniformly bounded smooth functions $u_ j\downarrow u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ by theorem 5.32.1 . Their averages decrease pointwise to $Au$ by dominated convergence. The corresponding smooth base potentials $v_ j$ decrease to a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function $v$, so $Au=\pi ^*v$. Dominated convergence gives $u_ j	o u$ and $Au_ j	o Au$ in $L^2(X,
u )$, while bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives convergence of the total masses. Thus ( 23.1.39 ) passes to $u$. If the mass is $6$, the inequality gives $u=Au$ almost everywhere. Since both functions are bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, lemma 5.24.4 gives equality everywhere. Conversely, if $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})$, choose smooth $v_ j\downarrow v$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ by theorem 5.32.1 . The pullbacks decrease to $u$ and are uniformly bounded. They are strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic because the base forms are positive and $ eta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their vertical derivatives vanish, so ( 23.1.5 ) gives mass $6$ for each of them. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives the same mass for $u$. It remains to prove that the constant $2/3$ is optimal. Choose a nonzero real $ho \in C_ c^\infty (U_0)$. For $\delta \in \mathbb R$, the function \[  u(\xi ,w)=\delta ho (\xi )\cos (\operatorname {Im}w)  \] extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$. For sufficiently small nonzero real $\delta $, it satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Its fiber average is zero, and its only fiber frequencies are $(p,q)=(0,\pm 1)$, with eigenvalue $1/4$. Hence equality holds in the fiber inequality, and therefore in ( 23.1.39 ), with nonzero left-hand side. No smaller coefficient can hold. $\square$ Corollary 23.1.40 . 09DD8DF2EF76 The Hopf metric satisfies \[  v_-(\omega )=6,\qquad v_+(\omega )=+\infty .  \] Proof. The lower bound $v_-(\omega )\geq 6$ follows from ( 23.1.39 ), and it is attained by constants. Theorem 23.1.1 gives $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. $\square$ In particular, for any sequence of bounded potentials whose masses tend to $6$, the differences from their fiber averages tend to zero in $L^2(X,
u )$. This controls only the variation along the fibers; the averaged potentials can still be arbitrary bounded potentials on the base. For nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ on this threefold, proposition 13.15.9 gives finite damped measures for the weight $(1-u)^{-1}[\log (\mathrm{e}-u)]^{-a}$, $a>1$, at the threshold $r_3=1$, with uniform tails and capacity continuity. The optimal damping rate for all normalized potentials on this threefold remains open. Under unitary rotations of the last two coordinates, theorem 23.1.62 gives the exact square-root threshold.

title: Proposition 23.1.38
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Proposition 23.1.38 . E42306969D71 For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, the average $Au$ is the pullback of a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2$, and 18B65325175F 23.1.39 \begin{equation}  \| u-Au\| _{L^2(X,\nu )}^2 \leq \frac23\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3-6\right). \end{equation} The coefficient $2/3$ is optimal, even for smooth $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Moreover, \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=6 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\pi ^*v\quad \text{for some } v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})\cap L^\infty (\mathbb P^2).  \] Proof. First suppose that $u$ is smooth and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Averaging the positive forms $\tau _ a^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$ gives $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au>0$. Since $Au$ is smooth and constant on the fibers, $Au=\pi ^*v$ for a smooth function $v$ on $\mathbb P^2$. At each point, the kernel of $\partial s$ maps isomorphically onto the tangent space of the base, and $\beta $ vanishes on it. Restricting $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Au=\pi ^*(\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+\beta $ to this kernel therefore shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. For a smooth function $f:E\to \mathbb R$, the nonconstant Fourier characters in ( 23.1.11 ), indexed by $(p,q)\in \mathbb Z^2\setminus \{ (0,0)\} $, have eigenvalues $\pi ^2p^2+q^2/4\geq 1/4$ for $-\partial _ w\partial _{\bar w}$. Parseval's identity therefore gives \[  \int _ E\left|f-\int _ Ef\, \mathrm{d}A_ E\right|^2\mathrm{d}A_ E \leq 4\int _ E|f_ w|^2\, \mathrm{d}A_ E.  \] Applying this inequality on every fiber, integrating against $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^2$ and using the mass identity ( 23.1.5 ), we obtain ( 23.1.39 ). For bounded $u$, choose uniformly bounded smooth functions $u_ j\downarrow u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ by theorem 5.32.1 . Their averages decrease pointwise to $Au$ by dominated convergence. The corresponding smooth base potentials $v_ j$ decrease to a bounded $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function $v$, so $Au=\pi ^*v$. Dominated convergence gives $u_ j\to u$ and $Au_ j\to Au$ in $L^2(X,\nu )$, while bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives convergence of the total masses. Thus ( 23.1.39 ) passes to $u$. If the mass is $6$, the inequality gives $u=Au$ almost everywhere. Since both functions are bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, lemma 5.24.4 gives equality everywhere. Conversely, if $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\omega _{\mathrm{FS}})$, choose smooth $v_ j\downarrow v$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ by theorem 5.32.1 . The pullbacks decrease to $u$ and are uniformly bounded. They are strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic because the base forms are positive and $\beta $ is positive on the vertical line. Their vertical derivatives vanish, so ( 23.1.5 ) gives mass $6$ for each of them. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives the same mass for $u$. It remains to prove that the constant $2/3$ is optimal. Choose a nonzero real $\rho \in C_ c^\infty (U_0)$. For $\delta \in \mathbb R$, the function \[  u(\xi ,w)=\delta \rho (\xi )\cos (\operatorname {Im}w)  \] extends by zero to a smooth function on $X$. For sufficiently small nonzero real $\delta $, it satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Its fiber average is zero, and its only fiber frequencies are $(p,q)=(0,\pm 1)$, with eigenvalue $1/4$. Hence equality holds in the fiber inequality, and therefore in ( 23.1.39 ), with nonzero left-hand side. No smaller coefficient can hold. $\square$

title: 23.1.41 Sharp damping under unitary rotations
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: The general damping estimate controls mass by the depth of a potential. On the standard Hopf threefold, unitary symmetry gives a stronger estimate: after integration along the elliptic fibers, a positive radial flux has total mass one. A semiconvexity estimate bounds the remaining radial coefficient by the square root of the depth. The resulting damping threshold is sharp, and at its endpoint finite measures can still concentrate on a pole divisor. We retain the standard threefold $X$, form $\omega $, projection $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$, fiber $E$ and probability area $\mathrm dA_ E$ of this chapter. Let $\mathcal R$ be the class of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ invariant under \[  (z_0,z')\longmapsto (z_0,Az'),\qquad A\in U(2),\quad z'=(z_1,z_2).  \] This holomorphic action preserves $\omega $. The class includes bounded and unbounded potentials. For a positive $C^1$ nonincreasing function $W:[0,+\infty )\to (0,+\infty )$ tending to zero, write \begin{gather*}  \mu _ u=\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u),\qquad \nu _{W,u}=W(-u)\mu _ u,\\  Q_ T(W)=\sup _{t\geq T}(1+\sqrt{2t})W(t),\qquad Q(W)=Q_0(W). \end{gather*} The weighted measure gives zero mass to the pole set, as does the extended non-pluripolar measure. Capacity always means $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 5.29 .
