title: 14.8 Variation of the normalization scalar
text: Integration against the adjoint probability measure eliminates the derivatives of the potential from the first variation of $b$. In the second variation, the second derivative of the logarithmic determinant contributes a nonnegative square with a minus sign. This gives concavity of $b$ and identifies the equality case. Write $b(F)$ for the scalar in ( 14.1.1 ), and use the linear normalization $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. For a smooth family $F_ t$, with $t$ in an open interval $I\subset \mathbb R$, write $(u_ t,b_ t)$ for the corresponding solutions and put $\eta _ t=\omega _{u_ t}$. By proposition 14.4.1 these depend smoothly on $t$; a dot denotes differentiation in $t$. Theorem 14.8.1 . C611B2CA264A Let $A_ t=\eta _ t^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ be the endomorphism of the tangent bundle that represents the real $(1,1)$-form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ with respect to $\eta _ t$; it is Hermitian with respect to $\eta _ t$. The normalization constant satisfies 11F81D837A44 14.8.2 \begin{align}  \dot b_ t& =-\int _ X\dot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t},\\  \ddot b_ t& =-\int _ X\ddot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t} -\int _ X\operatorname {tr}(A_ t^2)\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}.\tag{14.8.3} \end{align} In particular, for smooth real functions $F_0,G$ on $X$ and the affine family $F_ t=F_0+tG$, the function $b_ t$ is concave. Its second derivative vanishes at a parameter value if and only if $G$ is constant on $X$. Proof. Differentiating the logarithm of ( 14.1.1 ) gives \[  L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=\dot F_ t+\dot b_ t.  \] Integration against $\mu _{u_ t}$ proves ( 14.8.2 ). For a smooth family of positive Hermitian matrices $H_ t$, differentiation of the inverse matrix gives \[  \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\log \det H_ t =\operatorname {tr}(H_ t^{-1}\ddot H_ t) -\operatorname {tr}\bigl ((H_ t^{-1}\dot H_ t)^2\bigr ).  \] Apply this pointwise to the matrices of $\eta _ t$, using $\dot\eta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t$ and $\ddot\eta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ddot u_ t$. The second derivative of the logarithmic equation is \[  L_{u_ t}\ddot u_ t-\operatorname {tr}(A_ t^2) =\ddot F_ t+\ddot b_ t.  \] Integrating against $\mu _{u_ t}$ at this fixed parameter proves ( 14.8.3 ); there is no need to differentiate the measure. The eigenvalues of the Hermitian endomorphism $A_ t$ are real, so $\operatorname {tr}(A_ t^2)\geq 0$. For affine $F_ t$ we have $\ddot F_ t=0$, so the second derivative of $b_ t$ is nonpositive. If it vanishes, strict positivity of the smooth density of $\mu _{u_ t}$ implies $A_ t=0$ everywhere. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u_ t=0$, and the maximum principle shows that $\dot u_ t$ is constant. The first differentiated equation then gives $G=-\dot b_ t$, a constant. Conversely, if $G$ is constant, the solution metric is independent of $t$ and $b_ t=b_0-tG$. $\square$ Corollary 14.8.4 . B9C312CB7069 For two smooth functions $F,G$, the normalization constants satisfy \[  -\sup _ X(G-F)\leq b(G)-b(F)\leq -\inf _ X(G-F).  \] In particular, $|b(G)-b(F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty $. If $G-F$ is nonconstant, both inequalities in the first display are strict. Proof. Apply ( 14.8.2 ) along $F_ t=F+t(G-F)$ and integrate over $0\leq t\leq 1$. Each $\mu _{u_ t}$ is a probability measure with strictly positive smooth density, so the integral of a nonconstant continuous function against it lies strictly between the minimum and the maximum of that function. $\square$ Thus $b$ is a decreasing, concave, Lipschitz functional of the logarithmic density, with $b(F+a)=b(F)-a$ for every real constant $a$. By uniform approximation, it extends uniquely to a Lipschitz functional of continuous $F$. This extension concerns the scalar functional only; the existence and regularity of corresponding potentials require further estimates.

title: Corollary 14.9.4
14.10 Prescribing a Gauduchon volume form
text: We now return to a general connected compact complex manifold $X$, of dimension $n\geq 2$. To stay in a fixed Aeppli class of Gauduchon metrics, we vary the $(n-1)$st power of the metric by a term of the form $\partial \xi +\bar\partial \bar\xi $. The resulting scalar ansatz contains first derivatives of the potential as well as its complex Hessian. Theorem 14.10.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove) . 76AF759A4024 Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma _0$, a Gauduchon form $\gamma $, and a smooth real function $F$. There is a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ such that the $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Gamma _ u=\gamma _0^{n-1}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left( \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2}) \right)  \] is strictly positive, and the Hermitian form $\eta _ u$ with $\eta _ u^{n-1}=\Gamma _ u$ satisfies \[  \eta _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\gamma ^ n.  \] Here we use the linear-algebra fact that a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form is strictly positive if and only if it is the $(n-1)$st power of a Hermitian form, and that this Hermitian form is unique; the matrix form of this correspondence is described in section 14.13 . Keep $\gamma _0$ and $\gamma $ fixed for the remainder of the chapter, and write $\mathcal D_\gamma u=\Gamma _ u-\gamma _0^{n-1}$ for the part of the ansatz that is linear in $u$. To see which geometry is preserved, set $\xi _ u=\mathrm i\, \bar\partial u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2}/(4\pi )$. The Leibniz rule gives $\Gamma _ u-\gamma _0^{n-1}=\partial \xi _ u+\bar\partial \overline{\xi _ u}$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\partial \xi _ u+\bar\partial \overline{\xi _ u})=0$, if $\gamma _0$ is Gauduchon then so is $\eta _ u$, and the $(n-1)$st powers of $\gamma _0$ and $\eta _ u$ have the same Aeppli class. The uniqueness in theorem 14.10.1 concerns this scalar ansatz; it does not assert uniqueness among all Gauduchon metrics in the Aeppli class.

title: Theorem 14.10.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove)
text: Theorem 14.10.1 (Székelyhidi–Tosatti–Weinkove) . 76AF759A4024 Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma _0$, a Gauduchon form $\gamma $, and a smooth real function $F$. There is a unique pair $(u,b)\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)\times \mathbb R$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ such that the $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Gamma _ u=\gamma _0^{n-1}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left( \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial u\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2}) \right)  \] is strictly positive, and the Hermitian form $\eta _ u$ with $\eta _ u^{n-1}=\Gamma _ u$ satisfies \[  \eta _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{F+b}\gamma ^ n.  \] of theorem 14.10.1 . Let \[  F_0=\log \frac{\gamma _0^ n}{\gamma ^ n},\qquad F_ t=(1-t)F_0+tF,\quad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] We use the continuity method along the path $F_ t$. At $t=0$, the pair $u=0$, $b=0$ solves the equation, since $\eta _0=\gamma _0$. During the continuity argument we normalize potentials by $\int _ Xu\, \gamma ^ n=0$; adding a constant does not affect the equation, and at the end we impose $\sup _ Xu=0$ instead. For openness, the derivative of the equation with respect to the mean-zero potential and the scalar is $(w,a)\mapsto \mathcal L_ uw-a$. Given a right-hand side $q$, integration against the adjoint probability measure of proposition 14.12.1 forces $a=-\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $. The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero solution $w$, and Schauder estimates bound this inverse between Hölder spaces. Since positivity of $\Gamma _ u$ is an open condition, the implicit function theorem gives solutions for all nearby parameters. For closedness, note that the functions $F_ t$ are uniformly bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. After supremum normalization, proposition 14.11.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, the second-order and rescaling estimates bound the gradient and the complex Hessian, and lemma 14.17.1 gives all higher bounds. Subtracting the mean preserves all derivative bounds and changes the potentials by uniformly bounded constants. A subsequence of mean-zero solutions along a convergent sequence of parameters therefore converges smoothly to a solution at the limiting parameter, and the bounds $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ preserve strict positivity in the limit. Thus the set of solvable parameters is nonempty, open and closed, hence equal to $[0,1]$. Finally, consider two solutions $(u,b)$ and $(w,c)$ for the same $F$. At a maximum of $u-w$ their gradients agree and their complex Hessians are ordered, so the first-order terms are equal there and, since $P_ n$ preserves the order, $Q_ u\leq Q_ w$. The equation then gives $b\leq c$, and at a minimum the reverse inequality gives $b\geq c$. Hence $b=c$. Along the segment between $u$ and $w$, the matrices $Q$ remain positive because the ansatz is affine in the potential. Integrating the derivative of the logarithmic determinant along that segment produces a uniformly elliptic scalar operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term that annihilates $u-w$. The maximum principle shows that $u-w$ is constant, and the supremum normalization makes the constant zero. $\square$

section: 14.12 The adjoint equation for Gauduchon volume
text: As for the Monge–Ampère equation, solving the linearized Gauduchon volume equation requires a compatibility condition, given by an adjoint probability measure. Taking the $(n-1)$st root multiplies the trace linearization by the factor $n/(n-1)$, and the first-order term of the ansatz introduces a drift term. We compute the linearized operator at any potential with $\Gamma _ u>0$, and then express its adjoint condition as an equation for a positive $(1,1)$-form. Throughout this section we put $K=\gamma ^{n-2}$. Proposition 14.12.1 . 706EB82AB6A2 On the open set of smooth potentials $u$ with $\Gamma _ u>0$, the derivative of \[  \mathcal G(u)=\log \frac{\eta _ u^ n}{\gamma ^ n}  \] is the real elliptic operator 62F6382D2CAC 14.12.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal L_ uv= \frac{n}{n-1}\frac{\eta _ u\wedge \mathcal D_\gamma v}{\eta _ u^ n}. \end{equation} It has no zeroth-order term, and its kernel consists of the constants. There is a unique smooth positive function $\rho _ u$, normalized by $\int _ X\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n=1$, such that the probability measure \[  \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n  \] satisfies $\int _ X\mathcal L_ uv\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =0$ for every smooth real $v$. Proof. For a smooth path of potentials $u(t)$, write $\eta =\eta _{u(t)}$ and $\Gamma =\Gamma _{u(t)}$. Differentiating $\eta ^{n-1}=\Gamma $ gives $(n-1)\dot\eta \wedge \eta ^{n-2}=\dot\Gamma $, where $\dot\Gamma =\mathcal D_\gamma \dot u$. Wedging with $\eta $ and dividing by $\eta ^ n$, we obtain \[  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log \eta ^ n =\frac{n}{n-1}\frac{\eta \wedge \dot\Gamma }{\eta ^ n},  \] which proves ( 14.12.2 ). Only the second-order term $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \gamma ^{n-2}$ of $\mathcal D_\gamma v$ contributes to the principal symbol. For a nonzero complex covector $\zeta $ of type $(1,0)$, the form \[  \eta _ u\wedge \mathrm i\zeta \wedge \overline\zeta \wedge \gamma ^{n-2}  \] is a positive volume form. Hence the principal symbol is positive definite, and by compactness the operator is uniformly elliptic for each fixed $u$. The remaining term is of first order, and constants are annihilated, so the strong maximum principle gives $\ker \mathcal L_ u=\mathbb R$. The Fredholm and positivity arguments in the proof of theorem 11.4.2 apply to this real elliptic operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term. Its index is zero by deformation to a Laplacian, so its formal adjoint with respect to $\eta _ u^ n$ has a one-dimensional kernel spanned by a smooth strictly positive function. Normalizing its integral to one gives $\rho _ u$ and proves uniqueness. $\square$ The adjoint condition can be expressed as an equation for the positive $(1,1)$-form $\rho _ u\eta _ u$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $A$, set \[  \mathcal A_\gamma (A) =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A\wedge \gamma ^{n-2} +\operatorname {Re}\left(\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi } \partial A\wedge \bar\partial (\gamma ^{n-2})\right).  \] This is a real form of top degree, and $\mathcal A_\gamma $ is the formal adjoint of $\mathcal D_\gamma $ under the pairing of $(1,1)$-forms with $(n-1,n-1)$-forms, as the proof below shows. Proposition 14.12.3 . 029A1D30A55E The function $\rho _ u$ of proposition 14.12.1 is characterized by BD3712C889A6 14.12.4 \begin{equation}  \mathcal A_\gamma (\rho _ u\eta _ u)=0, \qquad \int _ X\rho _ u\eta _ u^ n=1. \end{equation} When $n=2$, its first equation is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ u\eta _ u)=0$. When $\eta _ u=\gamma $, the function $\rho _ u$ is constant and $\mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. Proof. We first prove that, for every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $A$ and every smooth real function $v$ on $X$, 195CC5F57ABE 14.12.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X A\wedge \mathcal D_\gamma v =\int _ X v\, \mathcal A_\gamma (A). \end{equation} Write $c=\mathrm i/(2\pi )$. Since $A,K,v$ are real, expanding the real part gives \[  \mathcal D_\gamma v =c\, \partial \bar\partial v\wedge K +\frac c2\bigl (\partial v\wedge \bar\partial K -\bar\partial v\wedge \partial K\bigr ).  \] Integrating the first term by parts twice gives $\int _ Xv\, c\partial \bar\partial (A\wedge K)$, and integrating each first-order term by parts once gives the correction \[  \int _ Xv\, \frac c2 \bigl (-\partial A\wedge \bar\partial K +\bar\partial A\wedge \partial K -2A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K\bigr ).  \] Finally, \[  \partial \bar\partial (A\wedge K) =\partial \bar\partial A\wedge K -\bar\partial A\wedge \partial K +\partial A\wedge \bar\partial K +A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K.  \] Adding these contributions cancels the terms containing $A\wedge \partial \bar\partial K$ and leaves $\mathcal A_\gamma (A)$. This proves ( 14.12.5 ). Applied to $A=\rho _ u\eta _ u$, it shows by ( 14.12.2 ) that $\int _ X\mathcal L_ uv\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $ is a fixed positive multiple of $\int _ Xv\, \mathcal A_\gamma (\rho _ u\eta _ u)$, so the adjoint condition is equivalent to ( 14.12.4 ). For $n=2$, we have $K=1$, which gives the first special case. For the second, the product rule gives \[  \mathcal A_\gamma (\gamma ) =\frac1{n-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0.  \] By uniqueness, $\rho _ u$ is consequently the constant $(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{-1}$. $\square$ For $n>2$ the equation for $\rho _ u\eta _ u$ involves the first derivatives of $\gamma ^{n-2}$, so the fixed auxiliary metric $\gamma $ remains part of the adjoint equation; it is not simply the Gauduchon condition for $\eta _ u$.

title: 14.14 The largest-eigenvalue estimate
text:
The matrix structure now gives a bound for the complex Hessian in terms of the squared gradient. We apply the maximum principle to the largest eigenvalue of $g$, corrected by functions of the gradient and of the potential. The missing torsion indices allow the concavity square to absorb the third derivatives. If the smallest eigenvalue is not too negative, the positive background closes the estimate; otherwise that eigenvalue produces a large positive Hessian square. We keep the notation of section 14.13 . Plain subscripts on scalar functions and subscripts after a comma on matrix coefficients denote coordinate derivatives, and the coefficients of the Chern connection of $\gamma $ are written $\Gamma ^ q_{ik}$. Choose $	au >0$ with $Q_0\geq 	au \gamma $. Theorem 14.14.1 . 2763FB514B34 Fix smooth Hermitian forms $\gamma _0,\gamma $ on a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$. For a smooth real function $h$ on $X$, suppose that $v$ is a smooth solution of \[  Q=Q_0+P_\gamma (\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial v)+Z(\partial v)>0, \qquad \log \det _\gamma Q=h,  \] with the tensors of section 14.13 . If $\| v\| _{C^0}$ and $\| h\| _{C^2}$ are bounded, then \[  \sup _ X|\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial v|_\gamma \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial v|_\gamma ^2 igr ),  \] where $C$ depends only on these bounds and the fixed smooth data. Proof. Adding a constant, we may assume $\sup _ Xv=0$, and we write $-M\leq v\leq 0$. Set \[  K=1+\sup _ X|\partial v|_\gamma ^2,\qquad \phi (s)=-	frac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \psi (t)=D_1\mathrm{e}^{-D_2t}.  \] The positive constants $D_1,D_2$ will be chosen below using only the fixed data. On $0\leq s\leq K$, \[   rac1{4K}\leq \phi '\leq  rac1{2K},\qquad \phi ''=2(\phi ')^2,\qquad 0\leq \phi \leq 	frac 12\log 2.  \] Let $\lambda _1$ be the largest eigenvalue of $g=\chi +\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial v+W$ relative to $\gamma $. It is positive, because $\operatorname {tr}_\gamma g=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma Q>0$. Consider a maximum point of \[  H=\log \lambda _1+\phi (|\partial v|_\gamma ^2)+\psi (v).  \] It suffices to bound $\lambda _1/K$ at this point, because the other two terms of $H$ are uniformly bounded once $D_1,D_2$ are fixed. We may assume that this ratio exceeds any fixed constant specified in the course of the argument. Choose holomorphic coordinates that are unitary at the maximum point, with $g$ diagonal there and eigenvalues ordered as $\lambda _1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda _ n$. All estimates below are at this point, and repeated indices are summed only when a sum is written. Put $\lambda =\lambda _1$ and use the weights $t_ i,f_ k$ and their sum $\mathcal F$ from lemma 14.13.5 . Since $\sum _ i\lambda _ i>0$ and the eigenvalues are ordered, \[  |\lambda _ i|\leq (n-1)\lambda ,\qquad |v_{i ar j}|\leq C\lambda \quad \hbox{if }\lambda \geq K.  \] The constant $C$ may change from line to line; it is independent of $K$ and, until $D_1,D_2$ are fixed below, also of $D_1,D_2$. The pure second derivatives $v_{ij}$ are not covered by this bound. $\square$ 14.14.2 Differentiating the largest eigenvalue. 9994CF39B2B0 Since $\lambda _1$ need not be smooth where it is a multiple eigenvalue, we first perturb $g$. Choose a smooth local unitary frame that is parallel for the Chern connection at the point, with first vector an eigenvector for $\lambda $. Let $B$ be the tensor that is diagonal in this frame, with eigenvalues $0,\epsilon _0,\ldots ,\epsilon _0$, where $\epsilon _0>0$ is fixed and small. Then $B\geq 0$, $
abla B=0$ at the point, and its second derivatives are bounded by fixed constants. The largest eigenvalue $\widetilde\lambda $ of $g-B$ is simple near the point, is at most $\lambda _1(g)$, and equals $\lambda $ at the point. Hence the smooth function $\widetilde H$, defined like $H$ with $\widetilde\lambda $ in place of $\lambda _1$, also has a local maximum there. Only the largest eigenvalue needs to be simple. For a family of self-adjoint matrices with a simple largest eigenvalue, differentiate the equation for the normalized eigenvector. Its component in the $p$th eigenspace is the corresponding derivative of the matrix divided by the eigenvalue gap. Differentiating the eigenvalue once more therefore gives  egin{align*}  a_ k:=\widetilde\lambda _ k& =
abla _ k g_{1 ar1},\  \widetilde\lambda _{k ar k} & =
abla _{ ar k}
abla _ k g_{1 ar1}+O(1) +\sum _{p>1} rac{|
abla _ k g_{1 ar p}|^2+ |
abla _ k g_{p ar1}|^2}{\lambda -\lambda _ p+\epsilon _0}. \end{align*} This formula remains valid if some of the lower eigenvalues coincide, with the sum taken over any orthonormal basis of their eigenspaces. The gaps are positive and at most $n\lambda +\epsilon _0$. title: Theorem 14.14.1
text: Theorem 14.14.1 . 2763FB514B34 Fix smooth Hermitian forms $\gamma _0,\gamma $ on a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$. For a smooth real function $h$ on $X$, suppose that $v$ is a smooth solution of \[  Q=Q_0+P_\gamma (\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v)+Z(\partial v)>0, \qquad \log \det _\gamma Q=h,  \] with the tensors of section 14.13 . If $\| v\| _{C^0}$ and $\| h\| _{C^2}$ are bounded, then \[  \sup _ X|\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v|_\gamma \leq C\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial v|_\gamma ^2\bigr ),  \] where $C$ depends only on these bounds and the fixed smooth data. Proof. Adding a constant, we may assume $\sup _ Xv=0$, and we write $-M\leq v\leq 0$. Set \[  K=1+\sup _ X|\partial v|_\gamma ^2,\qquad \phi (s)=-\tfrac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \psi (t)=D_1\mathrm{e}^{-D_2t}.  \] The positive constants $D_1,D_2$ will be chosen below using only the fixed data. On $0\leq s\leq K$, \[  \frac1{4K}\leq \phi '\leq \frac1{2K},\qquad \phi ''=2(\phi ')^2,\qquad 0\leq \phi \leq \tfrac 12\log 2.  \] Let $\lambda _1$ be the largest eigenvalue of $g=\chi +\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v+W$ relative to $\gamma $. It is positive, because $\operatorname {tr}_\gamma g=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma Q>0$. Consider a maximum point of \[  H=\log \lambda _1+\phi (|\partial v|_\gamma ^2)+\psi (v).  \] It suffices to bound $\lambda _1/K$ at this point, because the other two terms of $H$ are uniformly bounded once $D_1,D_2$ are fixed. We may assume that this ratio exceeds any fixed constant specified in the course of the argument. Choose holomorphic coordinates that are unitary at the maximum point, with $g$ diagonal there and eigenvalues ordered as $\lambda _1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda _ n$. All estimates below are at this point, and repeated indices are summed only when a sum is written. Put $\lambda =\lambda _1$ and use the weights $t_ i,f_ k$ and their sum $\mathcal F$ from lemma 14.13.5 . Since $\sum _ i\lambda _ i>0$ and the eigenvalues are ordered, \[  |\lambda _ i|\leq (n-1)\lambda ,\qquad |v_{i\bar j}|\leq C\lambda \quad \hbox{if }\lambda \geq K.  \] The constant $C$ may change from line to line; it is independent of $K$ and, until $D_1,D_2$ are fixed below, also of $D_1,D_2$. The pure second derivatives $v_{ij}$ are not covered by this bound. $\square$

title: 14.15 A Liouville theorem for the limiting cone

section: 14.15 A Liouville theorem for the limiting cone
text:
Rescaling at a point of large gradient removes the background and first-order terms of the Gauduchon equation and leaves a degenerate equation on $\mathbb C^ n$, whose solutions are maximal for a cone of matrices. We show that its bounded Lipschitz solutions are constant. The proof argues by induction on the dimension: if the energy of a solution in some complex direction becomes small on large balls, a limit is independent of one variable; if all directional energies stay positive, they give a strictly admissible comparison function. On $\mathbb C^ n$ we use Euclidean coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$, the identity matrix $I$, the Euclidean balls $B(x,r)$ and Euclidean volume $\mathrm{d}y$. In this section $
abla $ and $\Delta $ denote the Euclidean real gradient and Laplacian, and $\partial _\xi $ denotes differentiation in a complex direction $\xi $. For $n\geq 2$ and a Hermitian matrix $H$, set \[  P_ n(H)= rac{(\operatorname {tr}H)I-H}{n-1}.  \] This is the map $P_\gamma $ of section 14.13 for the Euclidean metric. It preserves nonnegativity and satisfies $P_ n(I)=I$ and $\operatorname {tr}P_ n(H)=\operatorname {tr}H$. For a real function $v$ write $H(v)=(v_{i ar j})$ in Euclidean coordinates. A continuous function $v$ on an open set of $\mathbb C^ n$ is admissible if $P_ n(H(v))\geq 0$ in the sense of matrix-valued distributions. It is maximal for this cone if it is admissible and every smooth function $h$ touching $v$ from below at a point satisfies \[  P_ n(H(h))
ot>0  \] at that point. Here touching means that $v-h$ has a local minimum with value zero, which need not be a strict minimum. Maximality is thus the viscosity supersolution condition for the degenerate equation $\det P_ n(H(v))=0$ on the boundary of the cone, together with distributional admissibility. Taking the trace shows that admissible functions are subharmonic. Since $P_ n$ is linear, convolution preserves admissibility, and so do nonnegative linear combinations and integrals of admissible smooth functions. Translations and unitary changes of coordinates preserve both conditions, as do multiplication by a positive constant and addition of a constant. Lemma 14.15.1 . 6E3495B1A225 Local uniform limits of admissible maximal functions are admissible and maximal. If $v$ is maximal on a bounded open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $h$ is smooth and admissible on $D$, both functions are continuous on $\overline D$, and $h\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $h\leq v$ on $D$. Proof. Let $v_ j$ be admissible maximal functions converging locally uniformly to $v$. Distributional positivity is preserved under this convergence. For maximality, suppose that a smooth function $h$ touches $v$ from below at $z_0$ and $P_ n(H(h)(z_0))>0$. Choose a small ball on which $v-h\geq 0$. Replacing $h$ by $h-\delta |z-z_0|^2$, with $\delta >0$ sufficiently small, keeps its matrix strictly positive near $z_0$ and makes the minimum strict. Uniform convergence then produces interior minimum points of $v_ j-h+\delta |z-z_0|^2$ tending to $z_0$. Adding the minimum value to the test function gives a function touching $v_ j$ from below with strictly positive matrix, a contradiction. For comparison, choose $R$ with $\overline D\subset \{ |z|\leq R\} $. If $h>v$ somewhere, then for small $\delta >0$ the smooth function \[  h_\delta =h+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)  \] still exceeds $v$ at some interior point and is at most $v$ on the boundary. Hence the negative minimum of $v-h_\delta $ is attained in the interior. But $P_ n(H(h_\delta ))=P_ n(H(h))+\delta I>0$ there, which contradicts maximality after the minimum value is added to $h_\delta $. No boundary regularity of $D$ is needed for this argument. $\square$ Theorem 14.15.2 . AC61FE141521 A bounded globally Lipschitz function on $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 2$, that is maximal for this cone is constant. Proof. Let $v$ be a bounded globally Lipschitz maximal function on $\mathbb C^ n$. We argue by induction on $n$. For $n=2$, $P_2(H)\geq 0$ is equivalent to $H\geq 0$, so $v$ is plurisubharmonic, and lemma 5.24.5 shows that it is constant. We first explain the reduction in dimension for $n\geq 3$. If a function is independent of $z_ n$, its complex Hessian has the block form $H\oplus 0$. The first block of $P_ n(H\oplus 0)$ is \[   rac{n-2}{n-1}P_{n-1}(H),  \] and the last entry is $\operatorname {tr}H/(n-1)$. Nonnegativity of $P_{n-1}(H)$ implies $\operatorname {tr}H\geq 0$, and positive definiteness implies $\operatorname {tr}H>0$. Thus $P_ n(H\oplus 0)$ is nonnegative, respectively positive definite, exactly when $P_{n-1}(H)$ is. The distributional version follows from the same linear identities. A test function in $n-1$ variables extends to $\mathbb C^ n$ independently of $z_ n$, so maximality also passes to $n-1$ variables. Consequently the induction hypothesis applies to bounded Lipschitz maximal functions that are independent of one complex variable. Suppose now that $v$ is nonconstant. Adding a constant and multiplying by a positive constant, we may assume that $\inf v=0$ and $\sup v=1$. Let $L$ be the Lipschitz constant of $v$. Choose a smooth radial nonnegative probability kernel $\eta $, supported in the closed unit ball and strictly positive in its interior. For a bounded measurable function $f$ and $r>0$, write \[  [f]_ r(x)=\int _{\mathbb C^ n}f(x+y)\eta _ r(y)\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad \eta _ r(y)=r^{-2n}\eta (y/r),\qquad v_\epsilon =[v]_\epsilon .  \] Both $v$ and $v^2$ are subharmonic. For $v^2$, use $v_\epsilon \geq 0$ and $\Delta (v_\epsilon ^2)=2v_\epsilon \Delta v_\epsilon +2|
abla v_\epsilon |^2\geq 0$, and pass to the uniform limit as $\epsilon 	o 0$. For $f=v$ and for $f=v^2$, the averages $[f]_ r(x)$ increase with $r$, by the monotonicity of spherical means of subharmonic functions. Their limit as $r	o \infty $ is independent of $x$, since \[  |[f]_ r(x)-[f]_ r(y)| \leq \| f\| _\infty \| \eta _ r(\cdot -x)-\eta _ r(\cdot -y)\| _{L^1} \leq C rac{|x-y|}{r}.  \] By the submean inequality this limit is at least $f(x)$ for every $x$, while it is at most $\sup f=1$. Therefore B2C22D2540A1 14.15.3  egin{equation}  [v]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1,\qquad [v^2]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. First suppose that there exist $ho >0$, sequences $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ and $r_ k	o \infty $, points $x_ k$ and unit complex directions $\xi _ k$ such that C26DE70CAF39 14.15.4  egin{equation}  [v^2]_{r_ k}(x_ k)+[v]_ho (x_ k)-2v(x_ k)\geq  rac43, \qquad \int _{B(x_ k,r_ k)}|\partial _{\xi _ k}v_{\epsilon _ k}|^2\, \mathrm{d}y \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Translate $x_ k$ to the origin and make $\xi _ k$ the last complex direction by a unitary change of coordinates. The resulting functions have the same bounds and Lipschitz constant, so by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and lemma 14.15.1 a subsequence converges locally uniformly to a maximal function $a$. The corresponding mollifications at scale $\epsilon _ k$ have the same local uniform limit, and by the integral condition their derivatives in the last complex direction tend to zero in $L^2$ on every fixed ball. Hence $\partial a/\partial z_ n=0$ in the sense of distributions. Since $a$ is real and continuous, it is independent of $z_ n$. The dimension reduction and the induction hypothesis show that $a$ is a constant $c\in [0,1]$. In the first inequality of ( 14.15.4 ), the first term is at most one, while the average at the fixed radius $ho $ and the value at the origin both tend to $c$. It would follow that $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. In the remaining case, for every fixed $ho >0$ there is $C_ho \geq 1$ such that, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_ho ^{-1}$, $r>C_ho $, and \[  [v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_ho (x)-2v(x)\geq  rac43,  \] one has 89711B0B590A 14.15.5  egin{equation}  \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm{d}y \geq C_ho ^{-1} \quad \hbox{for every unit complex direction }\xi . \end{equation} Indeed, if this failed for $C_ho =k$ for every integer $k$, a diagonal choice would give sequences as in ( 14.15.4 ). After a translation we may assume that $v(0)<1/12$. By ( 14.15.3 ), choose $ho $ with $[v]_ho (0)>3/4$, and then $r>C_ho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_ho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. We claim that, for some $c>0$, \[  [v^2]_ r-c|z|^2  \] is smooth and admissible on $D$. To prove the claim, differentiate the square of the smooth mollification: \[  H(v_\epsilon ^2) =2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon ) +2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \, \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}.  \] Denote by $A_\epsilon $ and $B_\epsilon $ the convolutions at the fixed radius $r$ of these two terms. The first satisfies $P_ n(A_\epsilon )\geq 0$, because $v_\epsilon \geq 0$, $v_\epsilon $ is admissible, and $P_ n$ is linear. The second satisfies $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$ for small $\epsilon $, with a constant $c_0>0$. Here the passage from the unweighted integral in ( 14.15.5 ) to the convolution needs care. The bound $|
abla v_\epsilon |\leq L$ makes the energy of a sufficiently thin boundary annulus of $B(x,r)$ at most $C_ho ^{-1}/2$, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball, the fixed kernel $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. For points $x\in D$, ( 14.15.5 ) then gives a uniform positive lower bound for the weighted integral in every direction, which is the asserted matrix inequality for $B_\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Since $P_ n$ preserves nonnegative matrices, \[  P_ n igl (H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r)-cI igr )\geq 0 \quad \hbox{on }D.  \] As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, $v_\epsilon ^2	o v^2$ uniformly, and convolution at the fixed positive radius $r$ gives convergence of all derivatives. This proves the claim. The smooth function \[  h=	frac 12 igl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_ho -4/3 igr )  \] is therefore admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, it is bounded because $v$ and its averages are bounded, and it lies in $D$. Moreover $v=h$ on $\partial D'$. Lemma 14.15.1 , applied on $D'$, gives $h\leq v$ there, which contradicts the definition of $D'$. This excludes the second case and proves the theorem. $\square$ The Lipschitz bound is used both for the compactness of translates and for the annulus estimate. For $n>1$, the conclusion would not follow from boundedness and subharmonicity alone, since $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ carries nonconstant bounded subharmonic functions.

title: 14.16 The gradient bound by rescaling
text: If the gradients of a family of solutions were unbounded, rescaling at points of maximal gradient would produce functions on growing Euclidean balls with gradient one at the origin. The Hessian estimate makes these functions compact in $C^1$ on every fixed ball, so a limit is a bounded Lipschitz function on $\mathbb C^ n$ with nonzero gradient at the origin. The rescaled determinant tends to zero, so the limit is maximal for the cone of section 14.15 , which contradicts theorem 14.15.2 . Consider a family of smooth solutions $(u,b)$ of the equation in theorem 14.10.1 , normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, with $\| F\| _{C^0}\leq M$ for a fixed $M>0$. By proposition 14.11.1 , $\| u\| _{C^0}$ and $|b|$ are uniformly bounded. The following proposition shows that a Hessian estimate in terms of the squared gradient implies bounds for both. Proposition 14.16.1 . EFE7268223F4 Suppose there is a constant $K$ such that every solution in this family satisfies 977E6E7B264D 14.16.2 \begin{equation}  \sup _ X|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u|_\gamma \leq K\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\gamma ^2\bigr ). \end{equation} Then $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\gamma $ and $\sup _ X|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u|_\gamma $ are bounded by a constant depending only on $X,\gamma _0,\gamma ,M$ and $K$. Proof. We use the matrices $Q_ u$ of ( 14.13.1 ). Their background term $Q_0$ is fixed, and $Z$ is linear in the first derivatives of $u/(2\pi )$. Suppose that the gradient bound fails. Then there are solutions $(u_ j,b_ j)$ with prescribed functions $F_ j$ such that \[  A_ j=\sup _ X|\partial u_ j|_\gamma =|\partial u_ j(x_ j)|_\gamma \longrightarrow \infty .  \] After passing to a subsequence, the points $x_ j$ lie in one fixed coordinate neighborhood. Translate the coordinates so that $x_ j$ becomes the origin, and apply a uniformly controlled complex linear change of coordinates so that the matrix of $\gamma $ at $x_ j$ is the identity; a coordinate ball of fixed radius remains available around every $x_ j$. On balls whose radii tend to infinity define \[  v_ j(z)=u_ j(x_ j+z/A_ j),  \] in these coordinates. The coefficient matrices $g_ j(z)$ of $\gamma $ at the points $x_ j+z/A_ j$ converge smoothly to the identity on every fixed ball. In this notation \[  |v_ j|\leq C, \qquad |\partial v_ j|_{g_ j}\leq 1, \qquad |\partial v_ j(0)|=1.  \] The assumed estimate ( 14.16.2 ) gives a uniform bound for all complex Hessian entries of $v_ j$ on every fixed ball, since two derivatives contribute the factor $A_ j^{-2}$. Hence the Euclidean Laplacians of the $v_ j$ are uniformly bounded, and the interior estimates for the Laplacian give local $W^{2,p}$ bounds for every finite $p$. Choosing $p>2n$ and using Sobolev embedding and compactness, we extract a diagonal subsequence converging in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a function $v$ on $\mathbb C^ n$. This function is bounded and globally Lipschitz, and \[  |\partial v(0)|=1.  \] Now divide the matrix in ( 14.13.1 ) by $A_ j^2$ and evaluate it at the scaled points. The background term becomes $O(A_ j^{-2})$, and the first-order term becomes $O(A_ j^{-1})$, since one derivative of $u_ j$ is $A_ j$ times a derivative of $v_ j$. Since the complex Hessians of $v_ j$ are uniformly bounded and $g_ j\to I$, we obtain on any fixed ball 3DCC81BE4D1E 14.16.3 \begin{equation}  A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j} =P_ n\left(\frac{H(v_ j)}{2\pi }\right)+o(1), \qquad \det (A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j}) =A_ j^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)(F_ j+b_ j)}\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} To be precise, we compute in the unitary frames obtained from the positive square roots $S_ j=g_ j^{-1/2}$. In these frames the principal matrix is $P_ n(S_ jH(v_ j)S_ j/(2\pi ))$, which differs from $P_ n(H(v_ j)/(2\pi ))$ by an error tending to zero uniformly; no derivatives of the frames are taken, and the determinant identity is exact in unitary frames. Since the matrices on the left of ( 14.16.3 ) are positive and the positive factor $1/(2\pi )$ does not change the cone, passing to the limit in the sense of distributions gives $P_ n(H(v))\geq 0$. It remains to check maximality. Suppose that a smooth function $h$ touches $v$ from below at $z_0$ and $P_ n(H(h)(z_0))>0$. Subtract $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ with $\delta >0$ small; on a small ball this makes the contact strict and preserves strict positivity of the matrix. Local uniform convergence gives points $z_ j\to z_0$ at which $v_ j$ minus this perturbed test function has an interior local minimum. At such a minimum, \[  H(v_ j)(z_ j)\geq H(h)(z_ j)-\delta I.  \] Because $P_ n$ preserves nonnegative matrices, ( 14.16.3 ) now implies $A_ j^{-2}Q_{u_ j}(z_ j)\geq cI$ for a fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $j$. The determinant of this matrix is then at least $c^ n$, which contradicts the limit zero in ( 14.16.3 ). Thus $v$ is maximal for the cone of section 14.15 . By theorem 14.15.2 , $v$ is constant, which contradicts $|\partial v(0)|=1$. This proves the uniform gradient bound, and substitution in ( 14.16.2 ) gives the uniform complex Hessian bound. $\square$ For prescribed functions $F$ bounded in $C^2$, proposition 14.11.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, and theorem 14.14.1 , applied to $v=u/(2\pi )$ and $h=(n-1)(F+b)$, proves ( 14.16.2 ). Thus both the gradient and the complex Hessian are uniformly bounded.

title: 14.17 Existence for the Gauduchon ansatz
text: The potential, gradient and Hessian bounds put the matrices $Q_ u$ in a compact set of positive matrices. This yields uniform ellipticity after the real Hessian is projected to its complex part and transformed by $P_ n$, so local elliptic regularity gives the compactness needed for closedness in the continuity method; the adjoint probability measure gives openness. The maximum principle then proves uniqueness within the scalar ansatz. Lemma 14.17.1 . 19E4D601D907 Let $\gamma _0,\gamma $ be as in theorem 14.10.1 . If the prescribed functions $F$ range over a set of smooth functions bounded in every $C^ k$ norm, then the smooth solutions $(u,b)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$ are bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. Proof. Work with $v=u/(2\pi )$ and write $Q=Q_ u$ for the matrix in ( 14.13.1 ). By proposition 14.11.1 , theorem 14.14.1 , proposition 14.16.1 , the function $v$, its gradient and its complex Hessian are uniformly bounded, and so are the constants $b$. Hence the eigenvalues of $Q$ are uniformly bounded above, and by the equation its determinant is uniformly bounded below. Every eigenvalue is therefore also bounded below by a positive constant. Choose fixed numbers $0<a<b_0$ such that $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ in unitary frames for every solution. The function $\Delta _\gamma v=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma (\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v)$ is uniformly bounded, and $\Delta _\gamma $ is a fixed uniformly elliptic operator. Its interior $W^{2,p}$ estimates, applied on a finite cover, bound $v$ in $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$. Choose $p>2n$ and $0<\alpha <1-2n/p$; Sobolev embedding gives a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Thus the matrix $R(x)=Q_0(x)+Z_ x(\partial v(x))$ is uniformly bounded in $C^\alpha $. On a coordinate ball, let $\mathcal H_ x(A)$ denote the Hermitian matrix of $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial v$ at $x$ in a fixed smooth unitary frame, expressed as a function of the real Hessian $A=D^2_{\mathbb R}v(x)$. It is a real linear function of $A$ depending smoothly on $x$. If a real symmetric matrix $N$ is nonnegative, then $\mathcal H_ x(N)\geq 0$, and its trace is comparable to $\operatorname {tr}_{\mathbb R}N$ with uniform positive constants on the ball. This follows by evaluating on a vector and its rotation by $\mathrm i$, or from the coordinate formula for $v_{i\bar j}$. Freeze the function $\partial v(x)$ already obtained in $R(x)$, and define for all real symmetric matrices $A$ \[  \widetilde\Phi (A,x)= \inf _{aI\leq B\leq b_0I} \left\{ \log \det B+ \operatorname {tr}\left[B^{-1} \bigl (R(x)+P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(A))-B\bigr )\right]\right\} .  \] The infimum is over a fixed compact set of positive Hermitian matrices, and each expression in braces is an affine function of $A$, so $\widetilde\Phi $ is concave in $A$. If $R(x)+P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(A))$ lies in that compact set, then $\widetilde\Phi (A,x)$ equals its logarithmic determinant: each expression in braces is a tangent affine function of the concave logarithmic determinant, and the tangent at that matrix itself attains equality. For $N\geq 0$, each of these affine functions increases by \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B^{-1}P_ n(\mathcal H_ x(N))\bigr )  \] when $A$ is replaced by $A+N$. Since $P_ n$ preserves positivity and trace, this increment lies between fixed positive multiples of $\operatorname {tr}_{\mathbb R}N$, uniformly in $B$ and $x$. Taking infima preserves both inequalities, so $\widetilde\Phi $ is uniformly elliptic on all real symmetric matrices. Smoothness of $\mathcal H_ x$ and the uniform $C^\alpha $ bound for $R$ also give \[  |\widetilde\Phi (A,x)-\widetilde\Phi (A,y)| \leq C|x-y|^\alpha (1+\| A\| ).  \] These are the hypotheses of the local Evans–Krylov estimate for concave uniformly elliptic equations with Hölder dependence on $x$, in the formulation given in section 25.8 . The value $\widetilde\Phi (0,x)$ is uniformly bounded, by the compactness of the set of matrices $B$ and the bound for $R$. By the choice of $a$ and $b_0$, the given smooth function solves \[  \widetilde\Phi (D^2_{\mathbb R}v,x)=(n-1)(F+b)  \] on the ball. The Evans–Krylov estimate, applied on smaller balls of a finite cover, yields a uniform $C^{2,\beta }$ bound for some $\beta >0$. Differentiating the original matrix equation gives linear uniformly elliptic equations for the first derivatives of $v$, whose coefficients, including the first-order coefficients coming from $Z$, are now Hölder continuous. Local Schauder estimates give $C^{3,\beta }$ bounds, and differentiation and induction give all higher bounds. The finite coordinate cover makes the bounds global. The only regularity results used here are the standard $W^{2,p}$ estimates for the Laplacian, the Evans–Krylov estimate for concave equations, and the Schauder estimates. $\square$ of theorem 14.10.1 . Let \[  F_0=\log \frac{\gamma _0^ n}{\gamma ^ n},\qquad F_ t=(1-t)F_0+tF,\quad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] We use the continuity method along the path $F_ t$. At $t=0$, the pair $u=0$, $b=0$ solves the equation, since $\eta _0=\gamma _0$. During the continuity argument we normalize potentials by $\int _ Xu\, \gamma ^ n=0$; adding a constant does not affect the equation, and at the end we impose $\sup _ Xu=0$ instead. For openness, the derivative of the equation with respect to the mean-zero potential and the scalar is $(w,a)\mapsto \mathcal L_ uw-a$. Given a right-hand side $q$, integration against the adjoint probability measure of proposition 14.12.1 forces $a=-\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma $. The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero solution $w$, and Schauder estimates bound this inverse between Hölder spaces. Since positivity of $\Gamma _ u$ is an open condition, the implicit function theorem gives solutions for all nearby parameters. For closedness, note that the functions $F_ t$ are uniformly bounded in every $C^ k$ norm. After supremum normalization, proposition 14.11.1 bounds $u$ and $b$, the second-order and rescaling estimates bound the gradient and the complex Hessian, and lemma 14.17.1 gives all higher bounds. Subtracting the mean preserves all derivative bounds and changes the potentials by uniformly bounded constants. A subsequence of mean-zero solutions along a convergent sequence of parameters therefore converges smoothly to a solution at the limiting parameter, and the bounds $aI\leq Q\leq b_0I$ preserve strict positivity in the limit. Thus the set of solvable parameters is nonempty, open and closed, hence equal to $[0,1]$. Finally, consider two solutions $(u,b)$ and $(w,c)$ for the same $F$. At a maximum of $u-w$ their gradients agree and their complex Hessians are ordered, so the first-order terms are equal there and, since $P_ n$ preserves the order, $Q_ u\leq Q_ w$. The equation then gives $b\leq c$, and at a minimum the reverse inequality gives $b\geq c$. Hence $b=c$. Along the segment between $u$ and $w$, the matrices $Q$ remain positive because the ansatz is affine in the potential. Integrating the derivative of the logarithmic determinant along that segment produces a uniformly elliptic scalar operator with first-order terms and no zeroth-order term that annihilates $u-w$. The maximum principle shows that $u-w$ is constant, and the supremum normalization makes the constant zero. $\square$

title: 14.18 Normalization for the Gauduchon equation
text: By theorem 14.10.1 , every smooth real function $F$ determines a scalar $b_\gamma (F)$, the constant $b$ of that theorem. As for the Monge–Ampère equation, its variation is governed by the adjoint probability measure $\mu _ u^\gamma $ of proposition 14.12.1 and by the concavity of the logarithmic determinant. To differentiate solutions, we fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_0$ and use the normalization $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$ in place of $\sup _ Xu=0$. Lemma 14.18.1 . 1ECE72025D8E The solution $(u,b_\gamma (F))$, normalized by $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$, depends smoothly on the parameters of every smooth finite-dimensional family of functions $F$. Proof. The map $\Gamma \mapsto \eta $ with $\eta ^{n-1}=\Gamma $ is smooth on positive forms, since in a frame it is the inverse of the smooth map $\eta \mapsto \eta ^{n-1}$, whose differential is invertible. The openness argument in the proof of theorem 14.10.1 , with the $\mathrm{d}V_0$-mean in place of the $\gamma ^ n$-mean, gives a bounded inverse for the derivative with respect to the potential and the scalar between the relevant Hölder spaces. The implicit function theorem gives local smooth solution maps, and uniqueness shows that they agree on overlaps. Applying this for every order of Hölder regularity gives the assertion for smooth data. $\square$ For a smooth family of prescribed functions $F_ t\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, with $t$ in an open interval of $\mathbb R$, let $u_ t$ be the corresponding solutions with $\int _ Xu_ t\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$, and set $Q_ t=Q_{u_ t}$ as in ( 14.13.1 ). The expression \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr )  \] is independent of the chosen frame and nonnegative, because $Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t$ is similar to the Hermitian matrix $Q_ t^{-1/2}\dot Q_ t Q_ t^{-1/2}$. Theorem 14.18.2 . F90961841CA0 For a smooth family $F_ t$ and its solutions, \begin{align*}  \dot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\dot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma ,\\  \ddot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\ddot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma -\frac1{n-1}\int _ X \operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) \, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma . \end{align*} In particular, $b_\gamma $ is concave, and along $F_ t=F_0+tG$ its second derivative is strictly negative unless $G$ is constant. Moreover, for smooth real functions $F,G$ on $X$ and every real constant $a$, \[  b_\gamma (F+a)=b_\gamma (F)-a, \qquad |b_\gamma (G)-b_\gamma (F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty .  \] Proof. By ( 14.13.1 ), \[  \mathcal G(u)=\frac1{n-1}\log \det _\gamma Q_ u.  \] Differentiating $\mathcal G(u_ t)=F_ t+b_\gamma (F_ t)$ once gives $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=\dot F_ t+\dot b_\gamma (F_ t)$, and integration against the adjoint probability measure gives the first formula. Because $\Gamma _ u$ is affine in $u$, its second derivative along the family is $\mathcal D_\gamma \ddot u_ t$. The formula for the second derivative of $\log \det $ used in the proof of theorem 14.8.1 therefore gives \[  \mathcal L_{u_ t}\ddot u_ t -\frac1{n-1}\operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) =\ddot F_ t+\ddot b_\gamma (F_ t).  \] Integrating against $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ at this fixed parameter gives the second formula; no derivative of the measure is needed. For affine $F_ t$, we have $\ddot F_ t=0$, and positivity of the density of $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ proves concavity. If the second derivative vanishes, then $\dot Q_ t=0$, so $\dot\Gamma _{u_ t}=0$ and $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=0$. By proposition 14.12.1 , $\dot u_ t$ is constant, and the first differentiated equation forces $G$ to be constant. Conversely, adding a constant to $F$ changes only $b$, by the opposite constant. Finally, integrate the first derivative along the segment from $F$ to $G$: since $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ is a probability measure, the derivative lies between $-\sup _ X(G-F)$ and $-\inf _ X(G-F)$, which proves the Lipschitz bound. $\square$ The Lipschitz bound extends $b_\gamma $ uniquely to continuous functions $F$. Constructing corresponding weak solutions would require, in addition, a volume measure for the $(n-1)$st roots of singular forms in the Aeppli ansatz, compactness of their potentials, and stability of the adjoint equation. On a surface with Gauduchon background form $\gamma _0$, conservation of the total mass makes the scalar and the adjoint probability measure explicit. Example 14.18.3 . 8AC1A3B0F2AF If $n=2$ and $\gamma _0$ is Gauduchon, then $\Gamma _ u=\gamma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\eta _ u$, and $\eta _ u$ is also Gauduchon. The mass identity of theorem 11.1.7 gives $\int _ X\eta _ u^2=\int _ X\gamma _0^2$. Therefore \[  b_\gamma (F)=\log \int _ X\gamma _0^2- \log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2, \qquad \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}{\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}.  \] The adjoint equation of proposition 14.12.3 gives the same measure, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ u=0$ and hence $\rho _ u$ is constant. Along $F+tG$, the second derivative of $b_\gamma $ is minus the variance of $G$ with respect to this probability measure. In section 14.19 we return to the potential equation for $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Smooth approximation will extend its solvability to nonnegative, nonzero $L^ p$ densities, $p>1$; control of the normalization constant and uniform convergence of the potentials will replace the derivative estimates used here.

title: Lemma 14.18.1
text: Lemma 14.18.1 . 1ECE72025D8E The solution $(u,b_\gamma (F))$, normalized by $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}V_0=0$, depends smoothly on the parameters of every smooth finite-dimensional family of functions $F$. Proof. The map $\Gamma \mapsto \eta $ with $\eta ^{n-1}=\Gamma $ is smooth on positive forms, since in a frame it is the inverse of the smooth map $\eta \mapsto \eta ^{n-1}$, whose differential is invertible. The openness argument in the proof of theorem 14.10.1 , with the $\mathrm{d}V_0$-mean in place of the $\gamma ^ n$-mean, gives a bounded inverse for the derivative with respect to the potential and the scalar between the relevant Hölder spaces. The implicit function theorem gives local smooth solution maps, and uniqueness shows that they agree on overlaps. Applying this for every order of Hölder regularity gives the assertion for smooth data. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.18.2
text: Theorem 14.18.2 . F90961841CA0 For a smooth family $F_ t$ and its solutions, \begin{align*}  \dot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\dot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma ,\\  \ddot b_\gamma (F_ t)& =-\int _ X\ddot F_ t\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma -\frac1{n-1}\int _ X \operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) \, \mathrm{d}\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma . \end{align*} In particular, $b_\gamma $ is concave, and along $F_ t=F_0+tG$ its second derivative is strictly negative unless $G$ is constant. Moreover, for smooth real functions $F,G$ on $X$ and every real constant $a$, \[  b_\gamma (F+a)=b_\gamma (F)-a, \qquad |b_\gamma (G)-b_\gamma (F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty .  \] Proof. By ( 14.13.1 ), \[  \mathcal G(u)=\frac1{n-1}\log \det _\gamma Q_ u.  \] Differentiating $\mathcal G(u_ t)=F_ t+b_\gamma (F_ t)$ once gives $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=\dot F_ t+\dot b_\gamma (F_ t)$, and integration against the adjoint probability measure gives the first formula. Because $\Gamma _ u$ is affine in $u$, its second derivative along the family is $\mathcal D_\gamma \ddot u_ t$. The formula for the second derivative of $\log \det $ used in the proof of theorem 14.8.1 therefore gives \[  \mathcal L_{u_ t}\ddot u_ t -\frac1{n-1}\operatorname {tr}\bigl ((Q_ t^{-1}\dot Q_ t)^2\bigr ) =\ddot F_ t+\ddot b_\gamma (F_ t).  \] Integrating against $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ at this fixed parameter gives the second formula; no derivative of the measure is needed. For affine $F_ t$, we have $\ddot F_ t=0$, and positivity of the density of $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ proves concavity. If the second derivative vanishes, then $\dot Q_ t=0$, so $\dot\Gamma _{u_ t}=0$ and $\mathcal L_{u_ t}\dot u_ t=0$. By proposition 14.12.1 , $\dot u_ t$ is constant, and the first differentiated equation forces $G$ to be constant. Conversely, adding a constant to $F$ changes only $b$, by the opposite constant. Finally, integrate the first derivative along the segment from $F$ to $G$: since $\mu _{u_ t}^\gamma $ is a probability measure, the derivative lies between $-\sup _ X(G-F)$ and $-\inf _ X(G-F)$, which proves the Lipschitz bound. $\square$

title: Example 14.18.3
text: Example 14.18.3 . 8AC1A3B0F2AF If $n=2$ and $\gamma _0$ is Gauduchon, then $\Gamma _ u=\gamma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\eta _ u$, and $\eta _ u$ is also Gauduchon. The mass identity of theorem 11.1.7 gives $\int _ X\eta _ u^2=\int _ X\gamma _0^2$. Therefore \[  b_\gamma (F)=\log \int _ X\gamma _0^2- \log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2, \qquad \mathrm{d}\mu _ u^\gamma =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}{\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\gamma ^2}.  \] The adjoint equation of proposition 14.12.3 gives the same measure, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta _ u=0$ and hence $\rho _ u$ is constant. Along $F+tG$, the second derivative of $b_\gamma $ is minus the variance of $G$ with respect to this probability measure.

title: 14.19 Continuous solutions and normalization
text: Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive volume form on $X$. As in section 14.1 , we write $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; for a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, the power $\omega _ u^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of proposition 5.28.2 . We fix $p>1$ and a nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$ with $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V>0$. Norms and almost-everywhere statements refer to $\mathrm{d}V$ unless another measure is specified. We seek continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions of $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, with an unknown constant $c>0$, and of $\omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $\lambda >0$. Smooth positive approximations of $f$ give solutions by section 14.1 . To pass to a limit, we need uniform control of both their constants and their potentials. Integration against a Gauduchon metric bounds the constants and hence the $L^ p$ norms of the resulting densities. Modified comparison then turns normalized $L^1$ compactness into uniform compactness, which identifies the limiting Monge–Ampère measure. For the exponential equation, a weighted Gauduchon mean also controls the additive constants. Letting $\lambda $ decrease to zero determines the normalization constant $c$ from $f$, even when the normalized potential is not unique. When a bounded solution has a smooth positive density depending on the point and the potential, proper exponential equations with a frozen smooth approximation of that potential give a trace estimate and prove that the solution is smooth. On the Hopf threefold, the constant has a sharp lower bound, with equality exactly for densities pulled back from the projective plane. For densities of unit integral with a common $L^ p$ bound, $1<p<\infty $, near equality forces normalized potentials to approach their fiber averages uniformly and gives weak convergence in $L^ p$ for the density differences. Smooth oscillating examples show why strong $L^1$ convergence of the densities need not follow. For $n\geq 2$, the final two sections fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\chi $ and study concave functions of the eigenvalues of $\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$. An admissible reference with a strict asymptotic gap controls an auxiliary Monge–Ampère comparison, giving stability as positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Equicontinuous data then give uniform compactness. Nearby smooth admissible functions yield a gradient bound if the first derivatives of the data are uniformly bounded.

title: 14.19.1 Continuous solvability
text: There are two natural ways to normalize the prescribed density: by an unknown positive constant, or by an exponential of the potential. Theorem 14.19.2 (Kołodziej–Nguyen) . C8D798C2D2F0 There are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential can be normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The constant $c$ is uniquely determined by $f$, by proposition 14.19.34 . The normalized potential, however, need not be unique, even for a smooth density; see theorem 14.26.1 . Theorem 14.19.3 (Nguyen) . CFA579B45DF9 For every $\lambda >0$, there is a unique continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u_\lambda $ satisfying C01B1AA0FBCA 14.19.4 \begin{equation}  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 14.19.2 (Kołodziej–Nguyen)
text: Theorem 14.19.2 (Kołodziej–Nguyen) . C8D798C2D2F0 There are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential can be normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. of theorem 14.19.2 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. By theorem 14.2.1 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and constants $c_ j$ such that \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=c_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad c_ j>0.  \] We first bound the constants. For $n\geq 2$, fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. By proposition 11.5.4 , \[  c_ j^{1/n}A_ j\leq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \qquad A_ j=\int _ X(f_ j\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Since $|x^{1/n}-y^{1/n}|\leq |x-y|^{1/n}$ for $x,y\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality gives $A_ j\to A>0$, where $A=\int _ X(f\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Thus $c_ j$ is bounded above. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives the same estimate, with $A_ j=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The lower bound for the density norm in theorem 14.19.19 gives $c_ j\| f_ j\| _ p\geq c_ p$, so the constants are bounded away from zero. The densities $c_ jf_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded in $L^ p$, and the same theorem gives a common bound for the $u_ j$. By theorem 5.25.2 , we may pass to a subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. By theorem 14.19.21 , $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, with $u$ continuous and $\sup _ Xu=0$. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives $\omega _{u_ j}^ n\rightharpoonup \omega _ u^ n$, while $c_ jf_ j\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Hence $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, as required. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.19.3 (Nguyen)
text: Theorem 14.19.3 (Nguyen) . CFA579B45DF9 For every $\lambda >0$, there is a unique continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $u_\lambda $ satisfying C01B1AA0FBCA 14.19.4 \begin{equation}  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} of theorem 14.19.3 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 14.7.2 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and $\omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The preceding lemma bounds $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, and consequently bounds $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ in $L^ p$. The normalized potentials $\psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j$ are uniformly bounded by theorem 14.19.19 . We may pass to a subsequence with $M_ j\to M$ and $\psi _ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. Theorem 14.19.21 gives uniform convergence $u_ j\to u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Uniform convergence and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$ give $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f$ in $L^ p$, and continuity of bounded products therefore gives $\omega _ u^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Uniqueness, even among all bounded solutions, follows from bounded exponential comparison, corollary 14.19.12 . $\square$

title: Equation 14.19.4
text: C01B1AA0FBCA 14.19.4 \begin{equation}  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\lambda )^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation}

title: 14.19.5 The modified comparison principle
text: For a Hermitian background, the total Monge–Ampère mass varies with the potential, and the ordinary comparison principle fails in general (see 14.25.3 ). A weaker form survives. Replacing the comparison potential $v$ by $(1-\varepsilon )v$ leaves the strictly positive form $\varepsilon \omega $ in reserve, and this reserve absorbs the torsion terms. On a sublevel set of height $s$, integration by parts makes the error proportional to $s$, and a finite induction controls the intermediate mixed products. The resulting multiplicative correction tends to one as $s$ tends to zero with $\varepsilon $ fixed. Since $X$ is compact and $\omega $ is positive, we can choose $B_0\geq 1$ such that \[  -B_0\omega ^2\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq B_0\omega ^2, \qquad -B_0\omega ^3\leq \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \leq B_0\omega ^3.  \] These inequalities are understood after wedging with positive forms of complementary degree; forms of degree larger than $2n$ vanish, and the corresponding terms below are omitted. Theorem 14.19.6 . 492E047184B3 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $0<\varepsilon <1$. For $s>0$, put \[  m_\varepsilon =\inf _ X\bigl (u-(1-\varepsilon )v\bigr ),\qquad U_{\varepsilon ,s}=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m_\varepsilon +s\} .  \] If $0<s<\varepsilon ^3/(32B_0n^2)$, then, with $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$, 63BE08CDB80C 14.19.7 \begin{equation}  (1-4a)^ n\int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^{\, n} \leq \int _{U_{\varepsilon ,s}}\omega _ u^ n. \end{equation} In particular, the reverse factor $(1-4a)^{-n}$ tends to one as $s\downarrow 0$ for fixed $\varepsilon $. Proof. Write $v_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )v$, $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ and \[  \phi =\max (u,v_\varepsilon +m_\varepsilon +s),\qquad T_ k=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k},\qquad I_ k=\int _ U T_ k\quad (0\leq k\leq n).  \] Set $I_{-1}=I_{-2}=0$. Then $0\leq \phi -u\leq s$, this difference vanishes outside $U$, and on $U$ plurifine locality gives $\omega _\phi =\omega _{v_\varepsilon }\geq \varepsilon \omega $ in all bounded products. By lemma 5.28.3 , for every fixed positive mixed product $W$ of $n-1$ bounded-potential factors, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _ u\wedge W \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=\phi \} }\omega _\phi \wedge W.  \] For $0\leq k\leq n-1$, apply this with $W=\omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{n-k-1}$. Since $u=\phi $ on $X\setminus U$, the difference $T_ k-T_{k+1}=(\omega _\phi -\omega _ u)\wedge W$ is nonnegative there. Consequently 3A0FB1FFA628 14.19.8 \begin{equation}  I_ k-I_{k+1} \leq \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\phi -u)\wedge W =\int _ X(\phi -u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W. \end{equation} This integration by parts is valid for bounded potentials. To see this, approximate $u$ and $\phi $ by decreasing sequences of smooth, uniformly bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions, using theorem 5.32.1 . For smooth functions the identity is ordinary integration by parts. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W$ expands as below into bounded Hessian products and smooth forms, and bounded Bedford–Taylor convergence, also against bounded quasi-continuous coefficients converging in capacity, passes each term to the limit. Set $r=n-k-1$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u=\mathrm{d}\omega _\phi =\mathrm{d}\omega $, expansion gives \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}W={}& k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r +r\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +k(k-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-2}\wedge \omega _\phi ^ r\\ & +2kr\, \mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^{k-1}\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-1}\\ & +r(r-1)\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \omega _ u^ k\wedge \omega _\phi ^{r-2}. \end{split}  \] Terms containing a negative power have coefficient zero and are omitted. On $U$ we may replace each $\omega ^ j$ in an upper bound by $\varepsilon ^{-j}\omega _\phi ^ j$, since $\omega _\phi \geq \varepsilon \omega $ there. Using $\phi -u\leq s$ and $\varepsilon ^{-2}\leq \varepsilon ^{-3}$ in ( 14.19.8 ), we obtain \[  I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq B_0s\varepsilon ^{-3} \bigl (k(k-1)I_{k-2}+k(1+2r)I_{k-1}+r^2I_ k\bigr ).  \] Each coefficient is at most $n^2$, and $a=B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3}$. Hence C197626AD934 14.19.9 \begin{equation}  I_ k-I_{k+1}\leq a(I_{k-2}+I_{k-1}+I_ k). \end{equation} Put $q=1-4a$; the assumption on $s$ gives $a<1/32$, so $q>7/8$. Suppose inductively that $qI_ j\leq I_{j+1}$ for $j<k$. Then $I_{k-1}\leq q^{-1}I_ k$ and $I_{k-2}\leq q^{-2}I_ k$ whenever the indices exist. Since \[  1+q^{-1}+q^{-2}\leq 1+8/7+64/49<4,  \] ( 14.19.9 ) gives $qI_ k\leq I_{k+1}$. The case $k=0$ follows from the same formula with the two absent terms set to zero. By induction, $q^ n I_0\leq I_ n$. Since $T_0=\omega _{v_\varepsilon }^ n$ on $U$ and $T_ n=\omega _ u^ n$, this is the theorem. In dimension one all torsion terms vanish and the same argument applies. $\square$ A strict multiplicative inequality between the Monge–Ampère measures on $\{ u<v\} $ absorbs the error in modified comparison. One first chooses the positivity reserve $\varepsilon $, and then a sublevel set thin enough to preserve the strict inequality. Theorem 14.19.10 . C0DEE578BC5D Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n,  \] then $u\geq v$. In particular, $\omega _ u^ n(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Suppose $m=\inf _ X(u-v)<0$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n>c, \qquad 2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty <-m/4,  \] omitting the second restriction if $v=0$. Let $m_\varepsilon $ and $U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ be defined as in theorem 14.19.6 for this pair $u,v$. Since $|m_\varepsilon -m|\leq \varepsilon \| v\| _\infty $, for all sufficiently small $s>0$ the set $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ is contained in $\{ u<v\} $: there \[  u-v<m_\varepsilon +s-\varepsilon v \leq m+2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty +s<0.  \] The set $U$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum and has positive volume by lemma 5.24.4 . Decrease $s$ further so that theorem 14.19.6 applies and $(1-4B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3})^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$. Write the first factor as $q^ n$. Positivity of every mixed term gives \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^ n \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n\omega _ v^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\omega ^ n.  \] Modified comparison and the assumption would therefore imply \[  q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n\int _ U\omega _ v^ n +q^ n\varepsilon ^ n\int _ U\omega ^ n \leq \int _ U\omega _ u^ n\leq c\int _ U\omega _ v^ n.  \] All integrals are finite, so the choice $q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$ and the positive volume of $U$ make this impossible. Hence $m\geq 0$. $\square$ Corollary 14.19.11 . 7C5FAB3BA5DA Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has strictly positive Monge–Ampère mass. Proof. Let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. If $\omega _ u^ n=0$, then theorem 14.19.10 , applied with $c=0$ and the constant potential $v=\sup _ Xu+1$, would give $u\geq v$, a contradiction. $\square$ The positive lower bound in corollary 14.19.11 depends on the potential. A bound that is uniform over all bounded potentials is the condition $v_-(\omega )>0$ of definition 13.14.14 . Corollary 14.19.12 . AB62A0258D5D If $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\lambda >0$, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\omega _ v^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\omega _ u^ n \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v\leq u.  \] Proof. For every $t>0$, the assumption gives $\omega _ u^ n\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\omega _ v^ n$ on $\{ u<v-t\} $. Since $\omega _{v-t}=\omega _ v$, theorem 14.19.10 , applied to $u$ and $v-t$, gives $u\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ proves $v\leq u$. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.19.10
text: Theorem 14.19.10 . C0DEE578BC5D Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ u^ n \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\omega _ v^ n,  \] then $u\geq v$. In particular, $\omega _ u^ n(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Suppose $m=\inf _ X(u-v)<0$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n>c, \qquad 2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty <-m/4,  \] omitting the second restriction if $v=0$. Let $m_\varepsilon $ and $U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ be defined as in theorem 14.19.6 for this pair $u,v$. Since $|m_\varepsilon -m|\leq \varepsilon \| v\| _\infty $, for all sufficiently small $s>0$ the set $U=U_{\varepsilon ,s}$ is contained in $\{ u<v\} $: there \[  u-v<m_\varepsilon +s-\varepsilon v \leq m+2\varepsilon \| v\| _\infty +s<0.  \] The set $U$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum and has positive volume by lemma 5.24.4 . Decrease $s$ further so that theorem 14.19.6 applies and $(1-4B_0n^2s\varepsilon ^{-3})^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$. Write the first factor as $q^ n$. Positivity of every mixed term gives \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )v}^ n \geq (1-\varepsilon )^ n\omega _ v^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\omega ^ n.  \] Modified comparison and the assumption would therefore imply \[  q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n\int _ U\omega _ v^ n +q^ n\varepsilon ^ n\int _ U\omega ^ n \leq \int _ U\omega _ u^ n\leq c\int _ U\omega _ v^ n.  \] All integrals are finite, so the choice $q^ n(1-\varepsilon )^ n>c$ and the positive volume of $U$ make this impossible. Hence $m\geq 0$. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.19.11
text: Corollary 14.19.11 . 7C5FAB3BA5DA Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has strictly positive Monge–Ampère mass. Proof. Let $u$ be a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. If $\omega _ u^ n=0$, then theorem 14.19.10 , applied with $c=0$ and the constant potential $v=\sup _ Xu+1$, would give $u\geq v$, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.19.12
text: Corollary 14.19.12 . AB62A0258D5D If $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\lambda >0$, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\omega _ v^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\omega _ u^ n \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v\leq u.  \] Proof. For every $t>0$, the assumption gives $\omega _ u^ n\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\omega _ v^ n$ on $\{ u<v-t\} $. Since $\omega _{v-t}=\omega _ v$, theorem 14.19.10 , applied to $u$ and $v-t$, gives $u\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ proves $v\leq u$. $\square$

title: 14.19.13 Capacity estimates and uniform compactness
text: Let $\operatorname {Cap}=\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ denote the capacity of section 5.29 . Modified comparison bounds the capacity of a thin sublevel set by the Monge–Ampère mass of a slightly larger one. A bound by a power $1+\alpha $ of capacity, $\alpha >0$, makes the resulting iteration converge. For an $L^ p$ density, corollary 5.29.5 supplies the case $\alpha =1$. Iterating the two inequalities gives a lower bound for the capacity of every sublevel set of fixed height above the minimum. Since the capacity of deep sublevel sets of normalized potentials is small by the tail estimate ( 5.29.4 ), this bounds the depth of a normalized solution. Lemma 14.19.14 . 370AD0860DAD Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, with $-H\leq v\leq 0$ and $H\geq 1$. Fix $0<\varepsilon <1$, and put \[  m=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )v),\qquad U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m+s\} .  \] There are $\delta _\varepsilon >0$, depending only on $(X,\omega ,\varepsilon )$, and $C_ H>0$, depending only on $(n,H)$, such that F937FDFBF165 14.19.15 \begin{equation}  t^ n\operatorname {Cap}(U_ s)\leq C_ H\int _{U_{s+t}}\omega _ u^ n \qquad (0<s,t,\  s+t<\delta _\varepsilon ). \end{equation} Every $U_ s$, $s>0$, has positive capacity. Proof. Let $B_0$ be the constant of theorem 14.19.6 , and set \[  \delta _\varepsilon =\min \{ 1-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon ^3/(128B_0n^2)\} .  \] For a capacity test $0\leq \rho \leq 1$, put \[  \tau =\frac{t}{2(1-\varepsilon )(H+1)},\quad w=(1-\tau )v+\tau \rho ,\quad m'=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )w).  \] Then $0<\tau <1$ and $0\leq (1-\varepsilon )(w-v)\leq t/2$, so $m-t/2\leq m'\leq m$. Consequently \[  U_ s\subset V:=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )w+m'+s+t/2\}  \subset U_{s+t}.  \] We apply modified comparison to $u,w$ at height $s+t/2<\delta _\varepsilon $; by the choice of $\delta _\varepsilon $, its inverse factor is at most $(8/7)^ n$. Moreover, \[  \omega _{(1-\varepsilon )w} \geq (1-\varepsilon )\tau \omega _\rho =\frac{t}{2(H+1)}\omega _\rho .  \] Integrating over $U_ s\subset V$, applying modified comparison on $V$, and taking the supremum over $\rho $, we obtain ( 14.19.15 ) with $C_ H=[2(H+1)]^ n(8/7)^ n$. Finally, each $U_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of the infimum, so it has positive smooth volume by lemma 5.24.4 , and hence positive capacity, as the constant test function shows. $\square$ Lemma 14.19.16 . 9C1A40570E78 In the setting of lemma 14.19.14 , suppose that $A,\alpha >0$ and \[  \omega _ u^ n(E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (E\subset X\text{ Borel}).  \] For every $0<D<\delta _\varepsilon $, 3CFE977F80E0 14.19.17 \begin{equation}  D\leq C_\alpha (C_ HA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad C_\alpha =\frac{2}{1-2^{-\alpha }}. \end{equation} In particular, when $\alpha =1$, 623E09972ED8 14.19.18 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq \frac{D^ n}{4^ nC_ HA}. \end{equation} Proof. Put $a(s)=\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ s)^{1/n}>0$ and $K=(C_ HA)^{1/n}$. The thin-sublevel estimate gives \[  t\, a(s)\leq K a(s+t)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (0<s,t,\  s+t<\delta _\varepsilon ).  \] Suppose $C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha <D$. Starting with $s_0=D$, set \[  t_ j=2K a(s_ j)^\alpha ,\qquad s_{j+1}=s_ j-t_ j.  \] If $a(s_ i)\leq 2^{-i}a(D)$ for $0\leq i\leq j$, then \[  \sum _{i=0}^ jt_ i \leq 2K a(D)^\alpha \sum _{i=0}^ j2^{-i\alpha } <C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha <D.  \] Thus $s_{j+1}>0$, and the sublevel estimate, applied with $s=s_{j+1}$ and $t=t_ j$, gives $a(s_{j+1})\leq a(s_ j)/2$. Induction justifies every step. The decreasing sequence $s_ j$ has a limit \[  s_\infty \geq D-C_\alpha K a(D)^\alpha >0.  \] Monotonicity now gives $0<a(s_\infty )\leq 2^{-j}a(D)$ for every $j$, a contradiction. This proves ( 14.19.17 ), including the case in which $U_ D=X$. $\square$ Theorem 14.19.19 . EA32B8891E2B There are constants $C_ p,c_ p>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,p)$, such that, whenever $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \omega _ u^ n=F\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V),\quad F\geq 0,  \] we have F7083E3F1991 14.19.20 \begin{equation}  \| u\| _\infty \leq C_ p(1+\| F\| _ p), \qquad \| F\| _ p\geq c_ p. \end{equation} Proof. By corollary 14.19.11 , $F$ is not almost everywhere zero. Apply lemma 14.19.16 with $v=0$, $H=1$, $\varepsilon =1/2$, and $A=C\| F\| _ p>0$, where $C$ is the constant of corollary 5.29.5 . Fix $D=\delta _{1/2}/2$, and put $M=-\inf _ Xu$. Since $U_ D=\{ u<-M+D\} $, the resulting inequality reads \[  \operatorname {Cap}(\{ u<-M+D\} )\geq c/\| F\| _ p.  \] If $M>D+1$, ( 5.29.4 ) bounds this capacity above by $C/(M-D)$, and the first assertion follows; the case $M\leq D+1$ is immediate. Bounding the same capacity above by $\operatorname {Cap}(X)$ gives the second assertion. $\square$ Suppose that two uniformly bounded solutions are far apart at some point. The preceding estimates give a fixed positive lower bound for the capacity of a sublevel set of their difference. If their $L^1$ distance is small, this set has small volume, and the uniform $L^ p$ bound for the densities then makes its Monge–Ampère mass small. This contradicts the sublevel estimate ( 14.19.15 ), and so upgrades $L^1$ compactness to uniform compactness. Put $p'=p/(p-1)$. Theorem 14.19.21 . BF849D15DF41 Suppose $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$, $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, and \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=F_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad F_ j\geq 0,\qquad \sup _ j\| F_ j\| _ p<\infty  \] for the fixed $p>1$. If $(u_ j)$ is Cauchy in $L^1(X,\mathrm{d}V)$, then it is Cauchy uniformly. In particular, every such family has a subsequence converging uniformly to a continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. By theorem 14.19.19 , there is a common $H\geq 1$ with $-H\leq u_ j\leq 0$. Suppose that the sequence is not uniformly Cauchy. After exchanging indices if necessary, we find $a>0$ and arbitrarily large $j,k$ with \[  S:=\inf _ X(u_ k-u_ j)\leq -a.  \] Choose $0<\varepsilon <1$ such that $\varepsilon H<a/4$, and choose a fixed $D>0$ with $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $2D<a/4$. Apply the preceding sublevel lemmas with $u=u_ k$ and $v=u_ j$. Since $v\leq 0$, $m=\inf (u-(1-\varepsilon )v)\leq S$. Thus \[  U_{2D}\subset \{ u-v<S+2D+\varepsilon H\}  \subset \{ |u-v|>a/2\} .  \] The capacity lower bound ( 14.19.18 ), with a constant $A$ independent of $j,k$ given by corollary 5.29.5 , yields $\operatorname {Cap}(U_ D)\geq c>0$. On the other hand, ( 14.19.15 ) and the inequalities of Hölder and Chebyshev give \[  \begin{split}  D^ n\operatorname {Cap}(U_ D) & \leq C_ H\int _{U_{2D}}F_ k\, \mathrm{d}V\\ & \leq C_ H\| F_ k\| _ p \left(\frac{2\| u_ k-u_ j\| _1}{a}\right)^{1/p'} \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This contradiction proves that the sequence is uniformly Cauchy. For the last assertion, the normalized compactness theorem, theorem 5.25.2 , gives an $L^1$-Cauchy subsequence of any such family. Its uniform limit is continuous, and distributional convergence preserves $\omega $-plurisubharmonicity. $\square$
