title: 14.19.22 Stability under a power capacity bound
search_title: Stability under a power capacity bound
text: The capacity lower bound of lemma 14.19.16 turns an integral error against the solution measure into a uniform error. The argument uses only the power capacity bound on this measure and therefore applies to singular measures as well. Proposition 14.19.23 . 3B70BD39881D Fix $A,\alpha >0$ and $H\geq 1$. Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ satisfy $\sup _ Xu=0$ and $-H\leq v\leq 0$, and suppose \[  \mu (E)\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (E)^{1+\alpha }, \qquad \mu =\omega _ u^ n, \qquad E\subset X\text{ Borel}.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha ,H$, such that B0DB641874CE 14.19.24 \begin{equation}  \sup _ X(v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu \right)^{\sigma _\alpha }, \qquad \sigma _\alpha =\frac{\alpha }{3n(1+\alpha )+\alpha }. \end{equation} For the square-capacity bound, $\alpha =1$, the exponent is $1/(6n+1)$. Proof. Write $L=\int _ X(v-u)_+\, \mathrm d\mu $ and $S=\sup _ X(v-u)_+$. Apply lemma 14.19.16 with competitor zero, $\varepsilon =1/2$ and one fixed $0<D<\delta _{1/2}$. It bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ u<\inf _ Xu+D\} $ below by a positive constant. The tail estimate ( 5.29.4 ) therefore bounds $-\inf _ Xu$ in terms of $(X,\omega ),A,\alpha $. Consequently $S$ has a fixed upper bound. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/2$, choose a fixed small $c>0$ and put $D=c\varepsilon ^3$. The formula for $\delta _\varepsilon $ in lemma 14.19.14 allows $c$ to be chosen so that $2D<\delta _\varepsilon $ and $4D\leq \varepsilon $. With \[  m=\inf _ X(u-(1-\varepsilon )v),\qquad U_ s=\{ u<(1-\varepsilon )v+m+s\} ,  \] we have $m\leq -S$ when $S>0$, since $v\leq 0$. On $U_{2D}$, \[  v-u>S-\varepsilon H-2D.  \] If $S>2\varepsilon H+4D$, this is greater than $S/2$. The backwards and thin-sublevel estimates give \[  c_0D^{n(1+1/\alpha )} \leq D^ n\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (U_ D) \leq C_ H\mu (U_{2D})\leq \frac{2C_ HL}{S},  \] where $c_0>0$ depends only on the stated data. Hence $S\leq CL\varepsilon ^{-3n(1+1/\alpha )}$ in this case. In the other case, $S\leq (2H+1)\varepsilon $. For sufficiently small $L>0$, choose $\varepsilon =L^{\sigma _\alpha }$. The two alternatives give ( 14.19.24 ). The remaining positive values of $L$ are covered by the fixed upper bound for $S$. If $L=0$, the first alternative is impossible for every small $\varepsilon $, and the second gives $S=0$ on letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 14.19.25 Construction of continuous solutions
text: Smooth approximation gives solutions with unknown normalization constants. A Gauduchon trace bounds these constants above, and the lower bound for the density norm in theorem 14.19.19 bounds them away from zero. The resulting uniform $L^ p$ bound puts the potentials in the compact family of theorem 14.19.21 , so their limit solves the prescribed equation. of theorem 14.19.2 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. By theorem 14.2.1 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and constants $c_ j$ such that \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=c_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad c_ j>0.  \] We first bound the constants. For $n\geq 2$, fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. By proposition 11.5.4 , \[  c_ j^{1/n}A_ j\leq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \qquad A_ j=\int _ X(f_ j\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Since $|x^{1/n}-y^{1/n}|\leq |x-y|^{1/n}$ for $x,y\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality gives $A_ j\to A>0$, where $A=\int _ X(f\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Thus $c_ j$ is bounded above. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives the same estimate, with $A_ j=\int _ Xf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The lower bound for the density norm in theorem 14.19.19 gives $c_ j\| f_ j\| _ p\geq c_ p$, so the constants are bounded away from zero. The densities $c_ jf_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded in $L^ p$, and the same theorem gives a common bound for the $u_ j$. By theorem 5.25.2 , we may pass to a subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. By theorem 14.19.21 , $u_ j\to u$ uniformly, with $u$ continuous and $\sup _ Xu=0$. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity gives $\omega _{u_ j}^ n\rightharpoonup \omega _ u^ n$, while $c_ jf_ j\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Hence $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, as required. $\square$ For the exponential equation, the role of the normalization constant is played by $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu}$. Its upper bound comes from Jensen's inequality: weighting the Gauduchon volume by the $n$th root of the density relates $\sup _ Xu$ to the Gauduchon trace of $\omega _ u$, which does not depend on $u$. The lower bound for the density norm again gives the reverse bound. Lemma 14.19.26 . B2B0EF9B5807 Fix $\lambda >0$. Suppose that smooth functions $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ solve \[  \omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where the smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j$ converge in $L^ p$ to a nonnegative nonzero $f$. Then $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$ is bounded above and below, uniformly in $j$. Proof. Absorbing the fixed smooth positive ratio $\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n$ into $f_ j$ and $f$ preserves their $L^ p$ convergence, so we may assume $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. Choose $\rho >0$ smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \omega ^{n-1})=0$, using theorem 11.4.2 ; for $n=1$, take $\rho =1$. Put \[  \alpha =\int _ X\rho \omega ^ n,\quad A_ j=\int _ X f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n,\quad \psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j\leq 0.  \] Set $A=\int _ X f^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n$. The inequality for $n$th roots used in the preceding existence proof gives $A_ j\to A>0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho \omega ^{n-1})=0$, the trace $\int _ X\omega _{u_ j}\wedge \rho \omega ^{n-1}$ equals $\alpha $; the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality therefore implies \[  \alpha =\int _ X\omega _{u_ j}\wedge \rho \omega ^{n-1} \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j/n}\int _ X \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \psi _ j/n}f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n.  \] Applying Jensen's inequality to the probability measure $A_ j^{-1}f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n$ and taking logarithms, we obtain 74778A2A41BF 14.19.27 \begin{equation}  \lambda M_ j\leq n\log (\alpha /A_ j) +\frac{\lambda }{A_ j}\int _ X(-\psi _ j)f_ j^{1/n}\rho \omega ^ n. \end{equation} By lemma 5.26.2 , the normalized potentials $\psi _ j$ have uniform $L^ q$ bounds for every finite $q$. With $q=np/(np-1)$, Hölder's inequality gives a uniform bound for the last integral, since $\| f_ j^{1/n}\| _{np}=\| f_ j\| _ p^{1/n}$. This proves the upper bound for $M_ j$. Finally, the density $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ satisfies $\| F_ j\| _ p\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j}\| f_ j\| _ p$. The lower-density bound of theorem 14.19.19 , applied to $\psi _ j$, gives $c_ p\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_ j}\| f_ j\| _ p$, which bounds $M_ j$ below. $\square$ of theorem 14.19.3 . Choose smooth strictly positive functions $f_ j\to f$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 14.7.2 , there are smooth $u_ j$ with $\omega _{u_ j}>0$ and $\omega _{u_ j}^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. The preceding lemma bounds $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, and consequently bounds $F_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f_ j$ in $L^ p$. The normalized potentials $\psi _ j=u_ j-M_ j$ are uniformly bounded by theorem 14.19.19 . We may pass to a subsequence with $M_ j\to M$ and $\psi _ j$ Cauchy in $L^1$. Theorem 14.19.21 gives uniform convergence $u_ j\to u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Bounded exponential comparison gives this monotonicity even where the densities vanish. Lemma 14.19.28 . 8068BC80F22D Let $\lambda >0$, and let $f_ a,f_ b$ be nonnegative nonzero $L^ p$ densities. Suppose that $a,b\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ solve \[  \omega _ a^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}f_ a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \omega _ b^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda b}f_ b\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $f_ a\leq f_ b$ almost everywhere, then $b\leq a$ on $X$. Hence $b\leq a$ by corollary 14.19.12 , applied with $u=a$ and $v=b$. $\square$ Corollary 14.19.29 . AEA7DCEDBA8B Every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of $\omega _ u^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is continuous. Proof. title: 14.19.30 Smoothness of bounded solutions
text: The continuous solutions constructed above have low regularity when the density is merely integrable. If the density is a smooth positive function of the point and the potential, every bounded solution is smooth. Differentiating that density directly would require derivatives of the solution. We instead freeze its occurrence in a smooth approximation and solve a proper exponential equation. A square of the prescribed potential in the maximum-principle function gives a trace estimate independent of its derivatives. We first prove this estimate, retaining the matrix notation $g,h$, the traces $S,B$ and the torsion trace $\tau $ of lemma 14.5.1 . Lemma 14.19.31 . 55D3763AB355 Fix $M\geq 0$ and a smooth real function $G$ on $X\times [-M,M]$. There is $C$, depending only on $\omega $, $M$ and $\| G\| _{C^2}$, with the following property. If $v,u$ are smooth, $\omega _ v,\omega _ u>0$, $|v|\leq M$, and \[  \omega _ u^ n=\mathrm e^{u+G(x,v)}\omega ^ n,  \] then \[  |u|\leq \| G\| _{C^0},\qquad C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _ u\leq C\omega .  \] Proof. The extrema of $u$ give the first bound, as in theorem 14.7.2 . Put $k=g+(v_{i\bar j})$, $S_ v=\operatorname {tr}_ gk$, and $D=2\| G\| _{C^0}$. The chain rule and Cauchy–Schwarz give, for $H=u+G(x,v)$, \[  \Delta _ gH\geq -C_0\bigl (1+S_ v+|\partial v|_ g^2\bigr ).  \] Indeed $\Delta _ gu=S-n\geq -n$, $\Delta _ gv=S_ v-n$, and the mixed derivatives of $G(x,v)$ are bounded below by $-C_0(1+|\partial v|_ g^2)$. Here and below constants depend only on the declared data. Set $r=v+M+1$, $R=2M+1$ and $s=u-\inf _ Xu+1$, so $1\leq r\leq R$ and $1\leq s\leq D+1$. For constants $A,L>0$ to be chosen, maximize \[  Q=\log S+Ar^2-Lu+s^{-1}  \] on $X$. If $S<1$ at the maximum, the bounded ranges of $r,u,s$ already bound $S$ everywhere. Otherwise lemma 14.5.1 applies there. Positivity gives \[  SB\geq n^2,\qquad S_ v\leq S\operatorname {tr}_ hk, \qquad |\partial v|_ g^2\leq S|\partial v|_ h^2.  \] The middle inequality follows by diagonalizing $h$ relative to $g$: every eigenvalue of $h$ is at most $S$, and the diagonal entries of $k$ are positive. Consequently, \[  \frac{\Delta _ gH}{S} \geq -C_1 B-C_0\operatorname {tr}_ hk-C_0|\partial v|_ h^2.  \] At the maximum, \[  \frac{\partial S}{S}=(L+s^{-2})\partial u-2Ar\partial v.  \] Since $|\tau |_ h^2\leq C_ gB$, Young's inequality bounds the torsion term by \[  \left|\frac2{S^2}\operatorname {Re}(h^{i\bar j}\tau _ iS_{\bar j})\right| \leq s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2+A|\partial v|_ h^2 +\frac{C_ g\bigl ((L+1)^2(D+1)^3+AR^2\bigr )}{S^2}B.  \] Also \begin{align*}  \Delta _ h(Ar^2)& \geq 2A\operatorname {tr}_ hk-2AR B+2A|\partial v|_ h^2,\\  \Delta _ h(-Lu+s^{-1})& =(L+s^{-2})(B-n)+2s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2. \end{align*} Combining these inequalities with ( 14.5.2 ) yields \[  \begin{split}  0\geq \Delta _ hQ\geq {}&  \left(L-2AR-C_2- \frac{C_ g((L+1)^2(D+1)^3+AR^2)}{S^2}\right)B-n(L+1)\\ & +(2A-C_0)\operatorname {tr}_ hk+(A-C_0)|\partial v|_ h^2 +s^{-3}|\partial u|_ h^2. \end{split}  \] Choose $A>C_0+1$ and then $L>2AR+C_2+2$. If the fraction in the coefficient of $B$ is at least one, $S^2$ at the maximum is bounded by its numerator. Otherwise the displayed inequality gives $B\leq n(L+1)$ there. For $n\geq 2$, the bounded determinant gives \[  S\leq n\mathrm e^{2\| G\| _{C^0}}B^{n-1}.  \] For $n=1$, $S=\mathrm e^{u+G(x,v)}$ directly. Thus $S$ is bounded at the maximum in every case. Maximality of $Q$ and the bounded ranges of $r,u,s$ give the same bound globally. The positive lower determinant bound then bounds every eigenvalue of $h$ away from zero. $\square$ Theorem 14.19.32 . B9E6E7C4706B Let $F\in C^\infty (X\times \mathbb R,\mathbb R)$. Every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}\, \mathrm dV  \] is smooth on $X$, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Proof. The density $\mathrm e^{F(x,u)}$ is bounded and strictly positive, so corollary 14.19.29 makes $u$ continuous. Choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $v_ j\downarrow u$ by theorem 5.32.1 . They have a common bound $M$ and converge uniformly by Dini's theorem. Define \[  G(x,t)=F(x,t)-t+\log \frac{\mathrm dV}{\omega ^ n}.  \] By theorem 14.7.2 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $a_ j$ with \[  \omega _{a_ j}^ n=\mathrm e^{a_ j+G(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Put $\delta _ j=\| G(x,v_ j)-G(x,u)\| _{C^0}\to 0$. The given $u$ solves the proper equation with coefficient $G(x,u)$. The weighted measures of $a_ j-\delta _ j$ and $a_ j+\delta _ j$ bracket its coefficient, so corollary 14.19.12 gives \[  a_ j-\delta _ j\leq u\leq a_ j+\delta _ j.  \] Hence $a_ j\to u$ uniformly. By lemma 14.19.31 , $C^{-1}\omega \leq \omega _{a_ j}\leq C\omega $ uniformly. In particular $\Delta _ ga_ j$ is uniformly bounded. Fixed-operator elliptic estimates give uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$, so $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. We explain the uniformly elliptic passage to higher regularity, using the concave extension from corollary 14.5.8 . On a relatively compact coordinate chart, let $P$ send a real Hessian to its complex Hermitian part, with the coordinate normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. All matrices $g(x)+P(D^2a_ j)$ lie in a fixed compact interval $\mathcal K=\{ \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I\} $ of positive matrices. Define \[  \mathcal F(x,N)=\inf _{A\in \mathcal K} \left\{ \log \det A+\operatorname {tr}\bigl [A^{-1}(g(x)+P(N)-A)\bigr ]\right\}  -\log \det g(x).  \] The tangent inequality for the concave logarithmic determinant shows that this is the original operator whenever $g(x)+P(N)\in \mathcal K$. It is concave and uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices: for $N'\geq 0$, $P(N')\geq 0$ and its trace is a fixed positive multiple of $\operatorname {tr}N'$, while $A^{\pm 1}$ have uniform bounds. Its dependence on $x$ is uniformly Lipschitz on this chart. Thus the $a_ j$ are classical, and hence viscosity, solutions of \[  \mathcal F(x,D^2a_ j)=a_ j+G(x,v_ j).  \] Both sides converge uniformly except for the Hessian variable. Stability of viscosity solutions gives $\mathcal F(x,D^2u)=u+G(x,u)$ in the viscosity sense. The right-hand side is Hölder because $u\in C^{1,\alpha }$. The local Evans–Krylov estimate therefore gives $u\in C^{2,\beta }$ for some $\beta >0$. The metric bounds pass to the limit, so the original equation is now uniformly elliptic with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Differentiating it and applying Schauder estimates repeatedly proves $u\in C^\infty (X)$. $\square$

title: 14.19.33 The vanishing exponent and scalar uniqueness
search_title: The vanishing exponent and scalar uniqueness
text: To show that the constant in theorem 14.19.2 is unique, we compare the solution $u_\lambda $ of ( 14.19.4 ) with constant translates of a solution $u$ of the normalized equation. Translating $u$ by its maximum and by its minimum gives two barriers for the exponential equation, whose separation is the oscillation of $u$. After multiplication by $\lambda $, both barriers converge to the logarithm of the constant as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Since $u_\lambda $ depends only on $f$ and $\lambda $, the constant is determined by $f$. Proposition 14.19.34 . 880520C4A2B1 Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$ and $c>0$ satisfy $\omega _ u^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Set $m=\inf _ Xu$ and $M=\sup _ Xu$. Then, for every $\lambda >0$, the solution of ( 14.19.4 ) satisfies 3B8781BD8BF5 14.19.35 \begin{equation}  u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-M \leq u_\lambda \leq u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-m. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \| \lambda u_\lambda -\log c\| _\infty \leq \lambda (M-m), \qquad \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\longrightarrow c \quad \hbox{uniformly on }X\hbox{ as }\lambda \downarrow 0.  \] Consequently, $c$ is the only constant for which the equation $\omega _ v^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. Proof. Set $a=u+\lambda ^{-1}\log c-M$ and $b=u+\lambda ^{-1}\log c-m$. These translates of $u$ have the same Monge–Ampère measure as $u$, and since $m\leq u\leq M$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq cf\, \mathrm{d}V=\omega _ a^ n=\omega _ b^ n \leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda b}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\omega _ a^ n\geq f\, \mathrm{d}V=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u_\lambda }\omega _{u_\lambda }^ n\geq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda b}\omega _ b^ n$. Applying corollary 14.19.12 first to the pair $(u_\lambda ,a)$ and then to the pair $(b,u_\lambda )$ gives $a\leq u_\lambda \leq b$, which is ( 14.19.35 ). Multiplying these inequalities by $\lambda $ and using $m\leq u\leq M$ gives the norm bound, and the uniform convergence follows. If $(v,c')$ is another such pair, the same argument applied to $v$ gives $\lambda u_\lambda \to \log c'$, because $u_\lambda $ depends only on $f$ and $\lambda $. Hence $c'=c$. $\square$ The barriers also give $\operatorname {osc}_ Xu_\lambda \leq 2(M-m)$, and the densities $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f$ converge to $cf$ in $L^ p$. By theorem 14.19.21 , the normalized potentials $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ are therefore precompact in $C^0(X)$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, and every cluster point solves the equation with constant $c$. Uniqueness of the constant does not, however, single out one cluster point; proposition 15.20.1 describes the symmetries that these limits inherit. For $C^2$ potentials, uniqueness of the constant also follows directly from the maximum principle: replacing one potential $v$ by $(1+\varepsilon )v$ leaves a strictly positive multiple of $\omega $ in reserve at an extremum. Proposition 14.19.36 . 92CEFF8A020B Let $u,v\in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$, and set $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $B=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. If $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=cB^ n$ for a constant $c>0$, then $c=1$. Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a maximum point of $u-(1+\varepsilon )v$, the complex Hessian of this function is nonpositive, so that \[  A+\varepsilon \omega \leq (1+\varepsilon )B.  \] At this point $B>0$, because $A+\varepsilon \omega >0$. Monotonicity of the determinant and $A^ n=cB^ n$ give $c\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $c\leq 1$, and interchanging the two potentials gives $c^{-1}\leq 1$. $\square$

Then, for every $\lambda >0$, the solution of ( 14.19.4 ) satisfies 3B8781BD8BF5 14.19.35 \begin{equation}  u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-M \leq u_\lambda \leq u+\frac{\log c}{\lambda }-m. \end{equation} In particular, \[  \| \lambda u_\lambda -\log c\| _\infty \leq \lambda (M-m), \qquad \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\longrightarrow c \quad \hbox{uniformly on }X\hbox{ as }\lambda \downarrow 0.  \] Consequently, $c$ is the only constant for which the equation $\omega _ v^ n=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap C(X)$. title: Proposition 14.19.40
Example 14.19.41
text: Example 14.19.41 . F8EB82A5AD2B Choose $0<a<1/2$, and use the function $s=\log |z|^2$ on the covering space $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $ from section 23.1 . Since $s$ changes by $-2$ under the defining contraction, every $2$-periodic function of $s$ descends to $X$. For an integer $m\geq 1$, define the smooth normalized potential \[  u_ m=\frac{a}{\pi ^2m^2}\bigl (\cos (\pi m s)-1\bigr ), \qquad \| u_ m-Au_ m\| _{C^0}=\frac{a}{\pi ^2m^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Primes below denote derivatives with respect to $s$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=\alpha $ and $\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s=\beta $, the chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m=(1+u_ m')\alpha +(1+u_ m'')\beta , \quad u_ m'=-\frac{a}{\pi m}\sin (\pi m s),\quad u_ m''=-a\cos (\pi m s).  \] Both coefficients are bounded below by positive constants independent of $m$. The rank identities $\alpha ^3=\beta ^2=0$ imply \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m)^3=H_ m\omega ^3,\qquad H_ m=\left(1-\frac{a}{\pi m}\sin (\pi m s)\right)^2 \bigl (1-a\cos (\pi m s)\bigr ).  \] On each fiber, $s$ is twice the real Haar coordinate plus a constant depending on the base point, so its distribution modulo $2$ is uniform. When the periodic expression $H_ m=(1+u_ m')^2(1+u_ m'')$ is averaged, the terms $u_ m'$, $u_ m''$, $u_ m'u_ m''$ and $(u_ m')^2u_ m''$ contribute zero, since they are derivatives of periodic functions. Hence \[  I_ m:=\int _ XH_ m\, \mathrm{d}\nu =AH_ m =1+\frac{a^2}{2\pi ^2m^2}.  \] Set $f_ m=H_ m/I_ m$. These smooth densities have unit integral and common strictly positive lower and finite upper bounds. Uniqueness of the constant gives $c_{f_ m}=I_ m\to 1$, and $Af_ m=1$. Nevertheless, \[  \| f_ m-1+a\cos (\pi m s)\| _{C^0(X)}=O(m^{-1}), \qquad \lim _{m\to \infty }\| f_ m-Af_ m\| _{L^1(X,\nu )}=\frac{2a}{\pi }>0.  \] Here the constant in $O(m^{-1})$ depends only on $a$, and the last identity uses the fact that the average of $|\cos |$ over a period is $2/\pi $. Thus near equality does not imply strong $L^1$ convergence to the fiber average, even for uniformly positive bounded smooth densities. For any pullback $g$ of a function on the base, the contraction property gives $\| f_ m-Af_ m\| _1\leq 2\| f_ m-g\| _1$, so approximation by such pullbacks also fails in $L^1$.

title: 14.19.42 Stability for concave equations
text: We now consider fully nonlinear equations defined by a concave symmetric function of the eigenvalues of $\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)$. For such equations, a fixed admissible reference with a strict asymptotic gap replaces the determinant bounds used above: it bounds the positive matrix perturbations of the reference along which the operator stays below a given level. An auxiliary Monge–Ampère equation, whose density is concentrated where the difference of two solutions is nearly maximal, then shows that this set cannot be small. The resulting stability estimate remains uniform when the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Throughout this section and the next, $n\geq 2$, and $\chi $ is a fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. In these two sections the letter $f$ denotes the function of eigenvalues introduced below, not the density fixed at the beginning of the chapter. For a smooth real function $w$ and an endomorphism $A$ of $T^{1,0}X$ that is Hermitian with respect to $\omega $, put \[  A_ w=\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w),\qquad F(A)=f(\lambda (A)),  \] where $\lambda (A)\in \mathbb R^ n$ is the vector of eigenvalues of $A$. Let $\Gamma $ be an open convex symmetric cone with $\Gamma _ n\subseteq \Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, where $\Gamma _ n$ is the positive orthant and $\Gamma _1=\{ \sum _ i\lambda _ i>0\} $. Assume that $f\in C^\infty (\Gamma )\cap C^0(\overline\Gamma )$ is symmetric, concave, positive on $\Gamma $, zero on $\partial \Gamma $, and satisfies \[  f_ i>0,\qquad \lim _{t\to \infty }f(t\lambda )=+\infty \quad (\lambda \in \Gamma ),  \] where $f_ i=\partial f/\partial \lambda _ i$. We call $w$ admissible if $\lambda (A_ w)\in \Gamma $ everywhere. Write $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ for the standard basis of $\mathbb R^ n$ and $\mathbf1=(1,\ldots ,1)$. For $\mu \in \Gamma $, define \[  f_{\infty ,i}(\mu )=\lim _{t\to \infty }f(\mu +te_ i),\qquad f_\infty (\mu )=\min _ i f_{\infty ,i}(\mu ),  \] allowing the value $+\infty $. Fix a smooth admissible function $\underline u$ and positive constants $H_0,\delta _0$. We consider smooth admissible solutions $u$ of \[  F(A_ u)=h,\qquad 0<h\leq H_0,\qquad f_\infty (\lambda (A_{\underline u}(x)))\geq h(x)+\delta _0,  \] where the right-hand side $h$ is a positive function on $X$; the last condition is the strict asymptotic gap at the reference $\underline u$. The right-hand sides satisfying these two conditions form the family of right-hand sides, and the solutions are normalized by $\inf _ Xu=0$. We call $X,\omega ,\chi ,f,\Gamma ,\underline u,H_0,\delta _0$ the fixed data ; all constants in this section depend only on them. Norms are taken with respect to $\omega ^ n$, and $\langle a\rangle _\omega =(\int _ X\omega ^ n)^{-1}\int _ Xa\omega ^ n$ denotes the average of a function $a$. Lemma 14.19.43 . C3049F567279 There are a positive continuous function $H$ on $X$ and constants $r,R,\delta >0$ with the following properties. Every right-hand side in the family satisfies $h\leq H$; on $X$, \[  \mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma ,\qquad f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta , \qquad \mu =\lambda (A_{\underline u});  \] and at every point of $X$, every positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphism $P$ satisfies \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)\leq H+2\delta \quad \Longrightarrow \quad P\leq R\operatorname {Id}.  \] Proof. Each $f_{\infty ,i}$ is an increasing limit of positive concave functions, hence concave with values in $(0,+\infty ]$. Suppose it is infinite at one point and finite at another point of $\Gamma $. Extend the segment joining them slightly beyond the second point, inside the open cone. The second point is then an interior point of the longer segment, so concavity forces the value there to be infinite, a contradiction. Thus $f_{\infty ,i}$ is either finite everywhere, and then continuous, or infinite everywhere. By symmetry, the same alternative holds for every $i$. Take $\delta =\frac18\min \{ \delta _0,\min _ Xf(\mu )\} >0$. In the finite case set $H=\min \{ H_0,f_\infty (\mu )-4\delta \} $; otherwise set $H=H_0$. Since $f_\infty (\mu )\geq f(\mu )\geq 8\delta $, this function is positive. The conditions on the family give $h\leq H$ and $f_\infty (\mu )\geq H+4\delta $. Since $\mu (X)$ is a compact subset of $\Gamma $ and the functions $f_{\infty ,i}$ are continuous (or identically infinite), a sufficiently small $r>0$ gives $\mu -2r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $f_\infty (\mu -2r\mathbf1)\geq H+3\delta $ on $X$. If the matrix bound failed, there would be points $x_ j\to x_*$ and $P_ j\geq 0$ with unbounded norms and $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)\leq H(x_ j)+2\delta $. By monotonicity of eigenvalues, the ordered eigenvalues $\lambda ^{(j)}$ of $A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j$ satisfy $\lambda _ i^{(j)}\geq \mu _ i(x_ j)-r$. Their sum tends to infinity, so some component $k$ tends to infinity along a subsequence. For every fixed $t>0$, eventually \[  \lambda ^{(j)}\geq \mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1+te_ k.  \] Since $f$ is increasing in each variable, letting $t\to \infty $ shows that the lower limit of $F(A_{\underline u}(x_ j)-r\operatorname {Id}+P_ j)$ is at least $f_\infty (\mu (x_*)-2r\mathbf1)\geq H(x_*)+3\delta $, which contradicts the upper bound $H(x_ j)+2\delta $. Adding positive semidefinite matrices preserves the cone, so all these comparisons take place in $\Gamma $. $\square$ Proposition 14.19.44 . 877A402699F6 Every solution satisfies $0\leq u\leq C$. Proof. Put $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$ and $w=u-\underline u-\sup _ X(u-\underline u)\leq 0$. Since $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, we have $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -\operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta \geq -C$. The Green-kernel argument in the proof of proposition 14.11.1 , applied to the operator $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, therefore bounds $\| w\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. Center a holomorphic coordinate ball of fixed size at a minimum point of $w$, and rescale it to the real unit ball. For a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set $q=w+\varepsilon |x|^2$ and $m=\min _ Xw$. The real contact-set construction of ( 14.11.2 ) gives a compact set $E$ on which \[  D^2q\geq 0,\qquad q\leq m+\varepsilon /2, \qquad |B_{\varepsilon /2}|\leq \int _ E\det D^2q\, \mathrm dx.  \] On $E$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -C\varepsilon \omega $. Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $C\varepsilon <r$. Then $P=\omega ^{-1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+r\omega )\geq 0$ and \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)=F(A_ u)=h\leq H.  \] Lemma 14.19.43 bounds $P$, and hence the complex trace of the Hessian of $q$. The nonnegative real Hessian of $q$ on $E$ therefore has bounded trace, and hence bounded determinant, so the contact inequality implies $|E|\geq c>0$. Since $w\leq m+\varepsilon /2$ on $E$, the $L^1$ bound gives $c(-m-\varepsilon /2)\leq C$. This bounds the oscillation of $w$, hence that of $u$; with the normalization $\inf _ Xu=0$, this is the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 14.19.45 . 0F1A655FC651 There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that any two normalized solutions $u_1,u_2$ with right-hand sides $h_1,h_2$ in the family satisfy \[  \| u_1-u_2\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1}\bigr ).  \] In particular, $C$ does not depend on a positive lower bound for the $h_ i$ or on bounds for their derivatives. Proof. Set $a=u_1-\underline u$, $b=u_2-\underline u$ and $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$. By proposition 14.19.44 , $|a|,|b|\leq C_0$ for a fixed $C_0\geq 1$. It suffices to bound $s=\max _ X(b-a)$ when it is positive; the opposite difference is handled by interchanging the solutions. Fix $r,R,\delta $ from lemma 14.19.43 and put $\alpha =r\omega $. For every smooth positive $\rho $ with \[  \rho \geq \tfrac 12,\qquad \langle \rho \rangle _\alpha =1,\qquad \langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 4,  \] theorem 14.2.1 gives a smooth solution \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=c\rho \alpha ^ n,\qquad \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi >0,\qquad \sup _ X\psi =0.  \] At a maximum of $\psi $, $c\rho \leq 1$, so $c\leq 2$. Apply theorem 14.19.19 with $p=2$ and background $\alpha $. Its potential and lower-density bounds give fixed $c_0,C_\psi >0$ with \[  c\geq c_0,\qquad -C_\psi \leq \psi \leq 0.  \] These constants depend only on the three bounds for $\rho $, and not on the cutoff function chosen below. Choose $\kappa >0$ so that $2C_0\kappa \leq 1/4$, $\kappa C_0\leq 1/16$ and $\kappa C_\psi /2\leq 1/16$. Next choose $M\geq 1$ with $2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n$, and then $\varepsilon _0>0$ with \[  \tfrac {16}{7}\varepsilon _0\leq \min \{ (2M)^{-1},M^{-2}\} .  \] If one of the inequalities \[  \| h_1-h_2\| _\infty \leq \kappa \delta s, \qquad \langle (b-a)_+\rangle _\omega \leq \varepsilon _0s.  \] fails, then $s\leq C(\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1})$, with $C$ depending only on $\kappa ,\delta ,\varepsilon _0$ and the volume of $X$. We assume both and derive a contradiction. Put $t=\kappa s$; since $s\leq 2C_0$, we have $t\leq 1/4$. On $\Omega =\{ (1-t)b-a>s/2\} $, we have $b-a>7s/16$, so by Chebyshev's inequality the relative volume of $\Omega $ is at most $16\varepsilon _0/7$. Take a smooth $\zeta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, zero on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and one on $[3/4,\infty )$, and set \[  \rho =b_0+M\zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr ),\qquad b_0=1-M\bigl \langle \zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr )\bigr \rangle _\omega .  \] The second term is supported in $\Omega $, so $1/2\leq b_0\leq 1$ and $\langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 2+2M^2(16\varepsilon _0/7)\leq 4$; here we use that averages with respect to $\alpha =r\omega $ and $\omega $ agree. Thus the auxiliary solution for this $\rho $ satisfies the bounds with the same constants $c_0,C_\psi $. At a point where $b-a=s$, the function $\Phi =(1-t)b-a+t\psi /2$ is at least $7s/8$, by the choice of $\kappa $. At a maximum point $x_0$ of $\Phi $, therefore, $(1-t)b-a\geq 7s/8$ because $\psi \leq 0$, and so $\rho (x_0)\geq M$. The second derivative test gives, at $x_0$, \[  P=\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((a-(1-t)b)/t\bigr ) \geq \tfrac 12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )+\tfrac 12\alpha >0.  \] The identity \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a =t\bigl ((\theta -\alpha )+P\bigr )+(1-t)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)  \] and concavity imply \[  F\bigl (\omega ^{-1}((\theta -\alpha )+P)\bigr ) \leq h_2+(h_1-h_2)/t\leq H+\delta .  \] Both forms in the convex combination are admissible, since $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $P>0$. By lemma 14.19.43 , $P\leq R\omega $. On the other hand, $P\geq \frac12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )$, so the auxiliary equation gives \[  R^ n\geq P^ n/\omega ^ n \geq 2^{-n}c\rho r^ n\geq 2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n,  \] a contradiction. Hence one of the two smallness inequalities fails, which gives the required bound for $s$. Interchanging the solutions proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 14.19.46 . E9194EDCB1FF Let $\mathcal H$ be a set of right-hand sides in the family that is equicontinuous. Then the normalized solutions with right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$ and have a common modulus of continuity. Proof. Admissibility and $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$ give $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq -C$. By theorem 11.4.2 , there is a smooth function $\rho _0>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _0\omega ^{n-1})=0$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \rho _0\omega ^{n-1}=0$ for every smooth $\varphi $. Integrating the product rule $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)=2u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+2\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$ against $\rho _0\omega ^{n-1}$, and using $0\leq u\leq C$ from proposition 14.19.44 , we obtain a uniform bound for $\int _ X|\mathrm du|_\omega ^2\omega ^ n$, because $\rho _0$ is bounded above and below. Rellich's theorem therefore gives precompactness in $L^1$. Given a sequence of such solutions, the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence whose right-hand sides converge uniformly, since they are equicontinuous and bounded by $H_0$. A further subsequence of the solutions is Cauchy in $L^1$, and theorem 14.19.45 makes it uniformly Cauchy. This proves precompactness in $C^0(X)$. A common modulus of continuity follows from a finite uniform $\varepsilon /3$-net, since each of its finitely many members is uniformly continuous. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.19.44
text: Proposition 14.19.44 . 877A402699F6 Every solution satisfies $0\leq u\leq C$. Proof. Put $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$ and $w=u-\underline u-\sup _ X(u-\underline u)\leq 0$. Since $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$, we have $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -\operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta \geq -C$. The Green-kernel argument in the proof of proposition 14.11.1 , applied to the operator $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, therefore bounds $\| w\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. Center a holomorphic coordinate ball of fixed size at a minimum point of $w$, and rescale it to the real unit ball. For a fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set $q=w+\varepsilon |x|^2$ and $m=\min _ Xw$. The real contact-set construction of ( 14.11.2 ) gives a compact set $E$ on which \[  D^2q\geq 0,\qquad q\leq m+\varepsilon /2, \qquad |B_{\varepsilon /2}|\leq \int _ E\det D^2q\, \mathrm dx.  \] On $E$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq -C\varepsilon \omega $. Choose $\varepsilon $ so that $C\varepsilon <r$. Then $P=\omega ^{-1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+r\omega )\geq 0$ and \[  F(A_{\underline u}-r\operatorname {Id}+P)=F(A_ u)=h\leq H.  \] Lemma 14.19.43 bounds $P$, and hence the complex trace of the Hessian of $q$. The nonnegative real Hessian of $q$ on $E$ therefore has bounded trace, and hence bounded determinant, so the contact inequality implies $|E|\geq c>0$. Since $w\leq m+\varepsilon /2$ on $E$, the $L^1$ bound gives $c(-m-\varepsilon /2)\leq C$. This bounds the oscillation of $w$, hence that of $u$; with the normalization $\inf _ Xu=0$, this is the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.19.45
text: Theorem 14.19.45 . 0F1A655FC651 There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that any two normalized solutions $u_1,u_2$ with right-hand sides $h_1,h_2$ in the family satisfy \[  \| u_1-u_2\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1}\bigr ).  \] In particular, $C$ does not depend on a positive lower bound for the $h_ i$ or on bounds for their derivatives. Proof. Set $a=u_1-\underline u$, $b=u_2-\underline u$ and $\theta =\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline u$. By proposition 14.19.44 , $|a|,|b|\leq C_0$ for a fixed $C_0\geq 1$. It suffices to bound $s=\max _ X(b-a)$ when it is positive; the opposite difference is handled by interchanging the solutions. Fix $r,R,\delta $ from lemma 14.19.43 and put $\alpha =r\omega $. For every smooth positive $\rho $ with \[  \rho \geq \tfrac 12,\qquad \langle \rho \rangle _\alpha =1,\qquad \langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 4,  \] theorem 14.2.1 gives a smooth solution \[  (\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=c\rho \alpha ^ n,\qquad \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi >0,\qquad \sup _ X\psi =0.  \] At a maximum of $\psi $, $c\rho \leq 1$, so $c\leq 2$. Apply theorem 14.19.19 with $p=2$ and background $\alpha $. Its potential and lower-density bounds give fixed $c_0,C_\psi >0$ with \[  c\geq c_0,\qquad -C_\psi \leq \psi \leq 0.  \] These constants depend only on the three bounds for $\rho $, and not on the cutoff function chosen below. Choose $\kappa >0$ so that $2C_0\kappa \leq 1/4$, $\kappa C_0\leq 1/16$ and $\kappa C_\psi /2\leq 1/16$. Next choose $M\geq 1$ with $2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n$, and then $\varepsilon _0>0$ with \[  \tfrac {16}{7}\varepsilon _0\leq \min \{ (2M)^{-1},M^{-2}\} .  \] If one of the inequalities \[  \| h_1-h_2\| _\infty \leq \kappa \delta s, \qquad \langle (b-a)_+\rangle _\omega \leq \varepsilon _0s.  \] fails, then $s\leq C(\| h_1-h_2\| _\infty +\| u_1-u_2\| _{L^1})$, with $C$ depending only on $\kappa ,\delta ,\varepsilon _0$ and the volume of $X$. We assume both and derive a contradiction. Put $t=\kappa s$; since $s\leq 2C_0$, we have $t\leq 1/4$. On $\Omega =\{ (1-t)b-a>s/2\} $, we have $b-a>7s/16$, so by Chebyshev's inequality the relative volume of $\Omega $ is at most $16\varepsilon _0/7$. Take a smooth $\zeta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, zero on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and one on $[3/4,\infty )$, and set \[  \rho =b_0+M\zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr ),\qquad b_0=1-M\bigl \langle \zeta \bigl (((1-t)b-a)/s\bigr )\bigr \rangle _\omega .  \] The second term is supported in $\Omega $, so $1/2\leq b_0\leq 1$ and $\langle \rho ^2\rangle _\alpha \leq 2+2M^2(16\varepsilon _0/7)\leq 4$; here we use that averages with respect to $\alpha =r\omega $ and $\omega $ agree. Thus the auxiliary solution for this $\rho $ satisfies the bounds with the same constants $c_0,C_\psi $. At a point where $b-a=s$, the function $\Phi =(1-t)b-a+t\psi /2$ is at least $7s/8$, by the choice of $\kappa $. At a maximum point $x_0$ of $\Phi $, therefore, $(1-t)b-a\geq 7s/8$ because $\psi \leq 0$, and so $\rho (x_0)\geq M$. The second derivative test gives, at $x_0$, \[  P=\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((a-(1-t)b)/t\bigr ) \geq \tfrac 12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )+\tfrac 12\alpha >0.  \] The identity \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a =t\bigl ((\theta -\alpha )+P\bigr )+(1-t)(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)  \] and concavity imply \[  F\bigl (\omega ^{-1}((\theta -\alpha )+P)\bigr ) \leq h_2+(h_1-h_2)/t\leq H+\delta .  \] Both forms in the convex combination are admissible, since $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $ and $P>0$. By lemma 14.19.43 , $P\leq R\omega $. On the other hand, $P\geq \frac12(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )$, so the auxiliary equation gives \[  R^ n\geq P^ n/\omega ^ n \geq 2^{-n}c\rho r^ n\geq 2^{-n}c_0Mr^ n>R^ n,  \] a contradiction. Hence one of the two smallness inequalities fails, which gives the required bound for $s$. Interchanging the solutions proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Corollary 14.19.46
text: Corollary 14.19.46 . E9194EDCB1FF Let $\mathcal H$ be a set of right-hand sides in the family that is equicontinuous. Then the normalized solutions with right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$ and have a common modulus of continuity. Proof. Admissibility and $\Gamma \subseteq \Gamma _1$ give $\operatorname {tr}_\omega \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq -C$. By theorem 11.4.2 , there is a smooth function $\rho _0>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _0\omega ^{n-1})=0$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge \rho _0\omega ^{n-1}=0$ for every smooth $\varphi $. Integrating the product rule $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)=2u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u+2\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$ against $\rho _0\omega ^{n-1}$, and using $0\leq u\leq C$ from proposition 14.19.44 , we obtain a uniform bound for $\int _ X|\mathrm du|_\omega ^2\omega ^ n$, because $\rho _0$ is bounded above and below. Rellich's theorem therefore gives precompactness in $L^1$. Given a sequence of such solutions, the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives a subsequence whose right-hand sides converge uniformly, since they are equicontinuous and bounded by $H_0$. A further subsequence of the solutions is Cauchy in $L^1$, and theorem 14.19.45 makes it uniformly Cauchy. This proves precompactness in $C^0(X)$. A common modulus of continuity follows from a finite uniform $\varepsilon /3$-net, since each of its finitely many members is uniformly continuous. $\square$

title: 14.19.47 Gradient bounds for concave equations
text:
We keep the fixed data, the family of right-hand sides and the normalization of subsection 14.19.42 , and assume in addition that $\| \partial h\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq H_1$; throughout the section, $u$ denotes a solution with such a right-hand side $h$. The gradient bound is obtained by comparison with a nearby smooth admissible function $V$. A maximum principle for a weighted gradient quantity bounds the gradient of $u$ in terms of that of $V$, provided $\| u-V\| _\infty $ is below a threshold that does not depend on the derivatives of $V$. The $C^0$ compactness of corollary 14.19.46 then shows that finitely many such comparison functions suffice for all solutions. For the derivative calculation, write $U=u/(2\pi )$ and $\underline U=\underline u/(2\pi )$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial U$. For any smooth real $V$, put $\mathcal A_ V=\omega ^{-1}(\chi +\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial V)$ and call $V$ admissible if $\lambda (\mathcal A_ V)\in \Gamma $. We use the Chern connection of $\omega $, and define the endomorphism $B=DF(\mathcal A_ U)$ by $ rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}F(\mathcal A_ U+tM)|_{t=0}=\operatorname {tr}(BM)$. Write $\lambda =(\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n)=\lambda (\mathcal A_ U)$. At a point where $\mathcal A_ U$ is diagonal in a unitary frame, set \[  B_ i=f_ i(\lambda ),\qquad \mathcal Lq=\sum _ iB_ iq_{i ar i},\qquad T=\sum _ iB_ i, \qquad |\partial q|_ B^2=\sum _ iB_ i|q_ i|^2.  \] Here subscripts denote frame derivatives, $U_{ki}=
abla _ iU_ k$ and $U_{i ar j}=\partial _ i\partial _{ ar j}U$; the second derivatives $U_{ki}$ need not be symmetric. The trace expressions below do not depend on the unitary frame. Lemma 14.19.48 . D049243EB2FA There are fixed $	au ,\kappa >0$ such that  egin{gather*}  T\geq 	au ,\qquad 0\leq \operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h,\  \mathcal L(U-V)\leq h\quad (V	ext{ admissible}),\qquad \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -h. \end{gather*} Moreover, at every point at least one of the alternatives \[  \mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq \kappa T, \qquad B\geq \kappa T\operatorname {Id}  \] holds. The constants depend only on the fixed data; in particular they are uniform for all right-hand sides in the family. Proof. If $\lambda (P)\in \Gamma $, then $\mathcal A_ U+tP$ is admissible for $t\geq 0$. The function $t\mapsto F(\mathcal A_ U+tP)$ is positive and concave on $[0,\infty )$, so its derivative at $t=0$ cannot be negative; thus $\operatorname {tr}(BP)\geq 0$. Since $F$ is concave and $F(0)=0$, the tangent inequality at $\mathcal A_ U$, evaluated at the origin, gives $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq h$. Choose $a_*>0$ with $F(a_*\operatorname {Id})>H_0+1$. Concavity gives \[  H_0+1<F(a_*\operatorname {Id}) \leq h+a_*T-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)\leq H_0+a_*T.  \] Thus $T\geq a_*^{-1}$. Since $\mathcal L(U-V)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)=\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})-\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ U)$, the remaining two bounds follow from the nonnegativity of $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_ V)$ and $\operatorname {tr}(B\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. We derive the alternative from the strict gap. Fix $r,H,\delta $ from lemma 14.19.43 , and put $\mu =\lambda (\mathcal A_{\underline U})$. Compactness and the gap give one $S>r$ such that \[  f(\mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i)>H+2\delta \qquad (1\leq i\leq n)  \] everywhere. We first prove a scalar alternative. At a point of $X$, let $\lambda \in \Gamma $ satisfy $f(\lambda )=\sigma $, where $\sigma =h$ at that point, and consider the set \[  K=\{ v\geq \mu -r\mathbf1:f(v)\leq \sigma \} .  \] It is contained in $\Gamma $ because $\mu -r\mathbf1\in \Gamma $, it is closed, and the matrix bound of lemma 14.19.43 , applied to diagonal matrices, makes it bounded; thus $K$ is compact. When nonempty, it contains $\mu -r\mathbf1$ and is star-shaped about that point: moving along a segment toward it decreases each coordinate, hence decreases $f$. Thus $K$ is connected. Let $N=
abla f(\lambda )$, whose entries are positive, and let $\Pi $ be the tangent hyperplane $N\cdot (v-\lambda )=0$. If $f(\mu -r\mathbf1)>\sigma $, concavity gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. Otherwise $\mu -r\mathbf1\in K$. The diagonal ray $\mu -r\mathbf1+t\mathbf1$, $t\geq 0$, meets $\{ f=\sigma \} $, since $f$ diverges along it; at the meeting point $v$, the tangent inequality gives $N\cdot (v-\lambda )\geq 0$. If $\Pi $ misses $K$, connectedness makes $N\cdot (v-\lambda )$ strictly positive throughout $K$, and in particular at $\mu -r\mathbf1$; this again gives $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$. If $v\in \Pi \cap K$, put $z_ i=v-r\mathbf1+Se_ i$. Then $z_ i\geq \mu -2r\mathbf1+Se_ i$, so $f(z_ i)>\sigma $. The tangent inequality at $\lambda $ gives \[  0<N\cdot (z_ i-v)=SN_ i-r\sum _ jN_ j.  \] Thus $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for every $i$. We have proved that $N\cdot (\mu -\lambda )>r\sum _ iN_ i$ or $N_ i>(r/S)\sum _ jN_ j$ for all $i$, at every positive level $\sigma $, with constants independent of $\sigma $. To pass to matrices, take $\lambda =\lambda (\mathcal A_ U)$, and order $\lambda $ and $\mu $ decreasingly. By concavity and symmetry, the numbers $f_ i(\lambda )$ are then ordered increasingly. In the eigenframe of $\mathcal A_ U$, the diagonal of $\mathcal A_{\underline U}$ is a doubly stochastic average of permutations of $\mu $, so the rearrangement inequality gives \[  \operatorname {tr} igl (B(\mathcal A_{\underline U}-\mathcal A_ U) igr ) \geq \sum _ if_ i(\lambda )(\mu _ i-\lambda _ i).  \] Since $N=(f_ i(\lambda ))_ i=(B_ i)_ i$, taking $\kappa $ smaller than $\min \{ r,r/S\} $ proves the matrix alternative. $\square$ Lemma 14.19.49 . BD78CDB91D24 Put $Q=1+|\partial U|_\omega ^2$. For any smooth real $\xi $, one has  egin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+Q\mathcal L\xi +|\partial \xi |_ B^2\ & \quad +2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{ ar i} -2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i ar k}U_ k\xi _{ ar i} -C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|_\omega , \end{align*} where $C_ g$ depends only on $\omega $ and $\chi $. Proof. Write $\mathscr T^ p_{ik}$ and $R^ p_{i ar jk}$ for the torsion and curvature of the Chern connection. The commutation formula and the differentiated equation read  egin{gather*}  
abla _{ ar j}
abla _ iU_ k =
abla _ kU_{i ar j}+\sum _ p igl (R^ p_{i ar jk}U_ p-\mathscr T^ p_{ik}U_{p ar j} igr ),\  \sum _ iB_ i
abla _ kU_{i ar i}=h_ k-\sum _ iB_ i
abla _ k\chi _{i ar i}. \end{gather*} The product rule for $|\partial U|^2$ gives both squares $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}|^2$ and $\sum B_ i|U_{k ar i}|^2$, the term $2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ kh_ kU_{ ar k}$, a curvature error bounded by $CT|\partial U|^2$, and the errors from $
abla \chi $ and torsion. The latter are bounded by \[  CT|\partial U|+CT|\partial U|^2 +C|\partial U|T^{1/2}\Bigl (\sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{k ar i}|^2\Bigr )^{1/2}.  \] Absorb the last term into half of the mixed square. Since $U_{i ar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}-\chi _{i ar j}$, the remaining half is at least $ rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-CT$. Hence \[  \mathcal L|\partial U|^2\geq \sum _{i,k}B_ i|U_{ki}|^2 + rac14\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2-C_ gTQ-2H_1|\partial U|.  \] Finally, \[  \partial _ i|\partial U|^2 =\sum _ kU_{ki}U_{ ar k}+\lambda _ iU_ i-\sum _ k\chi _{i ar k}U_ k.  \] In the product rule for $\mathrm e^\xi Q$, combine the cross term coming from the first sum with $|\partial U|^2|\partial \xi |_ B^2$ and with the square $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}|^2$. This gives $\sum B_ i|U_{ki}+U_ k\xi _ i|^2$, while the remaining weight term is $|\partial \xi |_ B^2$. $\square$ Proposition 14.19.50 . F13386AF12E0 There are constants $\eta ,C>0$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that every smooth admissible $V$ with $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \eta $ satisfies \[  \| \partial U\| _\infty \leq C igl (1+\| \partial V\| _\infty ^2 igr ).  \] The comparison radius $\eta $ is independent of the derivatives of $V$. Proof. Let $a\geq 1$ and $ eta >1$ be constants, to be chosen below. Assuming $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq  eta ^{-1}$, put \[  w=U-V- eta ^{-1},\qquad \xi =a(\underline U-U)+ eta w^2,\qquad K_ V=1+\| \partial \underline U\| _\infty +\| \partial V\| _\infty .  \] Then $-2 eta ^{-1}\leq w\leq 0$ and \[  \xi _ i=a(\underline U_ i-V_ i)+(-a+2 eta w)(U_ i-V_ i), \qquad |-a+2 eta w|\leq a+4.  \] Writing $D=|\partial (U-V)|_ B^2$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives  egin{align*}  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{ ar i}ight| & \leq  rac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_ aK_ V^4T+C_ a(Q+K_ V^2)D,\  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i ar k}U_ k\xi _{ ar i}ight| & \leq 	frac 12QD+C_ aT+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}T. \end{align*} For the first line, split $\xi _ i$ as above and use $\sum B_ i|U_ i|^2\leq 2D+2K_ V^2T$; then apply Young's inequality to the resulting three products, each absorbing at most $ rac1{24}\sum B_ i\lambda _ i^2$. Combining the preceding bounds with lemma 14.19.49 , we obtain, at every point where $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$ for a suitable constant $C'$,  egin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq  rac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2\ & \quad +Q igl [a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-(C_ g+2)T + eta D-(4H_0+2H_1) igr ]. \end{align*} Indeed, the coefficient of $D$ before absorption is $(2 eta -C_ a-1/2)Q-C_ aK_ V^2$, which is at least $ eta Q$ once $C'$ is large enough. The other errors satisfy $C_ aK_ V^4\leq Q$ and $C_ a+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}\leq Q$, and they account for the additional term $-2T$ in the bracket. Consider a maximum point of $\mathrm e^\xi Q$ at which $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$. In the first alternative of lemma 14.19.48 , the bracket is positive by the choice of $a$, since $T\geq 	au $. In the second, $D\geq \kappa T|\partial (U-V)|^2$. For $Q\geq 4(1+K_ V^2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|\partial (U-V)|^2\geq c_*Q$, where $c_*=(\sqrt3-1)^2/4$. Since $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -H_0$, the bracket is then at least \[  ( eta \kappa c_*Q-C_ g-2)T-(a+4)H_0-2H_1.  \] This is positive once $C'$ is large enough, because $T\geq 	au $. In both cases $\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q)>0$ at a maximum point, which contradicts the second derivative test. Thus $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ at the maximum point. The weight has uniformly bounded oscillation: \[  \operatorname {osc}_ X\xi \leq a(\operatorname {osc}_ X\underline U+\operatorname {osc}_ XU)+4/ eta .  \] By the potential bound in proposition 14.19.44 , this oscillation is bounded independently of $V$, so the estimate at the maximum point gives $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ everywhere. Taking square roots and setting $\eta = eta ^{-1}$ proves the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 14.19.51 . 979B56319AA1 There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that $\| \mathrm du\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq C$ for every normalized solution $u$ whose right-hand side $h$ lies in the family and satisfies $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$. In particular, the bound is uniform as the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Proof. The right-hand sides in the family with $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$ form an equicontinuous set. By corollary 14.19.46 , the corresponding functions $U$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$. Choose a finite $\eta $-net in this set, consisting of smooth admissible functions $V_1,\ldots ,V_ N$. Each solution is within $\eta $ of some $V_ j$, so proposition 14.19.50 bounds its gradient by $C(1+\max _ j\| \partial V_ j\| _\infty ^2)$. The set of solutions, and hence the chosen finite net, depends only on the fixed data and $H_1$. Finally, $u=2\pi U$, so the same conclusion holds for $\mathrm du$. $\square$ In section 14.20 we return to the Monge–Ampère equation for $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and ask when two potentials with the same density agree up to a constant. The uniqueness of the normalization scalar does not determine the potential: where the density vanishes, the polarized linear equation for the difference can be degenerate.

text:

title: Proposition 14.19.50
text: Proposition 14.19.50 . F13386AF12E0 There are constants $\eta ,C>0$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that every smooth admissible $V$ with $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \eta $ satisfies \[  \| \partial U\| _\infty \leq C\bigl (1+\| \partial V\| _\infty ^2\bigr ).  \] The comparison radius $\eta $ is independent of the derivatives of $V$. Proof. Let $a\geq 1$ and $\beta >1$ be constants, to be chosen below. Assuming $\| U-V\| _\infty \leq \beta ^{-1}$, put \[  w=U-V-\beta ^{-1},\qquad \xi =a(\underline U-U)+\beta w^2,\qquad K_ V=1+\| \partial \underline U\| _\infty +\| \partial V\| _\infty .  \] Then $-2\beta ^{-1}\leq w\leq 0$ and \[  \xi _ i=a(\underline U_ i-V_ i)+(-a+2\beta w)(U_ i-V_ i), \qquad |-a+2\beta w|\leq a+4.  \] Writing $D=|\partial (U-V)|_ B^2$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \begin{align*}  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ iU_ i\xi _{\bar i}\right| & \leq \frac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_ aK_ V^4T+C_ a(Q+K_ V^2)D,\\  \left|2\operatorname{Re}\sum _{i,k}B_ i\chi _{i\bar k}U_ k\xi _{\bar i}\right| & \leq \tfrac 12QD+C_ aT+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}T. \end{align*} For the first line, split $\xi _ i$ as above and use $\sum B_ i|U_ i|^2\leq 2D+2K_ V^2T$; then apply Young's inequality to the resulting three products, each absorbing at most $\frac1{24}\sum B_ i\lambda _ i^2$. For the second line, use $|\partial \xi |_ B\leq aK_ VT^{1/2}+(a+4)D^{1/2}$ and the bound for $\chi $. In both lines, $C_ a$ depends on $a$ but not on $\beta $ or on the derivatives of $V$. By lemma 14.19.48 and $w\leq 0$, \[  \mathcal L\xi \geq a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-4H_0+2\beta D.  \] Choose $a$ so large that $(a\kappa -C_ g-2)\tau >4H_0+2H_1+1$, and then $\beta \geq 2C_ a+2$. Combining the preceding bounds with lemma 14.19.49 , we obtain, at every point where $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$ for a suitable constant $C'$, \begin{align*}  \mathrm e^{-\xi }\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q) & \geq \frac18\sum _ iB_ i\lambda _ i^2\\ & \quad +Q\bigl [a\mathcal L(\underline U-U)-(C_ g+2)T +\beta D-(4H_0+2H_1)\bigr ]. \end{align*} Indeed, the coefficient of $D$ before absorption is $(2\beta -C_ a-1/2)Q-C_ aK_ V^2$, which is at least $\beta Q$ once $C'$ is large enough. The other errors satisfy $C_ aK_ V^4\leq Q$ and $C_ a+C_ aK_ VQ^{1/2}\leq Q$, and they account for the additional term $-2T$ in the bracket. Consider a maximum point of $\mathrm e^\xi Q$ at which $Q\geq C'(1+K_ V^4)$. In the first alternative of lemma 14.19.48 , the bracket is positive by the choice of $a$, since $T\geq \tau $. In the second, $D\geq \kappa T|\partial (U-V)|^2$. For $Q\geq 4(1+K_ V^2)$, the triangle inequality gives $|\partial (U-V)|^2\geq c_*Q$, where $c_*=(\sqrt3-1)^2/4$. Since $\mathcal L(\underline U-U)\geq -H_0$, the bracket is then at least \[  (\beta \kappa c_*Q-C_ g-2)T-(a+4)H_0-2H_1.  \] This is positive once $C'$ is large enough, because $T\geq \tau $. In both cases $\mathcal L(\mathrm e^\xi Q)>0$ at a maximum point, which contradicts the second derivative test. Thus $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ at the maximum point. The weight has uniformly bounded oscillation: \[  \operatorname {osc}_ X\xi \leq a(\operatorname {osc}_ X\underline U+\operatorname {osc}_ XU)+4/\beta .  \] By the potential bound in proposition 14.19.44 , this oscillation is bounded independently of $V$, so the estimate at the maximum point gives $Q\leq C(1+K_ V^4)$ everywhere. Taking square roots and setting $\eta =\beta ^{-1}$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.19.51
text: Theorem 14.19.51 . 979B56319AA1 There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data and $H_1$, such that $\| \mathrm du\| _{L^\infty (\omega )}\leq C$ for every normalized solution $u$ whose right-hand side $h$ lies in the family and satisfies $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$. In particular, the bound is uniform as the positive right-hand sides tend to zero. Proof. The right-hand sides in the family with $\| \partial h\| _\infty \leq H_1$ form an equicontinuous set. By corollary 14.19.46 , the corresponding functions $U$ form a precompact subset of $C^0(X)$. Choose a finite $\eta $-net in this set, consisting of smooth admissible functions $V_1,\ldots ,V_ N$. Each solution is within $\eta $ of some $V_ j$, so proposition 14.19.50 bounds its gradient by $C(1+\max _ j\| \partial V_ j\| _\infty ^2)$. The set of solutions, and hence the chosen finite net, depends only on the fixed data and $H_1$. Finally, $u=2\pi U$, so the same conclusion holds for $\mathrm du$. $\square$

title: 14.20 Uniqueness for degenerate equations
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form. For a nonzero nonnegative density $f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm dV)$, $p>1$, the preceding chapter determines the constant $c$ in $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=cf\, \mathrm dV$. We now ask whether the potential is determined up to a constant. For real potentials $u,v$, with the regularity stated in each result, set \[  A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\qquad B=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v,\qquad w=u-v, \qquad T=\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}A^ j\wedge B^{n-1-j}.  \] Then 2EA7CA32AE91 14.20.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=A^ n-B^ n. \end{equation} For $A,B\geq 0$ with equal Monge–Ampère measures, $w$ solves $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$, whose cofactor may be degenerate or nonclosed. Coefficient products for Sobolev potentials are interpreted almost everywhere. For $C^{1,1}$ solutions with a common continuous density, perturbing $w$ locates its extrema in elliptic regions; the maximum principle propagates their values along the corresponding components. For $C^2$ potentials, a continuous weight $h>0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions gives a global energy identity forcing $\mathrm dw$ to vanish in the positive directions of the cofactor. For bounded solutions, an energy measure replaces the pointwise gradient calculation. A continuous density whose positive set is connected and dense then gives uniqueness. When the background has invariant mass, ordinary comparison proves uniqueness for nonzero nonnegative $L^ p$ densities, $p>1$, even if the density vanishes on an open set. The examples on $\mathbb P^3$ have bounded mass and a smooth nonclosed Hermitian background, yet distinct smooth normalized solutions share one density. Its zero set separates the elliptic regions: it can be an open band or two hypersurfaces with quadratic vanishing, even for a real analytic density. Finite upper mass therefore does not ensure uniqueness.

Take the $C^{1,1}$ representative of $z$, write $M=\sup _\Omega z$, and suppose that $K=\{ z=M\} $ is a nonempty proper subset of $\Omega $. Near a relative boundary point of $K$, choose $y

e k}\lambda _\ell .  \end{equation} For $n\geq 2$, ( 14.21.8 ) and ( 14.21.9 ) show that $Q$ is locally uniformly elliptic exactly on $E_{m unif}$, that is, where $H$ has a local essential positive lower bound. Every eigenvalue is therefore bounded below by the determinant lower bound divided by a fixed power of the upper bound. Thus $U\subset E_{m unif}$. By ( 14.20.1 ), $w$ solves a linear equation in nondivergence form with measurable coefficients, whose principal quadratic form is a fixed positive multiple of $Q$. On each relatively compact coordinate ball in $E_{m unif}$, these coefficients are uniformly elliptic. 14.21.6 , applied to $w$ and to $-w$, makes $w$ constant on the component of $E_{m unif}$ containing the maximum point found above, and constant on the component containing the minimum point found above. Continuity extends the two constant values to the closures, proving ( 14.21.4 ). Distinct extrema force disjoint closures. The same argument applies on $U$ itself, since $U$ contains the extremal points found in $P_\chi $ and the cofactor is locally uniformly elliptic on $U\subset E_{m unif}$. This proves the assertions with $U$ in place of $E_{m unif}$. The component criteria are immediate except for the dense two-component case. If an open dense subset of connected $X$ has at most two components with disjoint closures, those closures are disjoint nonempty closed sets whose union is $X$, contradicting connectedness. Finally, when $Z=\{ f=0\} $ is a connected embedded real hypersurface, flattening charts assign to each point of $Z$ the unordered pair of components containing its two local sides. This pair is locally constant along $Z$, so connectedness makes it independent of the point; the two labels may coincide or be exchanged along a loop. Every component of $X\setminus Z$ has a nonempty boundary in $Z$, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $X$. Near such a boundary point it contains a local side. Thus the pair accounts for every component, and $U$ has at most two components. It is dense because a hypersurface has empty interior. This proves the last assertion without choosing a global side. $\square$ In this argument, the $C^{1,1}$ bound controls the measurable coefficients, and continuity of the density places the limiting contact points in $\{ f>0\} $. The next criterion gives a quantitative condition for $\{ f>0\} $ to be connected.

Continuity extends the two constant values to the closures, proving ( 14.21.4 ). Distinct extrema force disjoint closures. The same argument applies on $U$ itself, since $U$ contains the extremal points found in $P_\chi $ and the cofactor is locally uniformly elliptic on $U\subset E_{\rm unif}$. This proves the assertions with $U$ in place of $E_{\rm unif}$. The component criteria are immediate except for the dense two-component case. If an open dense subset of connected $X$ has at most two components with disjoint closures, those closures are disjoint nonempty closed sets whose union is $X$, contradicting connectedness. Finally, when $Z=\{ f=0\} $ is a connected embedded real hypersurface, flattening charts assign to each point of $Z$ the unordered pair of components containing its two local sides. This pair is locally constant along $Z$, so connectedness makes it independent of the point; the two labels may coincide or be exchanged along a loop. Every component of $X\setminus Z$ has a nonempty boundary in $Z$, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $X$. Near such a boundary point it contains a local side. Thus the pair accounts for every component, and $U$ has at most two components. It is dense because a hypersurface has empty interior. This proves the last assertion without choosing a global side. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.21.5
text: Lemma 14.21.5 . 59B8A4C8DA05 In Euclidean space $\mathbb R^ m$, let $B(p,r)$ be the ball of center $p$ and radius $r>0$, and let $I$ be the identity matrix. Let $g\in C^{1,1}$ near $\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \mathbb R^ m$, suppose $g\leq g(p)$ on the ball, and let $E$ be any subset of full measure in the ball at whose points $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion. For every $\delta >0$ and $0<\rho <r$, there is $x\in E\cap B(p,\rho )$ such that \[  D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I.  \] Proof. Put $g_\delta (x)=g(x)-\delta |x-p|^2$. The gradient map $F=\nabla g_\delta $ is Lipschitz on the ball, so it maps the null set $N=\overline{B(p,r)}\setminus E$ to a null set. Choose $s\in B(0,\delta \rho )\setminus F(N)$ and maximize $g_\delta (x)-s\cdot (x-p)$ on the closed ball. At any point with $|x-p|\geq \rho $, its value is strictly smaller than its value at $p$, because \[  g(x)-g(p)-\delta |x-p|^2-s\cdot (x-p) \leq -\delta |x-p|^2+|s|\, |x-p|<0.  \] Thus a maximizer $x$ lies in $B(p,\rho )$. The first-order condition at $x$ gives $F(x)=s$, so $x\notin N$. The second-order Taylor expansion at this upper contact point gives $D^2g(x)\leq 2\delta I$. Finally, sets $E$ as in the statement exist: by Rademacher's theorem, applied to the Lipschitz gradient of $g$, the function $g$ has a second-order Taylor expansion almost everywhere. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.21.6
text: Lemma 14.21.6 . 96D40C4808C2 Let $a=(a^{ij})$ be a measurable symmetric matrix field on a connected domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$. For each compact $K\Subset \Omega $, suppose there are constants $0<\lambda _ K\leq \Lambda _ K<\infty $ such that \[  \lambda _ K I\leq a(x)\leq \Lambda _ KI  \] almost everywhere on $K$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. Repeated indices $i,j=1,\ldots ,m$ are summed, and $z_{ij}=\partial _ i\partial _ jz$. If $z\in W^{2,\infty }_{\rm loc}(\Omega )$, $a^{ij}z_{ij}\geq 0$ almost everywhere, and $z$ attains its supremum at a point of $\Omega $, then $z$ is constant. Proof. We first prove strict weak comparison on a relatively compact domain: if $b\in C^{1,1}$, $Lb:=a^{ij}b_{ij}\geq \kappa >0$ almost everywhere, and $b\leq M$ on the boundary, then $b\leq M$ inside. Otherwise an interior maximum point lies in a closed ball on which $a\leq \Lambda I$. Apply 14.21.5 to the set of full measure where both the differential inequality and the Taylor expansion hold. Choosing $2\delta m\Lambda <\kappa $ gives the contradiction $\kappa \leq Lb\leq 2\delta \operatorname {tr}a\leq 2\delta m\Lambda $. Take the $C^{1,1}$ representative of $z$, write $M=\sup _\Omega z$, and suppose that $K=\{ z=M\} $ is a nonempty proper subset of $\Omega $. Near a relative boundary point of $K$, choose $y\notin K$ so that the ball of radius $r=\operatorname {dist}(y,K)>0$ is compactly contained in $\Omega $ and touches $K$ at $x_0$. On the closed annulus $r/2\leq |x-y|\leq r$, use fixed bounds $\lambda I\leq a\leq \Lambda I$ and set \[  b(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha r^2}.  \] For sufficiently large $\alpha $, \[  Lb=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha |x-y|^2} \bigl (4\alpha ^2 a^{ij}(x_ i-y_ i)(x_ j-y_ j) -2\alpha \operatorname {tr}a\bigr )\geq \kappa >0  \] almost everywhere on the annulus. On its inner sphere $z<M$ uniformly; on its outer sphere $b=0$. Choose $\eta >0$ small enough that $z+\eta b\leq M$ on both spheres. Strict weak comparison, applied to $z+\eta b$, gives this inequality throughout the annulus. At $x_0$, however, $z=M$, $b=0$, $\nabla z=0$, and $b$ increases to first order in the inward radial direction, which contradicts that inequality. Thus $K$ has no relative boundary point in $\Omega $, and connectedness proves the assertion. The argument uses no derivatives of the measurable coefficients. $\square$

title: 14.21.12 A square-root threshold
text: A nonnegative $C^{1,1}$ density grows at most quadratically away from each of its zeros. If its zero set separates a small ball, a family of parallel segments crossing the zero set therefore contributes at least a constant times $\sqrt t$ to the volume of $\{ f\leq t\} $ for small $t>0$. Excluding this lower bound makes $\{ f>0\} $ connected, and 14.21.3 then gives uniqueness. Write $\operatorname {Vol}(E)=\int _ E\mathrm{d}V$ for Borel sets $E$. Theorem 14.21.13 . 61851D05B072 Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is $C^{1,1}$. If B72083672909 14.21.14 \begin{equation}  \liminf _{t\downarrow 0} \frac{\operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} }{\sqrt t}=0,  \end{equation} then $\{ f>0\} $ is connected and $u-v$ is constant. In particular this holds when $f^{-1/2}\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, with $f^{-1/2}=+\infty $ on $\{ f=0\} $. The exponent $1/2$ is sharp in every dimension $n\geq 3$. Proof. Write $Z=\{ f=0\} $. Condition ( 14.21.14 ) first implies $\operatorname {Vol}(Z)=0$. We show that the complement of $Z$ in every sufficiently small coordinate ball is connected. Fix such a ball with convex Euclidean image. If the complement of $Z$ in it were disconnected, choose points $a,b$ in different components and small closed disks centered at $a$ and $b$, perpendicular to the segment $[a,b]$ and contained in those respective components. By making the disks small, all parallel segments between corresponding points stay in the ball. Each segment meets $Z$, since otherwise it would connect the two components. On a fixed coordinate region containing the closed ball, the gradient of $f$ is Lipschitz with some constant $K>0$. Since $f\geq 0$, we have $\nabla f(z)=0$ at every zero $z$, hence BB22D6F8FAF9 14.21.15 \begin{equation}  f(x)\leq \frac K2|x-z|^2 \end{equation} whenever the segment from $z$ to $x$ stays in that region. The endpoint disks are compact and disjoint from $Z$, so the parts of the segments near them contain no zeros. Thus every parallel segment contains a zero at a fixed positive distance from its endpoints. For small $t>0$, ( 14.21.15 ) gives on that segment an interval of length $2\sqrt{2t/K}$ contained in $\{ f\leq t\} $. Integrating over the transverse disk, which has positive measure, and using that $\mathrm{d}V$ is comparable to coordinate volume, we obtain \[  \operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} \geq c\sqrt t  \] for all sufficiently small $t$, contradicting ( 14.21.14 ). This proves the local connectedness assertion. For each such ball, the complement of $Z$ in it is nonempty, since $Z$ has zero volume, and it lies in one component of $U=X\setminus Z$. Two overlapping balls give the same component, because their open overlap contains a point outside $Z$. Since $X$ is connected, all these balls give the same component. Hence $U$ is connected, and 14.21.3 shows that $u-v$ is constant. If $f^{-1/2}\in L^1$, then, outside the null zero set, \[  \frac{\operatorname {Vol}\{ f\leq t\} }{\sqrt t} \leq \int _{\{ f\leq t\} }f^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}V\longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence. This proves the sufficient integrability condition. The sharpness assertion follows from the examples in 14.29 , as quantified at the end of that section. $\square$

title: 14.22 Polarized cofactors and propagation
text: Uniform ellipticity is sufficient for the propagation of an extremum, but it is not necessary: the directions in which the cofactor is positive may already connect enough points to force constancy. For $C^2$ potentials, the quadratic form $Q$ in ( 14.21.7 ) is continuous, and its polarization defines $Q^\sharp :T^*X\to TX$ by $\eta (Q^\sharp \xi )=Q(\xi ,\eta )$. The reachable set of a point consists of the endpoints of absolutely continuous curves starting there whose velocity lies in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ almost everywhere. The control orbit of a point consists of the endpoints of finite concatenations of flow lines, starting there, of locally Lipschitz vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. A positive weight $h$ satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ gives an energy identity that controls $\mathrm{d}w$ everywhere. Without such a weight, a degenerate maximum principle gives propagation only from the extremal sets. This distinction accounts for the different density assumptions on reachable sets and on orbits in the following theorem. Theorem 14.22.1 . 919310C73DBE Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n$, and put $w=u-v$. If there is a continuous $h>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions, then 24A83D889133 14.22.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}\, \partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T\equiv 0.  \end{equation} It follows that $w$ is constant if the set where $T$ is strictly positive is dense, or if the reachable set of one point is dense. Without the weight hypothesis, the sets where $w$ attains its maximum and its minimum are invariant under the flow of every locally Lipschitz vector field with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. If every control orbit is dense, then $w$ is constant. For smooth data it is enough that smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $, for example the columns of the symbol $a$ in ( 14.22.10 ) below, together with their iterated Lie brackets, span $TX$ at every point.

title: Theorem 14.22.1
text: Theorem 14.22.1 . 919310C73DBE Let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n$, and put $w=u-v$. If there is a continuous $h>0$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ in distributions, then 24A83D889133 14.22.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}\, \partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T\equiv 0.  \end{equation} It follows that $w$ is constant if the set where $T$ is strictly positive is dense, or if the reachable set of one point is dense. Without the weight hypothesis, the sets where $w$ attains its maximum and its minimum are invariant under the flow of every locally Lipschitz vector field with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $. If every control orbit is dense, then $w$ is constant. For smooth data it is enough that smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $, for example the columns of the symbol $a$ in ( 14.22.10 ) below, together with their iterated Lie brackets, span $TX$ at every point. of 14.22.1 (1). The product rule gives A2BD70AF14EC 14.22.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w =2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\pi }\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w. \end{equation} Approximate $w^2$ in $C^2$ by smooth functions $\varphi $ in ( 14.22.4 ). Since $hT$ is continuous and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ by ( 14.20.1 ), this gives A832621F5643 14.22.6 \begin{equation}  0=\frac1\pi \int _ X h\, \mathrm{i}\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T. \end{equation} The continuous integrand is nonnegative, so it vanishes identically, which is ( 14.22.2 ). By ( 14.21.7 ), ( 14.22.2 ) says that $Q(\mathrm{d}w)=0$. For the nonnegative quadratic form $Q$, this implies $Q(\mathrm{d}w,\eta )=0$ for every $\eta $. Therefore A81FFABB4E8D 14.22.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}w_ x\bigl (Q_ x^\sharp \eta \bigr )=0\qquad (x\in X,\  \eta \in T_ x^*X). \end{equation} By the chain rule and ( 14.22.7 ), $w$ is constant along every absolutely continuous curve whose velocity lies in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ almost everywhere. Thus $w$ is constant on each reachable set, and by continuity one dense reachable set suffices. If instead $Q$ is positive definite on a dense set, ( 14.22.6 ) gives $\mathrm{d}w=0$ there, and hence everywhere. $\square$ of 14.22.1 (2). Apply the preceding argument to $W=w$ and to $W=-w$ in each chart; both satisfy $LW=0$ by ( 14.20.1 ). The maximum set of $w$ is nonempty, closed, and contains every control orbit starting in it. If every orbit is dense, this maximum set is all of $X$, proving constancy. The argument for the minimum set is identical. It remains to prove the bracket criterion. Suppose that a family of smooth vector fields with values in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ is bracket generating. At $p$, let $\mathcal D_ p$ be the span of the values of all original fields pushed forward by finite compositions of their local flows and inverse flows. This distribution contains the original fields and is invariant under their flows. Differentiation of pushed-forward fields along a flow shows that it contains their nested Lie brackets; finite-dimensional subspaces are closed, so the derivative remains in $\mathcal D_ p$. Induction and the Jacobi identity give every iterated bracket. The assumed rank condition therefore gives $\mathcal D_ p=T_ pX$. Choose $2n$ such pushed-forward fields independent at $p$. The flow of each is a conjugate of an original flow and hence preserves its orbit. The map obtained by successively flowing for $2n$ small times has invertible derivative at zero. The inverse function theorem puts a neighborhood of $p$ in its orbit. All orbits are open, and their partition of connected $X$ has only one member. This proves the Hörmander-type sufficient condition; it requires neither a constant-rank hypothesis nor a smooth matrix square root of $a$. In particular, the columns of a smooth symbol $a$ may be used as the original vector fields. $\square$

title: 14.22.3 Weighted energy
text: Testing the weighted cofactor against $w^2$ produces a nonnegative gradient integral. Only distributional $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closedness of $hT$ is needed: for a continuous $h>0$, the condition is 271FE8625215 14.22.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge hT=0\qquad (\varphi \in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)). \end{equation} of 14.22.1 (1). The product rule gives A2BD70AF14EC 14.22.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)=2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+2\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w =2w\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\pi }\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w. \end{equation} Approximate $w^2$ in $C^2$ by smooth functions $\varphi $ in ( 14.22.4 ). Since $hT$ is continuous and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ by ( 14.20.1 ), this gives A832621F5643 14.22.6 \begin{equation}  0=\frac1\pi \int _ X h\, \mathrm{i}\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w\wedge T. \end{equation} The continuous integrand is nonnegative, so it vanishes identically, which is ( 14.22.2 ). By ( 14.21.7 ), ( 14.22.2 ) says that $Q(\mathrm{d}w)=0$. For the nonnegative quadratic form $Q$, this implies $Q(\mathrm{d}w,\eta )=0$ for every $\eta $. Therefore A81FFABB4E8D 14.22.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}w_ x\bigl (Q_ x^\sharp \eta \bigr )=0\qquad (x\in X,\  \eta \in T_ x^*X). \end{equation} By the chain rule and ( 14.22.7 ), $w$ is constant along every absolutely continuous curve whose velocity lies in $\operatorname {im}Q^\sharp $ almost everywhere. Thus $w$ is constant on each reachable set, and by continuity one dense reachable set suffices. If instead $Q$ is positive definite on a dense set, ( 14.22.6 ) gives $\mathrm{d}w=0$ there, and hence everywhere. $\square$ The argument uses only the test function $w^2$. For general test functions, integration by parts introduces derivatives of $hT$; the condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hT)=0$ alone does not make $L\varphi =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \wedge T)/\mathrm{d}V$ a symmetric operator in divergence form.
