title: 14.22.12 The unweighted energy defect
text: Integration against $w^2$ also measures the obstruction to using the unweighted cofactor, that is, the case $h=1$. For smooth potentials, the error is exactly the pairing of $w^2$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$. On a surface, the Gauduchon condition makes this error vanish for every pair of potentials; in dimension three, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ contains an additional term depending on the potentials. Proposition 14.22.13 . F563CACF5D7D Let $n\geq 2$, and let $u,v$ be smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ for a smooth function $f\geq 0$. Then 475D4376A313 14.22.14 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X w^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\{ f>0\} $ is dense in $X$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. By ( 14.20.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$. Integrating ( 14.22.5 ) against $T$, and applying Stokes' theorem twice to the left-hand side, yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)\wedge T=\int _ Xw^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] Substitution proves ( 14.22.14 ). For the uniqueness assertion, apply 14.22.1 (1) with $h=1$. At every point where $f>0$, the form $B$ is positive definite, so the term $B^{n-1}$ makes the cofactor $T$ strictly positive. The set where $T$ is strictly positive is therefore dense, as required. $\square$ Corollary 14.22.15 . EAC3CF41BD99 Assume $n=2$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. Let $f\geq 0$ be smooth, with a zero set of empty interior, and let $c>0$. Then any two smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions of \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2=cf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$ coincide. Proof. Here $T=A+B$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$. The set $\{ f>0\} $ is dense, so the proposition, applied to the density $cf$, makes the difference of the two solutions constant, and the normalization makes this constant zero. $\square$ In dimension three, direct expansion gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=3\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)+3\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v).  \] The Gauduchon condition cancels the first term but need not cancel the second. For instance, take both potentials equal to the perturbation $sv$ in example 11.23.5 . The common form $A=B$ is positive and satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A^2)\ne 0$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=3\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A^2)\ne 0$. Thus even for two equal positive solution forms, the cofactor need not be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed.

title: Proposition 14.22.13
text: Proposition 14.22.13 . F563CACF5D7D Let $n\geq 2$, and let $u,v$ be smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ for a smooth function $f\geq 0$. Then 475D4376A313 14.22.14 \begin{equation}  \int _ X \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X w^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\{ f>0\} $ is dense in $X$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. By ( 14.20.1 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$. Integrating ( 14.22.5 ) against $T$, and applying Stokes' theorem twice to the left-hand side, yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w^2)\wedge T=\int _ Xw^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] Substitution proves ( 14.22.14 ). For the uniqueness assertion, apply 14.22.1 (1) with $h=1$. At every point where $f>0$, the form $B$ is positive definite, so the term $B^{n-1}$ makes the cofactor $T$ strictly positive. The set where $T$ is strictly positive is therefore dense, as required. $\square$

title: 14.23 Integral rigidity in dimensions two and three

section: 14.23 Integral rigidity in dimensions two and three
text: In dimensions two and three, if two positive forms $A,B$ have equal determinants, an algebraic expression quadratic in $A-B$ has a strict sign unless the two forms agree. On a surface its integral vanishes because it is exact. On a threefold the integral is a term involving $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, so a sign condition on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ leads to the same conclusion. Approximation in the Sobolev norm justifies the integral identities for $W^{2,n}$ potentials. In this section $n\in \{ 2,3\} $. Norms of coefficients of forms are taken with respect to a fixed smooth metric and $\mathrm{d}V$. Theorem 14.23.1 . AF9D036E600F Let $u,v\in W^{2,n}(X,\mathbb R)$, and assume that $A,B\geq 0$ almost everywhere and \[  A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad f>0\quad \hbox{almost everywhere}.  \] If $n=3$, assume in addition that 6127DB916FC9 14.23.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{i}\eta \wedge \bar\eta \leq 0  \end{equation} for every $(1,0)$-covector $\eta $; for $n=2$ no condition on $\omega $ is needed. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)=0$ in the sense of distributions, and $u-v$ is almost everywhere constant. For the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic representatives of $u$ and $v$, the difference is constant everywhere. Proof. Put \[  \begin{gathered} s=(u+v)/2,\qquad D=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=A-B,\\ C=(A+B)/2=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s. \end{gathered}  \] The coefficients of $C$ and $D$ lie in $L^ n$, so their products of top degree are integrable by Hölder's inequality. At almost every point the common determinant is positive, so $A$ and $B$ are positive definite there, and we may diagonalize them simultaneously by congruence: for a suitable coframe of $(1,0)$-covectors $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$, write $A=\sum e_ j$, $B=\sum \lambda _ j e_ j$, where $e_ j=\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$, $\lambda _ j>0$, and $\prod \lambda _ j=1$. In dimension two, CB4E143A2628 14.23.3 \begin{equation}  D^2=A^2+B^2-2A\wedge B =2(2-\lambda _1-\lambda _2)e_1\wedge e_2\leq 0, \end{equation} with equality if and only if $A=B$. In dimension three, 899D523AFD3C 14.23.4 \begin{equation}  2C\wedge D^2=A^3+B^3-A^2\wedge B-A\wedge B^2\leq 0. \end{equation} Indeed, with $E=e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3$, the four terms on the right are \[  6E,\qquad 6E,\qquad 2\Bigl (\sum _ j\lambda _ j\Bigr )E, \qquad 2\Bigl (\sum _{i<j}\lambda _ i\lambda _ j\Bigr )E.  \] By the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and $\prod _ j\lambda _ j=1$, each sum is at least three, and equality forces all $\lambda _ j=1$, that is, $A=B$. Choose smooth real functions $w_ k\to w$ in $W^{2,n}$ and set $D_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k$; such approximations are obtained by a partition of unity and convolution, and they need not preserve semipositivity. For $n=2$, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XD_ k^2=0$, since $D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge D_ k)$. For a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, \[  \| D_ k^2-D^2\| _{L^1} \leq C_0\| D_ k-D\| _{L^2}(\| D_ k\| _{L^2}+\| D\| _{L^2})\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\int _ XD^2=0$, and the nonpositive integrand in ( 14.23.3 ) vanishes almost everywhere. By the equality case, $D=0$ almost everywhere. For $n=3$, also choose smooth functions $s_ k\to s$ in $W^{2,3}$, and put $C_ k=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k$. We need the identity CFA2A8BCECDA 14.23.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X C_ k\wedge D_ k^2 =\int _ X\omega \wedge D_ k^2 =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The first equality holds because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2)$. For the second equality, including its sign, put $J_ k=\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k$. Using $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and $(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c})^2=0$, \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k=-D_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k=-D_ k^2.  \] Stokes, first for $\mathrm{d}(\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k)$ and then for $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge J_ k)$, gives \begin{align*}  \int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k& =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k,\\  0& =-\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge J_ k-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k. \end{align*} Combining them yields ( 14.23.5 ). With a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, strong $L^3$ convergence implies convergence in $L^1$ of all products of three factors. For example, \[  \| (C_ k-C)\wedge D_ k^2\| _1 \leq C_0\| C_ k-C\| _3\| D_ k\| _3^2\longrightarrow 0,  \] and \[  \| C\wedge (D_ k^2-D^2)\| _1 \leq C_0\| C\| _3\| D_ k-D\| _3(\| D_ k\| _3+\| D\| _3)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Also $\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\to \mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w$ in $L^{3/2}$, so the right side of ( 14.23.5 ) converges. Consequently 81191FBC0D41 14.23.6 \begin{equation}  \int _ XC\wedge D^2=-\int _ X\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0. \end{equation} The sign follows from $\mathrm{d}w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w=(\mathrm{i}/(2\pi ))\partial w\wedge \bar\partial w$ and ( 14.23.2 ). The integrand on the left is nonpositive by ( 14.23.4 ), so it vanishes almost everywhere, and the equality case, which applies where the common determinant is positive, gives $D=0$ almost everywhere. In both dimensions, therefore, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=0$ in the sense of distributions. By proposition 5.22.2 with background zero, $w$ has a plurisubharmonic representative on $X$. It attains its maximum on the compact manifold $X$, so the maximum principle and connectedness make it constant. For the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic representatives, lemma 5.24.3 upgrades the almost-everywhere equality $u=v+\text{constant}$ to equality everywhere. In particular, normalizing the means gives equality in the Sobolev class, and normalizing the suprema gives equality of the plurisubharmonic representatives. $\square$ Corollary 14.23.7 . 3DF5F7F34405 Let $n\in \{ 2,3\} $, and let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is continuous and positive on a dense set. If $n=3$, assume ( 14.23.2 ); for instance, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ suffices. Then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. Put $D=A-B$ and $C=(A+B)/2$. At a point where the common top power vanishes, the algebraic expressions in the proof of 14.23.1 are still nonpositive: in dimension two $D^2=-2A\wedge B$, and in dimension three $2C\wedge D^2=-A^2\wedge B-A\wedge B^2$. The same integral identities force these continuous expressions to vanish everywhere. The equality cases give $D=0$ on $\{ f>0\} $, and density and continuity then give $D=0$ on $X$. As in the proof of the theorem, $u-v$ is then constant. $\square$ For example, on the Hopf threefold $X$ of section 23.1 , with projection $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$ and the semipositive form $\alpha =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the Fubini–Study form, the Hermitian metric $\omega $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2$, and hence ( 14.23.2 ). 14.23.1 therefore applies to this metric, even though its upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 13.14.14 is infinite by theorem 23.1.1 . The following sections return to a general Hermitian background.

text: Theorem 14.23.1 . AF9D036E600F Let $u,v\in W^{2,n}(X,\mathbb R)$, and assume that $A,B\geq 0$ almost everywhere and \[  A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad f>0\quad \hbox{almost everywhere}.  \] If $n=3$, assume in addition that 6127DB916FC9 14.23.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm{i}\eta \wedge \bar\eta \leq 0  \end{equation} for every $(1,0)$-covector $\eta $; for $n=2$ no condition on $\omega $ is needed. For the $\omega $-plurisubharmonic representatives of $u$ and $v$, the difference is constant everywhere. Proof. For $n=2$, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XD_ k^2=0$, since $D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge D_ k)$. For a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, \[  \| D_ k^2-D^2\| _{L^1} \leq C_0\| D_ k-D\| _{L^2}(\| D_ k\| _{L^2}+\| D\| _{L^2})\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\int _ XD^2=0$, and the nonpositive integrand in ( 14.23.3 ) vanishes almost everywhere. By the equality case, $D=0$ almost everywhere. For $n=3$, also choose smooth functions $s_ k\to s$ in $W^{2,3}$, and put $C_ k=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k$. We need the identity CFA2A8BCECDA 14.23.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X C_ k\wedge D_ k^2 =\int _ X\omega \wedge D_ k^2 =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The first equality holds because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2=\mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s_ k\wedge D_ k^2)$. For the second equality, including its sign, put $J_ k=\mathrm{d}w_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k$. Using $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and $(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c})^2=0$, \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k=-D_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ k,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k=-D_ k^2.  \] Stokes, first for $\mathrm{d}(\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k)$ and then for $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge J_ k)$, gives \begin{align*}  \int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}J_ k& =-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k,\\  0& =-\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge J_ k-\int _ X\mathrm{d}\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}J_ k. \end{align*} Combining them yields ( 14.23.5 ). With a fixed norm-comparison constant $C_0>0$, strong $L^3$ convergence implies convergence in $L^1$ of all products of three factors. text: Corollary 14.23.7 . 3DF5F7F34405 Let $n\in \{ 2,3\} $, and let $u,v\in C^2(X)$ satisfy $A,B\geq 0$ and $A^ n=B^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f\geq 0$ is continuous and positive on a dense set. If $n=3$, assume ( 14.23.2 ); for instance, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$ suffices. Then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. Put $D=A-B$ and $C=(A+B)/2$. At a point where the common top power vanishes, the algebraic expressions in the proof of 14.23.1 are still nonpositive: in dimension two $D^2=-2A\wedge B$, and in dimension three $2C\wedge D^2=-A^2\wedge B-A\wedge B^2$. title: 14.24 Bounded uniqueness and connectedness
text: For a continuous density whose positive set is connected and dense, bounded solutions are unique up to a constant. An energy measure of $w=u-v$ recovers the information supplied by differentiability. Its pushforward under $w$ has a Lipschitz density vanishing at the extreme values. If $w$ were nonconstant, these properties would force both extremal sets to have zero mass for the common Monge–Ampère measure. A smooth test potential with a larger density near one of these sets then contradicts modified comparison. Theorem 14.24.1 . 98EC31947E4C Let $F\in C^0(X)$ satisfy $F\geq 0$, $F\not\equiv 0$, with $U=\{ F>0\} $ connected and dense. If bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$ satisfy \[  \omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n,  \] then $u-v$ is constant. In particular, $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$ implies $u=v$. Continuity of $F$ supplies the local positive lower bounds and the neighborhoods of the extremal set used below. The auxiliary test densities are chosen smooth independently of $F$. Bounded solutions are continuous by corollary 14.19.29 , so we may use pointwise extrema throughout the proof. We shall also use modified comparison in the following form. If $b$ is continuous and $\omega _ b\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $0<\varepsilon <1$, then $b/(1-\varepsilon )$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, so theorem 14.19.6 applies with $(1-\varepsilon )v=b$. Thus its thin-sublevel estimate applies directly to such a strictly positive comparison potential $b$, and the correction factor tends to one as the height of the sublevel set tends to zero, with $\varepsilon $ fixed. Proposition 14.24.2 . 2C3AA01F259B Let $u,v$ be continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, where $F\geq 0$ is bounded and measurable. Let $q$ be a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and write $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n$. Then for every $0<\kappa <1$ and $\eta >0$, C7BC3EE4D543 14.24.3 \begin{equation}  F\omega ^ n\bigl (\{ u-v<\min _ X(u-v)+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} \bigr )>0. \end{equation} The analogous assertion holds for the set $\{ u-v>\max _ X(u-v)-\eta \} $. Proof. Choose $\delta \in (0,1]$ with $\omega _ q\geq \delta \omega $. For $0<t<1$, put $b_ t=(1-t)v+tq$, $m_ t=\min _ X(u-b_ t)$, and $E_ s=\{ u<b_ t+m_ t+s\} $. Then $\omega _{b_ t}\geq t\delta \omega $. Write $\mu =F\omega ^ n$, $d=\kappa ^{-1/n}-1$, and $\gamma =nd$. By ( 5.28.9 ), \[  \omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq \bigl ((1-t)F^{1/n}+tG^{1/n}\bigr )^ n \omega ^ n.  \] On $L=\{ F\leq \kappa G\} $ this is at least $(1+\gamma t)\mu $, since $G^{1/n}\geq (1+d)F^{1/n}$ there, and on $R=\{ F>\kappa G\} $ it is at least $(1-nt)\mu $. Choose $s>0$ so small that the reverse comparison factor in ( 14.19.7 ), with $\varepsilon =t\delta $, is at most $1+\gamma t/2$. Modified comparison on $E_ s$, with $x=\mu (E_ s\cap L)$ and $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)$, gives \[  (1+\gamma t)x+(1-nt)y\leq (1+\gamma t/2)(x+y), \qquad \text{and hence}\qquad y\geq \frac{1-\kappa ^{1/n}}2\, \mu (E_ s).  \] The open set $E_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of $m_ t$. As $\omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq (t\delta )^ n\omega ^ n$, ( 14.19.7 ) forces $\mu (E_ s)>0$, hence $y>0$. Let $a=\min _ X(u-v)$ and $\Lambda =\| v-q\| _\infty $. Since $u-b_ t=u-v+t(v-q)$, we have $|m_ t-a|\leq t\Lambda $ and $E_ s\subset \{ u-v<a+2t\Lambda +s\} $. Given $\eta $, choose $t$ and then $s$ with $2t\Lambda +s<\eta $. Since $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)>0$, this proves ( 14.24.3 ). Interchanging $u$ and $v$ gives the assertion for the near-maximum set. $\square$

title: Theorem 14.24.1
text: Theorem 14.24.1 . 98EC31947E4C Let $F\in C^0(X)$ satisfy $F\geq 0$, $F\not\equiv 0$, with $U=\{ F>0\} $ connected and dense. If bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$ satisfy \[  \omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n,  \] then $u-v$ is constant. In particular, $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$ implies $u=v$. of theorem 14.24.1 . By corollary 14.19.29 , $u,v$ are continuous. In dimension one, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=0$, so the maximum principle makes $w$ constant. Assume $n\geq 2$. Suppose that $w=u-v$ is nonconstant. Let $a=\min _ Xw$, $K=\{ w=a\} $, and $\mu =F\omega ^ n$. By lemma 14.24.11 , $\mu (K)=0$. Choose $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be the constant from proposition 14.24.13 . Since $\mu (K)=0$, the compact set $K_0=K\cap \{ F\geq \varepsilon /2\} $ has zero $\omega ^ n$-volume. Fix $A>1$ with $\varepsilon A>\max _ XF$. By outer regularity of the smooth volume measure, choose an open neighborhood $O$ of $K_0$ so small that \[  \int _ X\omega ^ n+(A^2-1)\int _ O\omega ^ n<B_0^2.  \] Take a smooth $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one near $K_0$ and supported in $O$, and set $g=1+(A-1)\chi $. If $K_0=\varnothing $, take $\chi =0$. Then $g\geq 1$, $g=A$ on $K_0$, and $\| g\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}<B_0$. By proposition 14.24.13 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $q$ with $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n\geq \varepsilon g\omega ^ n$. On $K_0$ we have $G\geq \varepsilon A>F$; on $K\setminus K_0$ we have $F<\varepsilon /2<\varepsilon \leq G$. Thus $G>F$ throughout the compact set $K$. By compactness and continuity, we can choose $0<\kappa <1$ such that $F<\kappa G$ on $K$; put $W=\{ F<\kappa G\} $. The complement of this open neighborhood of $K$ is compact, and $w-a$ has a strictly positive minimum there if it is nonempty. Hence some $\eta >0$ satisfies $\{ w<a+\eta \} \subset W$. Proposition 14.24.2 asserts that $\mu (\{ w<a+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} )>0$. By the preceding inclusion, however, this set is empty. This contradiction shows that $w$ is constant. If $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$, the constant is zero. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.24.2
text: Proposition 14.24.2 . 2C3AA01F259B Let $u,v$ be continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, where $F\geq 0$ is bounded and measurable. Let $q$ be a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, and write $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n$. Then for every $0<\kappa <1$ and $\eta >0$, C7BC3EE4D543 14.24.3 \begin{equation}  F\omega ^ n\bigl (\{ u-v<\min _ X(u-v)+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} \bigr )>0. \end{equation} The analogous assertion holds for the set $\{ u-v>\max _ X(u-v)-\eta \} $. Proof. Choose $\delta \in (0,1]$ with $\omega _ q\geq \delta \omega $. For $0<t<1$, put $b_ t=(1-t)v+tq$, $m_ t=\min _ X(u-b_ t)$, and $E_ s=\{ u<b_ t+m_ t+s\} $. Then $\omega _{b_ t}\geq t\delta \omega $. Write $\mu =F\omega ^ n$, $d=\kappa ^{-1/n}-1$, and $\gamma =nd$. By ( 5.28.9 ), \[  \omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq \bigl ((1-t)F^{1/n}+tG^{1/n}\bigr )^ n \omega ^ n.  \] On $L=\{ F\leq \kappa G\} $ this is at least $(1+\gamma t)\mu $, since $G^{1/n}\geq (1+d)F^{1/n}$ there, and on $R=\{ F>\kappa G\} $ it is at least $(1-nt)\mu $. Choose $s>0$ so small that the reverse comparison factor in ( 14.19.7 ), with $\varepsilon =t\delta $, is at most $1+\gamma t/2$. Modified comparison on $E_ s$, with $x=\mu (E_ s\cap L)$ and $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)$, gives \[  (1+\gamma t)x+(1-nt)y\leq (1+\gamma t/2)(x+y), \qquad \text{and hence}\qquad y\geq \frac{1-\kappa ^{1/n}}2\, \mu (E_ s).  \] The open set $E_ s$ is nonempty by the definition of $m_ t$. As $\omega _{b_ t}^ n\geq (t\delta )^ n\omega ^ n$, ( 14.19.7 ) forces $\mu (E_ s)>0$, hence $y>0$. Let $a=\min _ X(u-v)$ and $\Lambda =\| v-q\| _\infty $. Since $u-b_ t=u-v+t(v-q)$, we have $|m_ t-a|\leq t\Lambda $ and $E_ s\subset \{ u-v<a+2t\Lambda +s\} $. Given $\eta $, choose $t$ and then $s$ with $2t\Lambda +s<\eta $. Since $y=\mu (E_ s\cap R)>0$, this proves ( 14.24.3 ). Interchanging $u$ and $v$ gives the assertion for the near-maximum set. $\square$

title: 14.24.4 The energy of the difference
text:
In this subsection, $u,v$ are continuous $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions with $A^ n=B^ n=F\omega ^ n$ for a bounded measurable function $F\geq 0$, and $w=u-v$. Although the cofactor $T$ is now only a current, its product with $\mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w$ still defines a positive measure. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ determines how this energy is distributed over the level sets of $w$. Proposition 14.24.5 . 25FABE38E60B There is a finite positive measure $E=\mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge T$, defined below as a limit of regularizations, with the following properties. For every smooth real function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$, 5EA1FD990FD5 14.24.6  egin{equation}  \int _ X\chi ''(w)\, \mathrm{d} E=\int _ X\chi (w)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T. \end{equation} The signed current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a finite measure. If $a=\min _ Xw$, $b=\max _ Xw$, and \[  k(t)=\int _ X(w-t)_+\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T,  \] then $k$ is nonnegative, globally Lipschitz, supported on $[a,b]$, and B3915B7974CA 14.24.7  egin{equation}  w_*E=k(t)\, \mathrm{d} t. \end{equation} In particular, $E$ charges no level set of $w$. Let $V$ be a relatively compact coordinate domain such that $F$ has a positive essential lower bound on a neighborhood of $\overline V$. Then there is $C_ V<\infty $ such that every piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz function $p$ on $[a,b]$ satisfies C45BFBEEAF7F 14.24.8  egin{equation}  \int _ V|\mathrm{d}(p(w))|\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C_ V\left(\int _ V|p'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} Eight)^{1/2}, \end{equation} where $\mathrm{d}\lambda $ is Euclidean coordinate volume. Proof. Locally, expand $T$ into powers of the smooth form $\omega $ multiplied by closed Bedford–Taylor products of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. The operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ then acts only on the powers of $\omega $, and the local mass bounds in section 5.27 show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a finite signed measure. We first construct $E$ and prove ( 14.24.6 ). On a coordinate ball, convolve $u$, $v$ and the coefficients of $\omega $ with a common nonnegative radial mollifier. Write the resulting smooth positive forms as $A_ho =\omega _ho +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ho $ and $B_ho =\omega _ho +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ho $, and let $T_ho $ be their mixed sum. On a slightly larger ball, add the same fixed multiple of $|z|^2$ to each potential to obtain plurisubharmonic functions. Their radial regularizations decrease to the originals, so Bedford–Taylor continuity applies to all closed Hessian products. Since $u,v$ are continuous, $u_ho ,v_ho ,w_ho $ converge uniformly on compact subsets. For a closed smooth product $S_ho $ appearing in $T_ho $, the identity D3E407319B3E 14.24.9  egin{equation}  \mathrm{d} w_ho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ho \wedge S_ho =	frac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w_ho ^2S_ho )-w_ho \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge S_ho \end{equation} has a distributional limit: both Hessian products on the right converge weakly with uniformly bounded local variation, and their weights converge uniformly. The same holds after multiplication by the convergent smooth factors coming from $\omega _ho $. Thus the positive measures $E_ho =\mathrm{d} w_ho \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w_ho \wedge T_ho $ converge to a finite positive measure $E$. By ( 14.24.9 ), this limit does not depend on the regularization, so the local limits agree on overlapping charts. For smooth regularizations, the chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (w_ho )\wedge T_ho =\chi ''(w_ho )E_ho +\chi '(w_ho )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge T_ho .  \] The last current tends to zero, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ho \wedge T_ho =A_ho ^ n-B_ho ^ n$ tends weakly to $A^ n-B^ n=0$ with uniformly bounded variation, and $\chi '(w_ho )$ converges uniformly. Passing to the limit and integrating by parts on the compact manifold $X$ gives ( 14.24.6 ). A partition of unity justifies this passage without a global regularization; the terms containing derivatives of the cutoff functions cancel after summation. Let $\sigma =w_*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T)$ and $
u =w_*E$. Equation ( 14.24.6 ) says that $
u ''=\sigma $ as distributions on $\mathbb R$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0$ give \[  \sigma (\mathbb R)=\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0,\qquad \int _{\mathbb R}s\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (s)=\int _ Xw\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=0.  \] Consequently $k(t)=\int (s-t)_+\, \mathrm{d}\sigma (s)$ is globally Lipschitz and vanishes outside $[a,b]$. It satisfies $k''=\sigma $, so the compactly supported distribution $
u -k(t)\, \mathrm{d} t$ has second derivative zero and therefore vanishes. Positivity of $
u $ and continuity of $k$ imply $k\geq 0$. This proves ( 14.24.7 ), and the assertion about level sets follows because $
u $ is absolutely continuous. We now prove ( 14.24.8 ). On a coordinate neighborhood of $\overline V$, set $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and choose $c_ V>0$ with $F\omega ^ n\geq c_ V eta ^ n$. Let $A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ denote the absolutely continuous part of the current $A$, whose coefficients are locally integrable functions. Applying lemma 5.28.10 with the constant function $g=c_ V^{1/n}$ and differentiating the coefficient measures, we obtain $\det _ eta A_{\mathrm{ac}}\geq c_ V$ almost everywhere. The local Sobolev regularity in section 5.27 gives $w_ho 	o w$ strongly in $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, so a subsequence of the gradients converges almost everywhere. Moreover, $A_ho 	o A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ almost everywhere, by differentiation of the coefficient measures. Since $T_ho $ contains the term $A_ho ^{n-1}$ and all its terms are positive, Fatou's lemma, applied to $E_ho $, yields the measure inequality 7EF7549DDD02 14.24.10  egin{equation}  E\geq \mathrm{d} w\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}w\wedge A_{\mathrm{ac}}^{n-1}. \end{equation} The cofactor matrix of $A_{\mathrm{ac}}$ has smallest eigenvalue at least $\det A_{\mathrm{ac}}/\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}\geq c_ V/\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}$, where traces and determinants are taken with respect to $ eta $. The trace is locally integrable because $A$ has locally finite mass. The chain rule for Sobolev functions, ( 14.24.10 ) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give \[  \int _ V|\mathrm{d}(p(w))|\, \mathrm{d}\lambda \leq C\left(\int _ V|p'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} Eight)^{1/2} \left(\int _ V rac{\operatorname {tr}A_{\mathrm{ac}}}{c_ V}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda ight)^{1/2}.  \] The last factor is finite and is absorbed into $C_ V$. The values of $p'$ at the finitely many corners of $p$ are immaterial, because $E$ charges no level set of $w$. $\square$ Lemma 14.24.11 . 4FB9051BD00E In the setting of proposition 14.24.5 , assume in addition that $F$ is continuous and that $U=\{ F>0\} $ is connected and dense. If $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, then \[  F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\min _ Xw\} )=F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\max _ Xw\} )=0.  \] Proof. Put $a=\min _ Xw<b=\max _ Xw$, and let $k$ be the function of proposition 14.24.5 . It is Lipschitz and nonnegative, and $k(a)=0$. Choose $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $a+\epsilon _ j<b$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  J_ j(\delta )=\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j} rac{\mathrm{d} t}{k(t)+\delta }.  \] If $L$ is a Lipschitz constant for $k$, then $k(t)\leq L(t-a)$ on this interval, so $J_ j(\delta )	o \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Choose $\delta _ j>0$ with $J_ j=J_ j(\delta _ j)\geq j$. Let $p_ j=0$ on $(-\infty ,a]$, $p_ j=1$ on $[a+\epsilon _ j,\infty )$, and \[  p_ j'(t)= rac{1}{J_ j(k(t)+\delta _ j)}\quad (a<t<a+\epsilon _ j).  \] The pushforward identity ( 14.24.7 ) gives \[  \int _ X|p_ j'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} E = rac{1}{J_ j^2}\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j} rac{k(t)}{(k(t)+\delta _ j)^2}\, \mathrm{d} t \leq  rac1{J_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Every point of $U$ has a coordinate neighborhood $V$ as in proposition 14.24.5 , since $F$ is continuous. By ( 14.24.8 ), therefore, $\mathrm{d}(p_ j(w))	o 0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The bounded functions $p_ j(w)$ converge pointwise and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $\mathbf1_{\{ w>a\} }$, whose distributional gradient therefore vanishes on $U$. Since $U$ is connected, this indicator function is almost everywhere constant on $U$. As $w$ is nonconstant, $\{ w>a\} $ is a nonempty open set, and its intersection with the dense open set $U$ is nonempty and open; hence the constant is one. Thus $\{ w=a\} \cap U$ has zero volume, and since $F=0$ off $U$, the first assertion follows. Applying the argument to $-w$ gives the assertion for the maximum set. $\square$

title: Lemma 14.24.11
text: Lemma 14.24.11 . 4FB9051BD00E In the setting of proposition 14.24.5 , assume in addition that $F$ is continuous and that $U=\{ F>0\} $ is connected and dense. If $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, then \[  F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\min _ Xw\} )=F\omega ^ n(\{ w=\max _ Xw\} )=0.  \] Proof. Put $a=\min _ Xw<b=\max _ Xw$, and let $k$ be the function of proposition 14.24.5 . It is Lipschitz and nonnegative, and $k(a)=0$. Choose $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $a+\epsilon _ j<b$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  J_ j(\delta )=\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j}\frac{\mathrm{d} t}{k(t)+\delta }.  \] If $L$ is a Lipschitz constant for $k$, then $k(t)\leq L(t-a)$ on this interval, so $J_ j(\delta )\to \infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Choose $\delta _ j>0$ with $J_ j=J_ j(\delta _ j)\geq j$. Let $p_ j=0$ on $(-\infty ,a]$, $p_ j=1$ on $[a+\epsilon _ j,\infty )$, and \[  p_ j'(t)=\frac{1}{J_ j(k(t)+\delta _ j)}\quad (a<t<a+\epsilon _ j).  \] The pushforward identity ( 14.24.7 ) gives \[  \int _ X|p_ j'(w)|^2\, \mathrm{d} E =\frac{1}{J_ j^2}\int _ a^{a+\epsilon _ j}\frac{k(t)}{(k(t)+\delta _ j)^2}\, \mathrm{d} t \leq \frac1{J_ j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Every point of $U$ has a coordinate neighborhood $V$ as in proposition 14.24.5 , since $F$ is continuous. By ( 14.24.8 ), therefore, $\mathrm{d}(p_ j(w))\to 0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. The bounded functions $p_ j(w)$ converge pointwise and in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to $\mathbf1_{\{ w>a\} }$, whose distributional gradient therefore vanishes on $U$. Since $U$ is connected, this indicator function is almost everywhere constant on $U$. As $w$ is nonconstant, $\{ w>a\} $ is a nonempty open set, and its intersection with the dense open set $U$ is nonempty and open; hence the constant is one. Thus $\{ w=a\} \cap U$ has zero volume, and since $F=0$ off $U$, the first assertion follows. Applying the argument to $-w$ gives the assertion for the maximum set. $\square$
